While these have traditionally been applied to identify risk, the time is right for integrating predictive models with existing technologies such as electronic health records, clinical decision support systems, and clinical data warehouses, to result in action and efficiencies. n 2019, the use of predictive modeling was reported among 60% of health care executives within their organizations, and another 20% of them expressed intent to begin using them the following year [30], again primarily for risk prediction and not necessarily action.

sections.title: Types and Applications
sections.text:
TLDR; Predictive models in healthcare span a broad range of applications from disease risk assessment to treatment outcome prediction. Key applications include identifying surgical complications, preventing hospital readmissions, managing chronic diseases, and personalizing care pathways through AI-powered clinical decision support systems. (7 sources)

Key applications of predictive modeling in healthcare include:

1. **Surgical Risk Assessment**

- Prediction of major post-surgical complications including respiratory problems, infections, and organ dysfunction

- Early detection of cardiac complications and adverse drug reactions

- Risk assessment for wound healing issues and thrombophlebitis  [40575711 | Artetxe et al. | 2018 | Citations: 13]

2. **Hospital Readmission Management**

- Development of standardized scoring systems for unplanned re-admission risk

- Integration with clinical pathways to guide preventive actions

- Creation of structured decision support frameworks for staff  [13727624 | Hoogendoorn et al. | 2016 | Citations: 87]

3. **Emergency Department Utilization**

- Optimization of ED operations and length of stay

- Identification of patients requiring special attention

- Resource allocation improvements  [225487992 | Lee et al. | 2020 | Citations: 71]

4. **Primary Care Disease Management**

- Proactive management of chronic conditions like asthma and COPD

- Estimation of disease control likelihood

- Enhancement of patient outcomes through early interventions  [272902429 | Ros et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]

5. **Treatment Pathway Planning**

- AI-driven clinical decision support systems integrated with EHR

- Real-time evaluation of different treatment strategies

- Collaborative decision-making between clinicians and patients regarding treatment goals  [234473856 | Tarumi et al. | 2021 | Citations: 43]

6. **Care Delivery Optimization**

- Enhanced clinical decision-making

- Improved patient care coordination

- More efficient and cost-effective healthcare delivery  [267406284 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]

7. **Patient Monitoring and Intervention**

- Real-time tracking of patient vitals and symptoms

- Alert generation for deterioration in condition

- Automated collection and analysis of daily vital signs <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

These applications demonstrate how predictive modeling serves as a cornerstone of modern healthcare delivery, transforming raw clinical data into actionable insights for improved patient outcomes  [225487992 | Lee et al. | 2020 | Citations: 71]  [267406284 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4].

citations.title: [225487992 | Lee et al. | 2020 | Citations: 71]
snippets: Predictive analytics is a rapidly expanding area of health care [1]. With widespread electronic health record (EHR) adoption [2](Cohen, 2016)[4], vast quantities of clinical data are available. EHR data have been employed to develop predictive models in a wide range of clinical applications, such as predicting major post-surgical complications [5][6][7], sepsis [8], readmission [9][10](Artetxe et al., 2018), heart failure [12], substance abuse (Alemi et al., 2018), and death [9,14,(Hoogendoorn et al., 2016). Computational advancements have enabled machine learning techniques to effectively use EHR data for medical diagnosis [16][17][18]. The stated promise of these predictive models is to improve identification and risk stratification of patients, thereby facilitating targeted interventions to improve patient outcomes. Embedding these models within EHR systems as components of clinical decision support (CDS) interventions may allow real-time risk prediction. As stated by Agrawal and colleagues [19], this "prediction technology" is core to the anticipated applications of artificial intelligence (AI) for improving health care.

citations.title: [234473856 | Tarumi et al. | 2021 | Citations: 43]
snippets: Using a dataset of 27,904 patients with diabetes, an analytical method was developed and validated for generating a treatment pathway graph which consists of models that predict the likelihood of alternate treatment strategies achieving care goals. An AI-driven clinical decision support system (CDSS) integrated with the electronic health record (EHR) was developed by encapsulating the prediction models in an OpenCDS Web service module and delivering the model outputs through a SMART on FHIR (Substitutable Medical Applications and Reusable Technologies on Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) web-based dashboard. This CDSS enables clinicians and patients to review relevant patient parameters, select treatment goals, and review alternate treatment strategies based on prediction results.

citations.title: [267406284 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]
snippets: This survey focuses on predictive modeling in healthcare, which refers to using machine learning techniques to analyze patients' historical health data along with current observations to support diagnosis or make predictions about future health events. This approach usually leverages large datasets, often derived from EHR systems, to identify patterns, trends, and relationships that can be used to forecast specific healthrelated events. Predictive modeling has various applications in healthcare, including but not limited to disease risk assessment, hospital discharge potential or readmission risk, treatment outcomes prediction, and health resource allocation. In other words, predictive modeling can enhance clinical decision-making, improve patient care, and contribute to more efficient and cost-effective healthcare delivery.

Statistically significant variables were incorporated into a logistic regression model to predict poor disease control in patients with asthma and COPD patients...Integrating this predictive model into primary care practice could enhance the proactive management of asthma and COPD, potentially improving patient outcomes and reducing the burden on healthcare systems.

sections.title: Data Sources and Modeling Approaches
sections.text:
TLDR; Modern predictive models in healthcare leverage diverse data sources ranging from EHRs to wearable devices and social determinants of health data. Advanced machine learning approaches, including specialized architectures for processing long patient histories and temporal patterns, are increasingly replacing traditional statistical methods for improved prediction accuracy. (8 sources)

The foundation of predictive modeling in healthcare rests heavily on the rich tapestry of available data sources. Electronic Health Records (EHRs) serve as the primary data source, containing comprehensive clinical information that forms the backbone of predictive models  [213335870 | Rongali et al. | 2019 | Citations: 20]. The scope of these data extends beyond clinical records to include lifestyle and environmental data, which have proven highly correlated with patient health outcomes and play a crucial role in early warning systems for acute exacerbations  [252397201 | Wu et al. | 2022 | Citations: 15].

Recent advances in modeling approaches have been marked by the emergence of more sophisticated architectural designs. Novel frameworks like EHRMamba have achieved significant breakthroughs in processing capabilities, allowing for sequence lengths up to four times longer than traditional models while maintaining computational efficiency  [276903114 | Zhang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [267297026 | Fallahpour et al. | 2024 | Citations: 23]. Additionally, specialized temporal models like MOTOR have enhanced real-time monitoring capabilities, particularly valuable for chronic disease management and intensive care settings  [276903114 | Zhang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [257183275 | Steinberg et al. | 2023 | Citations: 21].

The integration of social determinants of health (SDOH) data has emerged as a critical frontier in predictive modeling. These models increasingly incorporate both patient-specific and population-level data to systematically identify patients at risk of developing future social healthcare needs  [268361153 | Hatef et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]. This approach represents a significant shift from traditional demographic analyses toward more holistic prediction frameworks  [27347617 | Kontos et al. | 2014 | Citations: 807].

However, a persistent challenge remains in the interpretability of advanced machine learning models. While deep learning approaches have demonstrated impressive accuracy in predictions, their black-box nature limits their practical clinical application  [53245191 | Jin et al. | 2018 | Citations: 31]. This tension between predictive power and interpretability continues to shape the evolution of modeling approaches in healthcare settings.

citations.title: [276903114 | Zhang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets: One of the key innovations in this space is the push for more scalable architectures that can handle longer patient histories without sacrificing computational efficiency. EHRMamba (Fallahpour et al., 2024) exemplifies this trend by leveraging the Mamba architecture, which allows it to process sequences up to four times longer than traditional models while maintaining linear computational complexity. By introducing Multitask Prompted Finetuning (MTF), EHRMamba is capable of learning multiple clinical tasks simultaneously, making it an efficient choice for deployment across different healthcare applications. Its use of the HL7 FHIR data standard further enhances its interoperability with existing hospital systems, making it easier to integrate into real-world clinical workflows. Benchmarks on the MIMIC-IV dataset (Johnson et al., 2020) confirm its strong performance across six key clinical prediction tasks, positioning it as a state-of-the-art model in EHR forecasting. Beyond general-purpose EHR models, several efforts have focused on temporal modeling, as predicting the timing of future medical events is critical in clinical practice. MOTOR (Steinberg et al., 2023) is one such time-to-event foundation model designed to improve risk stratification and proactive patient management. By explicitly modeling the likelihood and timing of future clinical events, MOTOR enhances real-time monitoring capabilities, making it particularly valuable for chronic disease management and intensive care settings.

To this end, many techniques have been developed to extract meaningful insights from EHR data with a common focus on prediction of upcoming medical events (e.g., a diagnosis or treatment) (Crosson et al., 2005), (Grant et al., 2008). sections.title: Clinical Decision Support Integration
sections.text:
TLDR; Clinical decision support systems powered by predictive models are increasingly embedded directly into electronic health records, enabling real-time risk assessments and personalized care recommendations. These integrations face challenges with model interpretability and cross-population validity, requiring careful consideration of implementation approaches. (8 sources)

The integration of predictive models into clinical decision support systems represents a crucial step in translating analytical insights into actionable healthcare interventions. Modern implementations leverage the widespread adoption of electronic health records (EHR) to embed predictive capabilities directly into clinical workflows, allowing for immediate risk assessments and timely interventions  [211082536 | Laschet et al. | 2020 | Citations: 1].

Real-time implementation examples showcase the versatility of these systems. Advanced models can now track patient progress dynamically, as demonstrated in stroke rehabilitation where systems predict recovery profiles continuously throughout the 6-month recovery period  [231677225 | Selles et al. | 2021 | Citations: 31]. Similarly, predictive models have been successfully integrated into oncology care to support prognostic discussions and advance care planning, incorporating both clinical data and natural language processing of radiologists' reports  [256867767 | Roberts et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]  [210839459 | Rossi et al. | 2023 | Citations: 17].

To bridge the gap between sophisticated machine learning models and clinical understanding, various approaches have been developed. Explainable AI methods like SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) help clinicians understand model predictions, making the technology more trustworthy and clinically applicable  [256867767 | Roberts et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]  [12919233 | Lundberg et al. | 2017 | Citations: 18403]. This transparency is crucial for gaining clinician trust and ensuring appropriate use in clinical settings  [54437196 | Miller et al. | 2018 | Citations: 0].

A notable innovation in clinical decision support is the development of cascading alert systems that balance sensitivity with clinical relevance. Such systems can significantly reduce false alarms while maintaining adequate predictive performance, helping clinicians focus on truly urgent cases  [53293470 | Larburu et al. | 2018 | Citations: 24]. This approach demonstrates how predictive modeling can enhance clinical decision-making without overwhelming healthcare providers with excessive alerts.

sections.title: Factors Affecting Implementation Success
sections.text:
TLDR; Successful implementation of predictive models depends heavily on user acceptance and technological readiness. Key success factors include ease of use, perceived usefulness, user expertise levels, and customization of interfaces to match specific clinical workflows. (6 sources)

Key factors that influence the successful implementation of predictive models in health information services include:

1. **User Acceptance and Training**

- Prior experience with computer/health information technologies strongly influences adoption rates  [13609990 | Zhang et al. | 2015 | Citations: 257]

- User-friendly interfaces and perceived usefulness are critical drivers of system adoption  [18249054 | Wangia | 2012 | Citations: 4]

- Computer self-efficacy and confidence levels significantly impact system utilization  [18249054 | Wangia | 2012 | Citations: 4]

2. **Technical Infrastructure Requirements**

- System interface characteristics must be carefully designed for optimal usability  [18249054 | Wangia | 2012 | Citations: 4]

- Scalable architectures are needed to handle longitudinal patient data efficiently  [276903114 | Zhang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]

- Interoperability standards like FHIR are essential for smooth integration with existing hospital systems  [276903114 | Zhang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]

3. **Data Quality and Availability**

- Comprehensive clinical information improves prediction accuracy  [213335870 | Rongali et al. | 2019 | Citations: 20]

- High-dimensional data from multiple sources increases model applicability  [244513649 | Sufriyana et al. | 2021 | Citations: 4]

- Longitudinal data requirements demand consistent data collection protocols <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

4. **Personalization and Adaptability**

- Models need to accommodate varying literacy levels and cognitive abilities  [18730901 | Shahrabani et al. | 2016 | Citations: 23]

- Service quality and website quality must be customized according to specific healthcare contexts [258027761 | Nazari-Shirkouhi et al. | 2023 | Citations: 17]

- Computer literacy requirements need to be matched with user capabilities [258027761 | Nazari-Shirkouhi et al. | 2023 | Citations: 17]

5. **Organizational Considerations**

- Job task modifications may be necessary for successful implementation  [18249054 | Wangia | 2012 | Citations: 4]

- Subjective norms and organizational culture affect adoption rates  [18249054 | Wangia | 2012 | Citations: 4]

- Integration with existing workflows requires careful planning <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

sections.title: Challenges and Limitations
sections.text:
TLDR; Despite significant advances in predictive modeling, several key challenges persist including validation across different populations, integration with clinical workflows, and balancing sophistication with usability. Technical barriers are compounded by organizational complexities and the need for robust validation frameworks. (6 sources)

The implementation of predictive models in healthcare faces several significant technical and operational hurdles. One fundamental challenge is the limited external validation of these models across different healthcare settings. While many models perform well in controlled development environments, very few undergo rigorous evaluation in actual clinical workflows, and even fewer demonstrate consistent performance across different hospitals  [248139457 | Sun et al. | 2021 | Citations: 22].

The complexity of data integration poses another substantial barrier. Modern healthcare systems must process diverse data streams, from routine clinical measurements to mobile health data, while accounting for irregular recording intervals and measurement errors  [4388354 | Paige et al. | 2018 | Citations: 45]. This challenge becomes particularly acute when attempting to establish connections between different data sources and ensure consistent quality across disparate systems <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

A significant limitation exists in determining which patients will effectively utilize technology-based platforms. Research indicates that a complex interplay of sociodemographic variables and lifestyle factors influences portal adoption, with nearly 80% of predictive factors relating to individual behaviors and preferences rather than purely demographic characteristics  [259201407 | Chen et al. | 2022 | Citations: 4]. This complexity makes it challenging to develop universally applicable implementation strategies.

The growing volume of available data presents both opportunity and obstacle. While expanded access to patient-level data through health information exchanges offers unprecedented possibilities for predictive modeling  [220444366 | Kasthurirathne et al. | 2020 | Citations: 11] [25739755 | Vuik et al. | 2016 | Citations: 104], the quality and consistency of these data sources can vary significantly across institutions, affecting model reliability and generalizability.

Furthermore, the transition from retrospective analysis to prospective implementation represents a critical challenge. Many promising models are initially developed and validated using historical data, yet proving their effectiveness in real-time clinical applications requires overcoming numerous operational and technical barriers <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [220444366 | Kasthurirathne et al. | 2020 | Citations: 11]

Large-scale adoption of health information systems [3], increased use of interoperable health information exchange, and the availability of socioeconomic data sets have led to unprecedented and ever increasing accessibility to various patient-and population-level data sources. The availability of these data sets, together with a focus on mitigating patient social factors and uptake of machine learning solutions for health care present considerable potential for predictive modeling in support of risk prediction and intervention allocation (Kansagara et al., 2011)(Vuik et al., 2016).

citations.title: [4388354 | Paige et al. | 2018 | Citations: 45]
snippets: The benefits of using electronic health records (EHRs) for disease risk screening and personalized health-care decisions are being increasingly recognized. Here we present a computationally feasible statistical approach with which to address the methodological challenges involved in utilizing historical repeat measures of multiple risk factors recorded in EHRs to systematically identify patients at high risk of future disease. The approach is principally based on a 2-stage dynamic landmark model. The first stage estimates current risk factor values from all available historical repeat risk factor measurements via landmark-age–specific multivariate linear mixed-effects models with correlated random intercepts, which account for sporadically recorded repeat measures, unobserved data, and measurement errors. The second stage predicts future disease risk from a sex-stratified Cox proportional hazards model, with estimated current risk factor values from the first stage.

question: What vulnerabilities in software are most frequently explained in detail in academic papers?

sections.title: Background/Introduction
sections.text:
TLDR; Software vulnerabilities are critical weaknesses that threaten system security and are increasingly prevalent. Academic papers extensively cover these vulnerabilities due to their significant impact on cybersecurity. (3 sources)

The prevalence and severity of software vulnerabilities has grown dramatically, becoming a central focus of academic research. Recent data reveals a concerning trend in vulnerability reporting - from around 6,500 vulnerabilities documented in 2016, the number surged to 25,200 in 2022, reaching nearly 29,000 by late 2023  [269559461 | Bahaa et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5]. These vulnerabilities pose serious risks to information systems, security procedures, and internal controls, creating potential entry points for malicious actors seeking to compromise system confidentiality, integrity, or availability  [267301213 | Cao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]  [276574696 | Ghosh et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

Despite increased efforts in secure programming practices, software vulnerabilities remain persistent and widespread  [269559461 | Bahaa et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5]. This persistence underscores why software vulnerabilities are frequently detailed in academic literature - they represent fundamental challenges in software security that require ongoing research and solutions <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">. Early detection of vulnerabilities during the software lifecycle has emerged as a critical priority, driving innovation in automated detection methods and prompting extensive academic investigation into their identification and mitigation  [267301213 | Cao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6].

citations.title: [267301213 | Cao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]
snippets: Software vulnerabilities, sometimes called security bugs, are weaknesses in an information system, security procedures, internal controls, or implementations that could be exploited by a threat actor for a variety of malicious ends. As such weaknesses are unavoidable during the design and implementation of the software, and detecting vulnerabilities in the early stages of the software life cycle is critically important. Benefiting from the great success of DL in code-centric software engineering tasks, an increasing number of learning-based vulnerability detection approaches have been proposed. To reveal the decision logic behind the binary detection results (vulnerable or not), most efforts focus on searching for important code tokens that positively contribute to the model's prediction.

citations.title: [269559461 | Bahaa et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5]
snippets: Software vulnerabilities are a particular category of defects that make software less secure and make it possible for products to be used maliciously. Insecure coding is the primary cause of the significant number of security flaws that occur nowadays. Software vulnerabilities continue to be a major issue despite the effort put into developing secure programming. This can be explained by the fact that in 2016, there were roughly 6,500 vulnerabilities reported in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) database, which increased to approximately 25,200 vulnerabilities in 2022. As of the end of 2023, the number of published vulnerabilities had reached approximately 28,961 [1].

citations.title: [276574696 | Ghosh et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]
snippets: A software vulnerability is a flaw that malicious attackers can exploit to compromise a system's confidentiality, integrity or availability (CIA), such as buffer overflows, SQL injection, and XSS.

sections.title: Classification Systems and Frameworks
sections.text:
TLDR; Several standardized frameworks exist for classifying software vulnerabilities, with Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) being the primary system. CWE provides a comprehensive hierarchical structure containing over 1,000 distinct vulnerability types, organized into broad categories and specific subtypes. (6 sources)

* **Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)**: A widely-used categorization system that maintains a comprehensive catalog of over 1,000 software weaknesses  [1090795 | Andrade | 2015 | Citations: 2]  [231925177 | Paul et al. | 2021 | Citations: 29]. This standard helps developers understand and address security vulnerabilities systematically.

* **CWE Pillars**: The framework organizes vulnerabilities into key categories including:

  - Improper Access Control

  - Resource lifetime management

  - Incorrect Calculations

  - Control flow management

  - Protection Mechanism Failures

  - Improper Comparisons

  - Exception handling

  - Input/output neutralization failures

  - Coding standards violations  [277940581 | Li et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]

* **Hierarchical Structure**: CWE employs a parent-child relationship system where broader categories serve as parents to more specific vulnerabilities. For example, injection flaws (CWE-74) encompass specific variants like Cross-Site Scripting (CWE-79)  [268247814 | Alfasi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

* **Industry Recognition**: Major organizations like MITRE regularly publish updated lists of the top-25 most dangerous software weaknesses  [258557402 | He et al. | 2023 | Citations: 108].

* **Educational Gap**: Notably, these vulnerability classifications are rarely covered in formal computer science education, leaving developers largely self-taught in these crucial security aspects  [1090795 | Andrade | 2015 | Citations: 2].

Each violation could be subtle, and many are seriously tricky. Software developers are not taught about these issues in school, and most do not receive any training on the job about these problems. 20 Indeed, other researchers have found many problems in Java projects. 5,(Tripp et al., 2009)21,(Enck et al., 2011)

snippets:
The CWE-1000 provides a hierarchical structure for categorizing software weaknesses at various levels of abstraction. At the highest level, these weaknesses are grouped into pillars, which represent the most abstract categories of vulnerabilities. Below is an overview of the key pillars: 

 Improper Access Control: Weaknesses related to insufficient restrictions on access to resources or functionalities. 

 Improper Interaction Between Multiple Correctly-Behaving Entities: Issues arising from unintended interactions between components that function correctly in isolation. 

 Improper Control of a Resource Through its Lifetime: Weaknesses involving inadequate management of resources during their creation, usage, or destruction. 

 Incorrect Calculation: Errors in computations or logical operations that lead to incorrect results. 

 Insufficient Control Flow Management: Weaknesses related to improper handling of program execution paths. 

 Protection Mechanism Failure: Failures in security mechanisms designed to protect systems or data. 

 Incorrect Comparison: Issues caused by flawed comparisons, such as incorrect equality checks. 

 Improper Check or Handling of Exceptional Conditions: 

Weaknesses stemming from inadequate handling of error conditions or exceptions. 

 Improper Neutralization: Vulnerabilities involving failure to sanitize inputs or outputs, potentially leading to injection attacks. 

 Improper Adherence to Coding Standards: Weaknesses resulting from violations of established coding practices or guidelines.

sections.title: Most Frequently Studied Vulnerability Types
sections.text:
TLDR; Buffer overflows and related memory errors dominate academic research due to their historical significance and widespread occurrence. Web application vulnerabilities account for about 70% of reported security incidents, making them a primary focus of study. (11 sources)

Academic research consistently identifies several vulnerability types as the most frequently studied. Buffer overflows stand out as the predominant area of investigation, appearing over 13,700 times in the CVE database as of May 2021  [250253601 | Butt et al. | 2022 | Citations: 18]. Within the buffer overflow family of vulnerabilities, "improper restriction of operations within memory buffer bounds" (CWE-119) receives the most scholarly attention, particularly because it enables remote code execution and administrative privilege escalation  [258947741 | Fu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 30]  [259203805 | Harzevili et al. | 2023 | Citations: 10].

Among specific buffer-related vulnerabilities, "writing beyond buffer boundaries" (CWE-787) emerges as especially critical, capable of causing system crashes and exposing sensitive information  [273582192 | Zhu | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [259203805 | Harzevili et al. | 2023 | Citations: 10]. This vulnerability is particularly prevalent in C and C++ applications, reflecting these languages' direct memory manipulation features  [258947741 | Fu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 30].

Web application vulnerabilities constitute approximately 70% of all reported security incidents  [267586034 | Ezenwoye | 2024 | Citations: 0], focusing research on common web-specific issues. Path traversal vulnerabilities (CWE-22) emerge as a notable subset of web application flaws, allowing attackers to bypass access restrictions and access unauthorized files  [259203805 | Harzevili et al. | 2023 | Citations: 10].

Historical examples of highly-studied vulnerabilities include the infamous Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160), Shellshock (CVE-2014-6271), and the glibc buffer overflow (CVE-2015-7547)  [46943187 | Llanso et al. | 2018 | Citations: 9]. Programming language-specific vulnerabilities also draw significant academic attention, with C/C++ programs showing susceptibility to memory safety issues and performance bottlenecks, while JavaScript applications frequently exhibit logic bugs and missing-check vulnerabilities  [277321710 | Qian et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [1262782 | Filus et al. | 2020 | Citations: 88].

Modern research increasingly focuses on machine learning approaches to automatically detect and classify vulnerabilities  [261064908 | Ni et al. | 2023 | Citations: 23]. These techniques aim to improve upon traditional manual analysis methods by providing scalable solutions for large-scale codebases <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

sections.title: Root Causes and Contributing Factors
sections.text:
TLDR; Research shows that most software vulnerabilities stem from recurring programmer mistakes rather than unique circumstances. Key factors contributing to these vulnerabilities include changing requirements, complexity of modern software, and gaps in secure development knowledge and tools. (3 sources)

Analysis of vulnerability databases reveals a clear pattern: the vast majority of software vulnerabilities can be traced to a surprisingly small set of consistent root causes, with these issues typically originating from repeated human programming errors  [230994864 | Anu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 7]. Three primary factors have been identified as leading contributors to these recurring mistakes:

First, the constant evolution of software requirements creates significant pressure on developers, often leading to compromises in security considerations. Second, many programmers lack sufficient expertise to properly implement complex security features. Third, inadequate technological infrastructure exists for building secure software systematically  [232236728 | Nina et al. | 2021 | Citations: 23].

These underlying causes manifest specifically in the form of insecure coding practices, which represent the most commonly cited security risk in software development. When combined with implementation flaws, these patterns create exploitable weaknesses that can be broadly categorized into injection flaws and logic vulnerabilities  [277918213 | Khan et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. Prevention requires proper software development practices and formal design methodologies that can proactively address these root causes, particularly in areas such as buffer overflow prevention and improper data handling  [30554166 | Simpson et al. | 2014 | Citations: 0].

To mitigate these recurring issues, experts emphasize the need for better integration of security awareness throughout the software development lifecycle <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">. This includes improved tooling for secure coding assistance, enhanced developer education, and systematic approaches to incorporating security requirements into architectural decisions.

sections.title: Emerging Trends in Vulnerability Research
sections.text:
TLDR; Modern vulnerability research increasingly leverages artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques for automated detection. Researchers are developing sophisticated explainable AI models that can pinpoint specific code elements responsible for vulnerabilities while maintaining high detection accuracy. (3 sources)

Recent advances in vulnerability research reflect a shift toward more sophisticated analytical approaches powered by artificial intelligence. Machine learning has become a cornerstone of vulnerability detection, with researchers developing increasingly precise methods for identifying security flaws in code  [52831393 | Xu | 2020 | Citations: 48]. This field encompasses diverse technical approaches, from program verification to fuzzing techniques, each offering unique advantages in uncovering hidden vulnerabilities  [257906734 | Spring | 2023 | Citations: 10].

A particularly promising direction involves explainable AI models that not only detect vulnerabilities but also provide insights into why certain code segments are flagged as problematic. These models employ various architectures and approaches, including graph neural networks, transformers, and attention-based mechanisms, to deliver both accurate vulnerability predictions and meaningful explanations for their findings  [261064908 | Ni et al. | 2023 | Citations: 23]. Notable innovations include frameworks that can identify specific tokens contributing to vulnerability predictions and models that combine high detection capability with precise localization of vulnerable code segments  [261064908 | Ni et al. | 2023 | Citations: 23].

The trend toward explainable AI in vulnerability research represents a significant advancement, as it addresses both the practical need for reliable detection and the educational requirement for understanding how these detections are made  [261064908 | Ni et al. | 2023 | Citations: 23]. While traditional manual analysis remains valuable, these new approaches offer the potential for scaling security audits to much larger codebases <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
TLDR; Large Language Models (LLMs) represent the cutting edge of artificial intelligence, built on the transformer architecture with billions to trillions of parameters. Modern LLMs demonstrate unprecedented capabilities in natural language understanding and generation, marking a significant evolution from earlier models. (4 sources)

The landscape of Large Language Models has undergone dramatic transformation since their inception, driven primarily by two key innovations <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">. First, the introduction of the transformer architecture fundamentally changed how machines process language by focusing solely on relationships between elements rather than sequential processing  [13756489 | Vaswani et al. | 2017 | Citations: 114143]. Second, the rapid scaling of model parameters from millions to hundreds of billions has led to qualitative improvements in performance  [267211660 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 23].

Today's leading LLMs typically contain tens to hundreds of billions of parameters, with some reaching into the trillions - representing approximately 3,000 times the parameter count of early models like BERT  [277066208 | Chandra | 2025 | Citations: 0]. These models are trained on vast collections of internet text, books, and academic papers, enabling them to develop sophisticated understanding across numerous topics  [267211660 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 23].

The evolution of LLMs has revealed several important developments. Starting with foundational models like GPT-3 (175B parameters) and PaLM (540B parameters), the field saw a significant acceleration in capability emergence  [268249175 | Hartsock et al. | 2024 | Citations: 63]. More recent advances have focused on improving efficiency without sacrificing performance, exemplified by models like LLaMA, which achieved comparable results to much larger models while being an order of magnitude smaller  [272969458 | Feretzakis et al. | 2024 | Citations: 10].

citations.title: [267211660 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 23]
snippets: In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4 [37] have become a prominent trend in natural language processing. With billions of model parameters, LLM models are trained on meticulous collections of textual content, ranging from books to web texts and Wikipedia articles. This comprehensive learning process enables LLM models to comprehend a wide range of prompts and questions, resulting in higher accuracy and precision when handling complex tasks. GPT models, particularly the GPT-4 model, have demonstrated their superiority over state-of-the-art models in various NLP tasks, including machine translation, question-answering, and close tasks.

The era of even larger LLMs began in 2020, introducing models like GPT-3 (the 3-generation Generative Pre-trained Transformer) (Brown et al., 2020) (175 B parameters) and PaLM (Pathways Language Model) (Chowdhery et al., 2022) (540 B parameters). Some of the most recent LLMs are LLaMA (Large Language Model Meta AI) [Tou+23b], Vicuna [Chi+[23], Llama 2 [Tou+23a], and Mistral [Jia+[23].

citations.title: [272969458 | Feretzakis et al. | 2024 | Citations: 10]
snippets:
Prominent examples of LLMs are BERT, GPT, RoBERTa, T5, XLNet, and Meta's series of LLaMA. BERT is an abbreviation for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. Devlin et al. (Devlin et al., 2019) proposed this, conditioning on both left and right context to capture deep bidirectional representations. It is pre-trained on masked language modeling and next-sentence prediction tasks, therefore performing really well in a wide range of NLP tasks after fine-tuning. 

The best-known GPT series by OpenAI are GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) and GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020). They are autoregressive models that predict the next word in a sequence. GPT-3 is the largest, with 175 billion parameters, and has achieved impressive scores on few-shot learning and text generation. RoBERTa is an improved version of BERT proposed by Liu et al. [3]. RoBERTa works better than the abovedescribed models by training on more data and omitting the objective of next sentence prediction. 

Text-to-Text Transfer Learning, as proposed by Raffel et al. in T5 (Raffel et al., 2019), generalizes all NLP tasks into a unified task for easier implementation of transfer learning. XLNet, by Yang et al. (Yang et al., 2019), proposes a permutation-based training objective to model effective bidirectional contexts, which avoids the pretraining constraints of masked language models. Foundation-LLaMA (Large Language Model Meta AI) [42] has 7 and 65 billion parameters going to Meta AI. LLaMA is engineered for being highperformance with high efficiency; one order of magnitude smaller in size than other bulk models, it still achieves the highest performance.

sections.title: Leading Open Source Models
sections.text:
TLDR; Open-source LLMs have gained prominence through efficient scaling and strong performance relative to their size. Notable models include LLaMA, Mistral, and Mixtral, with recent evaluations highlighting specific strengths in areas like reasoning and code generation. (10 sources)

* **LLaMA and LLaMA 2 (Meta)**: The LLaMA series represents a breakthrough in efficient scaling, with LLaMA 2 offering enhanced capabilities while requiring significantly fewer compute resources during training compared to previous models. The second iteration benefits from 40% more training data and optimization through human preference alignment  [268820018 | Qian et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [263186060 | Touvron et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4294].

* **Mistral AI Models**: Mistral has established itself as a leader among open-source alternatives, with Mistral 7B demonstrating superior performance against both larger open-source models and commercial counterparts. Its architectural innovations, including grouped-query attention and sliding window attention, enable efficient processing of longer sequences  [268385552 | Chawla et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]  [268819697 | Panagiotopoulos et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

* **Mixtral**: This model combines the efficiency of open-source frameworks with advanced capabilities, representing a significant step forward in the open-source ecosystem [269042933 | García-Ferrero et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

* **Deepseek and Solar**: These newer entries in the open-source landscape have shown promising results, particularly in specific technical tasks. Deepseek performed particularly well in programming-related tasks, while Solar demonstrated strong performance in question-answering scenarios  [269042933 | García-Ferrero et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]  [265758592 | Fröbe et al. | 2023 | Citations: 267]  [264985409 | Kim et al. | 2023 | Citations: 101].

* **Size vs Performance Trade-offs**: Empirical evidence suggests that larger models don't always equate to better performance - Llama 2's approach of optimizing computational efficiency alongside scaling has proven particularly effective  [271645882 | Yeom et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]. Even relatively compact models like LLaMA2-70B have shown competitive performance against much larger proprietary models  [271903779 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

* **Architecture Innovation**: Recent developments emphasize architectural efficiency alongside parameter count, as evidenced by models like Phi-3.5 which deliver strong performance despite their smaller size  [273403548 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

citations.title: [268385552 | Chawla et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]
snippets: In our research, we leverage the capabilities of the many different robust open-source large language models ultimately settling on Mistral [4] due to its superior performance. Mistral 7B surpasses the performance of the leading open 13B model (Llama 2 [29]) across all benchmarks and outperforms the best released 34B model (Llama 1 [29]) specifically in reasoning, mathematics, and code generation tasks. Current benchmark comparisons highlight clear distinctions in performance across different LLM families. When evaluating Chinese-language capabilities, however, models like Ernie Bot 4 have demonstrated superior performance  [269757226 | Jiang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

Task-specific evaluations reveal interesting patterns in model specialization. In algorithmic tasks, GPT-4 has shown consistent excellence across varying problem difficulties  [268032846 | Petruzzellis et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7], while models like DepGPT have achieved impressive results in specialized applications such as speech understanding tasks, with accuracies approaching 0.98  [266999641 | Chowdhury et al. | 2024 | Citations: 9].

Notably, some comparative studies have found that traditional approaches can occasionally outperform LLM variants in specific contexts. However, this finding appears to be context-dependent and does not diminish the overall utility of LLMs in most applications.

Recent evaluations comparing leading models across different scales have shown that newer iterations, regardless of ownership model, continue to improve upon their predecessors. This is evident in the ongoing refinement of models like GPT-3.5 and the emergence of newer entrants like Gemma, which pushes boundaries in multimodal capabilities  [272832417 | Ma | 2024 | Citations: 0]. sections.title: Application-Specific Best Practices

TLDR; Different LLMs excel in specific use cases based on their inherent capabilities and resource requirements. Understanding these specializations helps organizations choose the most suitable models for their particular needs, whether in healthcare, education, or technical applications. (9 sources)

When selecting an LLM for specific applications, several key considerations emerge from empirical evaluations and real-world deployments. For complex language processing tasks, particularly in English, GPT-4 continues to demonstrate superior capabilities, making it a preferred choice for high-stakes applications  [268201602 | Chen et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7]  [270380001 | Pordanesh et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

Translation services benefit significantly from modern LLMs' ability to understand context and produce coherent translations, often matching or exceeding traditional machine translation systems  (Zhang et al._1,  2024)  [265249578 | Vilar et al. | 2022 | Citations: 61]. This makes LLMs particularly valuable for cross-cultural communication and international business applications.

In technical domains, PaLM 2 has shown notable advantages for professional developers, supporting features like interactive debugging and incremental execution of code  [268201602 | Chen et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7]  [263571088 | Chowdhry et al. | 2024 | Citations: 17]. Similarly, models like ChatGLM have demonstrated exceptional performance in Chinese language applications, particularly in question-answering and dialogue systems  [270688665 | Su et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8]  [237451729 | Du et al. | 2021 | Citations: 1413].

The emergence of application-driven evaluation frameworks, such as A-Eval, provides organizations with structured methodologies for assessing model suitability for their specific needs  [270559009 | Lian et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]. These frameworks consider multiple dimensions beyond raw performance metrics, helping organizations identify the optimal balance between capabilities and operational constraints.

For scenarios requiring complex reasoning and detailed analysis, newer models like Claude 3.5 Sonnet have shown particular strength in handling nuanced queries, especially when dealing with complex, sentiment-laden content  [273351383 | Shamshiri et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. Meanwhile, GPT-4 remains stable and reliable for applications requiring consistent performance across varying demonstration sets  [273351383 | Shamshiri et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

question: The difference between cross-language summarization and multilingual summarization

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Text summarization has evolved to address the needs of a multilingual world through two distinct approaches: cross-lingual and multilingual summarization. These approaches emerged separately due to their unique technical requirements and challenges, though they share common goals of making content accessible across languages. (3 sources)

Text summarization systems have adapted to meet the growing demand for accessing and understanding content across different languages  [258714901 | Wang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 23]. Two primary approaches have developed to address this need: cross-lingual summarization (CLS) and multilingual summarization (MLS). While these approaches serve similar purposes of enabling multilingual content understanding, they have historically been researched and developed separately due to their distinct methodological requirements  [258714901 | Wang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 23]. With advances in technology, particularly in cross-lingual representations and large pre-trained models, both fields have seen significant growth and evolution  [243865371 | Perez-Beltrachini et al. | 2022 | Citations: 49]  [218675655 | Liu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 11441]. One notable advantage of modern approaches is their ability to handle diverse types of content while maintaining accessibility - for instance, some systems can now summarize live speech streams from various regional accents and languages simultaneously  [218675655 | Liu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 11414], demonstrating the sophisticated capabilities that have emerged in handling multilingual content.

citations.title: [243865371 | Perez-Beltrachini et al. | 2022 | Citations: 49]
snippets: Cross-lingual summarisation aims to produce a summary in a different target language (e.g., English) given a document in a source language (e.g., French). The practical benefits of this task are twofold: it not only provides rapid access to salient content, but also enables the dissemination of relevant content across speakers of other languages...While creating large-scale multi-lingual summarisation datasets has proven feasible (Straka et al., 2018;Scialom et al., 2020), at least for the news domain, cross-lingual datasets are more difficult to obtain...with the advent of cross-lingual representations (Ruder et al., 2019) and large pre-trained models (Devlin et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2020), research on multi-lingual summarisation (i.e., building monolingual summarisation systems for different languages) has been gaining momentum (Chi et al., 2020b;Scialom et al., 2020).

citations.title: [258714901 | Wang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 23]
snippets: To adapt text summarization to the multilingual world, previous work proposes multi-lingual summarization (MLS) and cross-lingual summarization (CLS). However, these two tasks have been studied separately due to the different definitions, which limits the compatible and systematic research on both of them.

sections.title: Core Definitions and Basic Concepts
sections.text:
TLDR; Cross-lingual summarization creates a summary in one language from content in another language, while multilingual summarization handles multiple languages simultaneously for outputs matching each input language. These approaches represent fundamentally different ways of approaching multilingual text summarization. (5 sources)

At their core, cross-lingual summarization and multilingual summarization represent distinct approaches to handling multilingual text summarization. Cross-lingual summarization specifically focuses on generating a summary in a target language from content written in a source language  [202541473 | Zhu et al. | 2019 | Citations: 133]  [213631816 | Cao et al. | 2020 | Citations: 26]. This means that regardless of the input language, the system produces output exclusively in the specified target language.

Multilingual summarization takes a broader approach, capable of processing and summarizing content in multiple languages simultaneously. What makes this approach unique is that it generates outputs in the same language as the respective inputs - if the input is in French, the summary remains in French; similarly for Japanese, the summary stays in Japanese  [258840886 | Huot et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7]  [264146402 | Wang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3].

These distinctions become clearer when considering specific examples. In a multilingual context, a system might process a mix of inputs in different languages (such as Hindi, English, and Gujarati) and generate corresponding outputs in the same languages. Conversely, a cross-lingual system operates primarily between pairs of languages, such as converting content from English to Hindi  [247958026 | Yadav et al. | 2022 | Citations: 49]. The choice between these approaches often depends on specific use cases and requirements <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [202541473 | Zhu et al. | 2019 | Citations: 133]
snippets: Cross-lingual summarization (CLS) is the task to produce a summary in one particular language for a source document in a different language. Existing methods simply divide this task into two steps: summarization and translation, leading to the problem of error propagation. To handle that, we present an end-to-end CLS framework, which we refer to as Neural Cross-Lingual Summarization (NCLS), for the first time. Moreover, we propose to further improve NCLS by incorporating two related tasks, monolingual summarization and machine translation, into the training process of CLS under multi-task learning. Due to the lack of supervised CLS data, we propose a round-trip translation strategy to acquire two high-quality large-scale CLS datasets based on existing monolingual summarization datasets. Experimental results have shown that our NCLS achieves remarkable improvement over traditional pipeline methods on both English-to-Chinese and Chinese-to-English CLS human-corrected test sets. In addition, NCLS with multi-task learning can further significantly improve the quality of generated summaries. We make our dataset and code publicly available here: http://www.nlpr.ia.ac.cn/cip/dataset.htm.

citations.title: [213631816 | Cao et al. | 2020 | Citations: 26]

citations.title: [247958026 | Yadav et al. | 2022 | Citations: 49]
snippets: Multilingual: In a Multilingual text summarizer, input is written in many languages (Hindi, English, and Gujarati), and output summary is generated likewise in these languages (Hovy & Lin, 1996).  Cross-Lingual: In a Cross-lingual text summarizer, the input document is in one language (say English), and the output summary is in another language (say Hindi) (Linhares Pontes et al., 2020)....SUMMARIST (Hovy & Lin, 1996) is a multilingual text summarization system based on an extraction strategy that generates summaries from English, Indonesian, Spanish, German, Japanese, Korean, and French sources. Cross-Language Text Summarization (CLTS) (Linhares Pontes et al., 2020) generates a summary in a target language from source language materials. It entails a combination of text summarising and machine translation methods. Unfortunately, this combination leads to mistakes, which lowers the quality of summaries. CLTS systems may extract relevant information from both source and destination languages through joint analysis, which improves the development of extractive crosslingual summaries.

citations.title: [258840886 | Huot et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7]
snippets: Given a document or multiple documents in a source language (e.g., English), cross-lingual summarization (Wang et al., 2022) aims to generate a summary in a different target language (e.g., Czech or German). It enables the rapid dissemination of relevant content across speakers of other languages. For instance, providing summaries of English news articles to Czech or German speakers; or making available to English speakers the content of product and service descriptions in foreign languages....While initial efforts have focused on English, more recently, with the advent of cross-lingual representations (Ruder et al., 2017) and large pre-trained models (Devlin et al., 2019)Liu et al., 2020), research on multilingual summarization (i.e., building monolingual summarization systems for different languages) has also gained momentum (Chi et al., 2019)(Scialom et al., 2020)Aharoni et al., 2022).

citations.title: [264146402 | Wang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3]
snippets: Multi-language summarization involves generating summaries for documents in various languages, but the output summary is in the same language as the input document. For instance, if the input is in French, the summary will be in French, if the input is in Japanese in the same model, the summary will be in Japanese [142]. Cross-lingual summarization refers to the task of generating a summary in a target language for a source document written in a different language [90](Orasan et al., 2008). This type of summarization task requires models to not only understand and extract the main ideas from the source document but also translate the extracted information into the target language.

sections.title: Technical Approaches and Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; Technical approaches to cross-lingual summarization generally fall into two categories: pipeline methods that combine separate summarization and translation steps, and end-to-end models that attempt direct cross-lingual generation. Recent developments include multi-task frameworks and unified decoders that aim to improve efficiency and performance. (8 sources)

The implementation of cross-lingual summarization systems follows several distinct technical approaches. The traditional pipeline approach first performs summarization in the source language before translating it to the target language  (Wang et al._1,  2023). While intuitive, this method suffers from error propagation issues since problems in either step can compound throughout the process  [259040743 | Li et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1].

More advanced approaches employ end-to-end models that attempt direct cross-lingual generation without intermediate translation steps  [259040743 | Li et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]  [202541473 | Zhu et al. | 2019 | Citations: 133]. These systems face significant challenges in simultaneously mastering both language understanding and summarization skills  (Cao et al._1,  2020).

Recent innovations have introduced more sophisticated architectures. For example, the Multi-Task framework for Cross-Lingual Abstractive Summarization (MCLAS) uses a unified decoder to generate both monolingual and cross-lingual summaries sequentially, treating monolingual summarization as a prerequisite task  [235247840 | Bai et al. | 2021 | Citations: 52]. Another approach involves adapting multilingual models like BERT, though this adaptation faces limitations since models are inherently trained to output text in the grammar of their source language  [237396364 | Zagar et al. | 2020 | Citations: 9].

Current research explores various model configurations, including two-stage pipeline approaches with independent summarization and translation components, as well as direct cross-lingual models  [260829737 | Takeshita et al. | 2023 | Citations: 8]. Despite these advancements, researchers acknowledge that simply breaking down cross-lingual summarization into multiple subtasks doesn't necessarily ensure optimal performance for each component  (Li et al._1,  2023).

Practical implementations have demonstrated success across multiple language pairs, including combinations of English with German, Italian, Chinese, and Japanese  [249192236 | Takeshita et al. | 2022 | Citations: 14]. These applications leverage state-of-the-art pre-trained language models to build systems capable of handling various cross-lingual summarization scenarios.

citations.title: [202541473 | Zhu et al. | 2019 | Citations: 133]
snippets: Cross-lingual summarization (CLS) is the task to produce a summary in one particular language for a source document in a different language. Existing methods simply divide this task into two steps: summarization and translation, leading to the problem of error propagation. To handle that, we present an end-to-end CLS framework, which we refer to as Neural Cross-Lingual Summarization (NCLS), for the first time. Moreover, we propose to further improve NCLS by incorporating two related tasks, monolingual summarization and machine translation, into the training process of CLS under multi-task learning. Due to the lack of supervised CLS data, we propose a round-trip translation strategy to acquire two high-quality large-scale CLS datasets based on existing monolingual summarization datasets. Experimental results have shown that our NCLS achieves remarkable improvement over traditional pipeline methods on both English-to-Chinese and Chinese-to-English CLS human-corrected test sets. In addition, NCLS with multi-task learning can further significantly improve the quality of generated summaries. We make our dataset and code publicly available here: http://www.nlpr.ia.ac.cn/cip/dataset.htm.

citations.title: [235247840 | Bai et al. | 2021 | Citations: 52]
snippets: Parallel cross-lingual summarization data is scarce, requiring models to better use the limited available cross-lingual resources. Existing methods to do so often adopt sequence-to-sequence networks with multi-task frameworks. Such approaches apply multiple decoders, each of which is utilized for a specific task. However, these independent decoders share no parameters, hence fail to capture the relationships between the discrete phrases of summaries in different languages, breaking the connections in order to transfer the knowledge of the high-resource languages to low-resource languages. To bridge these connections, we propose a novel Multi-Task framework for Cross-Lingual Abstractive Summarization (MCLAS) in a low-resource setting. Employing one unified decoder to generate the sequential concatenation of monolingual and cross-lingual summaries, MCLAS makes the monolingual summarization task a prerequisite of the CLS task. In this way, the shared decoder learns interactions involving alignments and summary patterns across languages, which encourages attaining knowledge transfer. Experiments on two CLS datasets demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms three baseline models in both low-resource and full-dataset scenarios. Moreover, in-depth analysis on the generated summaries and attention heads verifies that interactions are learned well using MCLAS, which benefits the CLS task under limited parallel resources.

citations.title: [237396364 | Zagar et al. | 2020 | Citations: 9]
snippets: Typically, this is done by multilingual models such as BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), or training the model on the resource-rich language (using monolingual embeddings in the source language) and then applying it to the less-resourced language where the input embeddings in the target language are mapped to the source language embeddings. Unfortunately, this standard procedure does not work for cross-lingual summarization, as the model is trained to output the sentences in the grammar of the source language. Blindly applying the procedure to a summarization model trained on English would produce sentences with English grammar in the target language. It is possible to achieve cross-lingual summarization using translation, but for summarization, this approach is unsatisfactory, as our baseline models, described in Section 5.1 show.

citations.title: [249192236 | Takeshita et al. | 2022 | Citations: 14]
snippets: Cross-lingual summarization processes English papers and generate summaries in German, Italian, Chinese and Japanese...In this paper, we fill this research gap and present an abstractive cross-lingual summarization dataset for four different languages in the scholarly domain, which enables us to train and evaluate models that process English papers and generate summaries in German, Italian, Chinese and Japanese...we benchmark the difficulty of cross-lingual extreme summarization with different models built on top of state-of-the-art pre-trained language models (Lewis et al., 2019)(Liu et al., 2020), namely a two-step approach based on monolingual summarization and translation, and a multilingual transformer model to directly generate summaries crosslingually.

citations.title: [259040743 | Li et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]
snippets:
Cross-lingual summarization (CLS) involves extracting the core content of a document in one language and expressing it in another language [1]. This task requires addressing both redundant information and language differences, which usually involves multiple steps. However, decomposing cross-lingual text summarization into multiple tasks does not guarantee optimal results for each individual neural network.

Given that the model integrates both monolingual and multilingual summarization tasks, it is necessary to configure the corresponding generation methods to enhance the quality of the generated summaries.

In cross-lingual summarization, we "train and evaluate models that process English papers and generate summaries in German, Italian, Chinese and Japanese." This approach includes a "two-stage pipeline approach that independently summarizes and translates, as well as a direct cross-lingual model."

sections.title: Challenges and Complexities
sections.text:
TLDR; Both cross-lingual and multilingual summarization face significant technical hurdles related to language complexity and information preservation. The challenges span from maintaining semantic accuracy across languages to managing cultural nuances and factual consistency. (7 sources)

Key challenges include:

1. **Combined Language Processing Complexity**: Cross-lingual summarization uniquely combines both translation and summarization challenges, making it more complex than single-language summarization  [257378170 | Zhang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5].

2. **Semantic Alignment Difficulties**: Systems must master dual competencies - understanding and compressing information while simultaneously managing cross-language semantics  [266578044 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

3. **Cultural References and Idioms**: Handling idiomatic expressions and cultural references poses a significant challenge during translation stages  [273022673 | Pernes et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [3520138 | Fadaee et al. | 2018 | Citations: 63].

4. **Factuality Maintenance**: Ensuring factual consistency between source and target documents remains a persistent challenge  [273022673 | Pernes et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [212966849 | Maynez et al. | 2020 | Citations: 352].

5. **Resource Limitations**: High-quality multilingual resources are scarce, limiting research progress in developing comprehensive solutions  [249048953 | T et al. | 2022 | Citations: 4].

6. **Model Configuration Challenges**: Finding the right balance between monolingual and multilingual aspects during model configuration affects summary quality  [259040743 | Li et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1].

7. **Error Propagation Risk**: Particularly in pipeline approaches, errors in either translation or summarization components can cascade and amplify problems  [259040743 | Li et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1].

8. **Many-to-Many Translation**: Modern systems aiming to handle multiple source-to-target language pairs face additional complexity in maintaining consistent quality across all language pairs  [273022673 | Pernes et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [239018575 | Xue et al. | 2021 | Citations: 634].

citations.title: [249048953 | T et al. | 2022 | Citations: 4]
snippets: One such application, Cross-lingual summarization (CLS), produces a summary in a particular language (target language) for an input document in a different language (source language). CLS can help people understand an article's gist written in an unfamiliar language by translating the summary to their familiar language. Current methods divide CLS into two methods: Summarization (Abstractive or Extractive) and Translation. Although there has been a tremendous amount of progress in abstractive summarization in recent years, most research focuses on monolingual summarization because of lack of high-quality multilingual resources.

Cross-lingual summarization refers to the task of producing a summary in a different language than the original document and has the potential to break language barriers by helping people to effectively capture the essence of documents written in foreign languages (Wang et al., 2022). This is a very challenging task, as it combines the difficulties of monolingual summarization, such as factual inconsistencies with respect to the source document (Maynez et al., 2020), with those of machine translation, such as translation of idiomatic expressions and cultural references (Fadaee et al., 2018).

sections.title: Applications and Benefits
sections.text:
TLDR; Cross-lingual and multilingual summarization technologies enable efficient content access and understanding across linguistic boundaries. These systems find practical applications in news consumption, business operations, education, and scientific communication, offering valuable tools for bridging language gaps. (7 sources)

Cross-lingual and multilingual summarization systems deliver significant practical benefits across various domains. At their core, these technologies enable rapid access to essential content across linguistic boundaries, helping users quickly grasp the main ideas of texts in unfamiliar languages [243865371 | Perez-Beltrachini et al. | 2022 | Citations: 49]  [257378170 | Zhang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5].

In the media sector, these systems facilitate the broad distribution of news content, allowing readers to stay informed about international events regardless of the original language of publication  [258840886 | Huot et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7]. Business applications benefit significantly through improved access to market intelligence and customer feedback across different regions  [258840886 | Huot et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7].

The educational sector has found valuable use cases, particularly in making academic content accessible to non-native speakers  [249836973 | Scialom et al. | 2020 | Citations: 385]. Research institutions and scholars benefit from being able to efficiently digest findings from publications in various languages, facilitating international collaboration and knowledge sharing  [249836973 | Scialom et al. | 2020 | Citations: 385].

Modern multilingual summarization systems offer enhanced capabilities compared to their cross-lingual counterparts, particularly in preserving subtle semantic meanings across languages  [272407713 | Phani et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. This advancement allows for more nuanced cross-cultural communication and understanding <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

The impact extends beyond individual users to organizations seeking to maintain competitive advantages in global markets. By enabling quick comprehension of foreign language content, these systems support faster decision-making and operational efficiency across international contexts  [268536633 | Parnell et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]  [270357490 | Park et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

question: Which 3D Gaussian Splatting methods exist that output mesh representations?

sections.title: Introduction/Background
sections.text:
TLDR; 3D Gaussian Splatting primarily excels at realistic rendering but has challenges when it comes to extracting proper mesh representations. This limitation has led researchers to explore various methods to combine 3D Gaussians with mesh representations. (3 sources)

While 3D Gaussian Splatting has gained popularity for its ability to achieve high-quality novel view synthesis at faster training speeds compared to traditional Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), it presents unique challenges when attempting to extract mesh representations  [259267917 | Kerbl et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3373]. One fundamental issue is that Gaussians lack inherent topological relationships, and without proper constraints, optimizing their attributes can lead to irregular geometry that makes extracting valid topological meshes problematic  [268513581 | Li et al. | 2024 | Citations: 24]. This challenge has spurred researchers to develop various approaches that either modify the Gaussian representation or combine it with mesh-based methods to overcome these limitations <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">. These developments have resulted in several distinct strategies for obtaining mesh representations from 3D Gaussian Splatting, ranging from refined mesh extraction algorithms to entirely new representations like 2D Gaussian Splatting.

citations.title: [268513581 | Li et al. | 2024 | Citations: 24]
snippets: To extract mesh surface from 3D Gaussians, SuGaR [13] serves as a refinement module to jointly optimize mesh and Gaussians.However, the method requires more GPU resources for training compared with 3DGS.

citations.title: [259267917 | Kerbl et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3373]
snippets: Radiance Field methods have recently revolutionized novel-view synthesis of scenes captured with multiple photos or videos. However, achieving high visual quality still requires neural networks that are costly to train and render, while recent faster methods inevitably trade off speed for quality. For unbounded and complete scenes (rather than isolated objects) and 1080p resolution rendering, no current method can achieve real-time display rates. We introduce three key elements that allow us to achieve state-of-the-art visual quality while maintaining competitive training times and importantly allow high-quality real-time (≥ 30 fps) novel-view synthesis at 1080p resolution. First, starting from sparse points produced during camera calibration, we represent the scene with 3D Gaussians that preserve desirable properties of continuous volumetric radiance fields for scene optimization while avoiding unnecessary computation in empty space; Second, we perform interleaved optimization/density control of the 3D Gaussians, notably optimizing anisotropic covariance to achieve an accurate representation of the scene; Third, we develop a fast visibility-aware rendering algorithm that supports anisotropic splatting and both accelerates training and allows realtime rendering. We demonstrate state-of-the-art visual quality and real-time rendering on several established datasets.

sections.title: Direct Mesh Extraction Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; Several methods have emerged to directly extract meshes from 3D Gaussian Splatting by adding specific constraints or modifications to the Gaussian representation. The most notable approaches include SuGaR's SDF-based regularization, 2DGS's surface-aligned 2D Gaussians, and Quadratic Gaussian Splatting's higher-order surface modeling. (7 sources)

Several key approaches have been developed to extract meshes directly from 3D Gaussian Splatting:

* **SuGaR**: Introduces a regularization term that aligns 3D Gaussians with the scene's surface using SDF-based optimization. This method then applies Poisson surface reconstruction to the aligned Gaussians to extract the final mesh  [265308825 | Guedon et al. | 2023 | Citations: 338]  [269605952 | Dalal et al. | 2024 | Citations: 20]. While effective, this approach requires significant GPU resources during training  (Li et al._1,  2024).

* **2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS)**: Instead of using 3D Gaussians, this method represents surfaces using 2D-oriented planar Gaussian disks. Each primitive contains two variance values and tangent vectors to define surface normals, ensuring view-consistent geometry  [270521286 | Ukarapol et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]  [272592871 | Yu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 53]. This approach addresses some of the fundamental limitations of 3D Gaussians by focusing on the fact that object surfaces are essentially 2D manifolds  [276580468 | Zhou et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [268692234 | Huang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 424].

* **Quadratic Gaussian Splatting (QGS)**: Enhances geometric fitting through higher-order surface representation, enabling more accurate mesh extraction from quadric models  [274234543 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

These methods represent different technical approaches to solving the core challenge of mesh extraction from 3D Gaussians, each offering specific advantages in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [265308825 | Guedon et al. | 2023 | Citations: 338]
snippets: We propose a method to allow precise and extremely fast mesh extraction from 3D Gaussian Splatting [15]. Gaussian Splatting has recently become very popular as it yields realistic rendering while being significantly faster to train than NeRFs. It is however challenging to extract a mesh from the millions of tiny 3D Gaussians as these Gaussians tend to be unorganized after optimization and no method has been proposed so far. Our first key contribution is a regularization term that encourages the Gaussians to align well with the surface of the scene. We then introduce a method that exploits this alignment to extract a mesh from the Gaussians using Poisson reconstruction, which is fast, scalable, and preserves details, in contrast to the Marching Cubes algorithm usually applied to extract meshes from Neural SDFs. Finally, we introduce an optional refinement strategy that binds Gaussians to the surface of the mesh, and jointly optimizes these Gaussians and the mesh through Gaussian splatting rendering. This enables easy editing, sculpting, animating, and relighting of the Gaussians by manipulating the mesh instead of the Gaussians themselves. Retrieving such an editable mesh for realistic rendering is done within minutes with our method, compared to hours with the state-of-the-art method on SDFs, while providing a better rendering quality.

citations.title: [268692234 | Huang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 424]
snippets: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has recently revolutionized radiance field reconstruction, achieving high quality novel view synthesis and fast rendering speed. However, 3DGS fails to accurately represent surfaces due to the multi-view inconsistent nature of 3D Gaussians. We present 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS), a novel approach to model and reconstruct geometrically accurate radiance fields from multi-view images. Our key idea is to collapse the 3D volume into a set of 2D oriented planar Gaussian disks. Unlike 3D Gaussians, 2D Gaussians provide view-consistent geometry while modeling surfaces intrinsically. To accurately recover thin surfaces and achieve stable optimization, we introduce a perspective-accurate 2D splatting process utilizing ray-splat intersection and rasterization. Additionally, we incorporate depth distortion and normal consistency terms to further enhance the quality of the reconstructions. We demonstrate that our differentiable renderer allows for noise-free and detailed geometry reconstruction while maintaining competitive appearance quality, fast training speed, and real-time rendering. Project page at https://surfsplatting.github.io.
