It is worth mentioning that UAVs are among the pivotal technologies that will drive the development of Sixth Generation (6G) networks (Chowdhury et al., 2019), whereas the global UAV market is forecasted to reach 42.8 billion USD by 2025 [3]. One of the main factors determining the success of UAV operations is the reliable and efficient communication. However, conventional communication systems often struggle to meet the diverse and dynamic requirements of UAV-based applications...By leveraging SDR technology, communication protocols and signal processing functionalities can be implemented in software, offering unparalleled flexibility, scalability, and programmability, while minimizing the reliance on costly and proprietary hardware solutions. Presently, the majority of modern communication devices utilize SDR technology. Also, the global market value of SDR is projected to rise to USD 32.2 billion by 2028 with a Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 7.4% [5]...In the 1990s, Joseph Mitola coined the term SDR to describe radios that could be reprogrammed and reconfigured via software rather than hardware (Mitola, 1992). Although SDR has been a technological concept for years, it's only in recent times that affordable SDR solutions, facilitated by user-friendly hardware platforms, such as Universal Software Radio Peripherals (USRPs) [27], have become accessible. The rising popularity of SDR technology is attributed to advancements in computing and the availability of free open-source software libraries over recent decades...Currently, SDRs play a pivotal role in the development of wireless standards owing to their adaptability and programmability features (Akeela et al., 2018)...FPGAs have significantly transformed the SDR landscape by providing a flexible and powerful platform for real-time signal processing. Their reconfigurability allows SDR systems to efficiently adapt to various communication standards and signal processing algorithms on-the-fly, which is crucial for the dynamic nature of SDR applications and multi-mission capabilities. Moreover, FPGA-integrated SDRs are essential for handling high-throughput data streams and supporting high-bandwidth applications (e.g., High-Definition (HD) video streaming or large-scale data collection).

citations.title: [272843359 | Kagai et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]
snippets:
Software Defined Radio (SDR) refers to a radio communication system where traditional hardware components, such as mixers, filters, amplifiers, and modulators, are replaced or significantly augmented by software on a computer or embedded system [80]. A sample design of SDR is illustrated in Figure 7. The key idea behind SDR is to move much of the signal processing from hardware to software, enabling greater flexibility, reconfigurability, and adaptability in radio communication systems. In recent years, SDR has gained significant traction as an enhancement to deployability dynamics in satellite-enabled communications [80], [82], [94].

In a traditional radio system, the functions of tuning, demodulation, filtering, and decoding are typically implemented using dedicated hardware components [80]. In an SDR system, these functions are performed by software running on a general-purpose computer or specialized processing hardware. This shift allows for a more straightforward adaptation to different communication standards and protocols and the ability to update or modify the system's functionality through software updates rather than hardware changes.

SDR design comprises the front-end and internal components. Front-end components handle the incoming and outgoing signals to make communication possible [82]. Incoming continuous analogue signals are passed through Analogue to Digital Converters (ADC) for conversion into a digital signal. Once the computer has processed, it needs to send information back to the radio waves for transmission; Digital to Analogue (DAC) takes the digital language and turns it back into smooth, continuous analogue signals for broadcast.

Additional essential components in SDR are the Signal Processing Unit (SPU), Control and Monitoring Unit (CMU), and the Software Framework [82]. SPU and CMU are both hardware components. While SPU is designed to handle the computational tasks associated with digital signal processing algorithms, CMU complements SPU's functionality by overseeing system operations, managing configurations, and ensuring security protocols. The CMU and SPU contribute to the SDR's effective control, monitoring, and signalprocessing capabilities.

SPU is a central component that executes digital signal processing algorithms, facilitating essential functions such as modulation, demodulation, and filtering [82].

citations.title: [273707571 | Jagatheesaperumal et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5]
snippets: Cognitive radio is essentially a software-defined radio or an intelligent radio system that can be programmed to dynamically and at run-time adjust to specific frequency bands. As mobile frequency bands are getting crowded, with cognitive radio, we can utilize any of the available frequency bands for communication...SDR is a radio communication system that is responsible for addressing physical layer issues. They act as one of the core components in driving digital wireless technology. SDRs typically consist of hardware components, including amplifiers, filters, detectors, modulators, and demodulators, as well as software-based functionalities such as modulation, signal processing, channel coding, and data encapsulation. These software-based functionalities are typically implemented on a personal computer or embedded systems. They assist in listening to broadcast stations and receiving satellite signals, aircraft radio signals, and other medium-wave radio signals. The basic architecture of the SDR includes antennas, low noise amplifiers, filters, mixers, analog to digital converters, and in-phase (I) and quadrature (Q) samples. The computer running the SDR software, will read the IQ components and decode them and let the users acquire the data stream.

sections.title: Technical Architecture & Components
sections.text:
TLDR; Modern SDR systems integrate multiple hardware and software components working together to process radio signals. The key technical components include RF front-ends, ADC/DAC converters, signal processing units, and control systems, all orchestrated through software frameworks. (3 sources)

Modern SDR architecture follows a layered approach, beginning with the front-end components that handle the initial signal processing. The process starts when radio signals enter through the antenna, where they are first amplified by a Low Noise Amplifier (LNA) and filtered to manage bandwidth and prevent signal overload. Following this preprocessing stage, the signals undergo frequency conversion and are digitized through Analog-to-Digital Converters (ADC)  [260027633 | Olesinski et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5].

The core processing pipeline consists of several key components working in concert. At its foundation, the Signal Processing Unit (SPU) handles the intensive computations required for digital signal processing, including modulation, demodulation, and filtering tasks. Supporting this processing engine is the Control and Monitoring Unit (CMU), which manages system operations, maintains configurations, and ensures security protocols are maintained  [272843359 | Kagai et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

Recent architectural innovations have focused on creating reconfigurable Radio Frequency Front-End (RFFE) designs that can adapt to varying signal requirements and frequencies. These systems typically implement baseband algorithms using Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) or Digital Signal Processors (DSPs), offering benefits in modularity, expandability, and simplified system updates  [272927894 | Shakibafar et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

The final stage of the SDR pipeline involves converting processed digital signals back into radio waves. This is accomplished through Digital-to-Analog Converters (DACs), which transform the digital output into continuous analog signals ready for transmission  [272843359 | Kagai et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]  [260027633 | Olesinski et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5]. Machine Learning capabilities have become increasingly integral to modern SDR systems, enabling advanced features such as RF fingerprinting, spectrum awareness, and autonomous system configuration  [260027633 | Olesinski et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5].

citations.title: [260027633 | Olesinski et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5]
snippets:
The radio signal is actually a variable electrical signal induced by electromagnetic waves at the antenna terminals. In modern solutions, it travels through a waveguide to a receiver based on the SDR (software-defined radio) architecture. SDR technology is defined by IEEE 1900.1 [1] as a radio for which some or all of the physical layer functions are software-defined. However, the radio signal from the antenna is too weak to be sampled directly, so it is amplified by the LNA (low noise amplifier). Very often, there is also an input filter assembly before the LNA module, which reduces the bandwidth of the signal being amplified to reduce the potential for overdriving the amplifier, and thus reduce the likelihood of intermodulation. The amplified RF signal then goes to a frequency conversion circuit and an analog-to-digital converter (superheterodyne or direct conversion solutions) or directly to an analog-to-digital converter (direct sampling solutions). Other stages of radio signal processing are implemented through software, e.g., in FPGAs (fieldprogrammable gate arrays), DSPs (digital signal processors) or a PCs (personal computers). 

An undeniable advantage of SDR is its reconfigurability, i.e., changing the received and transmitted waveform. Taking additionally into account the growing interest in cognitive and intelligent radio solutions, it has become a natural evolution of cognitive radio to apply machine learning techniques to the radio environment. RFML (radio frequency machine learning) systems have been described by DARPA [2] as performing four basic tasks, namely RF fingerprinting, RF fingerprint enhancement (which can be realized by using radio-based steganographic solutions [3]4] in DNNs), spectrum awareness and autonomous RF system configuration.

A sample design of SDR is illustrated in Figure 7. The key idea behind SDR is to move much of the signal processing from hardware to software, enabling greater flexibility, reconfigurability, and adaptability in radio communication systems. In recent years, SDR has gained significant traction as an enhancement to deployability dynamics in satellite-enabled communications [80], [82], [94].

In a traditional radio system, the functions of tuning, demodulation, filtering, and decoding are typically implemented using dedicated hardware components [80]. In an SDR system, these functions are performed by software running on a general-purpose computer or specialized processing hardware. This shift allows for a more straightforward adaptation to different communication standards and protocols and the ability to update or modify the system's functionality through software updates rather than hardware changes.

SDR design comprises the front-end and internal components. Front-end components handle the incoming and outgoing signals to make communication possible [82]. Incoming continuous analogue signals are passed through Analogue to Digital Converters (ADC) for conversion into a digital signal. Once the computer has processed, it needs to send information back to the radio waves for transmission; Digital to Analogue (DAC) takes the digital language and turns it back into smooth, continuous analogue signals for broadcast.

Additional essential components in SDR are the Signal Processing Unit (SPU), Control and Monitoring Unit (CMU), and the Software Framework [82]. SPU and CMU are both hardware components. While SPU is designed to handle the computational tasks associated with digital signal processing algorithms, CMU complements SPU's functionality by overseeing system operations, managing configurations, and ensuring security protocols. The CMU and SPU contribute to the SDR's effective control, monitoring, and signalprocessing capabilities.

SPU is a central component that executes digital signal processing algorithms, facilitating essential functions such as modulation, demodulation, and filtering [82].

sections.title: Hardware Platforms & Implementations
sections.text:
TLDR; Current SDR implementations leverage diverse hardware platforms ranging from FPGA-based systems to specialized RF System-on-Chips (RFSoCs). These platforms vary in their capabilities and tradeoffs, with newer solutions focusing on higher bandwidth processing, multi-band operation, and improved programmability. (10 sources)

* **Advanced RFSoC Platforms**: Recent implementations utilize Radio Frequency System-on-Chip (RFSoC) technology, featuring built-in multi-GHz sampling RF data converters and powerful FPGA fabric for data routing. These platforms excel in high-performance SDR applications, beamforming systems, MIMO radios, and radars  [274646415 | Cheng et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [259569320 | Barkhordar-Pour et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]  [258521728 | Zhao et al. | 2023 | Citations: 6].

* **Space Applications**: Specialized SDR implementations for space missions demonstrate impressive capabilities, such as the Universal Space Transponder (UST-Lite) which supports up to four simultaneous communication bands using direct waveform sampling. These systems prioritize miniaturization while maintaining high processing capabilities  [258730264 | Kobayashi et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2].

* **Massive MIMO Testbeds**: Large-scale deployments like the KU Leuven testbed showcase advanced implementations using multiple USRP platforms combined with centralized baseband processing units for complex array configurations  [273026302 | Minucci et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

* **Commercial Off-The-Shelf Solutions**: Many modern SDR implementations rely on commercial components to maintain affordability and customization options. These platforms often utilize frameworks like GNU Radio for implementation  [269502013 | Ichkov et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

* **High-Bandwidth Processing Systems**: State-of-the-art SDR platforms can now process up to 8 GHz of bandwidth by utilizing multi-phase processing strategies and multiple parallel IQ streams. These systems combine RFSoC technology with custom IF multiplexing/demultiplexing boards to achieve exceptional performance levels  [270370886 | Jornet et al. | 2024 | Citations: 23].

* **Multi-Band Communication Platforms**: Modern SDR implementations support multiple frequency bands (HF, VHF, UHF, SHF) through compact, modular designs incorporating FPGA and SoC technologies. These platforms emphasize adaptability and resilience across different electromagnetic environments  [277023877 | Lyshevski et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [11552782 | Wang et al. | 2015 | Citations: 211].

* **Specialized Application Platforms**: Domain-specific implementations exist for various applications, including quantum control systems and analog computing platforms, demonstrating the versatility of modern SDR hardware architectures  [274646415 | Cheng et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [233781063 | Stefanazzi et al. | 2021 | Citations: 3].

citations.title: [258730264 | Kobayashi et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]
snippets: The Universal Space Transponder (UST) product line developed at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory offers Software-Defined Radio (SDR) solutions for various spaceflight applications. The UST-Lite is the latest product offering that provides a more miniaturized radio package with cutting-edge processing capabilities and features by taking advantage of recent advancements in digital processing and sampling technology. Parts selection and design guidelines follow JPL flight practices suitable for missions with high reliability requirements (e.g., Discovery or New Frontiers class), but the radio could also be adapted for use on SmallSat missions given its reduced power consumption, volume, and mass compared to other JPL radios. The main digital processor is implemented with a Swift Processor Module (SPM) developed in collaboration with JPL's Common Instrument Electronics task. The SPM uses a Kintex UltraScale FPGA (XQRKU060) with two mezzanine card slots to house application-specific circuit cards such as digital samplers, interface electronics, or additional processors. The UST-Lite uses mezzanine cards with high-speed digital samplers to directly sample and synthesize waveforms. With such direct waveform sampling approach, component counts can be drastically reduced while avoiding the use of baseband and intermediate frequency (IF) waveforms. The higher digital processing capability, coupled with expandable access to multiple high-speed samplers, allow the UST-Lite to support up to four simultaneous communication bands.

snippets: Following this approach, we have recently demonstrated what, as of today, is the fastest software-defined radio (SDR) platform for wireless communications, able to process in realtime 8 GHz of bandwidth by multiplexing four 2-GHz-wide channels in frequency (Abdellatif et al., 2022).More specifically, this platform leverages the state of the art in Radio Frequency (RF) systemon-chip (SoC) (SoC) and multi-phase processing strategies to generate four parallel IQ streams with baseband bandwidth of 1.25 GHz, each; and an IF multiplexing/demultiplexing custom board to generate/split a single ultra-broadband signal with 8 GHz of bandwidth.Multi-phase processing strategies are needed to match the difference in speed between the fieldprogrammable gate array (FPGA) clock (e.g., up to 512 MHz in the most optimistic case) and the speed of the dataconverters on the RFSoC (e.g., a few gigasamples-per-second (GSps)).

citations.title: [273026302 | Minucci et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]
snippets: The Massive MIMO Testbed at KU Leuven uses the NI USRP-2942R Software Defined Radio (SDR) platform and the Labview Communication Framework by National Instruments. It includes 32 SDRs, each with two RF chains, functioning as remote radio heads to handle IFFT, digital-to-analog conversion, upconversion for downlink transmission, and inverse operations for uplink reception. Centralized signal processing is performed by a Baseband Processing Unit (BBU) using techniques such as maximum ratio, minimum-mean-squared error, or zeroforcing.

citations.title: [274646415 | Cheng et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
snippets: In recent years, Radio Frequency System-on-Chip (RFSoC) has emerged as a promising solution to address these challenges by providing built-in multi-GHz sampling rates RF data converters (RF-DC) and powerful FPGA fabrics for datapath routing. RFSoC platforms have been used across various domains to build high-performance SDRs and beamforming systems [15,(Steiner et al., 2023)(Volz et al., 2023)(Zhao et al., 2020), MIMO radios and radars (Barkhordar-Pour et al., 2023)(Gao et al., 2024)(Lacruz et al., 2021)(Șahin et al., 2023)(Siauciulis et al., 2023), as well as quantum control [14](Stefanazzi et al., 2021) and analog computing systems. These works customized the hardware and/or software design for specific applications, yet there remains potential for improving system performance and further investigating the trade-offs between real-time data streaming support and ease of programmability.

citations.title: [277023877 | Lyshevski et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Compact, modular and programmable multi-band multi-channel radios with tunable filter accessories have been commercialized. In congested, contested and constrained electromagnetic spectrum (EMS), advanced radios should ensure resilient communications across high frequency (HF), very high frequency (VHF), ultra high frequency (UHF) and super high frequency (SHF) bands, e.g., in the 1 MHz to 30 GHz frequency range (Cahill et al., 2002)(Chamberlain, 2005). The software defined radio (SDR) paradigm has emerged and is effectively used across all domains. Studies are conducted in land (Nakura et al., 2024)(Wang et al., 2007), air (Khaled et al., 2024)(Wang et al., 2015), sea (Romero-Godoy et al., 2022)(Wang et al., 2023), space (Wang et al., 2015)(Romero-Godoy et al., 2022) and cyber (Kacpura et al., 2014)(Xiong et al., 2017) domains. The SDR and communication platforms are commercialized with field-programmable gate arrays (FPGA) and system on a chip (SoC). Advanced algorithms, edge computing and parallelism empower adaptive signal processing in near real time (Coronado et al., 2019)(Efstathiou et al., 1999). There are a number of challenges and open problems in the design of SDRs (Haghighat, 2002)(Hall et al., 2012)(Sengupta et al., 2011)(Ulversoy, 2010). The 6G cellular technology requires new solutions, which amplify the use of multi-band SDRs (Jeon et al., 2022)(Karle et al., 2024). An all-domain command and control framework and 6G wireless technology imply the design of next-generation communication platforms to ensure communication superiority and seamless information sharing [19]. Robust multi-band wireless cellular technologies with learning capabilities (Hou et al., 2007)(Ru et al., 2009) are emerging. A consistent integration of a frontend module with a variable-gain amplifier and FPGA enables high-performance processing, networking, robustness, speed, control, filtering, reconfigurability, signal conversion and interfacing.

sections.title: Applications & Use Cases
sections.text:
TLDR; Software Defined Radio has found diverse applications across military, civil aviation, healthcare, and space communications sectors. Its flexibility and adaptability make it particularly valuable for emerging technologies like UAV communications, cognitive radio systems, and real-time multimedia transmission. (10 sources)

* **Military and Defense Applications**: SDR platforms are extensively used for RF detection and source localization, offering capabilities for monitoring wide areas through combinations of energy detection and cyclostationarity analysis  [263247899 | Slimeni et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]. These systems are particularly valuable for military surveillance and intelligence gathering operations.

* **Civil Aviation and UAV Communications**: SDR has become crucial for Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) communications, supporting applications in long-range communications, environmental monitoring, surveillance, and disaster management  [270515149 | Michailidis et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [262850511 | Gu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 98]. UAVs are expected to be pivotal drivers of 6G network development, with SDR enabling adaptable communication protocols for these aerial platforms.

* **Healthcare and Emergency Services**: Innovative applications include SDR-based systems for transmitting medical data in smart ambulances, utilizing OFDM technology across vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-infrastructure channels to ensure reliable data transmission during emergency situations  [274802919 | Pamungkas et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

* **Wireless Networking Research**: SDR serves as a vital tool for prototyping and testing new wireless networking methodologies, particularly in 5G communications research and implementation  [258895103 | Verdecia-Pena et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3] [257732302 | Hernandez-Solana et al. | 2022 | Citations: 13].

* **Cognitive Radio Systems**: Advanced cognitive radio implementations use SDR platforms for detecting, recognizing, and analyzing input signals in real-time, particularly valuable for dynamic spectrum access applications  [251973542 | Vardanyan et al. | 2022 | Citations: 1].

* **Internet of Things (IoT)**: SDR technology has proven valuable for IoT applications, particularly in validating, processing, and decoding multiple received signals simultaneously  [275188950 | Joossens et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

* **Space Communications**: Advanced space agencies utilize SDR technology in their communication systems, as demonstrated by NASA's Space Communications and Navigation (SCaN) Polylingual Experimental Terminal, which supports multiple waveforms and frequency bands  [258726326 | Angert et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0].

* **Quantum Computing Integration**: SDR systems are being explored for integration with quantum computing applications, marking a convergence of classical and quantum communication technologies  [276994867 | Sharma et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

citations.title: [251973542 | Vardanyan et al. | 2022 | Citations: 1]
snippets: Software-defined radio (SDR)-based cognitive communication radio systems are very popular at present, and there have been many investigations on this topic. This paper proposes a new type of cognitive radio transceiver (TRX) that can detect, recognize, and analyze input signals in real-time with minimal data loss. New hardware is designed and manufactured that combines a transmitter and a receiver in a dedicated integrated circuit. For data processing, a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) is used.

citations.title: [258726326 | Angert et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]
snippets: A next generation space software defined radio (SDR) has been designed and developed by the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory (JHU/APL) for use in the NASA Space Communications and Navigation (SCaN) Polylingual Experimental Terminal (PExT). The newest incarnation of the radio, Frontier Radio – Multi-Lingual (FR-ML), builds on years of work on the Frontier Radio family of SDRs. The FR-ML is designed to communicate at K/Ka-band and is tunable over a wide band supporting commercial, Space Network (SN), and Near Earth Network (NEN) bands. The radio supports Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS) compliant waveforms used in many NASA missions, as well as Digital Video Broadcast – Satellite – Second Generation (DVB-S2) waveforms typically used by commercial relay services. The FR-ML takes advantage of new component advancements enabling higher processing power and data rates in the high 100s of Mbits per second, approaching 1 Gbit per second with a variety of new features. New mission-enabling features include in-flight field programmable gate array (FPGA) reconfiguration as well as software re-programmability.

citations.title: [263247899 | Slimeni et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]
snippets: Radio frequency (RF) detection and source localization are critical requirements for military and civilian applications. This paper implements a multistep RF detection technique in a software defined radio (SDR) platform that starts by a fast energy detection then go through cyclostationarity feature detection to deal with low level signals. This combination offers range potential to monitor wider area. The system relies on the received signal strength indication (RSSI) measurements to estimate the distance between the sensing system and the detected RF source. General-purpose SDR platforms offer more flexibility and cost efficiency, compared to dedicated localization systems. It enables providing an embedded standalone system able to detect RF signals and to estimate the polar coordinates of the transmitter.

snippets: In recent years, driven by advancements in avionics and electronic systems, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), commonly referred to as drones, have emerged with applications spanning numerous domains, including long-range communications, environmental monitoring, surveillance, disaster management, target recognition, military reconnaissance, and beyond (Gu et al., 2023). One of the main factors determining the success of UAV operations is the reliable and efficient communication. However, conventional communication systems often struggle to meet the diverse and dynamic requirements of UAV-based applications...By leveraging SDR technology, communication protocols and signal processing functionalities can be implemented in software, offering unparalleled flexibility, scalability, and programmability, while minimizing the reliance on costly and proprietary hardware solutions. Presently, the majority of modern communication devices utilize SDR technology. Also, the global market value of SDR is projected to rise to USD 32.2 billion by 2028 with a Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 7.4% [5]...In the 1990s, Joseph Mitola coined the term SDR to describe radios that could be reprogrammed and reconfigured via software rather than hardware (Mitola, 1992). Although SDR has been a technological concept for years, it's only in recent times that affordable SDR solutions, facilitated by user-friendly hardware platforms, such as Universal Software Radio Peripherals (USRPs) [27], have become accessible. The rising popularity of SDR technology is attributed to advancements in computing and the availability of free open-source software libraries over recent decades...Currently, SDRs play a pivotal role in the development of wireless standards owing to their adaptability and programmability features (Akeela et al., 2018)...FPGAs have significantly transformed the SDR landscape by providing a flexible and powerful platform for real-time signal processing. Their reconfigurability allows SDR systems to efficiently adapt to various communication standards and signal processing algorithms on-the-fly, which is crucial for the dynamic nature of SDR applications and multi-mission capabilities. Moreover, FPGA-integrated SDRs are essential for handling high-throughput data streams and supporting high-bandwidth applications (e.g., High-Definition (HD) video streaming or large-scale data collection).

sections.title: Latest Advancements & Innovations
sections.text:
TLDR; Recent SDR innovations focus on improving flexibility, performance optimization, and standardized implementations. Key advances include automated control systems, enhanced monitoring capabilities, and specialized languages for efficient signal processing. (9 sources)

The field of Software Defined Radio continues to evolve through several groundbreaking innovations. A significant advancement is the development of automated control systems like WISCANet, which enables non-expert users to deploy over-the-air applications by simplifying hardware interactions and allowing real-time experimentation without hardware limitations  [252840046 | Holtom et al. | 2022 | Citations: 1].

Performance improvements have been achieved through optimized signal processing solutions. Novel approaches include Domain Specific Embedded Languages (DSEL) that enable efficient digital communication systems by exploiting both temporal and spatial parallelism in modern processor architectures  [249626202 | Cassagne et al. | 2022 | Citations: 5]. Code-generation-based libraries like Strymonas have demonstrated competitive performance in real-time applications, matching or even surpassing established solutions like GNU Radio in certain scenarios  [266934929 | Kobayashi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

Hardware-software co-design innovations have led to significant efficiency gains. The Terapool-SDR architecture demonstrates this progress through a cluster design featuring 1024 compact processing elements with shared memory architecture, specifically tailored for handling intense radio access network workloads  [269626475 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. Similarly, the integration of GNURadio with SDR platforms has enabled sophisticated RF signal processing applications, including frequency conversion systems for satellite communications and radar systems  [273042679 | Thavai et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

Standardization efforts have progressed notably, with organizations like ETSI developing frameworks for software radio reconfiguration. This standardization aligns with broader industry trends toward network "softwarization," emphasizing the movement of functionality from hardware to software  [246052171 | Kafetzis et al. | 2022 | Citations: 44]  [16838261 | Sun et al. | 2015 | Citations: 270]  [58760460 | Liu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 53].

Quality assurance and compliance monitoring have also seen innovation, with new systems like FDMonitor being developed to prevent signal violations and ensure adherence to spectrum regulations in city-scale SDR testbeds  [254823260 | Wang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0].

citations.title: [246052171 | Kafetzis et al. | 2022 | Citations: 44]
snippets: ETSI's Software Radio Reconfiguration model is described in a recent ETSI white paper [65] and in the EN 303 146 series of European Standards [66]. Its target is to enable device manufacturers to gradually implement software reconfigurable radios over different generations of equipment. Various use cases have been introduced, while the key challenges that have been identified are reproduced below from [65]...These latest standardization and research efforts, such as those presented in (Ramirez-Perez et al., 2016), (Sun et al., 2015), (Rosas et al., 2017), [71], and (Liu et al., 2020), indicate that SDR has become part of the broader "softwarization" endeavors that relate to the design and deployment of 5G networks. The term softwarization is used in many domains and can be defined as "moving functionality from hardware to software", (Liu et al., 2020). The main objective of softwarization is to improve the flexibility of the networks that will need to support a wide spectrum of services offered to wireless devices that are no longer as homogeneous as they used to be in the previous generations of cellular networks. In (Sun et al., 2015), the integration of Network Function Virtualization (NFV), SDN and SDR is examined in terms of standards, necessary standardization efforts and open research problems while a high-level architecture combining all three technologies is suggested. In [71], a software defined radio virtualization layer, called HyDRA, that enables the execution of multiple programmable air-interfaces on top of one RF front-end is presented.

citations.title: [249626202 | Cassagne et al. | 2022 | Citations: 5]
snippets: This article presents a new Domain Specific Embedded Language (DSEL) dedicated to Software‐Defined Radio (SDR). From a set of carefully designed components, it enables to build efficient software digital communication systems, able to take advantage of the parallelism of modern processor architectures, in a straightforward and safe manner for the programmer. In particular, proposed DSEL enables the combination of pipelining and sequence duplication techniques to extract both temporal and spatial parallelism from digital communication systems.

citations.title: [252840046 | Holtom et al. | 2022 | Citations: 1]
snippets: To accelerate the implementation and validation of numerous B5G/6G applications, we developed the WISCA Software-Defined Radio Network (WISCANet) (Holtom et al., 2021)[30]. WIS-CANet is a hardware-agnostic control software that automatically configures and controls a software-defined radio (SDR) network. By abstracting the hardware controls away from the user, WISCANet allows a non-expert user to deploy an over-the-air (OTA) application by simply defining a baseband processing chain in a high level language. WISCANet emulates real-time operations, allowing users to perform real-time experiments without the typical restrictions on processing speed and hardware capabilities.

citations.title: [254823260 | Wang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Software-defined radio (SDR) platforms, despite being an enabler of spectrum and infrastructure sharing, must ensure that their transmitted signals comply with spectrum rules. Violations may occur because of malware, misconfiguration, bugs in software, or RF frontend nonlinearities. We present FDMonitor, a full-duplex monitoring system attached between a transmitter's power amplifier and its antenna to monitor and control each SDR in the Platform for Open Wireless Data-driven Experimental Research (POWDER), an open city-scale SDR-based testbed.

citations.title: [266934929 | Kobayashi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
snippets: Strymonas is a code-generation--based library (embedded DSL) for fast, bulk, single-thread in-memory stream processing -- with the declarative description of stream pipelines and yet achieving the speed and memory efficiency of hand-written state machines. It guarantees complete stream fusion in all cases. So far, strymonas has been used on small examples and micro-benchmarks. In this work, we evaluate strymonas on a large, real-life application of Software-Defined Radio -- FM Radio reception, -- contrasting and benchmarking it against the synchronous dataflow system StreamIt, and the state-of-the art: GNU Radio. Strymonas, despite being declarative, single-thread single-core with no explicit support for SIMD, no built-in windowing or convolution, turns out to offer portable high performance, well enough for real-time FM Radio reception. It is on par with (or, on Raspberry Pi Zero, outstripping) GNU Radio, while providing static guarantees of complete fusion and type safety.

citations.title: [269626475 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Radio Access Networks (RAN) workloads are rapidly scaling up in data processing intensity and throughput as the 5G (and beyond) standards grow in number of antennas and sub-carriers. Offering flexible Processing Elements (PEs), efficient memory access, and a productive parallel programming model, many-core clusters are a well-matched architecture for next-generation software-defined RANs, but staggering performance requirements demand a high number of PEs coupled with extreme Power, Performance and Area (PPA) efficiency. We present the architecture, design, and full physical implementation of Terapool-SDR, a cluster for Software Defined Radio (SDR) with 1024 latency-tolerant, compact RV32 PEs, sharing a global view of a 4 MiB, 4096-banked, L1 memory.

The converter helps in frequency translation between the C/Ku and L bands, leading to a cost-effective and versatile solution for RF signal processing. By using open-source GNU Radio software, the proposed system enhances accessibility, enabling its deployment in diverse applications, from satellite communication to radar systems. The converter's unique features include real-time processing capabilities, customization through an intuitive graphical interface, and Python scripting.

sections.title: Background on Language Model Alignment
sections.text:
TLDR; Language model alignment aims to ensure AI systems understand and respond appropriately to human intentions and values. This involves various techniques including fine-tuning and human feedback to better match model outputs with human expectations. (1 source)

Language model alignment represents a crucial step beyond just pre-training, focusing on improving how well artificial intelligence systems understand and respond to human needs and intentions  [267636727 | Xiao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. While pre-trained models establish a foundational capability, they require additional alignment processes to effectively operate in real-world applications <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

One notable approach to alignment involves incorporating human expertise and feedback into the training process. For instance, specialized implementations like ClinicalGPT have demonstrated enhanced performance when combining traditional language modeling approaches (such as using Bloom-7B) with targeted fine-tuning in specific domains, utilizing both knowledge base improvements and human feedback mechanisms  [267636727 | Xiao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

The primary goals of alignment include enhancing model adaptability across various tasks and ensuring more accurate interpretation and generation of human-centered language responses <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">. This alignment process helps bridge the gap between a model's initial capabilities and its practical utility in serving human users effectively.

citations.title: [267636727 | Xiao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
snippets:
Although pre-training provides a solid foundation, aligning LLMs with human knowledge is often necessary to achieve optimal performance in specific tasks. Thus, aligning LLMs with professional human knowledge is a key technique for effectively leveraging their pre-trained capabilities across a wide range of language tasks [27,24]. This alignment not only enhances the models' adaptability but also enables a more precise understanding and response to human language and needs.

Improving the diverse task performance of LLMs through fine-tuning with human data has been extensively researched [24,16]. ClinicalGPT [26] fine-tuned Bloom-7B in the healthcare domain using knowledge-base retrieval enhancements and human feedback-based reinforcement learning techniques, showing better performance in Q&A tasks compared to baseline LLMs like LLaMA-7B and ChatGLM-6B assessed with GPT-4.

sections.title: Introduction to Expert Iteration
sections.text:
TLDR; Expert iteration is a powerful machine learning technique that alternates between generating examples and refining those examples through expert feedback. When applied to language models, it creates a cycle where experts review and correct model outputs, helping improve the model's capabilities over successive iterations. (1 source)

Expert iteration represents a fundamental approach to improving language model capabilities through iterative refinement. At its core, this methodology involves a systematic process where language models generate solutions or responses to specific problems, and then these outputs are reviewed and corrected by human experts who possess domain-specific knowledge  [273502014 | Wu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 22].

The process typically begins with a pre-defined dataset containing challenging problems or tasks that the language model needs to solve. After generating potential solutions, human experts analyze the model's attempts, identifying errors and areas for improvement. These expert-corrected versions then become part of the training data, allowing the model to learn from both its mistakes and the corrections made by specialists <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

Through repeated cycles of generation, evaluation, and correction, expert iteration enables language models to gradually enhance their performance and accuracy. This approach is particularly valuable because it leverages human expertise to guide the model's development while maintaining a structured and reproducible improvement process <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

sections.title: Applications and Performance Impact
sections.text:
TLDR; Expert iteration has shown significant positive impacts on language model performance, particularly in mathematical reasoning tasks. Studies demonstrate measurable improvements in success rates, though the implementation comes with substantial resource requirements. (3 sources)

Research has demonstrated concrete benefits of implementing expert iteration in language model alignment, particularly in specialized domains like mathematical reasoning. One study showed that applying expert iteration increased success rates in automated proof construction by approximately 5%, placing its effectiveness on par with newer alternative approaches like Thor  [248986108 | Jiang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 95].

However, the implementation of expert iteration requires careful consideration of resources and costs. While the technique can produce meaningful improvements, it demands significant human effort - estimates suggest around 100 human hours to create curriculum materials for 300 mathematical problems alone. Additionally, each iteration requires substantial computational resources, with evaluations suggesting approximately 500 TPU hours needed for just eight expert iterations  [248986108 | Jiang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 95].

Despite these resource demands, expert iteration remains a viable option for alignment, especially when combined with other training approaches. Research indicates that it can be integrated alongside reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), offering flexibility in implementation strategies  [246426909 | Ouyang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 11999]. More recent developments in alignment techniques continue to build upon these foundations, exploring ways to leverage weak-to-strong generalization to handle increasingly complex AI systems  [272592928 | Zakershahrak et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

Note: Given the relatively low citation counts of these papers, I've kept my assessments more neutral and focused primarily on describing the documented findings rather than making strong claims about impact <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

An important factor in choosing a suitable method is its cost. Expert iteration requires manually creating a set of "curriculum" problems, evaluating the language model on them, and training the language model on a growing training set for one epoch every iteration. We estimate that performing expert iteration on the same scale as (Zheng et al., 2021) for Isabelle, it would cost 100 human hours to formalise 300 maths problems, and 500 TPU hours to evaluate and fine-tune the language model for 8 expert iterations. Thor, on the other hand, incurs little extra computational cost compared with training a standard language model. We conclude that while requiring a much smaller computational budget, Thor can improve language models' success rates to a similar degree as expert iteration.

sections.title: Comparison with Other Alignment Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; Expert iteration exists alongside several other prominent alignment approaches, including search-based algorithms and learning-based methods like reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). Each method offers distinct trade-offs between computational efficiency and alignment effectiveness. (4 sources)

Here are the main alignment methods and their comparative characteristics:

* **Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)**: A widely adopted approach that uses human preference data to guide model optimization. While effective, RLHF can face stability issues and requires complex implementation procedures. Recent improvements have made it more manageable, with simplified variants like Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) showing comparable or superior results to traditional reinforcement learning approaches  [270095324 | Zhou et al. | 2024 | Citations: 20]  [258959321 | Rafailov et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3354]

* **Search-Based Algorithms**: These methods offer an efficient alternative that can utilize smaller language models to guide the decoding process in larger models. They represent a middle ground between pure expert iteration and full RLHF implementations  [270095324 | Zhou et al. | 2024 | Citations: 20]

* **Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)**: This newer approach simplifies the alignment process by reformulating RLHF as a straightforward classification problem. It eliminates the need for complex reinforcement learning steps and has shown promising results in controlling model outputs while maintaining simplicity  [270095324 | Zhou et al. | 2024 | Citations: 20]  [258959321 | Rafailov et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3354]

* **Behavior Cloning**: This represents a simpler alternative to expert iteration that focuses on supervised learning using selected comparison data. While potentially less sophisticated than expert iteration, it offers a more straightforward implementation path  (Ouyang et al._1,  2022)

* **Best-of-n Sampling**: This method addresses some of the limitations found in reward model optimization, though its effectiveness varies based on factors like reward model parameters and training dataset size  [270095324 | Zhou et al. | 2024 | Citations: 20]  [252992904 | Gao et al. | 2022 | Citations: 481]

citations.title: [270095324 | Zhou et al. | 2024 | Citations: 20]
snippets: There are two main categories of alignment algorithms: (1) search-based algorithms that optimize Eq. 1 with graph-based search during inference (Gao et al., 2022)13,18,19,11,12], and (2) learning-based algorithms that optimize Eq. 1 through gradient descent, aiming for a parametrized optimal language model [1,36,(Rafailov et al., 2023)[37]. Our work falls in the first category, proposing a search-based algorithm capable of using small language models to guide the decoding of a large language model to align with human preferences.

citations.title: [252992904 | Gao et al. | 2022 | Citations: 481]
snippets: In reinforcement learning from human feedback, it is common to optimize against a reward model trained to predict human preferences. Because the reward model is an imperfect proxy, optimizing its value too much can hinder ground truth performance, in accordance with Goodhart's law. This effect has been frequently observed, but not carefully measured due to the expense of collecting human preference data. In this work, we use a synthetic setup in which a fixed"gold-standard"reward model plays the role of humans, providing labels used to train a proxy reward model. We study how the gold reward model score changes as we optimize against the proxy reward model using either reinforcement learning or best-of-$n$ sampling. We find that this relationship follows a different functional form depending on the method of optimization, and that in both cases its coefficients scale smoothly with the number of reward model parameters. We also study the effect on this relationship of the size of the reward model dataset, the number of reward model and policy parameters, and the coefficient of the KL penalty added to the reward in the reinforcement learning setup. We explore the implications of these empirical results for theoretical considerations in AI alignment.

citations.title: [258959321 | Rafailov et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3354]
snippets: While large-scale unsupervised language models (LMs) learn broad world knowledge and some reasoning skills, achieving precise control of their behavior is difficult due to the completely unsupervised nature of their training. Existing methods for gaining such steerability collect human labels of the relative quality of model generations and fine-tune the unsupervised LM to align with these preferences, often with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). However, RLHF is a complex and often unstable procedure, first fitting a reward model that reflects the human preferences, and then fine-tuning the large unsupervised LM using reinforcement learning to maximize this estimated reward without drifting too far from the original model. In this paper we introduce a new parameterization of the reward model in RLHF that enables extraction of the corresponding optimal policy in closed form, allowing us to solve the standard RLHF problem with only a simple classification loss. The resulting algorithm, which we call Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), is stable, performant, and computationally lightweight, eliminating the need for sampling from the LM during fine-tuning or performing significant hyperparameter tuning. Our experiments show that DPO can fine-tune LMs to align with human preferences as well as or better than existing methods. Notably, fine-tuning with DPO exceeds PPO-based RLHF in ability to control sentiment of generations, and matches or improves response quality in summarization and single-turn dialogue while being substantially simpler to implement and train.

question: How do people in the field of NLP assess the organization of generated documents?

sections.title: Introduction & Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Document organization assessment in NLP combines traditional document classification with specialized evaluation approaches. The process spans from basic categorization to sophisticated coherence checking, reflecting the complexity of modern document analysis. (3 sources)

The assessment of document organization in Natural Language Processing has evolved significantly with the increasing volume of digital content requiring systematic evaluation. At its foundation lies document classification, which serves as a fundamental building block by organizing documents into predefined categories based on their content using both machine learning and text mining techniques  [229418167 | Nohuddin | 2021 | Citations: 3]. The scope of document organization assessment extends beyond mere categorization to encompass multiple facets of textual structure and coherence.

Modern approaches to evaluating document organization recognize distinct measurement categories. These include form-based measures, which focus on grammatical correctness, structural integrity, and overall coherence, as well as content-based measures that assess precision and recall in information representation [64497694 | Ba-Alwi et al. | 2015 | Citations: 5]. The complexity of document organization is further reflected in the multi-dimensional nature of assessment, which considers factors such as topical distribution patterns and reader engagement  [53835829 | Amin et al. | 2019 | Citations: 21].

When examining document organization from a reader perspective, research has revealed that readers actively engage in cognitive processing during reading, constantly monitoring and adjusting their mental models of the document structure <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">. This understanding has led to the development of increasingly sophisticated assessment frameworks that attempt to mirror the complexity of human comprehension while providing objective measures of organizational effectiveness.

This technique basically assigns a document into a set of predefined categories based on its content.

sections.title: Traditional Automatic Metrics
sections.text:
TLDR; Traditional automatic metrics for document organization primarily rely on variations of BLEU and ROUGE families of metrics. These metrics evaluate aspects like n-gram overlap, longest common subsequences, and consensus matching between generated and reference texts. (4 sources)

* **BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy)**: A precision-based metric that calculates how frequently n-gram words in the generated text appear in reference documents  [253265445 | Kaur et al. | 2022 | Citations: 9]  [11080756 | Papineni et al. | 2002 | Citations: 26280]. Originally developed for machine translation, BLEU has become a foundational metric for evaluating text generation quality.

* **ROUGE Family**: A recall-oriented family of metrics that determine how well the generated text captures content from reference documents. Key variants include:

  - ROUGE-L: Uses Longest Common Subsequence to evaluate how well the system maps sentence-level word order as n-grams  [253265445 | Kaur et al. | 2022 | Citations: 9]

  - ROUGE in Engineering Context: Widely adopted for evaluating generated text in technical domains, measuring similarity through precision, recall, and F1 scores  [267751173 | Prasad et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]

* **CIDEr (Consensus-based Image Description Evaluation)**: A hybrid metric combining both precision and recall components. It specifically focuses on evaluating consensus among multiple reference texts by measuring n-gram overlaps  [253265445 | Kaur et al. | 2022 | Citations: 9]  [6997039 | Vedantam et al. | 2014 | Citations: 4468]

While these metrics serve as valuable automated tools for quick evaluation, it's important to note that they primarily focus on surface-level similarities and may not fully capture semantic nuances or higher-level organizational principles <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [253265445 | Kaur et al. | 2022 | Citations: 9]
snippets:
The problem at hand was to generate a report similar to human-written reports. Thus to evaluate the generated report six evaluation metrics have been used: BLEU by (Papineni et al., 2002), ROUGE-L by (Lin, 2004), CIDEr by (Vedantam et al., 2014). BLEU (Bilingual evaluation understudy) is a precision-based metric that determines how many n-gram words in the generated report are present in the original report. Whereas complementing BLEU, ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) is a recall-based metric that determines how many words in the original report occur in the generated report. 

In particular, we have used ROUGE-L (Longest Common Subsequence), which uses in-sequence matches that map sentence-level word order as n-gram. CIDEr (Consensusbased Image Description Evaluation) metric is the precision and recall-based metric. It is a measure for consensus encoding how often n-grams in the generated report are present in the original report.

[22]. ROUGE, designed for the evaluation of generated text in tasks such as text generation and machine translation, systematically gauges similarity through precision, recall, and F1 score between the generated text and reference texts.

sections.title: Advanced Computational Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; Modern computational methods for assessing document organization combine structural analysis with semantic evaluation using advanced ML models. These approaches range from random forest implementations to transformer-based coherence detection and interactive network visualization. (8 sources)

Recent advances in computational methods for document organization assessment have moved beyond traditional metrics to incorporate more sophisticated analytical approaches. The evolution of neural networks has enabled breakthrough progress in modeling semantic relationships between sentences, allowing for more nuanced assessments of document structure  [257760070 | Celikyilmaz et al. | 2020 | Citations: 159].

One significant advancement has been the recognition that purely automated metrics fall short for document generation tasks, particularly when dealing with information density and narrative coherence. This limitation has driven the development of more holistic evaluation approaches  [23892230 | Wiseman et al. | 2017 | Citations: 581]. For instance, in structured text generation tasks like SQL statement creation, current evaluation methods often fail to adequately capture both structural and semantic aspects of document organization  [258041381 | Zhu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5].

Advanced computational frameworks now employ multiple complementary approaches:

* Hierarchical Coherence Models analyze document structure at varying granularity levels, enabling evaluation of organizational quality across different scales  [268146260 | Cho et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]  [235163887 | Liao et al. | 2021 | Citations: 14].

* Interactive Network Visualization provides intuitive ways to assess document structure, allowing analysts to examine connections and relationships between different components visually  [272629641 | Vierlboeck et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

Random Forest-based methods have emerged as effective tools for quality assessment, incorporating features related to organizational structure alongside network accessibility and content depth  [56053538 | He et al. | 2017 | Citations: 1].

Some innovative approaches now treat the evaluation process as a separate learning task, predicting label distributions for different annotation classes simultaneously. This method has shown promising results in reducing conflicts between annotator agreements and producing more reliable, fine-grained annotations  [257764363 | Zhong et al. | 2022 | Citations: 114].

Discourse-aware text representations have also been developed using unsupervised learning methods, helping to enhance both organizational coherence and argumentation strength in analyzed texts  [268146260 | Cho et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]  [201831454 | Mim et al. | 2019 | Citations: 41].

citations.title: [23892230 | Wiseman et al. | 2017 | Citations: 581]
snippets: We begin by discussing the evaluation of generated documents, since both the task we introduce and the evaluation methods we propose are motivated by some of the shortcomings of current approaches to evaluation. Text generation systems are typically evaluated using a combination of automatic measures, such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002), and human evaluation. While BLEU is perhaps a reasonably effective way of evaluating short-form text generation, we found it to be unsatisfactory for document generation. In particular, we note that it primarily rewards fluent text generation, rather than generations that capture the most important information in the database, or that report the information in a particularly coherent way. While human evaluation, on the other hand, is likely ultimately necessary for evaluating generations (Liu et al., 2016)Wu et al., 2016), it is much less convenient than using automatic metrics.

sections.title: Human Evaluation Approaches
sections.text:
TLDR; Human evaluation remains a cornerstone of document organization assessment, offering nuanced insights that automated metrics lack. Expert evaluators assess multiple dimensions including clarity, accuracy, completeness, and coherence, though this approach faces practical limitations around resources and scalability. (9 sources)

Despite the sophistication of automated evaluation methods, human assessment continues to be considered the gold standard for evaluating generated text, particularly for assessing qualities like relevance, coherence, and readability  [233476134 | Casola et al. | 2021 | Citations: 21]. This preference stems from humans' ability to grasp contextual meanings and subtle aspects of text that automated metrics might miss  [269930022 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

The human evaluation landscape encompasses several established approaches. Expert evaluation typically involves systematic assessment of generated outputs against reference models, though practitioners acknowledge that multiple valid interpretations of the same source material may exist  [272827578 | Woensel et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. This understanding has led to the development of structured evaluation frameworks that consider multiple aspects of document quality simultaneously.

A notable development in human evaluation methodology has been the adoption of standardized rubrics with specific rating scales. Many contemporary approaches utilize Likert-scale assessments (typically 1-5) across multiple dimensions, including grammaticality, factual accuracy, and coherence  [229363446 | Guo et al. | 2020 | Citations: 77]. This structured approach helps ensure consistent evaluation while maintaining the benefits of human judgment.

Research has identified core evaluation dimensions that tend to recur across disciplines. A factor analysis study revealed that approximately 58% of variance in document quality can be explained by four primary factors: organization, clarity, accuracy, and utility  [275544444 | Croxford et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]. Legal document evaluation exemplifies this multi-dimensional approach, incorporating specialized assessment criteria for correctness, form, completeness, and overall satisfaction  [276640146 | Fidelangeli et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

However, the human evaluation approach faces practical challenges. The process is notably labor-intensive and presents difficulties in recruiting qualified evaluators  [277043125 | Rallapalli et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. This has led to ongoing debates about the balance between human expertise and automated metrics, with some researchers exploring ways to better align human and machine evaluation approaches  [9482302 | Barzilay et al. | 2005 | Citations: 818]  [7949837 | Vaughan et al. | 1986 | Citations: 34].

snippets:
Systematic comparison of generated and reference output. The generated output, albeit individual module output or the final process model, is systematically compared to a reference model. This can be an element-by-element comparison or based on an aggregate measure, such as processes' behavioral profiles (Weidlich et al., 2011). Here, graphbased evaluations represent process models as graphs, and map the nodes between reference and extracted process graphs. A potential drawback is that the reference model may be only one of many valid process models for the same text (Sholiq et al., 2022). 

Expert evaluation of generated output. Experts manually evaluate the generated output, providing their opinions on metrics such as understandability, usefulness, their agreement with the output, or the model's equivalency with the text. Here, the evaluation can again be element-by-element (i.e., evaluating individual elements), or focusing on properties of the output as a whole (aggregate). This avoids the above issue of multiple valid reference models, as it does not involve comparisons with a reference. However, it is also resource-intensive and relies on subjective judgments 10 .

sections.title: Domain-Specific Considerations
sections.text:
TLDR; Different domains have unique requirements for document organization assessment, leading to specialized evaluation frameworks. Education, technical documentation, and legal fields each demand distinct approaches tailored to their specific needs and standards. (9 sources)

Domain-specific considerations play a crucial role in shaping how document organization is assessed across different fields. Educational contexts have developed specialized frameworks, as evidenced by initiatives like the Automated Student Assessment Prize (ASAP) dataset, which incorporates multiple grading dimensions including idea development, organization, and style  [265019065 | Zhou et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]  [12453064 | Stab et al. | 2014 | Citations: 414].

In technical documentation and software development, evaluation frameworks emphasize practical usability and verification capabilities. Recent approaches integrate structured assessment criteria including readability, consistency, coverage, diversity, flow, and usability testing  [270379798 | Bandyopadhyay et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5]. The impact of context window size on documentation quality has emerged as a critical consideration, with larger context windows showing superior performance in maintaining coherence, particularly in complex technical content  [274023514 | Barua et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

Legal document generation requires particularly rigorous evaluation approaches due to the critical nature of the content. Comprehensive assessment frameworks combine lexical analysis, semantic similarity checks, and expert reviews to ensure compliance with legal standards and maintain precision in documentation  [277596403 | Nigam et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. These frameworks often extend beyond basic organization to assess traceability and the effectiveness of documentation in supporting technical workflows  [271855602 | Dearstyne et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2] [262101525 | Hu et al. | 2022 | Citations: 18].

Recent innovations in domain-specific evaluation have begun incorporating systemic functional linguistics perspectives, recognizing that different types of self-documentation (Self-Docs) require distinct assessment approaches  [273403956 | Li et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. This has led to the development of specialized evaluation metrics that account for field-specific citation patterns and structural requirements  [271769794 | Nishimura et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1], demonstrating the importance of tailoring evaluation approaches to meet domain-specific needs.

For this purpose, we use the ASAP (the Automated Student Assessment Prize ) dataset (Stab et al., 2014), for it contains subsets suitable for carrying out this task. sections.title: Introduction/Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Mutual information (MI) is a fundamental concept in information theory that measures shared information between variables. Its conditional version extends this concept by considering the relationship between variables while accounting for additional information from a third variable. (LLM Memory)

Mutual information emerged from foundational work in information theory to provide a rigorous mathematical framework for understanding relationships between variables. At its core, MI quantifies how much information one variable contains about another, going beyond simple linear correlations. The concept was developed to address limitations of traditional statistical measures by offering insights into both linear and non-linear relationships between variables. <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

When extended to consider conditional relationships, mutual information becomes particularly powerful for analyzing complex systems where relationships might depend on additional context or confounding factors. The conditional version allows us to understand how strongly two variables relate to each other while controlling for or explicitly accounting for the influence of a third variable. This makes it especially valuable for studying real-world phenomena where direct relationships are often obscured by other factors. <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

sections.title: Definition and Properties of Mutual Information
sections.text:
TLDR; Mutual information (MI) measures the shared information between two variables or the reduction in uncertainty about one variable when knowing the other. It is mathematically defined through various equivalent expressions involving probabilities, joint distributions, and entropy concepts. (6 sources)

Mutual information between two random variables X and Y is fundamentally defined as the difference between the sum of their individual entropies and their joint entropy  [231603232 | Rame et al. | 2021 | Citations: 51]. This can be expressed mathematically through several equivalent formulations:

First, MI can be directly calculated from probability distributions using the formula:

$$ I(X;Y) = \sum p(x,y) \log \frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)} $$

where $ p(x,y) $ represents the joint probability distribution, and $ p(x) $, $ p(y) $ are the marginal distributions  [11353672 | Lizier et al. | 2013 | Citations: 68]. Another equivalent formulation uses entropy-based expressions:

$$ I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y) $$

where $ H(X) $ is the entropy (total uncertainty) of X, and $ H(X|Y) $ is the conditional entropy (remaining uncertainty in X after knowing Y)  [221132220 | Zhang et al. | 2020 | Citations: 19].

A crucial theoretical property of mutual information is its non-negativity, proven through the non-negativity of relative entropy (Kullback-Leibler divergence)  [117129189 | Ito et al. | 2015 | Citations: 10]. Furthermore, MI exhibits perfect independence from Pearson correlation coefficients - it can detect meaningful relationships between variables even when Pearson correlation suggests no connection  [174799135 | Mukherjee et al. | 2019 | Citations: 81].

An important characteristic is that mutual information is symmetric: $ I(X;Y) = I(Y;X) $, and it equals zero if and only if the variables are statistically independent  [174799135 | Mukherjee et al. | 2019 | Citations: 81]  [221132220 | Zhang et al. | 2020 | Citations: 19]. This symmetry property makes mutual information particularly useful for comparing relationships in either direction <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

These properties collectively establish mutual information as a robust and versatile tool for quantifying relationships between variables, regardless of whether those relationships are linear or non-linear  [174799135 | Mukherjee et al. | 2019 | Citations: 81]  [117129189 | Ito et al. | 2015 | Citations: 10].

sections.title: Definition and Properties of Conditional Mutual Information
sections.text:
TLDR; Conditional mutual information (CMI) extends the concept of mutual information by measuring shared information between two variables while accounting for the influence of a third variable. Like standard mutual information, CMI is non-negative and equals zero if and only if the variables are conditionally independent given the conditioning variable. (8 sources)

Conditional mutual information extends the fundamental principles of mutual information to situations where relationships between variables may be influenced by additional context or conditions. Formally, the conditional mutual information between variables X and Y given a third variable Z is defined similarly to standard mutual information but incorporates the conditioning variable  [11402791 | Feyzi et al. | 2017 | Citations: 26]  [11488413 | Braverman et al. | 2015 | Citations: 53].

Mathematically, conditional mutual information can be expressed in multiple equivalent forms. Using probability distributions, it is defined as:

$$ I(X;Y|Z) = \sum p(x,y,z) \log \frac{p(x,y|z)}{p(x|z)p(y|z)} $$

While using entropy-based expressions:

$$ I(X;Y|Z) = H(X|Z) - H(X|Y,Z) $$

Both these definitions emphasize that CMI measures the reduction in uncertainty about X when both Z and Y are known, compared to just knowing Z  [210911531 | Steinke et al. | 2020 | Citations: 159]  [221882635 | Liu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 12].

Like standard mutual information, CMI possesses several crucial properties. Most notably, it is non-negative, and the value equals zero if and only if X and Y are conditionally independent given Z  [252134145 | Zan et al. | 2022 | Citations: 8]  [258438200 | Wen et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7]. This property makes CMI particularly valuable for testing conditional independence hypotheses in probabilistic modeling  [117129189 | Ito et al. | 2015 | Citations: 10].

Intuitively, CMI can be understood as measuring the additional information shared between X and Y after accounting for the knowledge of Z  [235349061 | Lasserre et al. | 2021 | Citations: 2]  [13082365 | Villaverde et al. | 2013 | Citations: 61]. This interpretation helps reveal relationships that might be masked when only considering unconditional relationships between variables.

sections.title: Interpretation and Applications
sections.text:
TLDR; Mutual information serves as a powerful tool for measuring relevance and dependency between variables in practical applications, particularly in feature selection and system analysis. Its conditional form enables sophisticated analysis of information flow and relationships within complex networks of interacting components. (10 sources)

Mutual information finds extensive application in determining the relevance and importance of variables in various contexts. In machine learning and pattern recognition, MI serves as a crucial criterion for feature selection, where stronger MI values indicate greater relevance between features and target variables  [266839709 | Xin et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [760685 | Hor et al. | 2013 | Citations: 6].

The interpretational power of MI lies in its ability to quantify the reduction in uncertainty or information gain when moving between states. Practically, MI can be understood as the average number of bits saved in encoding or describing one variable when the value of another variable is known  [7252159 | Lizier | 2014 | Citations: 331]. This perspective makes it particularly valuable for data compression and efficient representation of information.

Conditional mutual information extends these interpretations to analyze complex interactions within multivariate systems. CMI reveals how much information persists between two variables after accounting for the influence of others, effectively capturing both redundant and synergistic information patterns  [254563939 | Ostergaard et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]. This capability is demonstrated in practical scenarios, such as analyzing academic peer reviews, where CMI can measure how much information is revealed beyond surface-level observations  [273963033 | Xu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

The versatility of these measures is further enhanced by their applicability in network reconstruction tasks, particularly in genetic regulatory networks where they excel at detecting nonlinear dependencies among genes  [50787689 | Pirgazi et al. | 2018 | Citations: 36]  [13054694 | Aghdam et al. | 2014 | Citations: 116]. In signal processing applications, CMI helps characterize directed functional connectivity in brain networks, providing insights into information transfer mechanisms  [40502475 | Batista et al. | 2016 | Citations: 58].

A notable advantage of both measures is their ability to quantify information relationships regardless of linearity or causality  [12544770 | Faes et al. | 2016 | Citations: 76]. This makes them particularly valuable for analyzing complex biological systems and neural networks, where traditional linear correlation measures may fail to capture meaningful relationships.
