sections.title: Challenges & Solutions
sections.text:
TLDR; While 3D Gaussian splatting with diffusion offers powerful capabilities, it faces several key challenges including artifact generation, multi-view inconsistency, and handling sparse inputs. Solutions focus on regularization techniques, structured representations, and advanced prior-based approaches. (4 sources)

The integration of diffusion models with 3D Gaussian splatting presents several significant technical challenges that researchers have addressed through various innovative solutions. A fundamental issue is the tendency of vanilla Gaussian splatting implementations to generate artifacts, particularly "floaters" - small spurious volume elements appearing between camera views and objects. This occurs because Gaussian splatting consists of independent Gaussian balls rather than having inherent smoothness properties like Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)  [268063640 | Fei et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

Multi-view consistency remains another persistent challenge, particularly when using diffusion-based editing models. The guidance images produced by these models can show significant discrepancies across different viewpoints, potentially leading to mode collapse and unwanted visual artifacts in the final 3DGS outputs  (Wang et al._1,  2024).

Researchers have developed several strategies to address these challenges. One approach involves incorporating structure priors through techniques like visual hull computations to locate Gaussians within object outlines and implement floaters elimination procedures. Additionally, Gaussian repair models powered by 2D large diffusion models have been deployed to address artifacts caused by incomplete or compressed object information  [272706275 | Yang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 19].

For scenes with sparse inputs, researchers have focused on addressing two critical issues: extrapolation beyond available viewpoints and handling occlusions. Recent approaches employ a reconstruction-by-generation pipeline that leverages video diffusion models to provide plausible interpretations for unobserved regions. To ensure consistency, some solutions implement scene-grounding guidance using optimized 3DGS-rendered sequences to control the diffusion model's generation process  [276884590 | Zhong et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

citations.title: [268063640 | Fei et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Gaussian Splatting is used in both stages. Unlike NeRF which consists of MLPs and as such has smoothness properties by construction (e.g., layers in an MLP, such as the ReLU, are piecewise linear), Gaussian Splatting consists of a set of independent Gaussian balls and thus does not automatically have such properties. Thus, a vanilla Gaussian Splatting implementation of text-to-3D would suffer from significant artifacts, such as floaters (i.e., small spurious volume elements in the space between the object and the camera views). To reduce these artifacts, we introduce a regularization term on the rendered alpha maps (i.e., the silhouette of the object projected onto a camera view)

Benefiting from its point-like structure, we design several techniques for introducing object structure priors, e.g. the basic/rough geometry of the object, to help build multi-view consistency, including visual hull (Laurentini, 1994) to locate Gaussians within the object outline and floater elimination to remove outliers. To erase artifacts caused by omitted or highly compressed object information, we propose a Gaussian repair model driven by 2D large diffusion models (Rombach et al., 2021), translating corrupted rendered images into high-fidelity ones.

snippets: Despite recent successes in novel view synthesis using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), modeling scenes with sparse inputs remains a challenge. In this work, we address two critical yet overlooked issues in real-world sparse-input modeling: extrapolation and occlusion. To tackle these issues, we propose to use a reconstruction by generation pipeline that leverages learned priors from video diffusion models to provide plausible interpretations for regions outside the field of view or occluded. question: What is the state of the art in cross subject EEG emotion recognition?

sections.title: Background & Challenges
sections.text:
TLDR; Cross-subject EEG emotion recognition faces significant challenges due to individual differences in brain responses and data quality issues. While excellent accuracy is achievable within-subject recognition, transferring models between subjects remains difficult despite various technical solutions being proposed. (8 sources)

Cross-subject EEG emotion recognition aims to classify emotions from brain activity data collected from different subjects than those used to train the model  [248399824 | Tao et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3]. However, several fundamental challenges limit its practical implementation. Individual differences manifest in three main ways: EEG signals exhibit weak amplitude, non-stationary behavior, and low signal-to-noise ratios  [251293664 | Li et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3]. These characteristics violate the standard assumption in machine learning that training and testing data comes from identical distributions  [245934372 | Ning et al. | 2021 | Citations: 17].

Traditional approaches face substantial accuracy drops when moving between subjects. While models can achieve impressive accuracies of around 96% for within-subject recognition, cross-subject performance can plummet to as low as 58% on standard benchmarks like the SEED dataset  [272632215 | Alameer et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [237572066 | Shen et al. | 2021 | Citations: 141]. Several practical challenges compound this issue:

1. Data annotation is time-intensive and costly  [269156360 | Pang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]

2. Signal quality varies significantly between subjects  [248399824 | Tao et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3]

3. Artifacts and noise frequently contaminate recordings  [269156360 | Pang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]

Various technical solutions have been attempted, including transfer learning approaches combining domain adaptation with deep neural networks  [272632215 | Alameer et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [198602410 | Wu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 9]. While these methods have shown promise, bridging the gap between subjects remains challenging, particularly when trying to maintain performance across different datasets  [276003730 | Alameer et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

citations.title: [237572066 | Shen et al. | 2021 | Citations: 141]
snippets: EEG signals have been reported to be informative and reliable for emotion recognition in recent years. However, the inter-subject variability of emotion-related EEG signals still poses a great challenge for the practical applications of EEG-based emotion recognition. Inspired by recent neuroscience studies on inter-subject correlation, we proposed a Contrastive Learning method for Inter-Subject Alignment (CLISA) to tackle the cross-subject emotion recognition problem. Contrastive learning was employed to minimize the inter-subject differences by maximizing the similarity in EEG signkal representations across subjects when they received the same emotional stimuli in contrast to different ones. Specifically, a convolutional neural network was applied to learn inter-subject aligned spatiotemporal representations from EEG time series in contrastive learning. The aligned representations were subsequently used to extract differential entropy features for emotion classification. CLISA achieved state-of-the-art cross-subject emotion recognition performance on our THU-EP dataset with 80 subjects and the publicly available SEED dataset with 15 subjects. It could generalize to unseen subjects or unseen emotional stimuli in testing. Furthermore, the spatiotemporal representations learned by CLISA could provide insights into the neural mechanisms of human emotion processing.

citations.title: [245934372 | Ning et al. | 2021 | Citations: 17]
snippets: Due to the individual differences and nonstationary of EEG signals, it is difficult to classify EEG emotions with traditional machine methods, which assume that the training and testing set come from the same data distribution, but this assumption is usually not true in the EEG field, therefore the accuracy of emotion recognition is very poor. In this paper, a Single-Source Domain Adaptive Few-Shot Learning Networks (SDA-FSL) was proposed for cross-subject EEG emotion recognition. This is the first time that domain adaptation method with few-shot learning has been used in the field of EEG emotion recognition. A CBAM-based feature mapping module was designed to extract the common features of the two domains, and the domain adaptation module was used to align the data distribution of two domains. In addition, Prototypical Networks with instance-attention mechanism is introduced to preserve domain-specific information.

To this end, transfer learning has been introduced to alleviate the data distribution difference between subjects. However, most of the existing methods have focused only on domain adaptation and failed to achieve effective collaboration with label estimation.

citations.title: [276003730 | Alameer et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]
snippets:
The non-stationarity of EEG signals across different subjects and datasets poses major challenges in developing practical EEG-based emotion recognition models.

Most of the research on learning a generalizable EEG-based emotion recognition method focuses on cross-subject and cross-session settings.

Domain adaptation (DA) methods using adversarial learning and feature alignment have been explored in EEG-based emotion recognition methods [1], [2], [3], [4] to address the challenges posed by inter-subject variability. DA reduces the domain gap between the source and target domains, typically by aligning the feature distributions of EEG signals from different subjects or sessions.

Domain generalization(DG) has been utilized to learn a cross-subject emotion classifier in [5], [6], and [7]. DG learns cross-subject emotion classifiers without relying on target domain data during training. However, these methods often need to learn a specific model for each subject in the source domain, which limits their applications in large-scale settings.

Some methods [8], [9], [10] have used contrastive learning [11] to improve model generalization in EEG-based emotion recognition, particularly in cross-subject settings. In these methods different augmentations of the same EEG signal or EEG signals of the same emotion are used to create positive pairs while EEG samples from different subjects or sessions are treated as negative pairs. This approach encourages the model to learn discriminative and subject or session invariant features.

While existing cross-subject methods achieve acceptable results on some EEG emotion datasets, their performance declines in cross-dataset scenarios [12]. Furthermore, existing cross-dataset methods still underperform compared to those trained and tested on the same dataset.

sections.title: Current Performance Benchmarks
sections.text:
TLDR; Current cross-subject EEG emotion recognition systems achieve varying levels of accuracy depending on the dataset and number of emotion classes. Recent advances have pushed accuracies above 80% for basic valence-arousal classification, though performance generally decreases as the complexity of emotion categories increases. (6 sources)

Recent benchmark performances on widely-used datasets reveal a pattern of progress in cross-subject emotion recognition capabilities. On the SEED dataset, researchers have demonstrated strong performance for basic emotion dimensions, achieving accuracy rates of nearly 99.63% for three-class valence recognition  [227244508 | Jin et al. | 2020 | Citations: 20].

More recent evaluations show slightly lower but still encouraging results for more complex emotion categorizations. The STGATE model achieved accuracies of 90.37% on SEED, 76.43% on SEED-IV, and 76.35% on DREAMER datasets across various emotion recognition tasks  [258082897 | Li et al. | 2023 | Citations: 29]. Similarly, DFF-Net demonstrated strong performance with 93.37% on SEED and 82.32% on SEED-IV  [265268281 | Lu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 8].

Even more recent developments continue to push boundaries. A label-refined domain adversarial neural network achieved accuracies of 93.35±4.14% and 84.08±6.01% on SEED and SEED-IV datasets respectively  [272022765 | Fu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. This represents a notable advancement given earlier reports of baseline performance at just 58% on the SEED dataset with simpler approaches  [272632215 | Alameer et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

Looking at more complex emotion classification tasks, the DAEST model demonstrated comprehensive evaluation metrics across multiple datasets. It achieved 88.1% accuracy for three-class classification on SEED, 73.6% for five-class classification on SEED-V, and notably 75.4% accuracy for binary classification of positive versus negative emotions and 59.3% for nine-class emotion recognition on the FACED dataset  [273877510 | Shen et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

citations.title: [273877510 | Shen et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Recently emerging deep learning architectures have significantly improved the performance of EEG emotion decoding. However, existing methods still fall short of fully capturing the complex spatiotemporal dynamics of neural signals, which are crucial for representing emotion processing. This study proposes a Dynamic-Attention-based EEG State Transition (DAEST) modeling method to characterize EEG spatiotemporal dynamics. The model extracts spatiotemporal components of EEG that represent multiple parallel neural processes and estimates dynamic attention weights on these components to capture transitions in brain states. The model is optimized within a contrastive learning framework for cross-subject emotion recognition. The proposed method achieved state-of-the-art performance on three publicly available datasets: FACED, SEED, and SEED-V. It achieved 75.4% accuracy in the binary classification of positive and negative emotions and 59.3% in nine-class discrete emotion classification on the FACED dataset, 88.1% in the three-class classification of positive, negative, and neutral emotions on the SEED dataset, and 73.6% in five-class discrete emotion classification on the SEED-V dataset.

sections.title: Key Technical Approaches
sections.text:
TLDR; Modern cross-subject EEG emotion recognition employs sophisticated deep learning frameworks that focus on domain adaptation and alignment. Key approaches include contrastive learning, graph neural networks, and specialized architectures that handle both spatial and temporal aspects of EEG signals. (13 sources)

Several distinct technical approaches have emerged to address the cross-subject EEG emotion recognition challenge:

1. **Deep Transfer Learning Frameworks**

- Deep Adaptation Neural Networks (DANN) enable unsupervised domain translation between EEG data domains  [52929260 | Long et al. | 2018 | Citations: 11178]

- Bidirectional DANN (BiDANN) improves performance by optimizing gradient reversal layers bidirectionally  [52067847 | Li et al. | 2018 | Citations: 439]

2. **Graph-Based Methods**

- Self-Organized Graph Neural Network (SOGNN) uses dynamic graph structures to construct correlations across subjects  [235382838 | Li et al. | 2021 | Citations: 77]

- Instance-adaptive graph networks explore dynamic connectivity across brain regions  [277313926 | Liu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]

3. **Contrastive Learning Approaches**

- CLISA (Contrastive Learning for Inter-Subject Alignment) maximizes similarities in EEG representations across subjects when experiencing same stimuli  (Shen et al._1,  2021)

- Transformers combined with adversarial discriminative domain adaptation show improved results for valence and arousal classification  [261979897 | Gao et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3]

4. **Multi-Source Adaptation Methods**

- Robust multi-source co-adaptation framework minimizes statistical and semantic distribution differences between source and target domains  [234475127 | Tao et al. | 2021 | Citations: 17]

- MASTF-net implements cross-subject multi-source adaptive method focusing on spatio-temporal and frequency domain information  [266827012 | Xu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]

5. **Style-Based Transfer Solutions**

- EEG Emotion Style Transfer Network (E²STN) addresses domain mismatches by separating content and style information  [260866172 | Zhou et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4]

- Progressive Graph Convolutional Networks (PGCN) learn features from coarse to fine granularity  [268681370 | Zhou et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]

6. **Hybrid and Multi-Modal Approaches**

- Integration of Differential Entropy (DE) features with eye movement data shows improved recognition accuracy  [270122917 | Dong et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]  [243220569 | Liu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 17]

- Emotion Preceptor combines static spatial adapters with temporal causal networks for robust encoding  (Dong et al._1,  2024)

citations.title: [234475127 | Tao et al. | 2021 | Citations: 17]
snippets: Focusing on cross-subject or cross-dataset automated emotion recognition with EEG features, we propose in this article a robust multi-source co-adaptation framework by mining diverse correlation information (MACI) among domains and features with l2,1−norm as well as correlation metric regularization. Specifically, by minimizing the statistical and semantic distribution differences between source and target domains, multiple subject-invariant classifiers can be learned together in a joint framework, which can make MACI use relevant knowledge from multiple sources by exploiting the developed correlation metric function.

citations.title: [235382838 | Li et al. | 2021 | Citations: 77]
snippets: As a physiological process and high-level cognitive behavior, emotion is an important subarea in neuroscience research. Emotion recognition across subjects based on brain signals has attracted much attention. Due to individual differences across subjects and the low signal-to-noise ratio of EEG signals, the performance of conventional emotion recognition methods is relatively poor. In this paper, we propose a self-organized graph neural network (SOGNN) for cross-subject EEG emotion recognition. Unlike the previous studies based on pre-constructed and fixed graph structure, the graph structure of SOGNN are dynamically constructed by self-organized module for each signal. To evaluate the cross-subject EEG emotion recognition performance of our model, leave-one-subject-out experiments are conducted on two public emotion recognition datasets, SEED and SEED-IV. The SOGNN is able to achieve state-of-the-art emotion recognition performance. Moreover, we investigated the performance variances of the models with different graph construction techniques or features in different frequency bands. Furthermore, we visualized the graph structure learned by the proposed model and found that part of the structure coincided with previous neuroscience research. The experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed model for cross-subject EEG emotion recognition.

citations.title: [260866172 | Zhou et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4]
snippets: Previous methods have performed well for intra-subject EEG emotion recognition. However, the style mismatch between source domain (training data) and target domain (test data) EEG samples caused by huge inter-domain differences is still a critical problem for EEG emotion recognition. To solve the problem of cross-dataset EEG emotion recognition, in this paper, we propose an EEG-based Emotion Style Transfer Network (E2STN) to obtain EEG representations that contain the content information of source domain and the style information of target domain, which is called stylized emotional EEG representations. The representations are helpful for cross-dataset discriminative prediction.

citations.title: [261979897 | Gao et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3]
snippets: CLISA (Contrastive Learning method for Inter-Subject Alignment), a method developed by Shen et al. [28], leverages contrastive learning to minimize inter-subject differences and improve cross-subject EEG-based emotion recognition by extracting aligned spatiotemporal representations from EEG time series. Domain adaptation with adversarial adaptive processes has recently gained increasing attention, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Wang et al. [29] proposed a multimodal domain adaptive variational autoencoder method by learning shared cross-domain latent representations and reducing distribution differences, demonstrating superior performance in emotion recognition with small labeled multimodal data. Guo et al. [30] proposed a multi-source domain adaptation with a spatiotemporal feature extractor for EEG emotion recognition, effectively reducing cross-subject and cross-session, demonstrating its powerful generalization capacity. He et al. [31] proposed a method that combines temporal convolutional networks and adversarial discriminative domain adaptation for EEG-based cross-subject emotion recognition, effectively addressing the domain-shift challenge. Sartipi and Cetin [32] proposed an approach that combined transformers and adversarial discriminative domain adaptation for cross-subject EEG-based emotion recognition, achieving improved classification results for valence and arousal.

citations.title: [266827012 | Xu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]
snippets: In the field of neuroscience, the electroencephalogram (EEG) is a crucial indicator of emotion. The EEG emotion recognition method based on domain adaptation (DA) has good objectivity and high time resolution and is the preferred method to study the brain's response to emotional stimuli. However, due to the obvious instability of EEG emotion characteristics, it is difficult to predict the emotion corresponding to EEG signals of cross-subjects by a model that combines all source domains into a single source. In order to solve the problem of cross-subject emotion analysis, we propose an EEG emotion recognition net with a cross-subject multi-source adaptive method (MASTF-net), where EEG features of different subjects are regarded as different domains. Through analyzing the invariance of the target domain and the uniqueness of the source domain, this method realizes the emotional analysis of different objects according to the spatio-temporal images and frequency domain information. First, features of EEG image are extracted from frequency and time dimensions. Secondly, combined with the serialized EEG frequency characteristics of local brain regions, independent classification module are established for different domains to recognize the emotion feature distribution of different subjects. In addition, a feature extraction method of differential entropy(DE) data of EEG is proposed based on frequency band division, which can provide stable feature input for our network structure. Finally, experiments are conducted on the SEED dataset. The experimental results show that our method has better classification accuracy in the experiment on the problem of cross multiple subjects. MASTF-net is superior to other relevant methods and models in multi-source domain. On the issue of cross subject emotion analysis, the highest accuracy of our method can reach $88.19\%$.

citations.title: [268681370 | Zhou et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]
snippets: Advanced performance in addressing distribution differences between training and test data in cross-subject EEG emotion recognition tasks has been demonstrated by methods like BiDANN (Li et al., 2018) and TANN [Li et al., 2021]...Zhou et al. proposed an innovative solution known as the Emotional EEG Style Transfer Network (E$^2$STN)...Extensive experiments demonstrate that E$^2$STN achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-dataset EEG emotion recognition tasks...PGCN achieves state-of-the-art performance by progressively learning discriminative features from coarse-to fine-grained emotion categories (Zhou et al., 2021).

citations.title: [270122917 | Dong et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]
snippets: Motivated by the recent emergence of pre-trained models and their outstanding performance in downstream tasks (Chen et al., 2022)8,(Luo et al., 2023)(Li et al., 2023)(Chen et al., 2023), we recognized that the high-dimensional semantic information of EEG extracted by encoders trained on large-scale subject-independent datasets may contain global generic representations beneficial for emotion recognition tasks.Simultaneously, considering the DE feature, which has been proven to be the most effective individual computational characteristic for EEG-based emotion recognition tasks (Du et al., 2020)(Tao et al., 2023)(Shen et al., 2021), as well as eye movement features often used as an additional modality to aid emotion recognition tasks and confirmed to improve recognition accuracy (Liu et al., 2021), we propose Mood Reader, a novel multi-modal and cross-scale fusion model for cross-subject emotion recognition that integrates global generic representations of EEG and the spatio-temporal interaction information in specific DE features.

citations.title: [277313926 | Liu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]
snippets: Cross-subject EEG emotion recognition is challenged by significant inter-subject variability and intricately entangled intra-subject variability. Existing works have primarily addressed these challenges through domain adaptation or generalization strategies. However, they typically require extensive target subject data or demonstrate limited generalization performance to unseen subjects. Recent few-shot learning paradigms attempt to address these limitations but often encounter catastrophic overfitting during subject-specific adaptation with limited samples...Early approaches to this task focused on handcrafted statistical features combined with simple classifiers, which yielded limited performance [25]. Recent works [19], [20], [26] primarily address this issue in a supervised learning manner. Song et al. proposed the instanceadaptive graph network, which explores dynamic connectivity across brain regions [26]. GMSS [20] leveraged multi-task self-supervision for generalized representations. Jin et al. introduced the pyramidal GCN, which fully exploits multi-scale information to improve performance [19]. More recently, semisupervised learning paradigms have been applied to EEG emotion recognition to refine individual-specific mappings better. Li et al. combined meta-learning and semi-supervised learning to facilitate subject-adaptation representations [27]. Guarneros et al. proposed semi-supervised multi-source joint distribution adaptation to align distributions across different subjects [28].

sections.title: Recent Breakthroughs & Innovations
sections.text:
TLDR; Recent innovations in cross-subject EEG emotion recognition focus on dynamic adaptation mechanisms and interconnection-aware approaches. New methods combine domain adaptation with dynamic graph structures and label refinement techniques to achieve improved generalization across subjects. (3 sources)

Recent breakthroughs in cross-subject EEG emotion recognition have centered around more sophisticated approaches to handling domain shifts and individual differences. One notable innovation is the development of the Interconnection Dynamic Domain Adaptation (IDDA) method, which combines dynamic graph convolution with domain adaptation to better capture both channel relationships and domain-invariant features. This approach includes a multi-source selection algorithm to optimize subject pairing and has achieved strong results with 85.75% accuracy on SEED and 72.36% on SEED-IV datasets  [268591733 | An et al. | 2024 | Citations: 9].

Another significant advancement has been the integration of few-shot learning with domain adaptation techniques. The Single-Source Domain Adaptive Few-Shot Learning Networks (SDA-FSL) represent a pioneering effort in applying few-shot learning to EEG emotion recognition. This approach uses CBAM-based feature mapping modules alongside domain adaptation components to balance common feature extraction and domain-specific preservation  [245934372 | Ning et al. | 2021 | Citations: 17].

Label refinement has emerged as a powerful technique for improving cross-subject performance. By dividing EEG samples into six groups based on users' brain activity patterns under different movie stimuli, researchers have achieved impressive results with classification accuracies of 93.35±4.14% and 84.08±6.01% on SEED and SEED-IV datasets respectively. This approach demonstrates the potential of detailed label refinement in enhancing cross-subject generalization  [272022765 | Fu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

These innovations collectively show a trend toward more nuanced approaches that consider both the structural relationships in EEG data and the temporal dynamics of emotional responses <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

snippets: To achieve more optimal cross-subject emotion recognition, a cross subject emotion recognition method based on interconnection dynamic domain adaptation (IDDA) is proposed. In IDDA, dynamic graph convolution (DGC) is employed to dynamically learn the intrinsic relationships between different EEG channels and to extract domain invariant features. And dynamic domain adaptation (DDA) is employed to align the source domain and target domain, at the same time the emotional sub-domains is aligned, achieving more optimal cross subject emotion recognition. IDDA enhances the emotion discrimination ability of domain invariant features, thereby improving the accuracy of cross-subject EEG emotion recognition. sections.title: Future Directions & Limitations
sections.text:
TLDR; Current cross-subject EEG emotion recognition faces limitations in handling fine-grained temporal variations and lacks standardized evaluation protocols. Future directions point towards more sophisticated temporal modeling, unified representation learning, and improved assessment methodologies. (6 sources)

Despite recent advances, several key limitations persist in current cross-subject EEG emotion recognition systems. Many existing methods rely heavily on global alignment between source and target domains while neglecting important fine-grained information  [266838904 | Li et al. | 2024 | Citations: 19]. Additionally, conventional approaches struggle to fully capture the complex spatiotemporal dynamics of neural signals that are essential for accurately representing emotion processing  [273877510 | Shen et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

One significant limitation lies in the treatment of multiple source domains, where existing methods often oversimplify by treating distinctly distributed sources as a single domain. This simplification fails to account for the complex joint distribution differences between domains  [252224934 | Liang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 9].

Looking ahead, several promising directions emerge:

1. Development of more sophisticated temporal modeling approaches that can better capture the intricate timing variations in EEG signals <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

2. Creation of unified representation learning frameworks that can bridge domain gaps while preserving task-relevant information  [256821232 | Wu et al. | 2022 | Citations: 22]

3. Implementation of more rigorous evaluation protocols that test performance across both seen and unseen subjects  [256821232 | Wu et al. | 2022 | Citations: 22]

Recent success stories suggest promising paths forward. The EMOTIONAL framework, for instance, has shown capability in extracting interpretable visual representations of emotional experiences while maintaining competitive classification performance  [256821232 | Wu et al. | 2022 | Citations: 22]. Similarly, approaches combining spatiotemporal feature learning with soft attention mechanisms have demonstrated improved performance across subjects  [248207471 | Li et al. | 2021 | Citations: 32].

A particular area needing attention is the development of standardized evaluation protocols that can fairly compare different approaches while accounting for real-world deployment scenarios  [249874500 | Zhang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 10]. Such standardization would help accelerate progress in the field by enabling more meaningful comparisons between different methodological approaches <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [252224934 | Liang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 9]

question: Downlink scheduling of satellite image data

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Satellite image downlink scheduling manages the transfer of collected image data from satellites to ground stations. This process occurs in two phases - data collection via imaging followed by data transmission either immediately during visibility or later during planned downlink sessions. (2 sources)

Earth observation satellites play a vital role in various applications including environmental monitoring, land surveys, and detailed investigations of sensitive areas  [250244012 | Chang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]. These satellites operate through a dual-phase mission cycle consisting of data acquisition (imaging) followed by data downlink (transmission). During the imaging phase, satellites capture and store observational data onboard until it can be transferred to ground stations  [250244012 | Chang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0].

The satellite image data downlink scheduling problem (SIDSP) has evolved significantly with modern technological developments. Traditionally, image data had to be transmitted in a strict "First observed, First downlink" sequence and couldn't be divided into segments  [250244012 | Chang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]. However, contemporary satellites are equipped with advanced on-board file systems that allow images to be split into smaller fragments and transmitted in any order, adding new dimensions of complexity to the scheduling challenge  [250244012 | Chang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0].

Each downlink session can handle partial imaging data, complete imaging data, or combinations of both, creating flexible options for managing data transmission  [250244012 | Chang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]. The primary goal remains consistent: to optimize the scheduling of downlink operations while ensuring timely data delivery to satisfy customer demands  [250244012 | Chang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]  [20907249 | Wang et al. | 2011 | Citations: 20].

citations.title: [250244012 | Chang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]
snippets:
The satellite image data downlink scheduling problem (SIDSP) plays a crucial role in the mission planning operation of earth observation satellites (EOSs) (Li et al., 2014). With the increase in the number of on-orbit EOSs (Wang et al., 2020) and modern technological developments (Chang et al., 2020, Lu et al., 2021, Chang et al., 2021b), the traditional meaning of SIDSP is now shifted, and the role of effective downlink scheduling in satellite mission planning becomes increasingly important.

Many existing research works on the traditional SIDSP implicitly assume that image data cannot be segmented (Karapetyan et al., 2015) and have to be transmitted in "First observed, First downlink (FOFD)" order (Wang et al., 2011). Under these conditions, SIDSP is equivalent to the satellite range scheduling problem (SRSP) (Luo et al., 2017, Marinelli et al., 2011, She et al., 2019). But with the development of on-board file systems in EOS (Huang et al., 2018), an original image data can be split into several fragments, referred to as "Segment", and then transmitted without prioritizing the capturing order, referred to as "rearrange". Because of this additional dimension of complexity, SIDSP is no longer a simple downlink request permutation problem (DRPP) (Karapetyan et al., 2015). The modern SIDSP is more complicated than SRSP (Zufferey et al., 2008, Vazquez and Erwin, 2014, Barbulescu et al., 2004) and the traditional SIDSP (Wang et al., 2011, She et al., 2019).

sections.title: Core Components and Constraints
sections.text:
TLDR; The core components of satellite image downlink scheduling include ground stations, satellites, and communication windows. Key constraints involve limited ground station availability, satellite visibility masks, and storage capacities that require timely data deletion if not properly transmitted. (3 sources)

Key components and constraints:

* **Ground Stations**: Limited number of ground stations exist to receive satellite data, creating competition for available receiving infrastructure  [115615066 | Song et al. | 2019 | Citations: 6].

* **Communication Windows (VTWs)**: Data transmission can only occur during specific visibility time windows when both the satellite and ground station are positioned to establish communication  [273488649 | Ferrari et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

* **Two Transmission Protocols**:

  - Real-time transmission: Data sent immediately during simultaneous observation and visibility

  - Record-playback: Stored data transmitted during planned downlink sessions

   [273488649 | Ferrari et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]

* **Visibility Mask Requirements**: Data transmission must begin when the satellite enters the designated ground station visibility mask. Missed transmissions during available windows result in failed data delivery  [115615066 | Song et al. | 2019 | Citations: 6].

* **Storage Constraints**: Satellites have limited storage capacity that requires timely data management. Untransmitted data will be deleted from storage, potentially resulting in lost customer demands  [115615066 | Song et al. | 2019 | Citations: 6]  [73650522 | Song et al. | 2018 | Citations: 18].

* **Oversubscription Challenge**: Customer demands typically exceed available ground resources, making it necessary to select which requests can be fulfilled rather than accepting all submissions  [73650522 | Song et al. | 2018 | Citations: 18].

* **Code Rate and Bit Error Rate**: Data transmission must comply with specific technical parameters regarding data encoding rates and acceptable error levels  [73650522 | Song et al. | 2018 | Citations: 18].

citations.title: [115615066 | Song et al. | 2019 | Citations: 6]
snippets: The small satellite image downlink scheduling problem (SSIDSP) mainly solves the problem of how to better match the limited receiving capacity of the ground station with the limited satellite resources. The limitation on the storage capacity of satellites requires that the picture data obtained should be downlinked as soon as possible; otherwise, the image data will be deleted from the storage. However, the number of ground stations is limited and the downlink tasks could only be performed when the ground stations and satellites establish communication and are visible to each other. The diagram of imaging satellite data downlink tasks is shown in Figure 1, which vividly demonstrates the satellite operation flow and time progress, respectively. The overall process of photographing and data downlinking is that the imaging satellite photographs the task during T 0 to T 1 . After the satellite completes the attitude maneuver, it downloads the data during T 2 to T 3 . The data transmission task can only begin when the satellite passes the visibility mask of the ground station. If a satellite cannot downlink the data after it has passed through the visible mask of all the ground stations, the task will not meet users' requests.

citations.title: [273488649 | Ferrari et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
snippets:
Download Scheduling Problem. The generation of effective download schedules is very important since image downlink often becomes the bottleneck in the efficiency of the whole system. Indeed, satellites have finite storage capacity and need to empty their memory before continuing to collect data. To do this, they dispose of a set of TWs available for the transmission of data to the Earth. Data transmission can follow two protocols: real-time transmission, requiring the satellite being within an available VTW while undertaking observation tasks, and record playback, that consists in storing data before transmission to the Earth.

The objective of the optimization problem is to maximize the global profit or quantity of the transmitted data, while respecting the process constraints. Additionally, some authors aim at minimizing the total tardiness, i.e., the total delay of all observing data from observation to transmission. Karapetyan et al. (2015) considered the optimization of the data transmission tardiness in the downlink scheduling problem for Canada's Earth observing satellite, RADARSAT-2, and proposed a schedule generation procedure that schedules urgent and regular requests in two consecutive steps, respecting task priorities.

citations.title: [73650522 | Song et al. | 2018 | Citations: 18]
snippets: The satellite image downlink scheduling problem (SIDSP) is included in satellite mission planning as an important part. A customer demand is finished only if the corresponding images are eventually downloaded. Due to the growing customer demands and the limited ground resources, SIDSP is an oversubscribed scheduling problem...The image downlink scheduling is a process of selecting a subset of downlink requests among the candidate set. Only if the image is successfully transmitted can the utility of the corresponding demand be counted. Considering all kinds of constraints, the subset of requests that can eventually be transmitted, their corresponding ground stations and downlink time windows are the output of SIDSP with the purpose of maximizing the utility function. SIDSP is a complex constrained optimization problem...Satellite image downlink mission is to transmit the original or compressed data to the ground station by satelliteground data link under the certain code rate and bit error rate...Downlink also can be classified into two ways: (1) the observed images are transmitted to the ground station in real time when the observation target and the ground station are simultaneously visible to the satellite; (2) first store observed images in the onboard memory and then transmit data to the ground station when the satellite is passing...Adapting to the characteristic of SIDSP, we exploit the serial scheduling scheme involving two key parts: (1) determining a permutation of the downlink requests and (2) producing a schedule from the given ordered requests. A schedule generation algorithm (SGA) is proposed to assign the downlink time window for each scheduled request.

sections.title: Modern Evolution of Downlink Capabilities
sections.text:
TLDR; Modern satellites have evolved beyond simple "first seen, first transmitted" limitations through onboard file systems and data segmentation capabilities. This evolution allows for more flexible data management strategies, though it introduces additional complexity to scheduling decisions. (4 sources)

The landscape of satellite image downlink capabilities has undergone significant transformation with technological advancement. Traditional systems operated under restrictive assumptions where image data had to be transmitted in a rigid "First observed, First downlink" sequence without the possibility of segmentation  [250244012 | Chang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]  [20907249 | Wang et al. | 2011 | Citations: 20].

Modern developments have introduced much greater flexibility through enhanced onboard file systems. These systems now allow images to be split into smaller segments called "Segmented Image Data (SID)" that can be transmitted independently and in any order  (Chang et al._1,  2022). This capability fundamentally changes how satellite operators can manage their data downlinks, moving away from the simpler "downlink request permutation problem" toward a more sophisticated scheduling challenge  [250244012 | Chang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0].

However, this increased flexibility comes with its own challenges. Recent research has highlighted that observation data often exhibits strong correlations between related images, necessitating coordinated transmission timing. For instance, failure to transmit even a portion of correlated data related to a specific topic can significantly diminish the overall value of the collected dataset  [220363282 | Chen et al. | 2020 | Citations: 11].

These evolving capabilities have prompted a shift in how we conceptualize the satellite image downlink scheduling problem (SIDSP), making it more complex than traditional range scheduling problems and requiring new approaches to optimization  [250244012 | Chang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]. The ability to segment and rearrange data adds new strategic considerations to the scheduling process <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

The observation data belonging to a specific topic usually has a strong correlation with each other. The value of a topic observation data may be decayed sharply, even if a small part of the observation data belonging to the topic cannot be transmitted to the ground in time. Therefore, the current models and algorithms can hardly meet the requirements of satellite observation data topic transmission scheduling (SDTTS) problem.

sections.title: Optimization Approaches and Algorithms
sections.text:
TLDR; Various optimization methods have been developed to address satellite downlink scheduling, ranging from Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) to heuristic approaches. These methods balance computational complexity with scheduling effectiveness, incorporating factors like data priority, ground station allocation, and temporal constraints. (3 sources)

Several key approaches have emerged for optimizing satellite image downlink scheduling:

* **Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP)**:

  - Used for scheduling large satellite constellations, MILP optimizes the coordination of imagery collections and data downlinks

  - Can handle complex networks of satellites and ground stations simultaneously

  - Often employs dynamic programming heuristics to break down the scheduling problem into manageable steps  [19809641 | Augenstein et al. | 2016 | Citations: 48]

* **Utility-Based Scheduling**:

  - Maximizes a composite utility function considering:

    - Number of successful downlinks

    - Request priority values

    - Tardiness penalties relative to requested windows

  - Allows selective rejection of lower-priority requests to optimize higher-value transmissions

   [16461240 | Karapetyan et al. | 2012 | Citations: 69]

* **Decoupled Planning Approach**:

  - Separates image collection and downlink scheduling to simplify computation

  - Uses heuristics to estimate onboard data volume over time

  - Allocates downlink time based on expected priority-weighted data accumulation

  - Provides faster solutions compared to fully integrated approaches

   [252263914 | Cox et al. | 2022 | Citations: 2]

* **Hybrid Heuristic Methods**:

  - Combine multiple techniques to balance computational efficiency with solution quality

  - Particularly useful for large-scale constellation management

  - Enable practical implementation while maintaining reasonable scheduling performance

   [252263914 | Cox et al. | 2022 | Citations: 2]

citations.title: [16461240 | Karapetyan et al. | 2012 | Citations: 69]
snippets: We consider the problem arising in satellite industry that deals with scheduling downlinks of images assuming that the schedule for image acquisition is already generated. We study RADARSAT-2 satellite that orbits the Earth to acquire images that can be downlinked to a set G of stationary ground stations for further processing. Since the problem has a lot in common with scheduling problems and, in particular, with the Resource Constrained Project Scheduling Problem, our notations are close to the ones used in the scheduling literature...Note that SIDSP deals with the problem of finding an image downlink schedule so that a utility function is maximized. The utility function considers the number of downlinks scheduled, their priority values, and the difference between the downlink start time and the start time of the request time window (tardiness). Rejection of requests is allowed, and a rejected request is referred to as unscheduled.

snippets: A mixed-integer linear program (MILP) approach to scheduling a large constellation of Earth-imaging satellites is presented. The algorithm optimizes the assignment of imagery collects, image data downlinks, and "health & safety" contacts, generating schedules for all satellites and ground stations in a network...This is achieved by a partitioning of the problem into sequential steps for downlink scheduling and image scheduling, with a novel dynamic programming (DP) heuristic providing a stand-in for imaging activity in the MILP when scheduling the downlinks.

snippets: To address this problem they separate the immediate coupling that exists between image collection opportunities and downlink opportunities. Separating the imaging and downlink planning decouples the variables present in the MILP but requires a method to appropriately allocated downlink time based on estimated image collection and current onboard memory state of each vehicle. To accomplish this, they provide a heuristic that estimates the amount of priority-weighted image data likely onboard the satellite as a function of time and the number of priority-weighted image collection opportunities a satellite would encounter during specific time periods. The authors demonstrate that with these two pieces of information it is possible to reasonably allocate downlink time among the constellation of vehicles and then also schedule the additional image collection opportunities. This modification yields dramatically reduced solve times and enables the efficient, yet sub-optimal, scheduling of the TerraBella constellation of satellites [31].

sections.title: Real-world Considerations and Challenges
sections.text:
TLDR; Real-world satellite downlink scheduling faces complex operational tradeoffs between cost, data latency, and resource contention. The rapid growth of satellite constellations has created new challenges around ground station allocation and data delivery timeliness. (3 sources)

The reality of satellite image downlink scheduling operates under significant commercial and technical pressures. One of the most pressing concerns is the substantial financial investment required for ground station access, with antenna rental costs reaching approximately $22 per minute  [275212693 | Zhao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [255599740 | Velusamy et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3]. This economic constraint has led operators to adopt strategic approaches to ground station utilization, sometimes choosing to defer data transmission to minimize expenses, which unfortunately increases overall data latency  [275212693 | Zhao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

Resource contention presents another major challenge, particularly in centralized architectures. Studies have shown that a single ground station can detect up to 100 satellites simultaneously, leading to intense competition for limited bandwidth and processing power  [275212693 | Zhao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [236961696 | Vasisht et al. | 2021 | Citations: 93]. This situation has driven innovation in ground station deployment strategies, with newer approaches exploring hybrid models that utilize subsets of ground stations specifically for downlink purposes  [236961696 | Vasisht et al. | 2021 | Citations: 93].

The emergence of distributed ground station networks has begun addressing some of these challenges, offering potential improvements in data delivery latency <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">. However, the fundamental tension between optimal data delivery and operational costs continues to shape how satellite operators approach downlink scheduling decisions in practice.

citations.title: [275212693 | Zhao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets:
Data downlink scheduling: Transmitting image data to data centers involves two stages: from the satellite to a ground station, and then from the ground station to the data center. 

During the initial stage, image data remain onboard the satellite until it establishes contact with a ground station. A single ground station equipped with multiple antennas can communicate with several satellites concurrently, with each antenna dedicated to one satellite. However, the decision to downlink data is influenced by several factors, even when satellites are within the ground station's range. Contention is a common issue. As shown in work (Vasisht et al., 2021), a ground station can simultaneously detect up to 100 satellites. Even when satellites are spaced evenly in orbit, they may compete for the same ground stations [22]. When multiple satellites vie for communication, priority is generally assigned based on several criteria including the amount of data backlog onboard and the quality of the GSL. Since renting a ground station antenna can cost 22 dollars per minute (Velusamy et al., 2022), operators may choose to skip some satellite passes to reduce costs, allowing data to accumulate. While this strategy is cost-effective, it leads to increased data latency.

citations.title: [236961696 | Vasisht et al. | 2021 | Citations: 93]
snippets: Large constellations of Low Earth Orbit satellites promise to provide near real-time high-resolution Earth imagery. Yet, getting this large amount of data back to Earth is challenging because of their low orbits and fast motion through space. Centralized architectures with few multi-million dollar ground stations incur large hour-level data download latency and are hard to scale. We propose a geographically distributed ground station design, L2D2, that uses low-cost commodity hardware to offer low latency robust downlink. L2D2 is the first system to use a hybrid ground station model, where only a subset of ground stations are uplink-capable. We design new algorithms for scheduling and rate adaptation that enable low latency and high robustness despite the limitations of the receive-only ground stations. We evaluate L2D2 through a combination of trace-driven simulations and real-world satellite-ground station measurements. Our results demonstrate that L2D2's geographically distributed design can reduce data downlink latency from 90 minutes to 21 minutes.

citations.title: [255599740 | Velusamy et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3]
snippets: Recent advances in satellite technology and the introduction of the Space-Data-as-a-Service business models are attracting interest for using the platform in a wide range of applications that include earth observations, 5G integration, aeronautical and maritime tracking and communications, asset tracking, sensor data collection, among others. In this new scenario, it becomes of interest not only selecting a ground station provider based on the monetary cost, but also the download features with prevailing atmospheric conditions to achieve high reliability and low data delivery latency. To this end, the Cognitive Space Gateway approach is used to route data bundles in a Ground Station-as-a-Service context with multiple providers to find a suitable balance between data latency and the ground station monetary costs, exploiting as possible site-diversity when available. The approach is tested experimentally using NASA's High-Rate Delay-Tolerant Networking (HDTN).

sections.title: Background/Introduction
sections.text:
TLDR; Large Language Models (LLMs) have evolved into sophisticated autonomous agents capable of various tasks, but face challenges with ambiguity in interpretation. Understanding and managing ambiguity is crucial for reliable LLM agent interactions, particularly in areas like emotional recognition and complex decision-making. (6 sources)

The rise of Large Language Models has ushered in a new era of artificial intelligence agents that demonstrate remarkable capabilities in autonomy, reactivity, and pro-activeness  [264172149 | Shu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 14]. These agents have shown promising results in various domains, from supporting intelligent urban planning to demonstrating adaptive learning abilities in virtual environments  [264172149 | Shu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 14].

However, a fundamental challenge lies in the inherent ambiguity of natural language, which can significantly impact LLM agent performance. Users often employ elliptical expressions and imprecise statements to optimize communication efficiency, leading to varied interpretations based on different assumptions and backgrounds  [269214521 | Kim et al. | 2024 | Citations: 14]. This challenge is compounded by the fact that LLMs are not specifically trained to handle ambiguous utterances, and their interpretation of ambiguity can vary based on their knowledge base  [269214521 | Kim et al. | 2024 | Citations: 14].

The importance of addressing ambiguity becomes particularly critical in emotional intelligence applications, where LLMs must comprehend complex and subtle emotional nuances  [272969068 | Hong et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. Beyond just language processing, ambiguity also affects how LLM agents perceive and respond to verbal instructions, potentially leading to unreliable outputs and unsafe decisions  [271709656 | Sun et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4].

Current efforts to improve LLM agent capabilities include developing sophisticated frameworks that integrate multiple components, such as control ends, perception ends, and action ends, drawing inspiration from cognitive science  [264172149 | Shu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 14]. These developments aim to create more dependable and controllable AI systems  [258959352 | Song et al. | 2022 | Citations: 154], though the challenge of managing ambiguity remains a central concern in advancing LLM technology <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

sections.title: Types and Sources of Ambiguity
sections.text:
TLDR; Ambiguity in LLM responses manifests in distinct forms, including entity-related confusion, query interpretation challenges, and knowledge application inconsistencies. These ambiguities can be categorized into aleatory uncertainty arising from inherent data ambiguity and epistemic uncertainty stemming from model knowledge gaps. (8 sources)

Research has identified several key categories of ambiguity affecting LLM performance:

1. **Entity Type Ambiguity**

- Occurs when models struggle to choose between multiple possible interpretations of named entities

- Studies show LLMs achieve only 75-85% accuracy in correctly interpreting ambiguous entities, with lower performance using underspecific prompts  [271404871 | Sedova et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]

2. **Query Ambiguity**

- Arises from vague or insufficient user instructions lacking sufficient detail

- Particularly problematic in interactive code generation and automated task execution  [276422341 | Vijayvargiya et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2]

- Can manifest as multiple possible interpretations of the same request [277272775 | Izquierdo-Badiola et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]

3. **Knowledge Application Ambiguity**

- Results from models possessing knowledge but struggling to apply it consistently

- Manifests as systematic discrepancies in model behavior and self-inconsistencies  [271404871 | Sedova et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]

4. **Task-Specific Instructions Ambiguity**

- Emerges from unclear task parameters (e.g., sorting direction, criteria)

- Cannot be resolved through simple design fixes but requires explicit user clarification  [276782028 | Chen et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]

5. **Contextual and Temporal Ambiguity**

- Arises from inherent ambiguity in questions and unclear task instructions  [265213190 | Hou et al. | 2023 | Citations: 49]

- Includes challenges related to temporal and geographical contexts  [273403502 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]  [235629374 | Zhang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 167]

6. **Aleatory vs. Epistemic Uncertainty**

- Aleatory uncertainty comes from inherent randomness or ambiguity in data

- Epistemic uncertainty relates to models' knowledge gaps  [265213190 | Hou et al. | 2023 | Citations: 49]

7. **Translation-Based Ambiguity**

- Manifests when sentences have multiple valid translations

- Can be detected through analysis of multilingual LLM hidden representations  [273403502 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]  [273901591 | Mehrparvar et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]

citations.title: [265213190 | Hou et al. | 2023 | Citations: 49]
snippets:
For many applications, it is necessary to distinguish between different types of uncertainty and decompose the source into these types, a problem we refer to as uncertainty decomposition. 

As discussed more formally below, it is always possible to decompose a predictive model's uncertainty into two components: aleatoric (data) uncertainty and epistemic (model) uncertainty. Epistemic uncertainty arises when correct outputs are predictable in principle, but models lack the knowledge required for prediction. For example, the question What is 2+3? requires the knowledge of algebraic operations. Without such knowledge, the uncertainty will be high. On the other hand, aleatoric uncertainty arises from ambiguity or inherent randomness in the data-generating process itself: in language processing applications, it may result from ambiguous questions (Min et al., 2020;(Guo et al., 2021)Kuhn et al., 2023) and unclear task instructions (Tamkin et al., 2022). In particular, an important source of aleatoric uncertainty is the input ambiguity. For example, the answer to the input question Who is the president of this country will have a high aleatoric uncertainty because it is ambiguous what country and time the question intends to query about.

citations.title: [271404871 | Sedova et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: One of the major aspects contributing to the striking performance of large language models (LLMs) is the vast amount of factual knowledge accumulated during pre-training. Yet, many LLMs suffer from self-inconsistency, which raises doubts about their trustworthiness and reliability. This paper focuses on entity type ambiguity, analyzing the proficiency and consistency of state-of-the-art LLMs in applying factual knowledge when prompted with ambiguous entities. To do so, we propose an evaluation protocol that disentangles knowing from applying knowledge, and test state-of-the-art LLMs on 49 ambiguous entities. Our experiments reveal that LLMs struggle with choosing the correct entity reading, achieving an average accuracy of only 85%, and as low as 75% with underspecified prompts. The results also reveal systematic discrepancies in LLM behavior, showing that while the models may possess knowledge, they struggle to apply it consistently, exhibit biases toward preferred readings, and display self-inconsistencies. This highlights the need to address entity ambiguity in the future for more trustworthy LLMs.

citations.title: [273403502 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]
snippets: Ambiguity has been studied extensively in NLP in across a variety of tasks. In machine translation, works have studied instances where sentences in a source language have multiple valid translations in a target language (Yin et al., 2021)Lopes et al., 2020;(155089628). In natural language inference (NLI), (Nie et al., 2020) collected a dataset of highly crossannotated examples that contain high disagreement in annotator judgments. (Liu et al., 2023) then found that these disagreements are often the result of ambiguity in the input. Recent work has studied various sources of ambiguity, from entity-linking (Lee et al., 2024), co-reference ambiguities (Yuan et al., 2023), to temporal and geographical contexts (Zhang et al., 2021).

citations.title: [273901591 | Mehrparvar et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
snippets: In this project, we propose a method to detect the ambiguity of a sentence using translation by multilingual LLMs. In particular, we hypothesize that a good machine translator should preserve the ambiguity of sentences in all target languages. Therefore, we investigate whether ambiguity is encoded in the hidden representation of a translation model or, instead, if only a single meaning is encoded. In our experiments, we have been able to predict ambiguity of sentences with high accuracy using machine translation without direct use of semantics and only based on the reconstruction error of a function that maps the forward and backward translation hidden representations to each other. The potential applications of the proposed approach span i) detecting ambiguous sentences, ii) fine-tuning existing multilingual LLMs to preserve ambiguous information, and iii) developing AI systems that can generate ambiguity-free languages when needed.

citations.title: [276422341 | Vijayvargiya et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2]
snippets: AI agents are increasingly being deployed to automate tasks, often based on ambiguous and underspecified user instructions. Making unwarranted assumptions and failing to ask clarifying questions can lead to suboptimal outcomes, safety risks due to tool misuse, and wasted computational resources. In this work, we study the ability of LLM agents to handle ambiguous instructions in interactive code generation settings by evaluating proprietary and open-weight models on their performance across three key steps: (a) leveraging interactivity to improve performance in ambiguous scenarios, (b) detecting ambiguity, and (c) asking targeted questions. Our findings reveal that models struggle to distinguish between well-specified and underspecified instructions. However, when models interact for underspecified inputs, they effectively obtain vital information from the user, leading to significant improvements in performance and underscoring the value of effective interaction.

When given ambiguous input, the LLM could interpret it differently. For example, if a user requests to "sort the elements in the table, " several questions arise: Should the sorting be ascending or descending? Should LLM sort it based on the name alphabetically or the ID values? Our study shows that simple clarification questions could greatly mitigate the effect of ambiguous intent. However, current LLM systems [8,13,34]98] rarely check with users or help them clarify intent, instead synthesizing output in one shot.
