sections.title: Background & Motivation
sections.text:
TLDR; The growing adoption of AI/ML workloads in cloud environments creates competing demands between QoS requirements and cost optimization. Managing these workloads effectively requires sophisticated scheduling approaches that balance resource utilization, performance isolation, and operational expenses. (2 sources)

The explosive growth of artificial intelligence and machine learning applications in cloud computing environments has created significant challenges in workload management and optimization. Modern cloud infrastructures host multiple users deploying various applications simultaneously on shared server resources, creating inherent tension between maximizing Quality of Service (QoS) and minimizing operational costs  [262967314 | Ferikoglou et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4].

This scenario presents several fundamental challenges that necessitate specialized scheduling solutions. First, the sharing of computing resources among multiple users inherently leads to potential interference between workloads <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">. Second, cloud providers face pressure to maximize resource utilization to maintain profitability while still delivering acceptable performance levels to their customers. Third, the diversity of AI workloads - spanning both training and inference tasks - adds additional layers of complexity to scheduling decisions  [262967314 | Ferikoglou et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4].

These challenges become particularly acute in the context of cloud-based AI deployments, where organizations must balance multiple competing objectives: ensuring consistent performance for individual workloads, preventing interference between parallel tasks, and maintaining cost-effective resource utilization  [258352522 | Mungoli | 2023 | Citations: 24]. Effective resolution of these challenges requires sophisticated approaches to resource allocation, load balancing, and dynamic scaling that can adapt to changing workload patterns while maintaining desired service levels  [258352522 | Mungoli | 2023 | Citations: 24].

citations.title: [258352522 | Mungoli | 2023 | Citations: 24]
snippets: Efficiently managing and optimizing AI workloads in the cloud is crucial for ensuring high performance, cost-effectiveness, and resource utilization. In this chapter, we discuss various strategies for load balancing and resource allocation, explore auto-scaling and dynamic resource provisioning techniques, and examine performance benchmarking and optimization approaches to improve the overall efficiency of cloud-based AI systems. By adopting these strategies and techniques, researchers and practitioners can significantly enhance the performance of their AI applications while minimizing the associated costs and complexities of managing cloud-based resources (Singh, 2018) [2].

citations.title: [262967314 | Ferikoglou et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4]
snippets: Over the last years, the ever-growing number of Machine Learning(ML) and Artificial Intelligence(AI) applications deployed in the Cloud has led to high demands on the computing resources required for efficient processing. Multiple users deploy multiple applications on the same server node to maximize Quality of Service(QoS); however, this leads to increased interference. In addition, Cloud providers aim to minimize their operating costs by efficiently utilizing the available resources. These conflicting optimization goals form a complex paradigm where efficient scheduling is required.

sections.title: Core Scheduling Approaches
sections.text:
TLDR; Modern AI workload scheduling operates at different granularities - from fine-grained operator-level scheduling to coarse-grained query-level routing. Key approaches include elasticity-enabled scheduling, proactive resource scaling, and intelligent workload coordination to prevent interference while maximizing resource utilization. (5 sources)

At the core of modern AI scheduling architectures lies a spectrum of approaches ranging from fine-grained to coarse-grained scheduling granularity. Fine-grained scheduling focuses on individual components within deep learning computations, treating DNN operators as basic scheduling units. While this approach offers precise control and potentially better performance optimization, it faces scalability limitations when dealing with numerous concurrent workloads  [244714777 | Yu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 9].

Coarse-grained scheduling takes a broader view, handling complete inference queries or training jobs as primary scheduling units. This approach has gained prominence through implementations like Microsoft's Deep Learning Inference Service (DLIS), where intelligent placement of multiple queries helps achieve high utilization while avoiding resource contention  [244714777 | Yu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 9].

Modern scheduling systems increasingly incorporate elasticity and fault tolerance features. For instance, Microsoft's Singularity system implements workload-aware scheduling that enables transparent preemption, migration, and dynamic resizing of deep learning workloads. This approach allows live job migrations across nodes, clusters, and regions while preserving execution state upon interruption  [246867134 | Shukla et al. | 2022 | Citations: 16].

Recent innovations include specialized mechanisms for concurrent execution of multiple workloads. Research has demonstrated the feasibility of running simultaneous inference and training tasks on GPUs, though this requires careful optimization to prevent memory exhaustion and maintain latency targets  [272195707 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. Advanced architectural approaches, such as Octopus, employ sophisticated scheduling strategies including dual-scheduling mechanisms and adaptive task block processing to optimize workflow execution  [270063186 | Deng et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

The ultimate goal of these scheduling approaches is to enable high resource utilization while maintaining service quality and preventing interference between workloads. This represents a delicate balance between maximizing infrastructure usage and ensuring individual job performance remains within acceptable bounds  [273760608 | Mangalampalli et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

citations.title: [244714777 | Yu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 9]
snippets:
Software-Level Workload Scheduling
As we mentioned before, one of the major challenges in multi-tenant inference is to avoid job interference. Therefore, many research works [5, 28, 50, 52] conduct workload scheduling among different DL jobs temporally to reduce such interfering, as shown in Figure 5. Such solutions aims to avoid interference by scheduling different DL model workloads along the time dimension, thus we categorize such works as software-level scheduling solutions. 

In practice, such workload scheduling granularity could be fine-grained, e.g., scheduling the DNN operators, or coarse-grained, e.g., scheduling the entire inference query. 

Operator Scheduling To achieve fine-grained scheduling, works [9,52] regard the DL model operators (e.g., conv, batch-norm, identity) as the minimum scheduling units. They first abstract multiple DNN's computation graph with many operators into an intermediate representation (IR). To explore the huge scheduling space, they design a ML-based auto-search method by defining three main factors: scheduling search space, profiling-guided latency cost model, and the machine learning-based search algorithm to find the best scheduling for a balanced GPU utilization without interference and reduced latency. Such fine-grained operator scheduling could achieve better performance, but usually face scalability issues when the number of workloads increases to very large, such as hundreds of DNN queries. 

Service Router Therefore, other works like [5,28,50] use a more coarse scheduling granularity, e.g., regarding each query as the minimum scheduling units, which thus reduces the scheduling complexity. For example, one of the querylevel workload scheduling example is the service router in large-scale data center, such as Microsoft Deep Learning Inference Service (DLIS) system [42]. To achieve high utilization while avoid resource contention, service router needs to understand different models' requirements and place one or multiple queries intelligently onto hardware.

citations.title: [246867134 | Shukla et al. | 2022 | Citations: 16]
snippets: Lowering costs by driving high utilization across deep learning workloads is a crucial lever for cloud providers. We present Singularity, Microsoft's globally distributed scheduling service for highly-efficient and reliable execution of deep learning training and inference workloads. At the heart of Singularity is a novel, workload-aware scheduler that can transparently preempt and elastically scale deep learning workloads to drive high utilization without impacting their correctness or performance, across a global fleet of AI accelerators (e.g., GPUs, FPGAs). All jobs in Singularity are preemptable, migratable, and dynamically resizable (elastic) by default: a live job can be dynamically and transparently (a) preempted and migrated to a different set of nodes, cluster, data center or a region and resumed exactly from the point where the execution was preempted, and (b) resized (i.e., elastically scaled-up/down) on a varying set of accelerators of a given type.

snippets: To address these challenges, we present Octopus, a scale-out spatial architecture and a suite of advanced scheduling strategies optimized for executing Orchestrated AI Workflows, such as the Discriminate Dual-Scheduling Mechanism, Adaptive Task Block Processing Unit (TBU) Scheduling Strategy, and Proactive Cluster Scheduling Strategy.

snippets: The scheduling method of Corun undertakes offline profiling to find the maximum number of concurrent inferences that can be executed along with a retraining job on a single GPU without incurring an out-of-memory error or significantly increasing the latency.

citations.title: [273760608 | Mangalampalli et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Workflow Scheduling is a crucial challenge in cloud computing as different task dependencies involved in workflows which makes task scheduling process more complex and incurs huge energy consumption for Cloud Service Provider (CSP). Inefficient scheduling of workflows onto VMs without considering runtime capacity of tasks leads to increase in consumption of energy, makespan and operational costs for CSP.

sections.title: Resource Management Strategies
sections.text:
TLDR; Modern resource management strategies emphasize dynamic provisioning and predictive scaling to handle fluctuating AI workload demands while minimizing waste. Key approaches include capacity optimization through automatic resource switching and cost optimization via accelerator selection and workload consolidation. (4 sources)

Effective resource management for AI workloads requires sophisticated approaches to handle their inherent volatility and unpredictable demand patterns. A fundamental challenge is managing resource allocation during periods of fluctuating request volumes, where traditional static provisioning often leads to excessive resource overprovisioning during peak loads  [249017623 | Gao et al. | 2022 | Citations: 26].

Modern systems address this through dynamic resource exploitation strategies. During off-peak periods, when certain workloads consume less than their allocated resources, these idle capacities can be repurposed for other tasks. This approach has proven particularly effective with GPU resources, where higher utilization correlates with improved energy efficiency and reduced waste  [249017623 | Gao et al. | 2022 | Citations: 26].

Two complementary resource management paradigms have emerged: cost-optimized and capacity-optimized configurations. Cost-optimized strategies prioritize accelerators with lower inference costs while maintaining performance targets. Capacity-optimized approaches ensure system resilience by automatically redirecting workloads to alternative accelerators when capacity constraints arise, while still meeting SLA requirements for latency and throughput  [277322476 | Biran et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

Advanced monitoring and prediction capabilities play a crucial role in implementing these strategies effectively. Systems like Kube-Knots demonstrate how analyzing historical resource usage patterns can enable accurate predictions of peak utilization, allowing for more informed decisions about resource allocation and workload consolidation  [249017623 | Gao et al. | 2022 | Citations: 26]  [270391462 | Liang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]. This predictive capability becomes especially valuable when coordinating heterogeneous GPU fleets, where different devices have varying memory constraints and computational capabilities  [270391462 | Liang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

citations.title: [249017623 | Gao et al. | 2022 | Citations: 26]
snippets:
Due to the bursty and fluctuating requests, it is common for the inference application to receive bursty and fluctuating requests, which are unpredictable. This must be considered when determining the resources for the workload. How to guarantee the latency with the minimal operational cost even in extremely overloading scenarios raises a new challenge. In practice, resources are often over-provisioned for inference workloads to guarantee their latency during the rush hours. Then an efficient scheduler needs to consider how to exploit the unused resources of these workloads when there are less queries.

MArk [172,173] analyzes the cost of utilizing different levels of resource abstractions in Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google Cloud Platform (GCP) for inference.

Kube-Knots [137] minimizes the resource waste by allocating offline batch jobs to better utilize the spare resources. It discovers that the GPU energy efficiency increases with its utilization. Therefore, achieving higher GPU utilization indicates higher energy efficiency and less resource wastes. To this end, Kube-Knots colocates the predictable GPU batch jobs with the online inference workloads, as the inference jobs generally underutilize the GPUs. During the scheduling, it also predicts the peak resource utilization of the jobs from their online resource usages. Aryl [85] also observes the resource can be wasted due to the resource over-provisioning for burst inference requests.

citations.title: [270391462 | Liang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]
snippets: Cost efficiency is another critical factor for distributed inference, especially when used in cloud services. AutoDeep [62] automates cloud deployment for real-time online DNN inference, focusing on minimizing costs while satisfying latency constraints. To achieve this, AutoDeep utilizes Bayesian optimization combined with DRL, which enables the adaptive discovery of the optimal cloud configuration and device placement and reduces the required searching time significantly. Through this method, AutoDeep achieves a trade-off between operational costs and latency in DNN inference workloads efficiently. HexGen [52] improves distributed inference cost efficiency for large generative models over heterogeneous GPU devices. It applies asymmetric tensor-wise and layer-wise model partitioning for pipeline-parallel inference and aims to minimize communication and computation costs with heterogeneous GPU memory constraints.

sections.title: AI-Powered Scheduling Solutions
sections.text:
TLDR; Recent advances leverage Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and stochastic modeling to create intelligent scheduling solutions for AI workloads. These approaches enable dynamic decision-making across multiple resource dimensions while accounting for uncertainty in execution times and resource availability. (5 sources)

* **Hierarchical DRL Framework**: A novel scheduling framework uses DRL with a hierarchical action space design to distinguish between on-demand and spot instances. The system employs multiple actor networks coordinated by a common critic network to optimize workflow execution costs through strategic resource selection  [271720326 | Jayanetti et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. This builds on DRL's established success in complex control tasks across various domains  [234336138 | Zhou et al. | 2021 | Citations: 65].

* **ANDREAS Solution**: This advanced scheduling system optimizes both training runtime workloads and energy consumption in GPU clusters. Implementation results show impressive cost reductions of 30-62% compared to baseline approaches, with real-world validation demonstrating only 13% deviation between predicted and actual costs  [234357866 | Filippini et al. | 2021 | Citations: 7].

* **ECCOS Framework**: Specialized for multi-language model serving, ECCOS employs a two-stage scheduling approach. It combines a multi-objective predictor for estimating model capabilities and computational costs with a constrained optimizer that balances cost optimization against quality and workload requirements  [276724603 | Mei et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

* **Stochastic Resource Allocation System**: A mathematically formulated approach that treats execution time as a stochastic variable enables more robust resource allocation decisions. This system demonstrates cost reductions of 32-80% while optimizing GPU memory utilization through multi-job co-location opportunities  [265434101 | Filippini et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5].

* **Hybrid Learning-Based Approaches**: Various combinations of heuristic methods and machine learning techniques have been implemented to find near-optimal solutions for workflow scheduling in heterogeneous computing environments  [276249331 | Bai et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

citations.title: [234357866 | Filippini et al. | 2021 | Citations: 7]
snippets: In this paper we propose ANDREAS, an advanced scheduling solution that tackles these problems jointly, aiming at optimizing DL training runtime workloads and their energy consumption in accelerated clusters. Experiments based on simulation demostrate that we can achieve a cost reduction between 30 and 62% on average with respect to first-principle methods while the validation on a real cluster shows a worst case deviation below 13% between actual and predicted costs, proving the effectiveness of ANDREAS solution in practical scenarios.

citations.title: [265434101 | Filippini et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5]
snippets: In this article, we presented a stochastic approach to model and tackle the optimal resource selection and scheduling problem for DL training jobs in GPU-based systems. We provided a mathematical formulation of the problem by defining the execution time as a stochastic variable, and we developed a stochastic heuristic that allocates jobs to the available resources to minimize the average energy costs while meeting the imposed due dates...The results confirm that our heuristic guarantees significantly better results than the existing ones, with a percentage total cost reduction between 32% and 80% on average in all the considered scenarios. Moreover, the results demonstrate that, depending on the workload and GPU memory, the possibility of co-locating multiple jobs on a single GPU can yield a percentage cost reduction between 17% and 29% on average. Future developments of our work will include the support for multi-node executions, i.e., the possibility of running very demanding applications on GPUs hosted on different nodes involving, possibly, also mixed training and long inference workloads.

citations.title: [271720326 | Jayanetti et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets:
In particular, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) (Zhou et al., 2021) has emerged as an efficient means of solving highly complex problems as evidenced by the recent successes achieved by DRL agents in complex control tasks in fields such as robotics, autonomous driving, healthcare and so on. In this work, we leverage the advanced capabilities of DRL for designing a cost optimized workflow scheduling framework. 

The design of action space is a fundamental characteristic of a DRL based formulation of a problem. The action spaces of a vast majority of scheduling problems that are modeled as DRL problems, include a flat set of actions. The action space may be discrete or continuous, and the agent selects an action from the action space. In this work, we propose a novel hierarchical way of designing the action space of the DRL model such that there is a clear distinction between on-demand and spot instances in action selection. A DRL framework comprising multiple actor networks guided by a common critic network is then designed to select a combination of actions from the hierarchical action space, to optimize cost of workflow executions.

citations.title: [234336138 | Zhou et al. | 2021 | Citations: 65]
snippets: With the acceleration of the Internet in Web 2.0, Cloud computing is a new paradigm to offer dynamic, reliable and elastic computing services. Efficient scheduling of resources or optimal allocation of requests is one of the prominent issues in emerging Cloud computing. Considering the growing complexity of Cloud computing, future Cloud systems will require more effective resource management methods. In some complex scenarios with difficulties in directly evaluating the performance of scheduling solutions, classic algorithms (such as heuristics and meta-heuristics) will fail to obtain an effective scheme. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) is a novel method to solve scheduling problems. Due to the combination of deep learning and reinforcement learning (RL), DRL has achieved considerable performance in current studies. To focus on this direction and analyze the application prospect of DRL in Cloud scheduling, we provide a comprehensive review for DRL-based methods in resource scheduling of Cloud computing. Through the theoretical formulation of scheduling and analysis of RL frameworks, we discuss the advantages of DRL-based methods in Cloud scheduling. We also highlight different challenges and discuss the future directions existing in the DRL-based Cloud scheduling.

citations.title: [276249331 | Bai et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets:
Scheduling in Heterogeneous Distributed Systems has been addressed using various methods, including reinforcement learning and meta-heuristic algorithms. (Orhean et al., 2017) propose a scheduling approach using reinforcement learning for heterogeneous distributed systems, assuming known task execution times to optimize scheduling decisions. Similarly, (Shirvani, 2020), (Karatza, 2001) present heuristic-based algorithms for workflow scheduling in heterogeneous distributed computing systems, combining heuristic methods to find near-optimal solutions. (Vasile et al., 2015) introduce a system resource-aware hybrid scheduling algorithm that models hardware resources to enhance scheduling efficiency. 

In the context of distributed deep learning, HeterPS (Liu et al., 2021) employs reinforcement learning-based scheduling in heterogeneous environments, enabling resource-aware and pipelineparallel execution. However, these approaches often assume a given workload with known performance profiles, either by assumption or based on prior measurements. In contrast, our work addresses scenarios where rescheduling occurs at runtime based on data characteristics. Additionally, these studies typically focus on scheduling for single inference tasks without considering the streaming of continuous inferences, which is common in machine learning workloads.

citations.title: [276724603 | Mei et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]
snippets: This paper addresses this challenge by proposing an efficient capability-cost coordinated scheduling framework, ECCOS, for multi-LLM serving, which explicitly constrains response quality and workload to optimize LLM inference cost. Specifically, it introduces the two-stage scheduling by designing a multi-objective predictor and a constrained optimizer. The predictor estimates both model capabilities and computational costs through training-based and retrieval-based approaches, while the optimizer determines cost-optimal assignments under quality and workload constraints.

Implementation results show benefits ranging from 17-80% improvements in cost efficiency, with particular gains achievable through intelligent resource utilization and workload consolidation. Particularly noteworthy are the cost savings achievable through intelligent resource utilization strategies. Multi-job co-location opportunities on single GPUs can yield consistent cost reductions of 17-29%, representing a meaningful opportunity for improving infrastructure utilization efficiency  [265434101 | Filippini et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5]. The ability to maintain performance parity while reducing costs represents a key advantage of modern scheduling solutions. Energy efficiency improvements are closely tied to resource utilization rates, with higher GPU utilization correlating directly to enhanced energy efficiency and reduced operational waste  [249017623 | Gao et al. | 2022 | Citations: 26]. This relationship between utilization and efficiency provides a strong economic incentive for implementing sophisticated scheduling approaches that can effectively consolidate workloads while maintaining service level agreements <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

sections.title: Background & Basic Concepts
sections.text:
TLDR; Vision Transformers (ViTs) convert images into sequences of patches before applying transformer architecture. While originally successful for classification tasks, ViTs face challenges with high-resolution images due to computational constraints and information retention limitations. (5 sources)

The Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture represents a significant shift in computer vision by adapting the transformer architecture from natural language processing to image analysis. At its core, ViT processes images by splitting them into fixed-size patches (typically 16×16 pixels) and converting these into a sequence of embeddings  [239016306 | Yuan et al. | 2021 | Citations: 227]  [225039882 | Dosovitskiy et al. | 2020 | Citations: 39330].

While ViT initially showed promise in image classification tasks through its patch-based self-attention mechanism, it faces notable limitations when applied to dense prediction tasks. The primary challenge stems from the non-overlapping patches creating low-resolution feature maps, coupled with the quadratic computational complexity that escalates rapidly with high-resolution inputs  [246240657 | Wang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 5].

These limitations led to early approaches that intentionally used coarser patches (like 16×16 pixels) to manage computational demands. Various strategies emerged, including upsampling results from low-resolution ViT outputs to create high-resolution mappings, and applying transformers specifically to sparse image keypoints rather than the full image  [245837195 | Tang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 156].

A significant breakthrough came with the introduction of the Swin Transformer, which addressed these limitations through a novel approach of hierarchical shifted windows. This innovation enabled more efficient processing of high-resolution images while maintaining competitive performance  [244346076 | Liu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 1750].

citations.title: [225039882 | Dosovitskiy et al. | 2020 | Citations: 39330]
snippets: While the Transformer architecture has become the de-facto standard for natural language processing tasks, its applications to computer vision remain limited. In vision, attention is either applied in conjunction with convolutional networks, or used to replace certain components of convolutional networks while keeping their overall structure in place. We show that this reliance on CNNs is not necessary and a pure transformer applied directly to sequences of image patches can perform very well on image classification tasks. When pre-trained on large amounts of data and transferred to multiple mid-sized or small image recognition benchmarks (ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB, etc.), Vision Transformer (ViT) attains excellent results compared to state-of-the-art convolutional networks while requiring substantially fewer computational resources to train.

citations.title: [239016306 | Yuan et al. | 2021 | Citations: 227]
snippets: Vision Transformer splits an image into a sequence of image patches of size 16 × 16, and extracts the feature representation of each image patch. Thus, the output representations of Vision Transformer lose the fine-grained spatial details that are essential for accurate dense predictions. The Vision Transformer only outputs a single-scale feature representation, and thus lacks the capability to handle multi-scale variation. To mitigate the loss of feature granularity and model the multi-scale variation, we present High-Resolution Transformer (HRFormer) that contains richer spatial information and constructs multi-resolution representations for dense predictions.

citations.title: [244346076 | Liu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 1750]
snippets: In this paper, we present techniques for scaling Swin Transformer [35] up to 3 billion parameters and making it capable of training with images of up to 1,536x1,536 resolution.

citations.title: [245837195 | Tang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 156]
snippets: To utilize the standard transformer in vision tasks, many works opt to apply it on low resolution or sparse tokens. ViT (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020) uses coarse image patches of 16 × 16 pixels to limit the number of tokens. DPT (Ranftl et al., 2021) up-samples low-resolution results from ViT to high resolution maps to achieve dense predictions. SuperGlue (Sarlin et al., 2019) applies transformer on sparse image keypoints. Focusing on correspondence and stereo matching applications, Germain et al. (2021) and (Li et al., 2020) also apply transformers at a low resolution feature map...However, as demonstrated in several works (Wang et al., 2021c;Liu et al., 2021;(Sun et al., 2021)(Li et al., 2020)(Shao et al., 2020), applying transformers on high resolution is beneficial for a variety of tasks.

citations.title: [246240657 | Wang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 5]
snippets: Recently, transformers have drawn tremendous interests, due to its great success in capturing long-range dependency. As the first standard-alone transformer for computer vision, Vision Transformer(ViT) (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020) shows impressive result on image classification with patch-based selfattentions. However there is still a large room to improve when applying to dense prediction tasks due to its lowresolution feature map caused by non-overlapping patches and intractable computing costs. The complexity of a naive dense transformer scales rapidly w.r.t the high-resolution output, limiting its application to dense prediction problems.

sections.title: Current Standard Resolution
sections.text:
TLDR; While traditional image classification tasks commonly use 224×224 resolution, Vision Transformers can effectively operate at much lower resolutions (as low as 20×20) while maintaining good accuracy. Recent developments allow ViTs to handle resolutions up to 672×672, though computational constraints remain a key consideration. (5 sources)

Current standard practices for Vision Transformer implementations reveal interesting variations from traditional computer vision approaches. Unlike Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), which traditionally decrease resolution progressively through their network layers, ViTs tend to retain the initial patch resolution throughout their network  [251264819 | Alshammari et al. | 2022 | Citations: 55].

Research has shown that ViTs can maintain strong performance even at remarkably low resolutions. Studies demonstrate that Vision Transformers can achieve accuracy levels above 84% even with extremely low resolutions of 20×20 patches  [257632051 | Wang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5]. Both humans and machines reach high accuracy (>90%) at resolutions of 100×100 or greater, suggesting a sweet spot for practical applications  [257632051 | Wang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5].

Most current ViT implementations operate at moderate resolutions, with common choices being 224×224 or 448×448 pixels  [260683037 | Orhan | 2023 | Citations: 3]. More advanced architectures have pushed these boundaries further - some models now support resolutions up to 672×672 while managing approximately 2,304 tokens  [268384865 | McKinzie et al. | 2024 | Citations: 187]. Through innovative techniques like positional embedding interpolation and strategic image tiling, researchers have even achieved theoretical maximum resolutions of 1,792×1,792 pixels  [268384865 | McKinzie et al. | 2024 | Citations: 187].

Traditional computer vision benchmarks like ImageNet-1K typically use 224×224 as their standard training resolution, making any higher resolution usage technically an exercise in extrapolation  [268536717 | Heo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 34]. However, this doesn't necessarily mean that higher resolutions aren't viable - rather, they represent a more challenging testing ground for these models' ability to generalize <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [251264819 | Alshammari et al. | 2022 | Citations: 55]
snippets: Image classification networks based on CNN tend to transmit representations with a decreasing level of resolution. ResNet, for example, consists of five stages, with each stage decreasing the resolution by half, resulting in a final feature map that is 1/32 * 1/32 in each dimension. In ViT, on the other hand, tokens are initially set to a size of 16 × 16, which reduces the resolution in that dimension; yet the final layer continues at that resolution. As a result, ViT is more likely to retain location information than ResNet. It is not possible to say that ViT has an advantage over ResNet because it retains location information, since image classification tasks do not require location information for classification decisions...In addition, the strategy of gradually reducing resolution, similar to ResNet, has been widely used in recent studies of vision transformers. An example of this is the pyramid vision transformer, shown in the figure above on the right. Transformer systems use self-awareness, and the memory required to store an image grows proportionally with the fourth power of its size. is makes it difficult to process large resolutions, but by using a strategy that gradually reduces resolution, as is the case with CNN systems, it is possible to process high-resolution information in the first layer while saving storage space. is is achieved by a technique similar to that used in CNN systems.

citations.title: [257632051 | Wang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5]
snippets: Vision Transformer can maintain an accuracy of 84.4% even when the image resolution is as low as 20×20. However, such a resolution is far from enough for humans to recognize ADLs at an ideal accuracy level. For resolutions above 100×100, both humans and machines can achieve a high accuracy above 90%.

citations.title: [260683037 | Orhan | 2023 | Citations: 3]
snippets: We consider three different spatial resolutions: 224×224 (0.05 MP), 448×448 (0.2 MP), and 476×476 pixels (0.23 MP), covering a roughly 4.5-fold range in spatial resolution (number of pixels). Due to computational costs, we use the larger two resolutions with the ViT-H model only.

citations.title: [268384865 | McKinzie et al. | 2024 | Citations: 187]
snippets: Through positional embedding interpolation, we have fine-tuned our model to support image resolutions ranging from 448×448, 560×560, to 672×672. Note that, for a resolution of 672×672, with a patch size of 14×14, an image is represented with 2, 304 tokens...Computing self-attention among more than 2, 000 image tokens is computationally challenging, limiting further scaling to even higher image resolutions...for a high-resolution input image, e.g., 1344 × 1344, we construct five images of 672 × 672, and feed them as independent images into our visual encoder...we first downsample the input image to 672 × 672 as a high-level representation, and also resize the input image to 1344 × 1344 and divide the resized image into 4 sub-images of 672×672, which preserve more detailed visual information. Using positional embedding interpolation for each sub-image, we can support image resolution as high as 1792×1792 in experiments.

citations.title: [268536717 | Heo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 34]
snippets: We train ViTs and Swin Transformers on ImageNet-1k [4] training set with highperformance training recipes [17]32].We report the accuracy on the ImageNet-1k validation set as varying image sizes.Note that we use the ImageNet-1k standard image resolution 224 × 224 for training.Thus, a resolution larger than 224 can be considered as extrapolation.

sections.title: Evolution of Resolution Capabilities
sections.text:
TLDR; Vision Transformer resolution capabilities have evolved dramatically from initial 224×224 limits to handling thousands of pixels. Key architectural innovations like progressive scaling, multi-scale structures, and specialized attention mechanisms have enabled continuous pushing of resolution boundaries. (7 sources)

The evolution of Vision Transformer resolution capabilities reflects significant technological progress in addressing the fundamental challenge of scaling transformers to handle increasingly larger images. Early ViT implementations were constrained by the O(N²) self-attention memory scaling, which initially limited models to modest resolutions around 128×176 pixels  [251135282 | Guizilini et al. | 2022 | Citations: 15].

A major breakthrough came with the development of scalable architectures that could handle substantially larger images. Researchers began exploring various resolutions ranging from 1K to 4M pixels, spanning across different types of vision tasks including classification, segmentation, and detection  [254275405 | Sreedhar et al. | 2022 | Citations: 2].

The Swin Transformer marked a significant advancement in resolution scaling capabilities, successfully demonstrating the ability to process images up to 1,536x1,536 resolution  [244346076 | Liu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 1,750]. More recent models have pushed these boundaries even further, with some architectures now supporting resolutions up to 4K  [268264262 | Chen et al. | 2024 | Citations: 88].

To enable these dramatic improvements in resolution handling, several architectural innovations emerged. These included multi-scale model structures for efficient high-resolution encoding  [232404731 | Zhang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 329], and the development of more efficient attention mechanisms. For instance, Agent attention with linear complexity has made it possible to leverage global receptive fields while maintaining computational feasibility, leading to notable accuracy gains when scaling to higher resolutions  [266210414 | Han et al. | 2023 | Citations: 74].

Recent research suggests that increasing resolution might be more effective than simply increasing model depth or width for scaling Vision Transformers, particularly for architectures that employ efficient attention mechanisms  [266210414 | Han et al. | 2023 | Citations: 74]. This is evidenced by specific examples like Swin Transformer, where scaling input resolution from 224×224 to 384×224 resulted in a significant improvement in ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy from 83.5% to 84.5%  [268532440 | Yao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 15].

citations.title: [232404731 | Zhang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 329]
snippets: This paper presents a new Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture Multi-Scale Vision Longformer, which significantly enhances the ViT of [12] for encoding high-resolution images using two techniques. The first is the multi-scale model structure, which provides image encodings at multiple scales with manageable computational cost.

citations.title: [251135282 | Guizilini et al. | 2022 | Citations: 15]
snippets: One of the main challenges of training Transformer-based architectures has been the O(N 2 ) self-attention memory scaling with input size. This means that the resolution of recent models has been fairly limited (e.g. the view synthesis model of Sajjadi et al. [38] primarily trains on low-resolution images, with a highest resolution of 128 × 176), hindering their application to real-world scenes. Perceiver IO decouples input resolution from the the learned latent representation, which enables training and real-time inference at higher resolutions [58]. In our experiments, we found it advantageous to train using a resolution curriculum, first at a lower resolution (128 × 192), and then fine-tune at a higher resolution (240 × 320).

citations.title: [254275405 | Sreedhar et al. | 2022 | Citations: 2]
snippets: Unlike prior work that focuses on classification and a 224 by 224 image size (49K pixels) [83], our evaluation is across various image sizes (1K to 4M pixels), including those used in standard datasets for classification (ImageNet [83]), segmentation (ADE20K (Zhou et al., 2017), Cityscapes (Cordts et al., 2016)), and detection (COCO (Lin et al., 2014), Cityscapes (Cordts et al., 2016)). These results become important for emerging applications that call for larger image resolutions (Yu et al., 2018), (Zou et al., 2019).

citations.title: [266210414 | Han et al. | 2023 | Citations: 74]
snippets: Large Receptive Field. Modern vision Transformers often confine self-attention calculation to local windows to reduce computation complexity, such as Swin [29]. In Tab. 4, we gradually enlarge the window size of Agent-Swin-T, ranging from 7² to 56². Clearly, as the receptive field expands, the model's performance consistently improves. This indicates that while the window attention pattern is effective, it inevitably compromises the long-range modeling capability of selfattention and remains inferior to global attention. As shown in Fig. 7a, unlike the quadratic complexity of Softmax attention, the linear complexity of agent attention enables us to benefit from a global receptive field while preserving identical computation complexity. High Resolution. Limited by the quadratic complexity of Softmax attention, current vision Transformer models usually scale up by increasing model depth and width. Building on insights from [43], we discover that enhancing resolution might be a more effective approach for scaling vision Transformers, particularly those employing agent attention with global receptive fields. As shown in Tab. 5, Agent-DeiT-B achieves a 0.2 accuracy gain compared to DeiT-B, whereas Agent-DeiT-S at 448² resolution attains an accuracy of 83.1 with only a quarter of the parameters. We observed analogous trends when scaling the resolution of Agent-PVT-M and Agent-Swin-S (see Appendix). Fig. 7b shows the FLOPs comparison between Agent-DeiT and DeiT, with Agent-DeiT saving 75% of FLOPs for 1024² resolution images. In Fig. 7c, we progressively increase the resolution of Agent-Swin-S, Swin-S, and Swin-B. It is evident that in high-resolution scenarios, our model consistently delivers notably superior outcomes.

citations.title: [268264262 | Chen et al. | 2024 | Citations: 88]
snippets: For instance, Imagen (Saharia et al., 2022), GigaGAN (Kang et al., 2023) and Stable Diffusion (Rombach et al., 2021) introduce an additional super-resolution network, while Stable Cascade (Pernias et al., 2024) employs multiple diffusion networks to increase resolution progressively. These combined-model solutions, however, can introduce cumulative errors. On the other hand, works like SDXL (Podell et al., 2023), DALLE 2 [31], Playground [20] and PixArt-α [5] have attempted to generate high-resolution images using diffusion models directly. Nevertheless, these efforts are capped at generating images with resolutions up to 1024px due to computational complexity. In this paper, we push this boundary to 4K resolution, significantly enhancing the visual quality of the generated content.

citations.title: [268532440 | Yao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 15]
snippets: A common practice in CNN backbone design is to enlarge network depth/width/input resolution, thereby enhancing model capacity by capturing more finegrained patterns within inputs. Similar in spirit, our work wants to delve into the process of scaling CNN+ViT hybrid backbones with high resolution inputs. Nevertheless, in analogy to the scaling of CNN backbones, simply enlarging the input resolution of prevalent ViT backbones will introduce practical challenge especially the sharply increased computational costs. Taking a widely adopted ViT backbone, Swin Transformer, as an example, when directly enlarging the input resolution from 224×224 to 384×384, the top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K is evidently increased from 83.5% to 84.5%.

sections.title: Resolution Challenges & Solutions
sections.text:
TLDR; Vision Transformers face significant computational barriers when handling high-resolution images due to quadratic complexity in attention mechanisms. Various solutions have emerged, including patch size optimization, multi-scale architectures, and efficient attention variants, allowing models to process increasingly larger images while maintaining reasonable computational costs. (9 sources)

A fundamental challenge in Vision Transformer applications lies in managing computational resources when processing high-resolution images. The standard attention mechanism creates a quadratic increase in computation requirements as image resolution increases - for example, scaling from 224×224 to 448×448 multiplies the self-attention computation by 16 times  [268248559 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 9].

This computational burden becomes particularly acute when handling multimodal tasks, where high-resolution images contain crucial detail-rich information needed for precise object recognition and relationship understanding  [271334712 | Ma et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. Traditional approaches often resort to significant downsampling of input images, which can severely impact performance in dense prediction tasks like semantic segmentation and pose estimation  [269983733 | Kienzle et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

Several innovative solutions have emerged to address these challenges:

1. Patch Size Optimization: Increasing patch sizes from typical values of 8-14 pixels to 224 allows efficient processing of ultra-high-definition images while keeping computational costs below 50G MACs  [272832088 | Hosu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8].

2. Multi-scale Architectures: Advanced frameworks like Swin Transformer implement alternating stages of shifting windows and non-overlapping patch partitioning, enabling flexible feature extraction at multiple scales  [272957384 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [244346076 | Liu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 1,750].

3. Native Resolution Preservation: Recent advancements incorporate techniques to preserve and even exceed native resolution through multiple image crops, helping capture fine-grained details from subtle objects, charts, and embedded text  [273351506 | Thapa et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

4. Progressive Processing Strategies: Some approaches selectively choose which high-resolution patches to use for specific tasks, trading off comprehensive high-resolution processing for computational efficiency  [270285666 | Arnold et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

These solutions demonstrate that while computational challenges persist, they are increasingly surmountable through careful architectural design and optimization strategies  [252683593 | Liang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 25].

citations.title: [252683593 | Liang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 25]
snippets: Despite the great success of transformer, its computation cost increases significantly when handling high-resolution representations, which are critical for dense prediction tasks. This paper attempts to resolve this issue by reducing the computation complexity during the inference stage, and presents a very simple solution for generating a large number of efficient vision transformer models directly from a single trained vision transformer, requiring no further training or fine-tuning.

citations.title: [268248559 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 9]
snippets: For instance, increasing the image resolution from 224 × 224 (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) to 448 × 448 multiplies the self-attention computation by 16 times.

citations.title: [269983733 | Kienzle et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]
snippets: Nowadays, real-life images, e.g.captured with mobile phone cameras, are of high resolution.However, most computer vision applications still work with low resolution images due to the high computational cost.Especially vision transformers (ViT) (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020) struggle with the quadratic complexity of the selfattention mechanism in high resolutions images.Consequently, most ViT based architectures perform a significant downsampling of the input image resolution.While this might not be a huge problem for tasks like image classification, it is a major drawback for dense pixel tasks like semantic segmentation, monocular depth estimation or human pose estimation.As a result, modern architectures like Segformer (Xie et al., 2021) have been developed to handle higher resolution images.

citations.title: [270285666 | Arnold et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets:
Getting better results in a vision transformer comes by using a higher resolution image or using smaller patches in a greater number. In both of these cases, the amount of patches being used as input increases. For instance, if the initial patch inputs is n, halving the size of the patches, or doubling resolution of the image will result in 4n patch inputs.

Our method trades off the benefits of high resolution patches without the need for every high-resolution patch as input. At the scales of HSI data, it is not practical to apply methods like ViT segmentation for high-resolution input. Instead, we suggest that deciding which high-resolution patches the segmentation algorithm can use helps to address computational issues.

citations.title: [271334712 | Ma et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
snippets: High-resolution images offer significant advantages for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by enabling the capture of detailed object information and complex relationships between objects in images.However, directly inputting high-resolution images into the vision encoder results in prohibitive computational expenses, primarily due to the quadratic complexity associated with the Transformer architecture [92] and the substantial increase in the number of visual tokens.

citations.title: [272832088 | Hosu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8]
snippets: To address this issue, we propose an architecture that can efficiently compute with fewer patches for high-resolution images by increasing the patch size, typically around 12 or 14, to 224. Doing so enables us to effectively handle UHD images with Vision Transformer architecture less than 50G MACs.

citations.title: [272957384 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: However, the original vision transformer (ViT) produces single-scale, low-resolution feature maps, which are inadequate for dense prediction tasks that require high-resolution features. Therefore, improvements on transformer models are necessary for their effective use in dense prediction tasks. Ranftl et al. (Ranftl et al., 2021) address this issue by assembling tokens from various stages of the vision transformer into image-like representations at multiple resolutions, progressively combining them into full-resolution predictions using a convolutional decoder. Similarly, Wang et al. (Wang et al., 2021) introduce a spatialreduction attention mechanism, constructing a progressively shrinking feature pyramid structure, which enables the model to flexibly learn multi-scale and high-resolution features. The Swin transformer (Liu et al., 2021) achieves multi-scale feature extraction through alternating stages of shifting windows and non-overlapping patch partitioning. This hierarchical approach, which merges varying numbers of image feature patches to construct feature maps of different scales and performs self-attention calculations within local windows, facilitates effective feature extraction and modeling capabilities at multiple scales.

citations.title: [273351506 | Thapa et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated the advantages of processing images at higher resolutions and utilizing multi-crop features to preserve native resolution details. However, despite these improvements, existing vision transformers (ViTs) still struggle to capture fine-grained details from less prominent objects, charts, and embedded text, limiting their effectiveness in certain tasks. In this paper, we extend recent high-resolution and multi-crop techniques by not only preserving the native resolution, but zooming in beyond it and extracting features from a large number of image sub-crops.

sections.title: Performance Impact Analysis
sections.text:
TLDR; Higher resolution generally correlates with improved model performance across various vision tasks, particularly for detecting and recognizing small objects. However, the marginal gains diminish at very high resolutions, and the choice between resolution and patch overlap can significantly impact performance depending on the specific application. (6 sources)

Studies examining the relationship between image resolution and Vision Transformer performance reveal clear quantitative benefits of using higher resolutions. Research shows that increasing resolution from 576 × 320 to 864 × 480 yields a 2.8% improvement in MOT metrics, with further increases to 1088 × 608 providing an additional 2.3% improvement  [237341579 | Zhu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 16].

Comparative analyses demonstrate significant advantages of high-resolution processing. For instance, ResFormer-B-MR achieved 81.72% Top-1 accuracy at high resolution (640) compared to just 75.86% at low resolution (96), representing improvements of 48% and 7.49% respectively over baseline models  [254125281 | Tian et al. | 2022 | Citations: 32].

However, the relationship between resolution and performance isn't strictly linear. Experiments with 256×256 versus 128×128 resolutions indicate that while lower resolutions help maintain context of entire objects, very low resolutions risk losing crucial detail information. Interestingly, even smaller global resolutions (32×32) can provide reasonable reconstruction for much larger outputs (512×512)  [249395640 | Ikehata | 2022 | Citations: 21].

An important finding emerges regarding the balance between resolution scaling and computational constraints. For resolutions exceeding 2048 × 1024, performance gains become minimal, suggesting diminishing returns at extreme resolutions. This aligns with observations that vanilla Vision Transformers become impractical beyond this point due to global attention computational complexity  [256218348 | Cantone et al. | 2023 | Citations: 20].

Recent research has identified nuanced interactions between resolution settings and patch configuration. When high-resolution alone fails to improve performance, introducing patch overlap can yield better results. For example, while 336*336 resolution reached saturation, switching to 290*290 with 4-pixel patch overlap produced remarkable improvements  [252918244 | Shao et al. | 2022 | Citations: 7].

citations.title: [237341579 | Zhu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 16]
snippets: We compared the differences between the models from three different resolutions (576 × 320, 864 × 480, and 1088 × 608). Table 3 lists the experimental results. When the resolution increased from 576 × 320 to 864 × 480, MOTA improved by 2.8%; when it is increased to 1088 × 608, MOTA continued to improve by 2.3%. The improvement of the encoder's input resolution is positively correlated with the improvement of model performance. Therefore, model performance can be improved by improving the input resolution (or reducing the patch size) under the condition that the computing force is allowed.

citations.title: [249395640 | Ikehata | 2022 | Citations: 21]
snippets: Table 4 compared different canonical resolutions either from 128×128 or 256×256 and we observe that 256×256 worked slightly better. This result indicates that though the lower resolution is helpful to see the entire object, important information for details could be discarded at very low resolution. On the other hand, it is surprising to see that 32×32 global lighting contexts from 128×128 canonical resolution still provides a reasonable reconstruction for 512×512 output resolution.

citations.title: [252918244 | Shao et al. | 2022 | Citations: 7]
snippets: The potential trade-off between fine-tuning on high-resolution and overlapping patches. We found that when high-resolution can not help in improving performance, adding overlapping between patches will keep making performance better. After we use the 336*336 resolution to fine-tune our model, it seems hard to improve in this stage. Instead, we use 290*290 resolution with 4 pixels patch overlapping, and get remarkable result shown in Table 3

citations.title: [254125281 | Tian et al. | 2022 | Citations: 32]
snippets: For instance, ResFormer-B-MR achieves a Top-1 accuracy of 75.86% and 81.72% when evaluated on relatively low and high resolutions respectively (i.e., 96 and 640), which are 48% and 7.49% better than DeiT-B.

citations.title: [256218348 | Cantone et al. | 2023 | Citations: 20]
snippets: As the input resolution increased, the SwinV2 model closed the performance gap with respect to the convolutional counterparts. We believe this might be due to two related factors. First, the local receptive field enforces the CNN to attain a global view of the input only in the very last layers. On the other hand, SwinV2 windows size scales with input resolution. Vanilla Vision Transformer is practically unusable at these high resolutions because of the computational complexity of global attention. For resolutions greater than 2048 × 1024, it is difficult to expect an increase in performance for both EfficientNet and SwinV2 since the results from 1536 × 768 to 2048 × 1024 are very close to each other. Other medical fields that make use of very high-resolution imaging could benefit from the Swin transformers scaling capability. In the field of mammography image analysis, many works adopt an input resolution of 224 × 224, we recommend using a resolution of the input images after cropping greater than 1200 × 600.

sections.title: Best Practices & Recommendations
sections.text:
TLDR; Based on extensive experimentation, optimal Vision Transformer configurations depend heavily on balancing resolution and patch size according to specific use cases. Key recommendations include starting with standard resolutions and gradually adjusting based on empirical results, while carefully considering computational constraints. (4 sources)

Based on systematic evaluations and research findings, here are the key recommended practices for implementing Vision Transformers with varying resolutions:

1. **Patch Size Selection**

   - Start with standard patch sizes (16x16) for initial implementation and evaluation  [277622031 | Morlier et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]

   - Consider experimenting with different patch sizes relative to desired resolution - for example, a 16x16 patch size tends to work better at lower resolutions (~128x128), while 12x12 patches may be more suitable for higher resolutions (~132x132)  [277622031 | Morlier et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]

2. **Resolution Scaling Strategy**

   - Begin with resolution ranges that match your computational capabilities <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

   - Gradually increase resolution while monitoring both accuracy and computational costs until reaching a satisfactory balance  [277622031 | Morlier et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]

   - Expect only moderate accuracy improvements (around 1-2%) for significant resolution reductions, while gaining substantial computational benefits  [277622031 | Morlier et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]

3. **Adaptive Approaches**

   - Implement dynamic resolution adjustment capabilities to handle variable input sizes effectively  [268723731 | Fan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 14]

   - Consider using fuzzy positional encoding to maintain consistent performance across different resolutions  [268723731 | Fan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 14]

4. **Task-Specific Considerations**

   - For document analysis or text detection tasks, consider using higher base resolutions than typical image classification tasks  [272464123 | Zhu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]

   - Be aware that standard 224-256 resolution training may be insufficient for specialized applications requiring finer detail discrimination  [272464123 | Zhu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]

5. **Evaluation Protocol**

   - Test across different resolution combinations before deployment <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

   - Document the specific resolution and patch size combinations that work best for your particular use case  [277622031 | Morlier et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]

citations.title: [268723731 | Fan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 14]
snippets: Our work introduces two key innovations to address this issue. Firstly, we propose a novel module for dynamic resolution adjustment, designed with a single Transformer block, specifically to achieve highly efficient incremental token integration. Secondly, we introduce fuzzy positional encoding in the Vision Transformer to provide consistent positional awareness across multiple resolutions, thereby preventing overfitting to any single training resolution. Our resulting model, ViTAR (Vision Transformer with Any Resolution), demonstrates impressive adaptability, achieving 83.3\% top-1 accuracy at a 1120x1120 resolution and 80.4\% accuracy at a 4032x4032 resolution, all while reducing computational costs.

citations.title: [272464123 | Zhu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]
snippets: Vision Transformer models are commonly pre-trained to process images at a fixed resolution, such as 224 or 336 pixels, which is commonly used for many image understanding tasks (Goyal et al., 2016)20,(Marino et al., 2019)(Li et al., 2022)(Li et al., 2023). However, these resolutions might be insufficient for precisely discerning tightly packed text in higher-resolution documents.

citations.title: [277622031 | Morlier et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets: We first explore the impact of resolution scaling by training and evaluating ViTs across a range of resolutions {8, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15}, keeping the patch size fixed at 16x16. This allows us to assess the effect of varying resolution, and by extension image resolution, on both the accuracy and computational cost of the model during training and evaluation. The results are shown on Figure 9 and show that reducing the resolution has a limited impact on accuracy. Specifically, we observe only a 1% drop in accuracy while achieving a 28% reduction in FLOPs when comparing the baseline with a resolution of 14 tokens per column or line. However, Increasing the resolution at a fixed patch size implies training and evaluating the ViT with a higher resolution image that can lead to a mismatch between the optimal image resolution and the optimal architecture resolution (i.e. tokens per column/line). In order to evaluate the relationship between the patch size and the architecture resolution, we train and evaluate ViT-S at two different resolutions {9, 11} and multiple patch size {8x8, 12x12, 16x16, 24x24, 32x32}, the results are shown on Table I. The best results for an architecture resolution of 9 and 11 are respectively obtained with patch size of 16x16 and 12x12, we can observe that the image resolution obtained with these resolution are similar with respectively 128x128 and 132x132 showing the importance of evaluating the best image size for the task and dataset selected.

question: What are open challenges in fuzzing?

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Fuzzing has evolved significantly since its introduction in 1990 as an automated testing approach. Despite continuous improvements in effectiveness and efficiency, ongoing challenges exist in making fuzzing more usable and powerful while addressing increasingly complex software requirements. (8 sources)

Fuzzing, introduced as an automated testing methodology in 1990, has become a fundamental approach for identifying software vulnerabilities by feeding automatically generated inputs into systems  [276557891 | Yan et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [14043069 | Miller et al. | 1990 | Citations: 1709]. Over the past decade, significant progress has been made in enhancing its capabilities through innovations in effectiveness, efficiency, and usability  [276557891 | Yan et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. Notable advancements have included improvements in feedback-directed fuzzing  [5687609 | Böhme et al. | 2016 | Citations: 556], parallel execution techniques  [39069234 | Böhme et al. | 2017 | Citations: 466], and automated fuzz driver generation  [174007166 | Babic et al. | 2019 | Citations: 165].

Coverage-based greybox fuzzing has emerged as a particularly effective technique for discovering software vulnerabilities  [269130904 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. However, modern software's increasing complexity presents persistent challenges for fuzzing. Contemporary applications often handle highly complex grammars and input formats, requiring sophisticated approaches to effectively explore input spaces  [266594798 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]  [269667841 | Green et al. | 2022 | Citations: 38].

The evolution of fuzzing continues to face several core challenges, including the difficulty of reaching deeper states in stateful systems and maintaining effective exploration without human intervention  [14535881 | Böhme et al. | 2020 | Citations: 62]. Research priorities consistently emphasize improving automation capabilities and developing robust theoretical foundations for fuzzing practices  [14535881 | Böhme et al. | 2020 | Citations: 62].

snippets:
In recent years, coverage-based greybox fuzzing has proven to be an effective and practical technique for discovering software vulnerabilities...However, there are a few hard challenges, even for the state-of-the-art fuzzers.

Generation-based fuzzers [1,6] rely on an input model describing the input format to produce legitimate test cases. Although the input model can sometimes be recovered from execution traces or program source codes by reverse engineering techniques, in most cases, fuzzers require experts with domain knowledge to provide input specifications. However, the model may be too complex to be complete and lack semantic constraints dictating relations across multiple input fields. As a result, they may not lead to good path coverage. In addition, inputs exploiting vulnerabilities are usually ill-formed files that do not follow input models. Generation-based fuzzers lack the ability to generate such ill-formed seed inputs.

A more popular way is mutating existing seed inputs at the bit and byte level to generate variants that allow exploring new program regions [3]5]. While this approach works well for simple and less constrained inputs, it may not be effective for inputs with complex structure and/or intensive cross-field constraints. These fuzzers tend to spend much time generating numerous inputs which however are rejected in the initial parsing stage, resulting in little code coverage improvement.

These advancements have addressed several challenges, ranging from enhancing its effectiveness and efficiency (Böhme et al., 2020)(Böhme et al., 2017)(Böhme et al., 2016) to improving its usability, exemplified by approaches such as automated fuzz driver generation (Babic et al., 2019)(Green et al., 2022)(Ispoglou et al., 2020)(Jeong et al., 2023)(Zhang et al., 2021).

sections.title: Technical Challenges
sections.text:
TLDR; Modern fuzzing faces several technical hurdles including resource management in parallel execution, handling complex stateful systems, and managing input validation and redundancy. Key challenges involve optimizing computation allocation, dealing with underspecified schemas, and balancing effectiveness with computational efficiency. (8 sources)

* **Resource Management and Parallel Efficiency**: Managing computing resources in parallel fuzzing environments presents significant challenges. Issues include task conflicts where multiple instances process similar paths, high synchronization overhead in distributed settings, and difficulties in optimal power allocation across instances  [253362401 | Zhou et al. | 2020 | Citations: 5].

* **State Management**: Fuzzing stateful systems is notably more challenging than stateless ones due to increased state spaces and difficulties in reaching deeper states. Stateful fuzzing remains a relatively young field and lacks mature, generic solutions compared to stateless approaches  [255522661 | Daniele et al. | 2023 | Citations: 16]  [270380234 | Daniele | 2024 | Citations: 1].

* **Input Validation and Semantic Space**: A significant challenge exists in generating inputs that pass validation checks while also exploring meaningful behaviors. Random sampling often produces invalid inputs that trigger early rejections, wasting computational resources  [254408720 | Kang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 9].

* **Schema Specification**: Black-box fuzzers struggle with under-specified schemas, limiting their ability to generate meaningful test cases for APIs and protocols  [262013406 | Arcuri et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7].

* **OS-Level Bottlenecks**: Operating system-level bottlenecks affect fuzzing performance, particularly in environments with heavy I/O operations. New operating primitives have been developed to mitigate file system contention and improve scaling  [266933313 | Di et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [9030231 | Xu et al. | 2017 | Citations: 182].

* **Redundancy Management**: Efficiently avoiding redundant test cases while ensuring comprehensive coverage of different behavioral outcomes remains a crucial challenge <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

* **Cross-System Interactions**: Fuzzing systems that interact with external services, such as databases and other APIs, introduces additional complexities in tracking and managing dependencies  [248693670 | Zhang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 33].

citations.title: [253362401 | Zhou et al. | 2020 | Citations: 5]
snippets:
To optimize parallel fuzzing towards resource-saving, we still need to overcome the following technical challenges.

(1) Task conflicts. In parallel fuzzing, owing to the absence of global scheduling and timely update of fuzzing information among the instances, different fuzzing instances may mutate the same seeds or generate redundant test cases that execute the same path, causing task conflicts, which will lead to a severe waste of testing resources. Though some tools, such as P-fuzz [32] and PAFL [33], try to synchronize fuzzing information among fuzzing instances, a centralized scheduling scheme is still required to optimize parallel fuzzing from a global perspective.

(2) Synchronization overhead. In parallel fuzzing, various fuzzing information can be shared among fuzzing instances to increase performance, such as seeds, coverage, hangs, and crashes. However, the synchronization overhead inevitably deducts the performance, and such deduction becomes more severe as instances increase. Thus, what information to share and how to share it is critical, especially in a distributed environment. To alleviate performance deduction and improve resource efficiency, some approaches [30][31][32][34] adopt periodical synchronization to achieve a tradeoff between effectiveness and efficiency. However, timely updating of fuzzing status is critical to avoid task conflict.

(3) Computing power allocation.

snippets: Challenges. Fuzzing the deep learning libraries poses challenges related to the selection of suitable inputs. The first challenge is that the space of inputs is large and many generated inputs do not belong to the domain of semantically-valid inputs. By randomly selecting inputs from the large input space, the vast majority of inputs would be rejected by the library's input validation checks, and therefore, fail to adequately test the library's behaviors. A second challenge is related to the redundancy of inputs. Given the observation of a test outcome (e.g., an exception thrown when invoked with a particular input), an appropriate strategy should be employed to pick an input that tests a different behavior from the already observed test outcome. Otherwise, the same library behavior would be tested again, leading to redundancies in fuzzing.

sections.title: Input Handling & Grammar Complexity
sections.text:
TLDR; Handling complex input formats and grammars remains a fundamental challenge in fuzzing, affecting both model-based and mutation-based approaches. The difficulty stems from the need to accurately represent input structures while generating meaningful test cases that can discover security issues despite strict validation checks. (4 sources)

Managing complex input formats and grammars presents distinct challenges for fuzzing approaches. Model-based fuzzers, while theoretically sound, heavily depend on accurate input models derived either from execution traces or program source codes through reverse engineering  [269130904 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. These models often prove too complex to implement completely and frequently lack semantic constraints that govern relationships between multiple input fields, resulting in suboptimal path coverage  [269130904 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

Mutation-based approaches face their own set of challenges, particularly when dealing with complex structured inputs. While effective for simpler input types, these methods often generate numerous invalid inputs that get rejected during initial parsing, resulting in inefficient testing processes  [269130904 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. Modern software frequently handles highly complex grammars, requiring substantial expertise to properly explore input spaces and identify security vulnerabilities  (Zhang et al._1,  2024).

Recent advances in mining context-free grammars from parsers have shown promise in automating the creation of test input generators  [237605106 | Dutra et al. | 2021 | Citations: 12]  [215758362 | Gopinath et al. | 2020 | Citations: 289]. This approach allows for unsupervised extraction of grammars from binaries without requiring access to source code, supporting both standard and custom extensions like JSONPath expressions and regular expressions. However, successfully extracting and utilizing these grammars for effective fuzzing remains an active area of research, highlighting the continuing importance of developing robust input handling mechanisms  [215758362 | Gopinath et al. | 2020 | Citations: 289].

snippets:
While FormatFuzzer is a highly efficient choice for domain-specific fuzzing, its modularity also makes it a useful platform for creating future fuzzers. Besides extending FormatFuzzer with further formats, our future work will focus on the following topics: 

Black-box strategies. Recent advances in grammar-based fuzzing, such as systematically achieving grammar coverage (Havrikov et al., 2019) or learning and leveraging probability distributions [49] could easily be adopted for binary template fuzzing, too. Search-based fuzzing. The decision seed format opens way for easily integrating alternate fuzzing strategies. Of particular interest is genetic optimization as part of search-based testing, since FormatFuzzer already implements mutation and crossover operations. Mining binary formats. Recent techniques for mining context-free grammars from parsers (Gopinath et al., 2020)(Mathis et al., 2019) could be adapted to binary formats, simplifying template construction. Mining binary constraints. Extending a (mined) syntactic template, we can track processing of individual input elements using dynamic tainting and dynamic analysis, and extract context-sensitive constraints from input processors. Engaging the community. We will be creating tutorials and other material to engage the community in writing binary templates. The Wikipedia list of file formats [2] lists more than 1,000 formats-so there is still lots to do!
