sections.title: Benchmarking & Evaluation Challenges
sections.text:
TLDR; Evaluating fuzzers effectively requires addressing multiple interconnected challenges, from establishing standardized benchmarks to defining comprehensive performance metrics. Current evaluation frameworks face issues with reproducibility, realistic test scenarios, and biased measurement approaches. (5 sources)

Evaluating fuzzers presents a complex landscape of interrelated challenges that extend beyond simple performance measurements. One fundamental issue lies in the practical usability of fuzzers, where many tools, despite being open-sourced, suffer from implementation limitations that hamper reproducible comparisons and systematic analysis  [222132978 | Li et al. | 2020 | Citations: 92]. This usability gap creates significant barriers to meaningful evaluation and advancement of the field.

A critical aspect of evaluation involves the selection and definition of appropriate benchmarks. There remains considerable debate about how to construct representative test targets and develop unbiased measurement methodologies that accurately reflect real-world vulnerable systems  [231592362 | Natella et al. | 2021 | Citations: 70]. Web API fuzzers, for instance, currently lack proper benchmarks for experimental evaluation, complicating efforts to compare and validate different approaches  [270258097 | Putu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

The establishment of comprehensive performance metrics represents another significant challenge. Current evaluation frameworks often rely on insufficient and oversimplified metrics that fail to capture the full spectrum of fuzzer behaviors and effectiveness  [222132978 | Li et al. | 2020 | Citations: 92]. This limitation necessitates the development of more nuanced and comprehensive evaluation criteria that can account for various aspects of fuzzer performance.

The relationship between coverage maximization and bug discovery effectiveness adds another layer of complexity to evaluation. While current state-of-the-art fuzzers prioritize maximizing code coverage, this approach doesn't necessarily translate to superior bug-finding capabilities  [260126016 | Wang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]. This disconnect highlights the need for evaluation metrics that better align with practical security objectives rather than purely coverage-based measures.

citations.title: [222132978 | Li et al. | 2020 | Citations: 92]
snippets: Conducting comprehensive and pragmatic evaluations of fuzzers entails overcoming multiple important challenges. First, although many fuzzers have been open sourced, their usability in practice is often limited, as reported by recent research (Peng et al., 2018)(Zhu et al., 2019), which results in reproducibility issues, impeding comparison. Thus, it is necessary to test and enhance fuzzers' usability. Second, the evaluation of fuzzers should be conducted on pragmatic benchmark programs. Existing benchmark programs are not satisfactory (Klees et al., 2018). A reliable evaluation of fuzzers thus calls for pragmatic benchmarks. Third, the assessment must be conducted based on a comprehensive set of performance metrics. Nevertheless, existing metrics are insufficient and rough, leading to incomplete assessments. Thus, it is important to augment the performance metrics for comprehensive evaluation.

sections.title: Automation & Integration Challenges
sections.text:
TLDR; Automating fuzzing workflows and integrating different fuzzing approaches remains challenging due to limited toolchain maturity and configuration complexity. Key obstacles include the need for better automation of fuzz driver generation and the difficulty of optimally combining multiple fuzzers in collaborative settings. (7 sources)

The automation of fuzzing processes faces significant hurdles, particularly in reducing the manual effort required for setup and maintenance. A critical challenge lies in automating the creation of effective fuzz drivers for standalone libraries, which traditionally demands extensive programming knowledge and careful manual coding  [232076395 | Zhang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 31]. Despite recognition of this need, research focusing on comprehensive automation of the entire fuzzing workflow remains sparse  [259262388 | Rahalkar | 2023 | Citations: 1].

The integration of different fuzzing approaches presents another significant challenge. While ensemble approaches aim to leverage diversity across different fuzzers, concerns persist about the sufficient coverage of various fuzzing strategies and the scalability of ensemble architectures  [49557490 | Chen et al. | 2018 | Citations: 11]. The complexity of identifying optimal configurations across diverse techniques further complicates matters, particularly in collaborative fuzzing scenarios where multiple different fuzzers need coordination  (Zhang et al._2,  2024).

The emergence of AI-based approaches adds new layers of complexity to automation and integration. Large Language Models (LLMs) introduce specific challenges in areas such as automatic prompt construction and output validation  [266690829 | Lyu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 15]. These challenges are compounded by broader concerns about data quality and dataset bias, which can significantly impact the performance of AI-integrated fuzzing systems  [267365086 | Huang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 14]  [49882503 | Lemieux et al. | 2017 | Citations: 50].

citations.title: [232076395 | Zhang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 31]
snippets: Fuzzing is a technique widely used in vulnerability detection. The process usually involves writing effective fuzz driver programs, which, when done manually, can be extremely labor intensive. Previous attempts at automation leave much to be desired, in either degree of automation or quality of output. In this paper, we propose IntelliGen, a framework that constructs valid fuzz drivers automatically. First, IntelliGen determines a set of entry functions and evaluates their respective chance of exhibiting a vulnerability. Then, IntelliGen generates fuzz drivers for the entry functions through hierarchical parameter replacement and type inference. We implemented IntelliGen and evaluated its effectiveness on real-world programs selected from the Android Open-Source Project, Google's fuzzer-testsuite and industrial collaborators. IntelliGen covered on average 1.08X-2.03X more basic blocks and 1.36X-2.06X more paths over state-of-the-art fuzz driver synthesizers FUDGE and FuzzGen. IntelliGen performed on par with manually written drivers and found 10 more bugs.

The first potential threat is the insufficient diversity of the base fuzzers. In section III-A for the base fuzzers selection, we propose three different dimensions, including the coverage information granularity diversity, seed generation strategy diversity, and seed mutation as well as selection strategy diversity. For the implementation of EnFuzz, we select AFL, AFLFast, AFLGo and FairFuzz as the base fuzzers. They are open-source and can demonstrate the issue of generalization ability easily based on their previous evaluations and comparisons, but they partially cover those dimensions and may be insufficient...We can integrate other available fuzzers to improve the diversity of base fuzzers. Another problem related is regarding those three dimensions equally. For example, compared with same-type fuzzers' strategies (e.g. mutation or selection strategy), the diversity of different types of fuzzers (e.g. generation-based and mutation-based) is usually larger. Therefore, difference in fuzzers' types contribute more to the improvement in performance. We can assign different weights to different dimensions after empirical studies. Also, based on the three basic dimensions, we can try to adapt some diversity measures in ensemble learning to ensemble fuzzing, such as sub-sampling the training examples. 

The second potential threat is the mechanism scalability of the ensemble architecture. In section III-B about the ensemble architecture design, we propose the seed synchronization mechanism and result integration mechanism. sections.title: Future Research Directions
sections.text:
TLDR; Emerging research directions in fuzzing center on leveraging machine learning for smarter exploration and improving automation capabilities. Key areas include developing hybrid approaches that combine multiple fuzzing techniques, advancing performance prediction models, and creating more efficient ways to utilize cloud infrastructure. (7 sources)

* **Machine Learning Integration**: Research is needed to develop effective ML-guided fuzzing approaches that can achieve higher precision and recall rates while efficiently reducing search spaces. Particular attention must be paid to incorporating ML models specifically designed for cross-contract vulnerability detection  [249652483 | Xue et al. | 2021 | Citations: 41].

* **Automation Theory Development**: There is a pressing need to build a stronger theoretical foundation for fuzzing practices, moving beyond incremental improvements in specific techniques toward principled approaches to automated testing  [268388023 | Schloegel et al. | 2024 | Citations: 24]  [14535881 | Boehme et al. | 2020 | Citations: 62].

* **Hybrid Approaches**: Developing hybrid fuzzing strategies that combine protocol-specific and application-specific techniques shows promise for creating more effective testing approaches. Special attention is needed for systems with complex branching logic and messaging-based architectures  [260975154 | Mantu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0].

* **Human-Automation Interaction**: Further research is warranted in human-in-the-loop approaches, particularly given practitioner interest in combining automated efficiency with human insight  [14535881 | Boehme et al. | 2020 | Citations: 62].

* **Cloud Infrastructure Optimization**: Exploring innovative ways to harness cloud computing resources for fuzzing presents untapped opportunities, particularly in terms of improving performance prediction models and optimizing test suite execution  [2737956 | Papadakis et al. | 2018 | Citations: 333].

* **Performance Prediction Models**: Advancing models that can better predict fuzzer performance and experiment duration remains an important research direction, helping users make more informed decisions about resource allocation  [2737956 | Papadakis et al. | 2018 | Citations: 333].

* **LLM-Based Enhancement**: Research into leveraging Large Language Models for fuzzing purposes, addressing challenges in accuracy, scalability, and adaptation to different contexts, represents an emerging frontier  [269362337 | Jiang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 9].

sections.title: Introduction to NURBS
sections.text:
TLDR; NURBS (Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines) is a fundamental mathematical framework used across mathematics, computer science, and engineering disciplines. It serves as the standard mathematical foundation for describing both analytical and free-form shapes in computer-aided design systems. (4 sources)

NURBS represents a sophisticated mathematical framework that combines curves and surfaces into a unified approach for geometric modeling. Its significance spans multiple technical domains, including Mathematics, Computer Science, and Engineering, particularly in Computer Aided Design (CAD), Computer Aided Geometric Design (CAGD), and Computational Mathematics  [19875215 | Zhang et al. | 2017 | Citations: 3].

At its core, NURBS consists of three essential components: B-spline basis functions, control points, and weight vectors that collectively determine the degrees of freedom of the resulting curve or surface  [7282632 | Silva et al. | 2013 | Citations: 1]. This mathematical model gained widespread adoption because it provides a standardized way to describe both analytical curves and surfaces, as well as free-form shapes  [230567590 | Zhu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 1].

One of NURBS' most notable achievements is becoming the predominant mathematical description method in computer-aided design systems. Its universal applicability and straightforward computational implementation made it particularly valuable for defining product geometry in manufacturing contexts  [230567590 | Zhu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 1]. The technology has proven especially important in standard geometric exchange formats, serving as the mathematical foundation for industry-standard specifications like IGES (Initial Graphics Exchange Specification) and STEP (Standard for the Exchange of Product Model Data)  [216340432 | Liu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 4].

sections.title: Applications of NURBS
sections.text:
TLDR; NURBS finds extensive use across diverse domains including robotics, computer graphics, and manufacturing. Key applications include surface modeling, trajectory planning, and geometric design optimization, with particular strength in creating precise complex shapes and deformable surfaces. (5 sources)

* **Robotics Path Planning and Control**: NURBS serve as powerful tools for trajectory generation and path smoothing in robotic systems. Their ability to handle both control points and weights makes them highly adaptable for generating optimal movement patterns in industrial robots, autonomous vehicles, and mobile platforms  [52312991 | Ravankar et al. | 2018 | Citations: 245].

* **Surface Modeling and Animation**: NURBS excel in creating smooth, complex surfaces with high computational efficiency. The method uses control points, kernels, and weights to define surfaces, making it particularly valuable for industrial design and animation production  [266731910 | Yu | 2023 | Citations: 0].

* **Geometric Design Optimization**: NURBS demonstrate superior capability in representing both analytical shapes and free-form designs. Their geometric invariance under various transformations like translation, scaling, and projection makes them particularly efficient for design optimization tasks  [243917340 | Cui et al. | 2021 | Citations: 40].

* **Virtual Reality and Interactive Systems**: Advanced NURBS implementations enable interactive control and selection of specific regions of interest in surface models. This capability facilitates detailed editing and modification of complex geometric models within CAD environments  [123328604 | Fazanaro et al. | 2016 | Citations: 9].

* **Free-form Shape Generation**: NURBS provide an effective solution for creating compact and smooth shapes, combining flexibility with versatility. This characteristic makes them particularly valuable for applications requiring complex geometric representations  [3569001 | Mao et al. | 2018 | Citations: 8].

* **Manufacturing and Quality Control**: The technology enables accurate geometric modeling and measurement in manufacturing processes <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

sections.title: Ray Tracing Techniques for NURBS
sections.text:
TLDR; Ray tracing of NURBS surfaces involves specialized algorithms to compute intersections between rays and parametric surfaces. While traditional approaches focused on direct intersection calculations, modern techniques employ acceleration strategies like Bézier clipping and GPU-based tessellation to improve efficiency. (7 sources)

Ray tracing has emerged as a primary method for generating high-quality 3D images, though working with NURBS surfaces presents unique challenges since most modern renderers primarily handle triangular primitives  [60661774 | Sisojevs | 2012 | Citations: 0]. Early approaches to ray-NURBS intersection focused on direct computation methods, notably Kajiya's pioneering algorithm from 1982, which could handle bicubic surface patches without requiring preliminary subdivisions. However, this method proved computationally expensive, potentially requiring thousands of floating-point operations per ray-patch intersection  [60661774 | Sisojevs | 2012 | Citations: 0].

Modern techniques have evolved to address these computational challenges through various optimization strategies. One significant advancement is the Bézier clipping method, which projects the ray-surface intersection problem from 4D to 2D space and reduces arithmetic operations by approximately 50% per subdivision iteration  [60661774 | Sisojevs | 2012 | Citations: 0]. For containment checking within trimmed NURBS surfaces, advanced algorithms combine algebraic and geometric approaches, leveraging the convex hull property of Bézier curves to accelerate recursive subdivision  [268691772 | Spainhour et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6].

GPU acceleration has become increasingly important in handling NURBS tessellation, as traditional CPU-based approaches face performance limitations due to data transfer bottlenecks  [36930968 | Concheiro et al. | 2010 | Citations: 6]. Recent developments include adaptive stepping algorithms specifically designed for NURBS surfaces, which dynamically adjust sampling rates to balance accuracy and computational cost  [54833907 | Fu et al. | 2015 | Citations: 4].

Despite these advances, ray tracing NURBS surfaces remains computationally intensive, often leading to longer rendering times compared to simpler geometric representations  [55575737 | Gusiatin et al. | 2017 | Citations: 0]. Various field-oriented methods and parametric approaches continue to emerge, particularly for visualizing complex freeform surfaces  [215738930 | Wei et al. | 2019 | Citations: 0]. However, these specialized techniques remain less common in practical applications, where triangle-based representations often dominate due to their computational efficiency  [226551447 | Xu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 0].

citations.title: [215738930 | Wei et al. | 2019 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Low-frequency methods are typically limited to problems of small electrical size due to limitations of computation time and system memory. The ray-based high-frequency EM method, shooting and bouncing rays (SBR), are employed to solve THz target scattering. A very common way of representing arbitrary targets is via a surface mesh made of triangular facets. To guarantee the geometrical accuracy, a small size of the mesh elements must be chosen. Ray tracing becomes more time-consuming while in THz band. A special ray-tracing technique that combined geometric optics (GO) with non-uniform rational B-Splines (NURBS) has been implemented.

citations.title: [226551447 | Xu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Interpolation and approximation of curves and surfaces through an array of points have been researched very early (Nielson, 1984)(Meier et al., 1987)(Higashi et al., 1988)(Kallay, 1987)(Moreton et al., 1992)(Takahashi, 1998). The algorithm of merging several B-spline curves to one B-spline curve has been proposed by Tai et al. (Tai et al., 2003). They optimized the position of control points to merge two B-spline curves as precisely as possible, and adjusted the knots to avoid superfluous knots. Harish et al. (Pungotra et al., 2010) proposed an algorithm of merging two or more B-spline surfaces which is suitable for virtual reality applications. It's fast and robust, and even more robust than the common NURBS-based modeling software tool, Rhino. More B-spline curves and surfaces merging algorithms are referred in (Lu, 2014)(Shu et al., 2014)(Lin et al., 2015)(Yan et al., 2016) and the references therein.

citations.title: [268691772 | Spainhour et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]
snippets: Containment within regions defined by Bézier curves has also been studied in the context of 2D parametric trimming curves for 3D NURBS surface patches.In this sub-problem, it must be determined if a point in the 2D parameter space of the 3D surface is contained within the (often, but not necessarily watertight) trimming curves.Because this and other contemporary 2D containment problems are frequently solved with ray casting algorithms [Marussig and Hughes 2017], we note that they can largely be divided into two categories.In the algebraic approach, intersections between rays and arbitrary curves can be computed using typical root-finding techniques in parameter space [Patrikalakis and Maekawa 2010], although standard bisection and gradient descent methods can only identify at most a single point of intersection.In contrast, geometric approaches take place in physical space, decomposing the curve into subcurves until intersections with the ray can be identified [Farin 2001].The current state-of-the art method, Bézier clipping (Nishita et al., 1990)(Sellán et al., 2022)], lies at the intersection of these two approaches, where recursive algebraic subdivision is accelerated using the convex hull property of a Bézier curve.

citations.title: [36930968 | Concheiro et al. | 2010 | Citations: 6]
snippets:
NURBs (Non-Uniform rational B-splines) surfaces (Piegl and Tiller, 1997) have been widely employed in CAD/CAM tools and graphic applications due to their capabilities for modeling complex geometries. Together with the high quality associated with the NURBS models, another advantage of the NURBS representations is the compactness of the description and, as a consequence, the low storage and transmission requirements.

Current GPUs (Graphic Processing Unit) are triangle oriented and not designed for the direct rendering of parametric representations. Therefore, these representations are usually tessellated into triangles in the CPU (Central Processing Unit) before being sent to GPU to be displayed. This strategy presents some problems which diminishes system performance, for example, the amount of information to be sent from CPU to GPU or the increment in the storage requirements associated with the triangle mesh.

To synthesize parametric surfaces on the GPU the tessellation of the models is directly realizing on the GPU (Guthe et al., 2005;Dyken et al., 2009). In these proposals the rendering process is performed per patch (Guthe et al., 2005) or per set of patches according to the required level of detail (Dyken et al., 2009).

snippets: In this paper, aiming at improving the accuracy and efficiency of creeping ray tracing on arbitrarily shaped NURBS surface, we present a creeping ray tracing algorithm based on a novel adaptive variable step Euler method. Since the adaptive variable step Euler method is based on the conventional Euler method, the efficiency is ensured. And in the process of numerically iteratively solving the GDE, due to the introduction of shape factor , the discrete step sizes are adaptively corrected timely. Hence, compared with the conventional Euler method, the proposed method can easily ensure the accuracy of creeping ray tracing on arbitrarily shaped NURBS surface. Namely, it is more suitable for engineering applications. The efficiency and accuracy of the proposed method will be analyzed and verified by comparing the results of different methods.

The author proposed to transform the NURBS surface into rational Bezier regions at the stage of preliminary preparation of the algorithm to work which requires additional computational costs. A complex approach is presented in [5]. Parametrically free surface forms and the most suitable for them way of visualization by the ray tracing method are studied there. In general, analysis of works [4]5] makes it possible to note that the use of NURBS and other parametric curves and surfaces significantly lengthens time of rendering the scene by the ray tracing method. This makes it difficult to use standard algorithms for image synthesis with the help of the ray tracing method.

citations.title: [60661774 | Sisojevs | 2012 | Citations: 0]
snippets:
Ray tracing has become a popular method for generating high quality images. Most of the modern ray tracing based applications only deals with triangles as basic primitives. NURBS surface representation is common for most of 3D modelling tools because of its compactness and the useful geometric properties of NURBS surfaces. Using the direct ray tracing of NURBS surfaces, one can achieve better quality of rendered images (Efremov et al., 2005). There are many approaches to solving this problem.

In 1982 Kajiya (Kajiya, 1982) used ideas from algebraic geometry to obtain a numerical procedure for intersecting a ray with a bicubic surface patch. His method is robust, not requiring preliminary subdivisions to satisfy some a priori approximation. It proceeds more quickly for patches of lower degree. The algorithm is simply structured and does not require memory overhead. But unfortunately the algorithm has many disadvantages. It does not significantly utilize coherence. The algorithm computes all intersections of the given ray with a surface patch, even if just closest intersection need to be found. And finally the algorithm performs enormous amounts of floating point operations. Kajiya estimates that 6000 floating point operations may have to be performed in order to find all of the intersections between one ray and one bicubic patch. In the modern ray tracing applications global illumination algorithms are commonly used, and million of rays can be tested against one parametric patch. It makes the proposed algorithm unpractical [2].

T.Nishita, T.W.Sederberg, and M.Kakimoto (Nishita et al., 1990) described methods crossing for problem solution in star -rational Bezier surface. This method was called Bezier clipping. This method can be classified as an algorithm partly based on division and partly as calculation method. After ray representation as crossing of two planes, ray -surface crossing problem can be projected from 4D space to 2D space. This method reduces the number of arithmetical operations which is necessary to perform de Casteljau subdivision with 50% in every subdivision iteration. Nishita highlighted that Bezier cutting idea can be successfully applied in cases when we need to resolve problem of cropped region estimation. At the same time Nishita noted that described method does not resolve some tasks, one of them being the frequent point search problem and the instability of the method in some surface special cases.

sections.title: Challenges and Limitations
sections.text:
TLDR; Despite its versatility, NURBS faces several inherent technical constraints including tensor product limitations, computational complexity, and storage requirements. These challenges affect both the theoretical foundations and practical implementation of NURBS in ray tracing applications. (3 sources)

While NURBS offers powerful geometric modeling capabilities, it comes with several significant technical limitations that impact its use in ray tracing and related applications:

* **Tensor Product Constraints**: The fundamental tensor product nature of NURBS creates a structured grid dependency in the parametric space and control points. This architectural limitation leads to increased redundancy in degrees of freedom, affecting both memory usage and computational efficiency  [322926 | Lian et al. | 2012 | Citations: 13].

* **Integration Complexity**: Due to the rational function nature of NURBS, exact integration using traditional numerical methods like Gauss quadrature becomes challenging. This limitation affects applications requiring precise mathematical integration  [322926 | Lian et al. | 2012 | Citations: 13].

* **Patch Continuity Issues**: NURBS surfaces typically achieve only C⁰ continuity between adjacent patches, necessitating additional mathematical treatments for smooth transitions between segments  [322926 | Lian et al. | 2012 | Citations: 13].

* **Storage Requirements**: NURBS representations require substantial storage space due to their comprehensive control point and weight matrices  [52312991 | Ravankar et al. | 2018 | Citations: 245].

* **Parametrization Sensitivity**: The effectiveness of NURBS models heavily depends on proper initialization of weights. Poor weight initialization can result in undesirable parametrization outcomes  [52312991 | Ravankar et al. | 2018 | Citations: 245].

* **Geometry Repair Needs**: NURBS-based geometries often require post-processing repairs to address potential gaps or overlaps between patches, adding complexity to the modeling workflow  [322926 | Lian et al. | 2012 | Citations: 13].

These challenges have led to ongoing research into alternative approaches, such as T-splines, which aim to reduce the number of control points while maintaining similar modeling capabilities  [236521081 | Kermarrec et al. | 2021 | Citations: 6].

snippets:
Non-uniform Rational B-Splines (NURBS) [115](Scott et al., 2012) are an extension of Bsplines by introducing the weights for basis functions to represent a wider range of geometries such as conic sections. From a geometric point of view, NURBS in R d is a projective transformation of B-splines in R d+1 . NURBS inherit the properties of B-splines as mentioned above, but still have some drawbacks: 

Rational functions As NURBS are not polynomial functions, integrating them cannot be done exactly using Gauß quadrature. 

Tensor product The parametric space and control points rely on a structured grid due to the tensor product property of NURBS, which increases the redundancy of the degrees of freedom. 

Continuity NURBS usually achieve only C 0 continuity between the patches. 

Geometry repair From a computational geometry point of view, NURBS based geometry always requires some level of repair due to gaps or overlaps of the various patches making up a geometry.

sections.title: Current Implementations and Tools
sections.text:
TLDR; Modern implementations of NURBS ray tracing span academic libraries, optimization frameworks, and specialized design tools. These implementations focus on both geometric accuracy and computational efficiency, with recent developments emphasizing GPU acceleration and integrated optimization capabilities. (6 sources)

Recent implementations of NURBS processing in ray tracing applications showcase diverse approaches to balancing geometric fidelity with computational efficiency. The FORMIDABLE optical design library demonstrates one approach to simulating optical systems using ray-traced NURBS surfaces, incorporating features for quantitative performance assessment and integration with external optimization algorithms  [265410904 | Volatier | 2023 | Citations: 3].

Surface modeling implementations often integrate NURBS with intuitive interaction tools. These systems allow users to modify both curves and surfaces in 3D modeling environments, typically employing sets of control points and weighted parameters to achieve desired shapes  [266725295 | Chatterjee | 2024 | Citations: 1].

Advanced implementations now incorporate sophisticated mesh generation techniques for NURBS surfaces. These approaches begin with parametric curve definition, progress through control point mapping, and utilize molecular dynamics simulations to optimize sample point distributions for subsequent triangulation  [202559273 | Perumal | 2019 | Citations: 19].

Some modern frameworks treat NURBS as alternatives to traditional Bézier modules, offering improved differentiation capabilities. For instance, the NURBS-Diff implementation provides enhanced functionality for handling NURBS curves and surfaces in computational workflows  [265659865 | Worchel et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7].

Local Refinement NURBS (LR NURBS) represents a newer implementation direction, focusing on overcoming traditional NURBS limitations in terms of local adaptivity. This approach includes automated remeshing capabilities and has found applications in contact computations involving complex 3D geometries  [14006279 | Zimmermann et al. | 2017 | Citations: 38].

For real-world applications, some implementations emphasize the importance of initial conditions and boundary conditions during the development phase. This is particularly crucial in scenarios involving thermal gradients, stress loads, and varying material properties  [226194894 | Guessous et al. | 2020 | Citations: 0]  [110926753 | Zheleznyakova | 2015 | Citations: 1].

citations.title: [14006279 | Zimmermann et al. | 2017 | Citations: 38]
snippets: LR NURBS can model complex geometries exactly and are the rational extension of LR B-splines. The local representation of the parameter space overcomes the drawback of non-existent local refinement in standard NURBS-based isogeometric analysis. For a convenient embedding into general finite element codes, the Bézier extraction operator for LR NURBS is formulated. An automatic remeshing technique is presented that allows adaptive local refinement and coarsening of LR NURBS. In this work, LR NURBS are applied to contact computations of 3D solids and membranes.

citations.title: [202559273 | Perumal | 2019 | Citations: 19]
snippets: In (Zheleznyakova, 2015), the authors developed a method to form triangulations for 3D surfaces by first parametrising the NURBS curves in physical domain. NURBS hull is then formed through connection of control points (in rows and columns) in the actual physical domain. These control points are later mapped to a parameter domain. These control points in the parameter domain act as initial sample points for triangulation. Distribution of these initial sample points is made uniform or non-uniform (in case of adaptive meshing) through physical simulation such as molecular dynamics method. Once the distribution of the sample points has been optimised in the parameter domain, these sample points are then re-mapped to the physical domain. Finally triangulation takes place based on Delaunay method.

Unlike virtual clay, the NURBS-based surface modeling method only modifies  the object's surface. In this modeling approach, the objects utilized are typically represented using implicit curves or surfaces (Lamousin et al., 1994). Sometimes, the implicit surfaces are discretized into mesh data structures (Liverani et al., 2004); sometimes, the curves are tessellated with mesh as well. A set of control points defines the shape of the surface, and a set of weights controls the influence of each control point on the shape. Research by Liverani et al. (Liverani et al., 2004) and Schkolne et al. (Schkolne et al., 2001) used NURBS in different environments and interaction tools.

sections.title: Introduction/Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Faceted plots evolved from early concepts of small multiples and trellis displays into modern visualization tools. They emerged as a solution for displaying complex multivariate data through multiple coordinated views, becoming particularly important in data science and exploratory analysis. (6 sources)

Faceted plots trace their conceptual origins to two influential works in the late 1980s: Edward Tufte's "small multiples" approach and Robert Gentleman and Ross Ihaka's "trellis displays"  [231632301 | Hurley et al. | 2021 | Citations: 9]  [266499322 | Becker et al. | 1996 | Citations: 273]. Over time, these ideas merged into what we now know as "faceting," a fundamental visualization technique that became widely adopted through Hadley Wickham's innovations  [231632301 | Hurley et al. | 2021 | Citations: 9].

At their core, faceted datasets organize multivariate data items into multiple orthogonal categories, originally developed for browsing large data stores  [67750541 | Ghoniem et al. | 2019 | Citations: 95]. Modern faceted plots have evolved to become essential tools for analyzing complex datasets, particularly when dealing with multiple facets such as spatial, temporal, or textual information  [67750541 | Ghoniem et al. | 2019 | Citations: 95]  [16870232 | Hadlak et al. | 2015 | Citations: 84].

A key advantage of faceted visualization is that it enables analysts to examine different data subsets while maintaining consistency across views  [272616419 | Chen et al. | 2024 | Citations: 12]. This capability becomes especially valuable when analysts need to compare patterns across different conditions or categories, as it preserves the ability to understand relationships within each subset while facilitating cross-subset comparisons <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

snippets: Visualizing data via conditioning or slicing was popularized by the "small multiples" of Tufte (1986) and the trellis displays of (Becker et al., 1996). snippets: In faceted datasets, multivariate data items are grouped in multiple orthogonal categories. Originally used as an approach to search and browse large data stores and text corpora (Cao et al., 2010)(Smith et al., 2006), later work extended the faceted approach to include relationship visualization (Lee et al., 2009)(Zhao et al., 2013). citations.title: [16870232 | Hadlak et al. | 2015 | Citations: 84]
snippets: Graph visualization is an important ﬁeld in information visualization that is centered on the graphical display of graph-structured data. Yet real world data is rarely just graph-structured, but instead exhibits multiple facets, such as multivariate attributes, or spatial and temporal frames of reference. In an effort to display different facets of a graph, such a wealth of visualization techniques has been developed in the past that current surveys focus on a single additional facet only in order to enumerate and classify them. This report builds on existing graph visualization surveys for the four common facets of partitions, attributes, time, and space. It contributes a generic high-level categorization of faceted graph visualization that subsumes the existing classiﬁcations, which can be understood as facet-speciﬁc reﬁnements of the resulting categories. Furthermore, it extends beyond existing surveys by applying the same categorization to graph visualizations with multiple facets. For each of the introduced categories and considered facets, this overview provides visualization examples to illustrate instances of their realization.

sections.title: Core Definition & Components
sections.text:
TLDR; Faceted plots consist of multiple related visualizations arranged in a structured layout, typically sharing consistent axes and scales. They combine a 2D faceting structure with computed visual elements to display data subsets effectively. (5 sources)

At its foundational level, a faceted plot comprises two essential components: a 2-dimensional faceting structure (COORD) that determines how data is organized, and computational elements (ELEMENT) that define how data is rendered within each facet  [259287221 | Becker et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]. These components work together to display subsets of data in panels that maintain visual consistency across the entire plot.

Within the Grammar of Graphics framework, facets serve as a mechanism to partition data into meaningful subsets while ensuring that each panel shares the same coordinate system and visual properties  [272146358 | Guo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [247112928 | Dunnington et al. | 2022 | Citations: 18]. This standardization of scales and labels across panels facilitates direct comparison between different data subsets  [247112928 | Dunnington et al. | 2022 | Citations: 18].

A notable characteristic of faceted plots is their ability to arrange multiple similar visual components in a coordinated manner. Rather than duplicating entire visual structures for each subset, which could lead to confusion, faceting provides a cleaner approach to displaying concatenated visual elements  [253370347 | Ying et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]. Common implementations of this principle include scatterplot matrices and various forms of conditioned choropleth maps, where individual plots are organized within an overarching framework that maintains clear visual hierarchy  [60913436 | Grolemund et al. | 2015 | Citations: 13].

citations.title: [247112928 | Dunnington et al. | 2022 | Citations: 18]
snippets: In the Grammar of Graphics, facets are defined as displaying subsets of a data set in panels of the same graphic (Bailey, 2007). Using a data structure with one row per measurement, plotting multiple parameters on same plot using facets is a natural way to represent these data. In ggplot2, facets also coordinate the scales and labels for each panel.

citations.title: [253370347 | Ying et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]
snippets: For example, the component in Fig. 3(B2) can be regarded as "a layered visualization with a density plot and a graph" and "a facet visualization whose elements are pie charts" from the perspective of implementation...For another example, a faceted visualization can be considered as a concatenation of a list of similar visual components. Representing the chart with "concat" has to duplicate the structures of similar visual components multiple times. Instead, it is much neater and more accurate to use "facet" to represent it in the context of data visualization.

snippets:
Faceted plots are made up of (sub)plots which are themselves plotted within the coordinate system defined by the faceting (Wilkinson, 2005). Furthermore, we have shown that tables are faceted data visualizations. At its core, then, a table has two components: 

1. A 2-dimensional faceting structure (COORD), and 2. a set of computations to be performed within each facet (ELEMENT).

citations.title: [272146358 | Guo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: The Grammar of Graphics (implemented by ggplot2) [52] specification uses layered components to encode visual representation layers, scales for aesthetic attributes, a coordinate system to map the position on the plot, and facets to partition data into subsets.

citations.title: [60913436 | Grolemund et al. | 2015 | Citations: 13]
snippets: Other popular embedded plots combine common graphs into a table of subplots. These embedded plots include scatterplot matrices (Chambers 1983), conditioned choropleth maps (Carr et al., 2005), trellis plots (Sarkar 2008), and facetted plots (Wilkinson and Wills 2005). In these embedded plots, each subplot contains an explicit set of axes and the subplots are organized into a larger implicit frame-usually a visual table, which can be thought of as a cartesian graph that has categorical x and y variables.

sections.title: Types of Faceting Functions
sections.text:
TLDR; Two primary types of faceting functions dominate modern visualization software: facet_wrap() for creating ribbon-like arrangements and facet_grid() for 2D grid layouts. These functions offer distinct approaches to organizing and presenting multiple data subsets within a cohesive visualization. (4 sources)

* **Facet_wrap()**

  - Creates a linear sequence of plots that wraps into a 2D arrangement like a ribbon  [33661624 | Ito et al. | 2013 | Citations: 626]

  - Automatically arranges plots in a compact layout without requiring predefined grid dimensions

  - Particularly useful for exploring longitudinal data by distributing observations along one dimension while maintaining consistent axes and visual properties  [253508817 | Berker et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3]

* **Facet_grid()**

  - Generates a full 2D grid of panels that can be arranged by both rows and columns  [33661624 | Ito et al. | 2013 | Citations: 626]

  - Uses a formula syntax where:

    * ".~ group" creates plots arranged by column

    * "group ~ ." creates plots arranged by row

    * "group ~ sex" creates a 2D grid combining both variables  [33661624 | Ito et al. | 2013 | Citations: 626]

* **Variable-Based Faceting**

  - Binary variables: Simply splits data based on the presence/absence of the variable

  - Continuous variables: Calculates mean values to divide data into two sub-populations

  - All facets maintain identical axes ranges for easy cross-comparison  [257255382 | Guo et al. | 2023 | Citations: 14]

* **Network Visualization Faceting**

  - Specialized implementation for separating dense networks into smaller, comparable subnetworks

  - Allows edges to appear in only one panel while maintaining consistent node positions across all facets

  - Particularly useful for visualizing network structures as functions of temporal or categorical attributes  [65026250 | Tyner et al. | 2017 | Citations: 34]

While this use of multifaceted figures seems to be rare in some journals where space constraints are applied, they are a great way of inspecting longitudinal data by distributing them along one dimension while keeping all other aesthetics (e.g., axes, colors, etc.) consistent.

However, if a faceting variable is continuous, the TreatmentEffectExplorer module first calculates the variable mean, which is then used to divide the cohort into two sub-populations...All faceted plots in the TreatmentEffectExplorer module share the same  and  axes ranges to support easy comparison across the different visualizations.

citations.title: [33661624 | Ito et al. | 2013 | Citations: 626]
snippets: The concept of conditioning plots by the levels of one or more factors is called faceting in ggplot2. There are two faceting functions: facet_wrap() and facet_grid(). Both use a formula to determine the layout, and both share a common argument scales =, but otherwise, they are separate entities. facet_grid() is capable of generating a 2D grid of graphics panels-by column and/or by row. For example, facet_grid(.~ group) generates multipanel plots per level of a factor group by column, but facet_grid(group ~.) will generate plots by row. The dot (.) indicates that no variable is specified for that side of the formula. By specifying both sides, such as facet_grid(group ~ sex), a 2D grid of multipanel plots by group and by sex will be produced. In contrast, facet_wrap() reshapes a 1D ribbon of plots into a 2D arrangement. Instead of a 2D grid of panels associated with the level combinations of two variables, facet_wrap() creates a string of panels and "wraps" them into the graphics region like a ribbon, patterned on how the lattice behaves.

  - Multidimensional data exploration: Investigating patterns across multiple experimental conditions  [270285568 | Hao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [233394038 | Xie et al. | 2021 | Citations: 12]

* **Data Exploration and Discovery**

* **Scientific Visualization Systems**

  - Interactive exploration: Enabling quick navigation between different data facets for complex analytical tasks  [59604472 | Renoust et al. | 2019 | Citations: 3]

  - Network visualization: Separating dense networks into manageable subnetworks for detailed comparative analysis  [65026250 | Tyner et al. | 2017 | Citations: 34]

snippets: In the first stage, we aim to capture meaningful data facets of the input table as comprehensively as possible. If we use violent enumeration, it will produce a lot of candidate data facets, and many of them will not include data trends. citations.title: [233394038 | Xie et al. | 2021 | Citations: 12]
snippets: Multi‐dimensional data exploration is a classic research topic in visualization. Most existing approaches are designed for identifying record patterns in dimensional space or subspace. In this paper, we propose a visual analytics approach to exploring subset patterns. The core of the approach is a subset embedding network (SEN) that represents a group of subsets as uniformly‐formatted embeddings. We implement the SEN as multiple subnets with separate loss functions. The design enables to handle arbitrary subsets and capture the similarity of subsets on single features, thus achieving accurate pattern exploration, which in most cases is searching for subsets having similar values on few features. Moreover, each subnet is a fully‐connected neural network with one hidden layer. The simple structure brings high training efficiency. We integrate the SEN into a visualization system that achieves a 3‐step workflow. Specifically, analysts (1) partition the given dataset into subsets, (2) select portions in a projected latent space created using the SEN, and (3) determine the existence of patterns within selected subsets. Generally, the system combines visualizations, interactions, automatic methods, and quantitative measures to balance the exploration flexibility and operation efficiency, and improve the interpretability and faithfulness of the identified patterns. Case studies and quantitative experiments on multiple open datasets demonstrate the general applicability and effectiveness of our approach.

sections.title: Advantages & Limitations
sections.text:
TLDR; Faceted plots excel at enabling quick navigation between data subsets and supporting comparative analysis, but face challenges with scalability and customization. Their power lies in maintaining visual consistency while revealing patterns across multiple views, though careful consideration must be given to managing complexity. (7 sources)

Faceted plots offer several key advantages in data visualization. One of their strongest assets is their ability to support quick navigation between different data facets during complex analytical tasks  [59604472 | Renoust et al. | 2019 | Citations: 3]. This feature is particularly valuable when trying to understand relationships between different data items or identify outliers across multiple views.

However, as the number of facets increases, these advantages can transform into significant limitations. The practice of dividing data across multiple views inevitably leads to scalability challenges, necessitating thoughtful approaches to view selection and ranking  [269042820 | Montambault et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]. Traditional solutions to address these challenges include implementing methods for selecting informative views and utilizing visual quality metrics to rank them effectively.

From an implementation perspective, modern faceting systems often require balancing multiple visual encoding channels to maximize information conveyance. Current frameworks incorporate numerous encoding options, including position, length, angle, color variations, and shape  [256808747 | Zeng et al. | 2021 | Citations: 15]. While this richness of options enhances visual expression, it can also complicate the interpretation of faceted displays.

Some practical limitations exist in terms of customization capabilities. For instance, in popular visualization tools like ggplot2, while facet_wrap() and facet_grid() effectively manage data allocation across subplots, they restrict aesthetic customization within faceted plots. Features such as dynamic color schemes for different variable levels or complex hierarchical variable assignments can prove challenging to implement  [273009282 | Min | 2024 | Citations: 3].

Despite these limitations, faceted plots remain highly versatile tools that can adapt to different usage contexts. When properly implemented, they can efficiently embed various specialized plots including scatterplot matrices, conditioned choropleth maps, and other grid-based visualizations  [60913436 | Grolemund et al. | 2015 | Citations: 13]. Their effectiveness stems from combining small-multiple principles with aesthetic mapping capabilities, allowing users to simultaneously examine multivariate relationships across multiple conditions  [67411560 | Becker et al. | 2017 | Citations: 3].

citations.title: [256808747 | Zeng et al. | 2021 | Citations: 15]
snippets: Selecting appropriate visual encodings is critical to designing effective visualization recommendation systems, yet few findings from graphical perception are typically applied within these systems. We observe two significant limitations in translating graphical perception knowledge into actionable visualization recommendation rules/constraints: inconsistent reporting of findings and a lack of shared data across studies. How can we translate the graphical perception literature into a knowledge base for visualization recommendation? We present a review of 59 papers that study user perception and performance across ten visual analysis tasks. Through this study, we contribute a JSON dataset that collates existing theoretical and experimental knowledge and summarizes key study outcomes in graphical perception. We illustrate how this dataset can inform automated encoding decisions with three representative visualization recommendation systems. Based on our findings, we highlight open challenges and opportunities for the community in collating graphical perception knowledge for a range of visualization recommendation scenarios.

snippets: Faceting data, or dimensions, across multiple views quickly leads to scalability issues, and thus methods for selecting informative views (Wilkinson et al., 2005), used in conjunction with visual quality metrics to rank views (Bertini et al., 2011), are common approaches to handle such problems.

sections.title: Background & Basic Concepts
sections.text:
TLDR; Autoencoders are neural networks designed to learn efficient data representations by reconstructing their input. They consist of an encoder-decoder architecture that compresses data into a lower-dimensional representation while preserving key features, enabling tasks like dimensionality reduction and feature learning. (5 sources)

Autoencoders represent a fundamental advancement in unsupervised learning, operating as specialized neural networks that aim to replicate their input while working with reduced complexity  [153311019 | Mu et al. | 2019 | Citations: 171]. Their core functionality centers around learning efficient data representations through a two-part architecture: an encoder that compresses input data into a lower-dimensional latent space, and a decoder that reconstructs the original data from this compressed representation  [212689445 | Murari et al. | 2019 | Citations: 5]  [233420464 | Wijegunarathna et al. | 2021 | Citations: 3].

The architecture follows a straightforward design pattern where the input and output layers maintain identical dimensions, while the intermediate hidden layer operates at a lower dimensionality. This structural arrangement forces the network to learn essential features at the bottleneck layer, effectively serving as a mechanism for dimensionality reduction  [210181458 | Wen et al. | 2020 | Citations: 6]. Through backpropagation, the network optimizes its parameters to minimize the reconstruction error between the input and output, ensuring faithful reproduction of the original data  [233420464 | Wijegunarathna et al. | 2021 | Citations: 3].

Several notable variants of autoencoders have emerged to address specific challenges. Sparse autoencoders incorporate sparsity constraints to encourage selective feature usage, while denoising autoencoders add artificial noise during training to improve robustness. The development of deeper architectures through stacking multiple layers has enabled more sophisticated feature learning capabilities  [153311019 | Mu et al. | 2019 | Citations: 171]. The decoder architecture typically mirrors the encoder structure, though this symmetry isn't strictly mandatory - what matters most is maintaining matching input and output dimensions  [212689445 | Murari et al. | 2019 | Citations: 5].

citations.title: [153311019 | Mu et al. | 2019 | Citations: 171]
snippets:
Autoencoder is an unsupervised learning algorithm that applies backpropagation, setting the target values to be equal to the inputs. In 1986, Rumelhart et al. (Rumelhart et al., 1986) proposed the concept of autoencoder (AE), and used it for high-dimensional complex data processing. Autoencoder can extract the latent feature by reconstructing the input data to form the output data. The basic structure of autoencoder can be viewed as three-layer neural network: input layer x, hidden layer h, and output layer y, where the output layer and input layer has the same scale, and Fig. 1 is the schematic diagram of autoencoder. 

Where f() is a nonlinear function, such as sigmoid function,  ′ is the link weight of the hidden layer to the output layer, and b' is the bias of the output layer. y is treated as a prediction of x. In general, the weight matrix  ′ is limited to the transpose of the weight matrix W:  ′ =   . According to the different forms of data, the reconstruction error is usually defined as mean square error or cross entropy. 

Some researchers introduced the idea of sparse representation, proposed a sparse Autoencoder, in which the average value of the output signal by l 2 penalty or encouragement with a small mean value which approximated by a Gaussian distribution. In [32], a coarse-to-fine Autoencoder was trained to complete the task of locating key points on the face. In order to enhance the generalization of Autoencoder, Mikolov et al. [33] proposed denoising Autoencoder that added artificial noise to the training samples to allow the network to reconstruct the original clean input from the noisy signals. In [34], the deep Autoencoder is used to obtain a compact image high-level description and image retrieval. Many researchers have successfully applied the deep Autoencoder to the image feature representation. Autoencoders can reconstruct the input data through training the network, tuning the parameters, and cascading to form a deep neural network.

citations.title: [210181458 | Wen et al. | 2020 | Citations: 6]
snippets:
The architecture of an autoencoder is a three-layer feed-forward neuro network that contains an input layer, a hidden layer, and an output layer. All three layers are fully connected hierarchically through weighted connections that are updated by a backpropagation algorithm. An important property of the AE's structure is that the dimensions of the input layer and output layer are the same, while the dimension of the hidden layer is much smaller so that the output layer is forced to reconstruct the pattern of the input layer with the smaller size of the hidden nodes, the value in each hidden node could represent a lowdimension feature from the input data, and the whole AE could be interpreted as a dimension-reduction function. 

The basic principle behind training the AE is the minimizing of the residual error between the values of the input and output layers. Let X = [x 1 , x 2 , x 3 , . . . , x d ] denote all the FCs for the entire dataset, y = y 1 , y 2 , y 3 , . . . , y p denote the features that represent × after dimension reduction, and z = [z 1 , z 2 , z 3 , . . . , z d ] denote the corresponding reconstructed data. The number of input and output layer nodes is indicated by d, whose size is equal to the number of observations, and the number of hidden nodes is denoted by p p < d ; the weight and bias of the encoder and decoder can be denoted by w 

The features are computed by y = f w (1,0) x + b (1,0) where f (x) is a sigmoid function of the hidden nodes; the reconstructed data are computed by z = g W (2.1) x + b (2,1) , where g (x) is the tanh function of the output nodes. In this paper, we chose autoencoders to perform dimension reduction, and the weights were transferred to the DNN model for pretraining. In every training iteration, a set of edges generated by the Pearson's correlation of time courses in a window from a sample were fed to the AE, following which the AE was trained using a backpropagation algorithm.

citations.title: [212689445 | Murari et al. | 2019 | Citations: 5]
snippets:
Autoencoders are feedforward neural networks with a specific type of topology, reported in Figure 1. The defining characteristic of autoencoders is the fact that the output is the same as the input [12]. They are meant to compress the input into a lower-dimensional code and then reconstruct the output from this representation. To this end, an autoencoder consists of three components: Encoder, code, and decoder. The encoder compresses the input and produces the code, a more compact representation of the inputs. The decoder then reconstructs the input using this code only. The code constitutes a compact "summary" or "compression" of the input, which is also called the latent-space representation. In more detail, the input passes first through the encoder, which is a fully connected artificial neural network (ANN), and is translated into a code. The code is the input of the decoder, which is meant to produce an output, which is as similar as possible to the input. The decoder architecture is typically the mirror image of the encoder. sections.title: Manifold Learning Perspective
sections.text:
TLDR; Autoencoders inherently operate by learning to map data onto lower-dimensional manifolds while preserving crucial structural relationships. This mathematical foundation allows autoencoders to discover compact representations that maintain the essential geometric and topological properties of the input data. (6 sources)

From a geometric perspective, autoencoders fundamentally operate by discovering and learning the manifold structure of high-dimensional data  [271533596 | Lee et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. This understanding comes from the observation that real-world data often lies predominantly on or near a lower-dimensional manifold embedded within the higher-dimensional space, a principle known as the manifold hypothesis  [262012653 | Ramanaik et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1].

The mathematical framework of autoencoders aligns closely with classical manifold learning approaches. When restricted to linear transformations, autoencoders essentially learn the same subspace as Principal Component Analysis (PCA)  [211532485 | Ghosh et al. | 2020 | Citations: 23]  [11120398 | Baldi et al. | 1989 | Citations: 1340]. The nonlinear variant extends this capability, fitting within Whitney's theorem for manifold embeddings when allowing nonlinear transformations  [211532485 | Ghosh et al. | 2020 | Citations: 23].

Recent perspectives emphasize that the decoder in an autoencoder specifically maps from the representation space to a manifold in the input space  [237363987 | Schuster et al. | 2021 | Citations: 6]. This relationship creates a parametric representation of the input manifold in the latent space, where the decoder ensures that data points approximately lie on this learned manifold structure  [271533596 | Lee et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. This geometric interpretation has important practical implications, particularly in applications like image denoising, where noisy samples can be projected onto the cleaner manifold representation to achieve denoising  [44071471 | Lei et al. | 2018 | Citations: 145].

However, it's worth noting that this manifold learning perspective introduces complexities - there isn't necessarily a unique solution for either the manifold itself or its coordinate system, leading to multiple valid autoencoder solutions for the same dataset  [262012455 | Lee | 2023 | Citations: 6].

The nonlinear autoencoder has been proposed as a nonlinear version of PCA (Kramer, 1991)(Kramer, 1992). If we restrict g to be linear and allow h to be nonlinear then the autoencoder fits into the blueprint of Whitney's theorem for manifold embeddings (Broomhead et al., 2000)(Broomhead et al., 2001). Topologically sensitive nonlinear reduction use, e.g., topological circle or sphere encoding neurons (Kirby et al., 1999)(Kirby et al., 1996)[49] to capture shape in data.

citations.title: [237363987 | Schuster et al. | 2021 | Citations: 6]
snippets: Here, we take up a simple but not too well-known view on autoencoders and representation learning from a manifold learning perspective. We show that the decoder maps from the representation space to a manifold in the input space. We then show how a decoder can be trained without an encoder by optimizing the representations of the training data directly together with the weights of the decoder similar to manifold learning. In training we optimize towards a manifold that has the minimum distance between the training points and their projections onto the manifold. Learning of a representation along with an autoencoder has been introduced before as predictive sparse decompositions Kavukcuoglu et al. (2010), and others have even made the step of separating representation and decoder from the encoder Han et al. (2016).

citations.title: [262012455 | Lee | 2023 | Citations: 6]
snippets: This paper presents the geometric aspect of the autoencoder framework, which, despite its importance, has been relatively less recognized. Given a set of high-dimensional data points that approximately lie on some lower-dimensional manifold, an autoencoder learns the \textit{manifold} and its \textit{coordinate chart}, simultaneously. This geometric perspective naturally raises inquiries like"Does a finite set of data points correspond to a single manifold?"or"Is there only one coordinate chart that can represent the manifold?". The responses to these questions are negative, implying that there are multiple solution autoencoders given a dataset. Consequently, they sometimes produce incorrect manifolds with severely distorted latent space representations.

Systematic analysis and post-processing of highdimensional and high-throughput datasets (Pepperkok et al., 2006), (Perlman et al., 2004), is a current computational challenge across disciplines, such as neuroscience (Vogt, 2018)- (Zhang et al., 2020), plasma physics (Karniadakis et al., 2021)- (Willmann et al., 2021), or cell biology and medicine (Kobayashi et al., 2022)- (Nikitina et al., 2019). In the machine learning (ML) community, autoencoders (AEs) are commonly considered as the central tool for learning a low-dimensional oneto-one representation of high-dimensional datasets. The representations serve as a baseline for feature selection and classification tasks, heavily arising for instance in bio-medicine (Ronneberger et al., 2015)- (Andriasyan et al., 2021). 

AEs can be considered as a non-linear extension of classic principal component analysis (PCA), [18]- (Everitt et al., 2001), comparisons for linear problems are given in (Rolinek et al., 2018). citations.title: [271533596 | Lee et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
snippets:
In this section, we briefly introduce an autoencoder and its manifold learning perspective [29]- [36]. Consider a highdimensional data space X and a set of data points D = {x i ∈ X } N i=1 , and assume the data points {x i } lie approximately on some lower-dimensional manifold M in X (the manifold hypothesis). Suppose M is an m-dimensional manifold and let Z be a latent space R m . 

An autoencoder consists of an encoder, a mapping g : X → Z, and a decoder, a mapping f : Z → X . These are often approximated with deep neural networks and trained to minimize the reconstruction loss 

given a distance metric d(, ) on X . We note that, given a sufficiently low reconstruction error, all the data points {x i } should lie on the image of the decoder f . Under some mild conditions -that are (i) m is lower than the dimension of the data space X and (ii) f is smooth and its Jacobian ∂f ∂z (z) ∈ R dim(X )×m is full rank everywhere -, the image of f is an m-dimensional differentiable manifold embedded in X . In other words, the decoder produces a lower-dimensional manifold where the data points approximately lie.

snippets: The main focus of various deep learn methods is to learn the manifold structure from the real data and obtain a parametric representation of the manifold. In general, there is a probability distribution µ in the ambient space X , the support of µ is a low dimensional manifold Σ ⊂ X . For example, an autoencoder learns the encoding map ϕ θ : X → F and the decoding map ψ θ : F → X , where F is the latent space. The parametric representation of the input manifold Σ is given by the decoding map ψ θ . The reconstructed manifold Σ = ψ θ  ϕ θ (Σ) approximates input manifold. Furthermore, the DNN also learns and controls the distribution induced by the encoder (ϕ θ ) * µ defined on the latent space. Once the parametric manifold structure is obtained, it can be applied for various application, such as randomly generating a sample on Σ as a generative model. Image denoising can be reinterpreted geometrically as projecting a noisy sample onto Σ representing the clean image manifold, the closest point on Σ gives the denoised image.

sections.title: Core Components & Architecture of Topological Autoencoders
sections.text:
TLDR; Topological Autoencoders extend traditional autoencoders by incorporating a topological loss term that preserves the structural relationships of data. The architecture maintains the basic encoder-decoder structure but adds a differentiable topological regularization component that ensures the latent space preserves key topological features of the input data. (4 sources)

* **Encoder and Decoder Structure**: The foundational architecture consists of an encoder that maps input data to a lower-dimensional latent space and a decoder that reconstructs the input from this latent representation [173990640 | Moor et al. | 2019 | Citations: 145]. The decoder architecture is typically the mirror image of the encoder, though this symmetry isn't strictly required - the critical requirement is that input and output dimensions match  [212689445 | Murari et al. | 2019 | Citations: 5].

* **Persistent Homology Integration**: The key innovation in topological autoencoders is the incorporation of persistent homology calculations from both the input and latent spaces [173990640 | Moor et al. | 2019 | Citations: 145]. During forward propagation, these calculations yield persistence diagrams that capture topological features at different scales  [235189653 | Hensel et al. | 2021 | Citations: 187].

* **Differentiable Topological Loss**: The framework includes a differentiable topological regularization term that compares the topological signatures of both the input and latent spaces [173990640 | Moor et al. | 2019 | Citations: 145]. This comparison involves analyzing the persistence diagrams derived from the Vietoris-Rips complexes of each space, treating them as vectors for direct comparison  [235189653 | Hensel et al. | 2021 | Citations: 187].

* **Training Process**: The network is trained using standard backpropagation while simultaneously optimizing the topological loss term alongside the traditional reconstruction error  [276647247 | Clément et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. The topological regularization term specifically considers the lengths of carefully selected edges in both the input and latent spaces to maintain structural consistency  [276647247 | Clément et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

* **Distance Matrix Comparison**: The topological preservation mechanism relies on comparing selected distances from the full distance matrix of point clouds in both the input and latent spaces  [235189653 | Hensel et al. | 2021 | Citations: 187]. This comparison helps ensure that both global and local topological features are maintained during dimensionality reduction [173990640 | Moor et al. | 2019 | Citations: 145].

citations.title: [173990640 | Moor et al. | 2019 | Citations: 145]
snippets: We propose a novel approach for preserving topological structures of the input space in latent representations of autoencoders. Using persistent homology, a technique from topological data analysis, we calculate topological signatures of both the input and latent space to derive a topological loss term. Under weak theoretical assumptions, we construct this loss in a differentiable manner, such that the encoding learns to retain multi-scale connectivity information. We show that our approach is theoretically well-founded and that it exhibits favourable latent representations on a synthetic manifold as well as on real-world image data sets, while preserving low reconstruction errors.
