snippets:
Autoencoders are feedforward neural networks with a specific type of topology, reported in Figure 1. The defining characteristic of autoencoders is the fact that the output is the same as the input [12]. They are meant to compress the input into a lower-dimensional code and then reconstruct the output from this representation. To this end, an autoencoder consists of three components: Encoder, code, and decoder. The encoder compresses the input and produces the code, a more compact representation of the inputs. The decoder then reconstructs the input using this code only. The code constitutes a compact "summary" or "compression" of the input, which is also called the latent-space representation. In more detail, the input passes first through the encoder, which is a fully connected artificial neural network (ANN), and is translated into a code. The code is the input of the decoder, which is meant to produce an output, which is as similar as possible to the input. The decoder architecture is typically the mirror image of the encoder. Even if this condition is not an absolute requirement, it is typically the case (the actual indispensable requirement is that the dimensionality of the input and output is the same). Autoencoders can be trained via backpropagation as traditional ANNs.

Overall, there are four hyperparameters that need to be to set before starting the training of an autoencoder: (1) Code size, i.e., the number of nodes in the middle layer; (2) the number of layers; (3) In more detail, the input passes first through the encoder, which is a fully connected artificial neural network (ANN), and is translated into a code. The code is the input of the decoder, which is meant to produce an output, which is as similar as possible to the input. The decoder architecture is typically the mirror image of the encoder. Even if this condition is not an absolute requirement, it is typically the case (the actual indispensable requirement is that the dimensionality of the input and output is the same). Autoencoders can be trained via backpropagation as traditional ANNs.

citations.title: [235189653 | Hensel et al. | 2021 | Citations: 187]
snippets: As a recent example, (Moor et al., 2019) propose a topological autoencoder, which aims to preserve topological features of the input data in low-dimensional representations. This is achieved via a regularisation term that incentivises the persistence diagrams of both the latent and input space to be topologically similar. This method acts on the level of mini-batches, treating each of them as a point cloud. Persistence diagrams are obtained from the Vietoris-Rips complex of each space. By tracking the simplices that are relevant for the creation and destruction of topological features, and by consistently mapping simplices to a given edge in the Vietoris-Rips complex, each filtration can be interpreted as a selection of distances from the full distance matrix of the point cloud. The proposed regularisation term then compares the "selected" distances in the data space with the corresponding distances in the latent space (and vice versa). Finally, this regularisation is differentiable under the assumption that the persistence diagram is discrete (i.e., for each of its points, there is an infinitesimal neighbourhood containing no other points). The scheme can thus be directly integrated into the end-to-end training of an autoencoder, making it aware of the topology in the data space.

sections.title: Mathematical Framework & Working Principle
sections.text:
TLDR; Topological Autoencoders combine traditional autoencoder mathematics with persistent homology calculations to preserve topological features. The framework uses distance matrices and persistence diagrams to create a differentiable loss function that maintains both local and global topological structures during dimensionality reduction. (6 sources)

The mathematical foundation of Topological Autoencoders begins with their treatment of input data as point clouds, where both the input space X and latent space Z are analyzed using persistent homology techniques  [173990640 | Moor et al. | 2019 | Citations: 145]. This approach characterizes the topology of a manifold through homology groups, which represent various topological features such as disconnected components and non-deformable cycles  [220514200 | Duque et al. | 2020 | Citations: 25]  [231792991 | Barannikov | 1994 | Citations: 70].

The implementation utilizes ε-ball neighborhood graphs to approximate the topological features of manifolds from which data is sampled  [220514200 | Duque et al. | 2020 | Citations: 25]. The crux of the framework lies in its ability to track how topological features persist as the ε-ball radius increases until the graph becomes fully connected  [231792991 | Barannikov | 1994 | Citations: 70].

The key mathematical innovation is the construction of a differentiable topological regularization term Lt that compares the topological signatures of both the input and latent spaces. This comparison occurs at the level of mini-batches, where persistence diagrams are extracted from the Vietoris-Rips complexes of each space  [173990640 | Moor et al. | 2019 | Citations: 145]. The framework retrieves values from these persistence diagrams and treats them as vectors, enabling direct comparison and integration into the standard backpropagation process  [235189653 | Hensel et al. | 2021 | Citations: 187].

The final optimization objective combines the traditional reconstruction loss with the new topological regularization term, where λ serves as a hyperparameter to balance the two objectives  [173990640 | Moor et al. | 2019 | Citations: 145]. The resulting loss function has demonstrated effectiveness in identifying consistent patterns in persistent homology of constructed Vietoris-Rips filtrations  [254043695 | Volkov | 2022 | Citations: 2], thereby strengthening the connection between persistent homology and dimensionality reduction.

The computation specifically focuses on comparing selected distances from the full distance matrix of point clouds in both spaces, creating a bridge between topological data analysis and deep learning frameworks  [235189653 | Hensel et al. | 2021 | Citations: 187]  [219365002 | Edelsbrunner et al. | 0 | Citations: 1236].

citations.title: [173990640 | Moor et al. | 2019 | Citations: 145]
snippets: We propose a novel approach for preserving topological structures of the input space in latent representations of autoencoders. Using persistent homology, a technique from topological data analysis, we calculate topological signatures of both the input and latent space to derive a topological loss term. Under weak theoretical assumptions, we construct this loss in a differentiable manner, such that the encoding learns to retain multi-scale connectivity information. We show that our approach is theoretically well-founded and that it exhibits favourable latent representations on a synthetic manifold as well as on real-world image data sets, while preserving low reconstruction errors.

citations.title: [220514200 | Duque et al. | 2020 | Citations: 25]
snippets: Recently, topological autoencoders (TAE) [41] were proposed which include a regularization based on a topological signature of the input data. The topology of a manifold can be characterized by homology groups, which, depending on their dimension, represent various topological features such as the number of disconnected components or the number of cycles on the manifold that cannot be deformed into each another. When data are sampled from a manifold, such topological features can be approximately derived from a ε-ball neighborhood graph of the data. Persistent homology (Edelsbrunner et al., 0), (Barannikov, 1994) was introduced as a means to identify the topological signature of manifolds based on how long topological features persist when progressively increasing the ε-ball of the neighborhood graph up to a point where the graph is fully-connected (topological features with a short ε lifespan are attributed to noise). TAE thus penalizes discrepancies between the topological signatures of the input space and the latent space.

citations.title: [235189653 | Hensel et al. | 2021 | Citations: 187]
snippets: As a recent example, (Moor et al., 2019) propose a topological autoencoder, which aims to preserve topological features of the input data in low-dimensional representations. This is achieved via a regularisation term that incentivises the persistence diagrams of both the latent and input space to be topologically similar. This method acts on the level of mini-batches, treating each of them as a point cloud. Persistence diagrams are obtained from the Vietoris-Rips complex of each space. By tracking the simplices that are relevant for the creation and destruction of topological features, and by consistently mapping simplices to a given edge in the Vietoris-Rips complex, each filtration can be interpreted as a selection of distances from the full distance matrix of the point cloud. The proposed regularisation term then compares the "selected" distances in the data space with the corresponding distances in the latent space (and vice versa). Finally, this regularisation is differentiable under the assumption that the persistence diagram is discrete (i.e., for each of its points, there is an infinitesimal neighbourhood containing no other points). The scheme can thus be directly integrated into the end-to-end training of an autoencoder, making it aware of the topology in the data space.

citations.title: [254043695 | Volkov | 2022 | Citations: 2]
snippets: One of the major relevant works is the topological autoencoder [7], where a loss term wrt A X , A Z , π X , π Z was proposed, corresponding to the distance matrices A and topologically relevant persistent pairings π of input space X and latent space Z, respectively. Proposed topological autoencoder has proven to find consistent patterns in observed persistent homology (PH) of constructed Vietoris-Rips filtrations, strengthening the assumption that persistent homology can be applied to dimensionality reduction.

sections.title: Advantages & Limitations
sections.text:
TLDR; Topological Autoencoders offer powerful capabilities for preserving data topology in lower dimensions but face trade-offs in computational efficiency and practical implementation. Key strengths include robust topology preservation and handling complex manifold structures, while limitations involve longer training times and potential overfitting risks. (5 sources)

**Advantages:**

* **Effective Topology Preservation**: TAEs excel at maintaining both global and local topological features during dimensionality reduction, enabling better representation of the data's shape and structure in lower dimensions  [227347303 | Cornell | 2020 | Citations: 0].

* **Multiple Manifold Handling**: Unlike many alternative methods, TAEs can effectively learn and represent multiple manifolds simultaneously, providing greater flexibility for complex data structures  [227347303 | Cornell | 2020 | Citations: 0].

* **Nonlinear Structure Capture**: The architecture is particularly effective at capturing highly non-linear structures through separate autoencoders for restoring global structure and node attributes  [245008514 | Tao et al. | 2021 | Citations: 0].

* **ε-Faithful Representations**: TAEs can provide quantitative measurements of topological and geometric approximation quality, helping ensure accurate representation of manifolds with non-trivial topology  [251741200 | Schonsheck et al. | 2022 | Citations: 5].

**Limitations:**

* **Computational Overhead**: Training TAEs requires significantly longer computation times compared to traditional autoencoders  [227347303 | Cornell | 2020 | Citations: 0].

* **Overfitting Risk**: The method is susceptible to overfitting, requiring careful regularization and monitoring during training  [227347303 | Cornell | 2020 | Citations: 0].

* **Architectural Complexity**: Success depends heavily on proper neural architecture choices and often requires larger datasets to achieve optimal performance  [227347303 | Cornell | 2020 | Citations: 0].

* **Homeomorphic Constraints**: There are fundamental limitations due to topological obstructions - for perfect reconstruction, the data manifold must be homeomorphic to its embedding space, which isn't always possible  [263608965 | Kvalheim et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]  [251741200 | Schonsheck et al. | 2022 | Citations: 5].

* **Local Coverage Issues**: When dealing with complex manifolds like the double torus, single autoencoders may fail to generate data covering the entire manifold, necessitating multi-chart approaches  [251741200 | Schonsheck et al. | 2022 | Citations: 5].

citations.title: [227347303 | Cornell | 2020 | Citations: 0]
snippets: We propose the idea that a candidate for a filtering function preserving global and local topology is the topological autoencoder (TAE), introduced by Moor et al. [2019]. These are autoencoders (AEs) regularized with a Persistent Homology loss to preserve the topology. As seen in their paper (see Moor et al. [2019]), the TAEs manage to preserve the shape and form of the data in lower dimensions to a certain extent, and manages to capture the global as well as local topology apart from other methods. As they also note, the TAE can learn multiple manifolds, which is a difficult task for many methods. When this topology is preserved for a distance metric of choice, we can derive a compact representation in lower dimensions that better represents the data's shape. TAEs do of course come with a longer training time, a risk of overfitting, neural architecture choices and a need for larger datasets. It does however provide a bridge between topology and deep learning.

citations.title: [251741200 | Schonsheck et al. | 2022 | Citations: 5]
snippets:
Topological Concerns Chart autoencoders (CAEs) were introduced in [42] to represent data from manifolds with non-trivial topology without prior knowledge of the topology. The authors introduce the concept of an ϵ-faithful representation, which quantitatively measures the topological and geometric approximation of autoencoders to the data manifold. An essential result of this work is that an auto-regressive model cannot accurately represent a manifold distributed dataset unless the latent space is homeomorphic to the data manifold. This motivates the use of multi-latent space models in which each chart covers only a compact region. 

Consider a double torus shown in Figure 2. In the case where the latent dimension is two, they fail to generate data to cover the whole manifold, in this case the manfiold has been 'flattened'. When the latent dimension is increased to three, the newly sampled data do not all stay on the manifold. Additionally, near by points on the manifold may be far apart in the latent space because homeomorphism is violated.

citations.title: [263608965 | Kvalheim et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Deep neural network autoencoders are routinely used computationally for model reduction. They allow recognizing the intrinsic dimension of data that lie in a $k$-dimensional subset $K$ of an input Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$. The underlying idea is to obtain both an encoding layer that maps $\mathbb{R}^n$ into $\mathbb{R}^k$ (called the bottleneck layer or the space of latent variables) and a decoding layer that maps $\mathbb{R}^k$ back into $\mathbb{R}^n$, in such a way that the input data from the set $K$ is recovered when composing the two maps. This is achieved by adjusting parameters (weights) in the network to minimize the discrepancy between the input and the reconstructed output. Since neural networks (with continuous activation functions) compute continuous maps, the existence of a network that achieves perfect reconstruction would imply that $K$ is homeomorphic to a $k$-dimensional subset of $\mathbb{R}^k$, so clearly there are topological obstructions to finding such a network.

sections.title: Applications & Extensions
sections.text:
TLDR; Topological Autoencoders have found diverse applications across scientific domains, from biomedical imaging to materials science. Recent extensions include hyper-spherical variational autoencoders and hybrid approaches combining graph convolutions with topology preservation. (7 sources)

* **Biomedical Imaging and Diagnostics**: TAEs have been successfully deployed in medical applications, including glioblastoma segmentation and cancer detection from histopathological images  [262012653 | Ramanaik et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]  [231764056 | Andriasyan et al. | 2021 | Citations: 14]  [257411467 | Kobayashi et al. | 2022 | Citations: 31].

* **Cell Biology and Single-cell Analysis**: The technology has proven valuable in analyzing high-dimensional cellular data, particularly in understanding immune cell populations and disease mechanisms  [262012653 | Ramanaik et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]  [191890672 | Perlman et al. | 2004 | Citations: 1947].

* **Materials Science**: TAEs have been applied to analyze electron energy-loss spectra from scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), enabling automated defect identification in crystalline materials  [262012653 | Ramanaik et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]  [235441265 | Willmann et al. | 2021 | Citations: 78].

* **Neuroscience Research**: The framework has been adapted for studying neural activity patterns and brain connectivity, contributing to our understanding of complex neurological processes  [262012653 | Ramanaik et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]  [210314598 | Zhang et al. | 2020 | Citations: 41].

* **Graph-based Applications**: Recent developments include graph convolutional autoencoders that handle structured graph data, particularly useful for preserving both node features and topological relationships in network analysis  [271949377 | Wang | 2024 | Citations: 0].

* **Enhanced Sampling Techniques**: Hyper-spherical Variational Autoencoders (S-VAE) represent an innovative extension that moves beyond Euclidean latent spaces, improving the reliability of sample generation by incorporating built-in topological structures  [255943613 | Bouayed et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0].

* **Feature Selection and Classification**: TAEs serve as a foundation for downstream tasks, providing robust feature representations that facilitate subsequent classification and analysis procedures  [262012653 | Ramanaik et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1].

citations.title: [255943613 | Bouayed et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]
snippets:
Hyper-spherical Variational Autoencoders (S − VAE) were introduced in (Davidson et al., 2018) and represent an attempt to move away from euclidean latent spaces and introduce built-in topological structures as constraints on the latent space. The use of topological structures can help reduce the probability of sampling a latent vector that the decoder cannot reconstruct into a real-world sample. 

One solution to address the continuity of the latent space is to fit a mixture model to the latent space of the training or validation dataset. New samples can then be drawn from the mixture model, which can lead to good performance in terms of synthetic data generation because the drawn samples are in areas where the decoder knows how to reconstruct them.

citations.title: [271949377 | Wang | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: The autoencoder is an unsupervised learning model for learning an efficient representation of data. It reconstructs the input data by mapping the input data to the potential feature space and then mapping the feature space back to the original data space (Azpúrua et al., 2022)(Yang et al., 2021). The autoencoder does not rely on label information but instead uses the input data as a reference. Its main applications include data reduction and feature extraction, which realize the purpose of data compression and extraction of important features by learning meaningful representations of data. Graph convolutional autoencoders combine the idea of graph convolutional neural networks with autoencoders to learn the representation of graphstructured data. The encoder encodes the node features and topology in the graph through the convolutional neural network to obtain the low-dimensional representation of the node, and the decoder maps the low-dimensional representation back to the original node features and topology through the reverse operation. A meaningful representation of the graph structure is learned by minimizing the reconstruction error, that is, the difference between the input graph and the decoder output graph.

sections.title: Introduction & Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Several standardized datasets are commonly used to evaluate core language model capabilities. These include comprehensive benchmarks like MMLU and ARC-Challenge, alongside other specialized datasets like HellaSwag and TruthfulQA. (1 source)

Multiple standardized datasets have emerged as essential tools for evaluating artificial intelligence language models (LLMs) across various cognitive abilities. These datasets form a comprehensive evaluation ecosystem that tests fundamental aspects of machine intelligence, including common sense reasoning, mathematical proficiency, question answering accuracy, and factual consistency  [264591440 | Boughorbel et al. | 2023 | Citations: 8]. The selection of specific datasets often depends on the particular aspect of model capability being investigated <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">. While newer datasets continue to emerge, the core set of evaluation benchmarks established early in the field remain foundational tools for assessing progress in AI development <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

sections.title: MMLU Training Sets & Usage
sections.text:
TLDR; MMLU is a comprehensive multitask benchmark that evaluates models across 57 subjects spanning STEM, humanities, and social sciences. Different approaches have emerged for using MMLU as a training resource, including standard splits, custom combined training sets, and filtered versions focused on specific domains. (7 sources)

The MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) dataset serves as a versatile tool for both evaluation and training purposes. At its core, MMLU functions as a comprehensive multitask benchmark that tests broad knowledge and problem-solving skills through multiple-choice questions across diverse academic disciplines  [266191741 | Zhu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 19].

Researchers have developed various approaches to utilizing MMLU's training resources. One notable implementation combines MMLU with other multiple-choice question-answering benchmarks to create a training set of approximately 100,000 examples and 30 million tokens [270764411 | Wu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 22] [266902714 | Meng et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]. For focused applications, particularly in mathematical reasoning, researchers have created specialized versions like MMLU-STEM, which extracts questions covering science, technology, engineering, and mathematics domains  [273351442 | Chia et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

Some researchers prefer to exclude the official MMLU training set during model development, opting instead to rely on alternative training resources  [267759981 | Li et al. | 2024 | Citations: 51]. Others have taken a more rigorous approach, creating curated versions like MMLU-Redux, which contains 3,000 manually re-annotated questions across 30 subjects  [272969471 | Choi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

When developing new models, practitioners often integrate MMLU into broader training strategies. For instance, some approaches combine MMLU with other domain-specific datasets, such as Pubmed Central for medicine, Stackexchange for programming Q&A, and Wikipedia for encyclopedic knowledge  [273185866 | Grangier et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]. This integration allows for targeted improvement in specific knowledge areas while maintaining strong performance across the full spectrum of covered subjects  [270764411 | Wu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 22].

sections.title: Math Training Sets
sections.text:
TLDR; Multiple specialized datasets exist for training mathematical reasoning in language models, ranging from elementary math word problems to advanced competition-level problems. Key resources include GSM8K, MATH, and newer collections like MathPile and DeepSeekMath Corpus, which together offer billions of tokens of mathematical content. (9 sources)

Here are the major training sets used for mathematical reasoning:

 **GSM8K (Grade School Math)**: Contains 7,473 training examples of grade-school-level word problems requiring two to eight calculation steps to solve. The problems are linguistically diverse and created by human experts  [258352268 | Liu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 25]  [271329091 | Tan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

 **MATH**: A collection of 12,500 competition-level mathematics problems with detailed step-by-step solutions. Unlike GSM8K, MATH problems require more sophisticated mathematical reasoning and haven't been widely used in training previous models  [271329091 | Tan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]  [262824824 | Li et al. | 2023 | Citations: 12].

 **Proprietary Large-Scale Collections**:

  - WebMath: 35 billion tokens from GitHub, arXiv, and Math StackExchange

  - Math Web Pages: 17.5 billion LaTeX-based tokens

  - DeepSeekMath Corpus: 120 billion tokens

 [272753509 | Han et al. | 2024 | Citations: 13]

 **Specialized Training Resources**:

  - MathMix: 1 billion high-quality mathematical tokens used in fine-tuning GPT-4

  - MathPile: Aggregates 9.5B tokens from multiple sources including textbooks, arXiv, Wikipedia, and StackExchange

  - AMPS: Over 100,000 Khan Academy problems and 5 million Mathematica-generated problems

 [272753509 | Han et al. | 2024 | Citations: 13]  [266999601 | Zhu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 28]

 **Combined Training Approaches**: Recent research shows success in combining multiple training sets strategically. For example, using GSM8K and MATH together has led to improved performance on both training sets and out-of-domain benchmarks like ARC-Challenge and MMLU-STEM  [272653955 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]. Researchers also supplement these core datasets with additional resources like MAWPS and SVAMP for enhanced training coverage  [270562752 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 12].

 **Advanced Problem Collections**: Modern evaluations include competition-level benchmarks like AMC23, AIME24, and OlympiadBench for assessment, though these are primarily used for evaluation rather than training  [273654982 | Cao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

sections.title: ARC-Challenge Training & Usage
sections.text:
TLDR; ARC-Challenge is a specialized dataset containing grade-school level science questions designed to test complex reasoning abilities. Research has shown success in using both ARC-Challenge and its easier counterpart ARC-Easy for training, leading to improved performance across various reasoning benchmarks. (6 sources)

The ARC-Challenge dataset stands apart from other training resources due to its explicit focus on testing higher-order reasoning capabilities in AI systems. Initially introduced as part of the AI2 Reasoning Challenge, the dataset is divided into two subsets: an Easy Set and a Challenge Set, collectively containing 3,548 questions  [276317712 | Zhang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 3].

Recent research has demonstrated successful outcomes when combining both training sets from ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge during the training process  [266977266 | Hase et al. | 2024 | Citations: 25]. This combined approach has proven particularly valuable when integrated with other specialized datasets like GSM8K and MATH, showing measurable improvements not just on ARC-related tasks but also across various out-of-domain reasoning benchmarks including HumanEval, GPQA, and MMLU-STEM  [272653955 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

The versatility of ARC-style datasets extends beyond pure scientific reasoning applications. When incorporated into broader pre-training strategies, ARC questions contribute to improved performance across multiple domains, including STEM subjects and general language understanding tasks  [266573694 | Wang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 38]  [273185541 | Li et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5]. The inclusion of ARC questions in training regimens helps ensure that models maintain robust scientific knowledge retention even under extensive training conditions  [59369731 | Clark et al. | 2018 | Citations: 1214].

sections.title: Background and Motivation
sections.text:
TLDR; Synthetic tabular data generation addresses critical challenges in modern data science, including data scarcity, privacy concerns, and class imbalance. The field has evolved from traditional statistical approaches to sophisticated deep learning methods, reflecting the increasing complexity and importance of tabular data in various sectors. (5 sources)

The generation of synthetic tabular data has emerged as a crucial solution to several persistent challenges in data science and machine learning applications  [266162999 | Ling et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3]  [277999654 | Shi et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2]. This field has gained prominence due to three fundamental factors: the limited availability of real data, data incompleteness, and growing privacy concerns  [244959037 | Lee | 2022 | Citations: 26].

Tabular data forms the backbone of decision-making systems across diverse sectors, including finance, healthcare, manufacturing, and natural sciences, though its application comes with unique challenges  [269282531 | Kim et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]. Unlike unstructured data modalities such as images or text, tabular data is structurally simpler yet semantically more complex, involving intricate inter-column relationships and domain-specific contexts  [276775588 | Long et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

The evolution of synthetic data generation methods reflects the progression from basic statistical approaches to more sophisticated techniques. Early approaches relied on relatively simple methods such as decision trees and Bayesian networks  [277999654 | Shi et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2]. However, these traditional methods faced limitations in handling complex data distributions and managing high-dimensional data  [244959037 | Lee | 2022 | Citations: 26].

Modern approaches now span multiple paradigms, including energy-based models, variational autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, and diffusion models  [277999654 | Shi et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2]. Notably, recent innovations have produced methods capable of generating data that maintains both privacy and utility  [276775588 | Long et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]. These advances have addressed critical challenges such as feature heterogeneity, complex inter-correlations, and intricate column-wise distributions that characterize tabular data  [273653942 | Shi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4].

citations.title: [244959037 | Lee | 2022 | Citations: 26]
snippets: Tabular data synthesis has received wide attention in the literature. This is because available data is often limited, incomplete, or cannot be obtained easily, and data privacy is becoming increasingly important. In this work, we present a generalized GAN framework for tabular synthesis, which combines the adversarial training of GANs and the negative log-density regularization of invertible neural networks. The proposed framework can be used for two distinctive objectives. First, we can further improve the synthesis quality, by decreasing the negative log-density of real records in the process of adversarial training. On the other hand, by increasing the negative log-density of real records, realistic fake records can be synthesized in a way that they are not too much close to real records and reduce the chance of potential information leakage. We conduct experiments with real-world datasets for classification, regression, and privacy attacks. In general, the proposed method demonstrates the best synthesis quality (in terms of task-oriented evaluation metrics, e.g., F1) when decreasing the negative log-density during the adversarial training. If increasing the negative log-density, our experimental results show that the distance between real and fake records increases, enhancing robustness against privacy attacks.

snippets: Synthetic data has been widely applied in the real world recently. One typical example is the creation of synthetic data for privacy concerned datasets. In this study, we concentrate on the first example, and introduce (a) the Howso engine, and (b) our proposed random projection based synthetic data generation framework. We evaluate these two algorithms on the aspects of privacy preservation and accuracy, and compare them to the two state-of-the-art synthetic data generation algorithms DataSynthesizer and Synthetic Data Vault. citations.title: [269282531 | Kim et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]
snippets:
Tabular data, consisting of mixed variable types such as numerical and categorical variables, represents a widely applicable and essential data format [30]. It plays a crucial role in enhancing decisionmaking and efficiency in various real-world applications, such as finance, healthcare, manufacturing, and natural sciences [1,3,26]. However, challenges such as data scarcity and class imbalance, particularly for rare yet crucial events, often significantly degrade the performance of machine learning (ML) models, often resulting in reduced accuracy for underrepresented classes. To address these challenges, efficient synthetic data generation methods have been developed to augment tabular datasets. Traditional methods, such as synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) and its variants [5,11,21], focus on generating minority class samples to alleviate class imbalance. Recently, advanced generative models, such as TVAE [35], CTAB-GAN [39], and TabDDPM [19], have shown promising results in producing high-quality synthetic tabular data.

Large language models (LLMs) have also demonstrated significant potential for generating realistic tabular data, effectively handling both numerical and categorical variables [4]37]. However, these models often require extensive, data-specific fine-tuning, which can increase the risk of overfitting to majority classes or dominant feature values, especially in small and highly imbalanced tabular datasets.

citations.title: [273653942 | Shi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]
snippets:
Synthesizing high-quality tabular data is an important topic in many data science tasks, ranging from dataset augmentation to privacy protection. However, developing expressive generative models for tabular data is challenging due to its inherent heterogeneous data types, complex inter-correlations, and intricate column-wise distributions.

Unlike image data, which comprises pure continuous pixel values with local spatial correlations, or text data, which comprises tokens that share the same dictionary space, tabular data features have much more complex and varied distributions (Xu et al., 2019;Borisov et al., 2023), making it challenging to learn joint probabilities across multiple columns. More specifically, such inherent heterogeneity leads to obstacles from two aspects: 1) typical tabular data often contains multi-modal data types, i.e., continuous (e.g., numerical features) and discrete (e.g., categorical features) variables; 2) within the same feature type, features do not share the exact same data property because of the different meaning they represent, resulting in different column-wise marginal distributions (even after normalizing them into same value ranges).

In recent years, numerous deep generative models have been proposed for tabular data generation with autoregressive models (Borisov et al., 2023), VAEs (Liu et al., 2023), and GANs (Xu et al., 2019) in the past few years. Though they have notably improved the generation quality compared to traditional machine learning generation techniques such as resampling (Chawla et al., 2002), the generated data quality is still far from satisfactory due to limited model capacity.

citations.title: [276775588 | Long et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]
snippets:
Synthetic tabular data have widespread applications in industrial domains such as healthcare, finance, and supply chains, owing to their potential to protect privacy and mitigate data scarcity. However, generating realistic synthetic tabular data while preserving inter-column logical relationships remains a significant challenge for the existing generative models.

Tabular data, often structured in a table with rows and columns and stored in relational databases (Vieira et al., 2020), is ubiquitous (van Breugel and van der Schaar, 2024) across various industries-ranging from medical records in healthcare and transaction data in finance to sales data in retail to inventory data in warehousing. Such data is often carefully designed and maintained by domain experts, with data schemes or structures that are domain-specific and where columns are interdependent. Compared to unstructured data modalities such as image, video, and text, tabular data is structurally simpler yet semantically more complex, featuring well-defined columns, rich inter-column interactions, high dimensionality and heterogeneity, as well as domain-specific context and complexity. Thus, synthetic tabular data generation is challenging and remains underexplored, with its development significantly lags behind these unstructured data modalities (van Breugel and van der Schaar, 2024).

Nevertheless, many methods (Chawla et al., 2002;Xu et al., 2019;Kotelnikov et al., 2023;Borisov et al., 2022)-mainly adapted from models designed for generating other data modalities-have been proposed in literature to generate tabular data. One of earliest such approaches is the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling TEchnique (SMOTE), originally proposed by Chawla et al. (2002) to address dataset imbalance problem. As a data augmentation method, this interpolation-based method has recently been found effective in generating tabular data (Wang et al., 2024a). However, despite its promising performance on several benchmark datasets, as reported in Long et al. (2025b), SMOTE inherently struggles to preserve data privacy effectively and capture complex column dependencies. To overcome these limitations, deep generative models-leveraging their success in image, text, and audio synthesis-have been increasingly explored for tabular data generation. For instance, Xu et al. (2019) proposed CTGAN, a generative adversarial network (GAN)-based method specifically designed for tabular data. CTGAN learns the distribution of tabular data and generates synthetic rows from the learned representation. Although CTGAN improves privacy preservation (Zhao et al., 2024), it struggles to capture the interdependencies between categorical and continuous columns (Zhang et al., 2023). More recently, diffusion model-based methods such as TabDDPM (Kotelnikov et al., 2023) and TabSyn (Zhang et al., 2023) have been introduced to synthesize tabular data by learning the denoising process in latent space. These approaches demonstrate superior performance compared to CTGAN, particularly in preserving intricate tabular structures. Furthermore, Borisov et al. (2022) proposed GReaT, a large language model (LLM)-based approach for tabular data generation. GReaT transforms tabular data into textual representations and fine-tunes generative models to produce synthetic data, enabling the learning of underlying distributions without requiring complex encoding and decoding processes.

citations.title: [277999654 | Shi et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2]
snippets: Tabular data remains one of the most prevalent and critical data formats across diverse real-world applications. However, its effective use in machine learning (ML) is often constrained by challenges such as data scarcity, privacy concerns, and class imbalance. Synthetic data generation has emerged as a promising solution, leveraging generative models to learn the distribution of real datasets and produce high-fidelity, privacy-preserving samples. Various generative paradigms have been explored, including energy-based models (EBMs), variational autoencoders (VAEs), generative adversarial networks (GANs), large language models (LLMs), and diffusion models. While several surveys have investigated synthetic tabular data generation, most focus on narrow subdomains or specific generative methods, such as GANs, diffusion models, or privacy-preserving techniques. This limited scope often results in fragmented insights, lacking a comprehensive synthesis that bridges diverse approaches. In particular, recent advances driven by LLMs and diffusion-based models remain underexplored. This gap hinders a holistic understanding of the field`s evolution, methodological interplay, and open challenges.

sections.title: Types of Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; Synthetic tabular data generation methods can be broadly categorized into statistical approaches and deep learning-based methods. The statistical approaches include Bayesian networks, decision trees, and Gaussian copulas, while deep learning methods encompass GANs, VAEs, and diffusion models. (7 sources)

## Statistical Distribution Methods

* **Bayesian Networks**: Used for modeling discrete variables and capturing causal relationships between features  [252780718 | Kim et al. | 2022 | Citations: 59]  [269148648 | Livieris et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8]

* **Decision Trees**: Employed for generating discrete variables and handling missing data  [244959037 | Lee | 2022 | Citations: 26]  [12280527 | Reiter | 2005 | Citations: 434]

* **Recursive Table Modeling**: Uses Gaussian copula to generate continuous variables by modeling multivariate distributions  [252780718 | Kim et al. | 2022 | Citations: 59]  [14311503 | Patki et al. | 2016 | Citations: 150]

## Deep Learning Methods

### GAN-Based Approaches

* **Conditional GAN (CTGAN)**: Addresses mixed data types and handles highly imbalanced categorical columns  [209180044 | Xu et al. | 2019 | Citations: 989]

* **MedGAN**: Specialized in generating discrete-valued patient records while preserving complex inter-variable relationships  [1769101 | Choi et al. | 2017 | Citations: 435]

* **TableGAN**: Employs CNN modules to improve synthetic data quality and predictive power  [52126543 | Park et al. | 2018 | Citations: 404]

### VAE-Based Approaches

* **Variational Autoencoders (TVAE)**: Creates a compressed latent representation of the input data to generate new samples while avoiding mode dropping  [209180044 | Xu et al. | 2019 | Citations: 989]

### Hybrid and Unified Approaches

* **Synthetic Data Vault (SDV)**: Combines multiple probabilistic graphical modeling and deep learning techniques to provide flexible data generation options  [266998802 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 18]

Each method offers distinct advantages in terms of computational efficiency and data quality  [266998802 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 18]. Statistical methods excel in speed and simplicity but may struggle with complex data structures, while deep learning approaches can better handle intricate data distributions but require more computational resources <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [252780718 | Kim et al. | 2022 | Citations: 59]
snippets: Tabular data synthesis is a long-standing research topic in machine learning. Many different methods have been proposed over the past decades, ranging from statistical methods to deep generative methods. However, it has not always been successful due to the complicated nature of real-world tabular data. In this paper, we present a new model named Score-based Tabular data Synthesis (STaSy) and its training strategy based on the paradigm of score-based generative modeling. Despite the fact that score-based generative models have resolved many issues in generative models, there still exists room for improvement in tabular data synthesis. Our proposed training strategy includes a self-paced learning technique and a fine-tuning strategy, which further increases the sampling quality and diversity by stabilizing the denoising score matching training. Furthermore, we also conduct rigorous experimental studies in terms of the generative task trilemma: sampling quality, diversity, and time. In our experiments with 15 benchmark tabular datasets and 7 baselines, our method outperforms existing methods in terms of task-dependant evaluations and diversity. Code is available at https://github.com/JayoungKim408/STaSy.

citations.title: [266998802 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 18]
snippets:
The most common synthetic tabular data generation methods can be divided into two main types, namely statistical distribution methods and deep learning-based methods [28,11]. The principle of the former group is to generate appropriate samples by considering the probability distribution of the real dataset. Representative methods include, for example, Gaussian multivariate [16], Chi-square, and Monte Carlo method [28]. While statistical distribution methods offer advantages such as speed, ease of application, minimal computing resource demands, and typically manageable parameters, they may not be suitable for handling large or complex data [28,(Hernadez et al., 2022). Deep learning, particularly generative adversarial networks (GANs), has rapidly gained traction due to its computation efficiency (Hernadez et al., 2022). There are many variants of GAN-based approaches, such as Wasserstein GAN [2] for hyperparametric search, HealthGAN (Yale et al., 2020) for health domain, and conditional GAN (CTGAN) for synthetic tabular data [53]. 

Furthermore, there is an important ecosystem for synthetic tabular and time series data generation, namely Synthetic Data Vault (SDV) (Patki et al., 2016). SDV consists of a combination of multiple probabilistic graphical modeling and deep learning (DL) based techniques (Hernadez et al., 2022). SDV is widely used in different fields of synthetic generation and has been shown to achieve similar results as using real data in the tested datasets (Patki et al., 2016)(Zhao et al., 2021).

citations.title: [269148648 | Livieris et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8]
snippets:
In this section, we briefly present some of the effective and widely used models for generating tabular data.It is worth mentioning that traditional approaches such as Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (Chawla et al., 2002) and Adaptive Synthetic Sampling (He et al., 2008) were not included, since they require labeled data for their application.Nowadays, Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) constitute the most widely used approaches proposed in the literature for generating synthetic data.These classes of models offer researchers to choose between probabilistic modeling based on the specific requirements of tabular data at hand and adversarial training dynamics.Another interesting approach for generating synthetic data is based on Gaussian Copula (Li et al., 2020), which is based on statistical methods for modeling features dependencies.It is able to capture linear dependencies in multivariate data by modeling the features' joint distribution given their marginal distributions.In contrast to GMM and GANs, which are dedicated to create synthetic data, Gaussian Copula is not a generative model in sense of creating new instances directly, but is often used in synthetic data generation by combining it with marginal distributions to generate synthetic instances with similar dependency structures.

Gaussian Mixture Models [1] are characterized by their ability to model complex multivariate distributions and offer an effective approach for synthetic data generation.GMM are based on a probabilistic framework for modeling complex data distributions by combining multiple Gaussian components.In detail, these models learns the distribution of the input data, focusing on explicitly capturing the interdependence between variables using mixture components for generating synthetic samples, which closely resemble the original dataset.The versatility of GMM lies in their ability to capture diverse patterns and dependencies within tabular data, making them well-suited for many real-words applications.

Generative Adversarial Networks (Gui et al., 2020) have emerged as a state-of-the-art models for synthetic data generation, demonstrating significant capabilities in preserving the statistical properties of original datasets by maintaining both the marginal distributions of individual features and complex inter-feature dependencies.Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Network (CTGAN) [16] constitutes a GAN-based model, which is dedicated for synthesizing tabular data.

sections.title: Deep Learning-Based Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; Deep learning methods for synthetic tabular data generation have evolved from early GAN-based approaches to more sophisticated models incorporating specialized architectures and techniques. The field has seen rapid advancement with the emergence of transformer-based models, diffusion models, and large language models, each bringing unique capabilities for handling tabular data complexities. (12 sources)

## GAN-Based Innovations

Early attempts at applying GANs to tabular data faced significant challenges due to the mixed nature of data types and non-Gaussian distributions  [238863014 | Bourou et al. | 2021 | Citations: 101]. CTGAN emerged as a breakthrough solution by introducing specialized preprocessing and mode-specific normalization to handle categorical variables and imbalanced datasets  [209180044 | Xu et al. | 2019 | Citations: 989].

The field saw further advancement with models specifically designed for mixed-type data. MedTGAN demonstrated superior performance for discrete-valued clinical records  [211191040 | Li | 2020 | Citations: 156], while CtabGAN+ addressed the challenges of imbalanced and long-tailed categorical features  [233444040 | Zhao et al. | 2021 | Citations: 158].

## Diffusion Models

Diffusion models have recently gained prominence in tabular data generation, marking a shift from earlier GAN-centric approaches  [270358021 | Lin et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]. TabDDPM pioneered the use of diffusion models for tabular data by implementing separate processes for categorical and continuous columns  [248200103 | Kotelnikov et al. | 2022 | Citations: 130]. This was followed by TabSyn, which incorporated a VAE-based embedding layer for more stable training and improved generation quality  [264146605 | Zhang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 82].

## Transformer and LLM-Based Approaches

The emergence of transformer-based models marked a significant evolution in the field  [270391998 | Tu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]. GReaT represented a novel approach by treating tabular data as sentences and fine-tuning GPT-2, achieving competitive performance particularly for categorical features  (Borisov et al._1,  2022).

More recently, transformer-based models have evolved to specifically address tabular data's structural characteristics. These models leverage the inherent structure of tabular data, including limited value ranges and column-specific distributions, leading to improvements in both efficiency and quality  [275788953 | Tiwald et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]. ForestFlow demonstrated particular promise by combining the strengths of tree ensemble models with diffusion approaches  [274965329 | D'souza et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

The field continues to evolve with hybrid approaches emerging, such as COdi, which enables controlled and interpretable generation by factorizing dependencies and allowing users to modify specific attribute combinations  [258309242 | Lee et al. | 2023 | Citations: 54].

citations.title: [238863014 | Bourou et al. | 2021 | Citations: 101]
snippets:
GAN models have shown great possibilities in the generation of synthetic images and text. Over the past few years, potential uses of GANs have been explored for tabular data generation, since they offer great flexibility to model data distributions in contrast with traditional statistical techniques. 

Giving the table Treal with real data, the task of synthetic data generation results in a synthetic table T syn. The T is partitioned into training set T train and test set T test . A GAN model is trained at T train . The data generator G learns the data distribution of each column in a table T, and then, it is used to generate the synthetic data of the table T syn . A successful data generator G for tabular data should be able to address the challenges associated with the nature of real-world tabular data. 

It is common for T to contain mixed data types of numerical and categorical columns. The numerical columns of table can have either discrete or continues values. Thus, the Generator G should be trained to simultaneously learn and generate a mix of data types. Additionally, the shape distribution of each column may differ, following usually non-Gaussian and multimodal distributions, where the min-max transformation causes vanishing gradient problems. In categorical columns of real-world tabular data, the imbalance problem often occurs, since some classes have more instances than others. Imbalanced data lead to mode collapse as well as to inadequate training of the minor classes. Furthermore, sparse one-hot-encoded vectors can cause issues at the training procedure of the Discriminator D, since it learns to distinguish real from fake data from the distribution's rareness rather to the realness of the value. 

Different GAN models have been created in order to solve some or all of the abovementioned issues. TGAN [22] is constructed to work on any tabular dataset. MedGAN (Choi et al., 2017) tries to generate simultaneously discrete and continuous samples. In this work, the most promising GAN models for tabular data generation are analyzed, which are TableGAN [28], CTGAN [23], and CopulaGAN [29].

citations.title: [258309242 | Lee et al. | 2023 | Citations: 54]
snippets: With growing attention to tabular data these days, the attempt to apply a synthetic table to various tasks has been expanded toward various scenarios. Owing to the recent advances in generative modeling, fake data generated by tabular data synthesis models become sophisticated and realistic. However, there still exists a difficulty in modeling discrete variables (columns) of tabular data. In this work, we propose to process continuous and discrete variables separately (but being conditioned on each other) by two diffusion models. The two diffusion models are co-evolved during training by reading conditions from each other. In order to further bind the diffusion models, moreover, we introduce a contrastive learning method with a negative sampling method. In our experiments with 11 real-world tabular datasets and 8 baseline methods, we prove the efficacy of the proposed method, called CoDi.

citations.title: [264146605 | Zhang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 82]
snippets: Recent advances in tabular data generation have greatly enhanced synthetic data quality. However, extending diffusion models to tabular data is challenging due to the intricately varied distributions and a blend of data types of tabular data. This paper introduces Tabsyn, a methodology that synthesizes tabular data by leveraging a diffusion model within a variational autoencoder (VAE) crafted latent space. The key advantages of the proposed Tabsyn include (1) Generality: the ability to handle a broad spectrum of data types by converting them into a single unified space and explicitly capture inter-column relations; (2) Quality: optimizing the distribution of latent embeddings to enhance the subsequent training of diffusion models, which helps generate high-quality synthetic data, (3) Speed: much fewer number of reverse steps and faster synthesis speed than existing diffusion-based methods. Extensive experiments on six datasets with five metrics demonstrate that Tabsyn outperforms existing methods. Specifically, it reduces the error rates by 86% and 67% for column-wise distribution and pair-wise column correlation estimations compared with the most competitive baselines.

Synthetic Tabular Data Generation(STDG) has long been studied by statisticians (Nowok et al., 2016)(Reiter, 2005)(Chawla et al., 2002).Recent success of deep generative models significantly advanced its boundary (Che et al., 2017)(Kim et al., 2021)(Figueira et al., 2022).In particular, CTGAN (Xu et al., 2019) combines conditional Generative Adversarial Network(GAN) and model-speicif normalization to model highly imbalanced and non-Gaussian columns.CtabGAN+ (Zhao et al., 2021)(Zhao et al., 2022) proposed a solution for mixed-type and long-tailed variable problems.Autodiff [57] and Tabsyn (Zhang et al., 2023) used a combination of latent-diffusion and data-specific autoencoder structure, which is the most similar work to ours but missing the critical transferable encoding/decoding ability.TabDDPM (Kotelnikov et al., 2022) achieved the current state-of-the-art in tabular generation with separate diffusion process for numerical and categorical columns.Some models also synthesizes data with Differential Privacy guarantee (Jordon et al., 2018)(Zhang et al., 2014)(McKenna et al., 2022)...Despite their effectiveness in modeling column distributions, none of the above methods is able to effectively boost the training of machine learning models with synthesized data, greatly limiting their usage in data augmentation [24].

snippets: Tabular data synthesis was initially based on classical deep generative models [Jordon et al., 2018, Xu et al., 2019, Morales-Alvarez et al., 2022], but has recently flourished with Transformer-based, LLM-based, and DFM-based methods.For example, to generate synthetic tabular data, [Gulati and Roysdon, 2023] applies a masked Transformer [Vaswani et al., 2017]; GReaT [Borisov et al., 2022] formulates tabular data as sentences and finetunes Generative Pre-trained Transformer 2 (GPT-2) [Radford et al., 2019]; TabDDPM [Kotelnikov et al., 2023], and CoDi [Lee et al., 2023] apply denoising diffusion probabilistic models [Ho et al., 2020]; STaSy [Kim et al., 2023] uses a score-based diffusion model [Song and Ermon, 2019]; Forest-VP and Forest-Flow [Jolicoeur-Martineau et al., 2024] use tree-based [Chen et al., 2015] deep diffusion and flow matching models [Lipman et al., 2023].Additionally, GOGGLE [Liu et al., 2023] uses an encoder-decoder model for generating tabular data, of which the decoder is a graph neural network to capture the dependencies between features.Since more and more tabular synthesis models are introduced every day, we mainly mentioned the representative ones for each category and benchmark on most of them in the experiments.Nevertheless, we highly suggest survey papers [Borisov et al., 2022, Li et al., 2023, Fang et al., 2024] for more detail about tabular synthesis models.

citations.title: [274965329 | D'souza et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets:
Handling imbalance in class distribution when building a classifier over tabular data has been a problem of long-standing interest. One popular approach is augmenting the training dataset with synthetically generated data. While classical augmentation techniques were limited to linear interpolation of existing minority class examples, recently higher capacity deep generative models are providing greater promise.

Among the transformer-based (Vaswani 2017) synthesizers, Generation of Realistic Tabular data i.e. GReaT (Borisov et al. 2023), TabuLA model (Zhao, Birke, and Chen 2023) and Tabular Masked transformers (Gulati and Roysdon 2023), TabLLM (Hegselmann et al. 2023) are noteworthy synthetic data generators. Normalizing flows are also used to estimate the data distribution (Papamakarios, Pavlakou, and Murray 2017). 

Of late, diffusion-based models are providing higher quality generations of synthetic data. These include the Denoising diffusion probabilistic model TabDDPM (Kotelnikov et al. 2022), TabSyn (Zhang et al. 2024) a Latent diffusion model, and Forestflow (Jolicoeur-Martineau, Fatras, and Kachman 2024) based on XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin 2016). We experiment with several categories of existing generators for tabular data, and found ForestFlow and Tab-Syn to provide the best accuracy.
