Both architectures have been adapted to handle mixed-type tabular synthetic data [VAE-based: (Akrami et al., 2022;(Liu et al., 2023); GAN-based: (Park et al., 2018;(Xu et al., 2019)(Zhao et al., 2021)Qian et al., 2023;(Li et al., 2021)(Zhao et al., 2022)]. 

With the rise in popularity of Large Language Models (LLMs), token-based transformers have also been applied to generate tabular synthetic data. Broadly, two classes of tabular-data LLMs can be identified. The first class leverages the knowledge embedded in pre-trained foundational models to create synthetic data "from scratch", relying solely on user prompts. The second class focuses on generating synthetic data that replicates a specific original dataset. This approach involves either fine-tuning pre-trained LLMs on the target dataset or training LLM-like architectures from scratch using the dataset. In this paper, we benchmark only against methods following the latter approach, where the model is explicitly trained to reproduce the statistical prop-erties of a given dataset (Borisov et al., 2022)Solatorio & Dupriez, 2023;Karami et al., 2024). 

In addition to token-based transformers, auto-regressive transformer models specifically designed for tabular data have also been proposed (Lee et al., 2023)Castellon et al., 2023;(Gulati et al., 2023). Unlike LLMs or token-based approaches, these models explicitly leverage the inherent structure of tabular data, such as limited value ranges, column-specific distributions, and inter-feature relationships, to enhance both the efficiency and quality of synthetic data generation. More recently, researchers have begun exploring hybrid approaches that combine transformers with diffusion to model discrete features (Zhang et al., 2024a).

sections.title: Challenges and Considerations
sections.text:
TLDR; Synthetic tabular data generation faces several key technical hurdles, including handling mixed data types, preserving complex relationships between columns, and maintaining data utility while ensuring privacy. The field must also contend with evaluation challenges and the need to balance computational efficiency with generation quality. (5 sources)

The generation of synthetic tabular data presents unique challenges that extend beyond those encountered in other data modalities  [253510877 | Gueye et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]. A fundamental challenge lies in modeling the complex interdependencies between columns while simultaneously handling the heterogeneous nature of tabular data, which typically contains both continuous and categorical features  [277038852 | Zhang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

One significant obstacle is the complexity of capturing and preserving the intricate relationships between variables in the generated data. While newer methods have made progress in addressing these challenges, the quality of synthetic data still falls short of real data standards  [273653942 | Shi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]. This limitation is particularly evident when dealing with multi-modal data types and complex column-wise distributions  [273653942 | Shi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4].

Privacy preservation emerges as another critical consideration, especially when working with sensitive data. While recent approaches have attempted to address privacy concerns through various mechanisms, balancing privacy protection with data utility remains an ongoing challenge  [272910781 | Umesh et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. The field has made progress in developing methods that can maintain both privacy and utility  [272910781 | Umesh et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [253510877 | Gueye et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6], but optimal solutions continue to evolve.

The scalability of synthetic data generation methods presents another significant consideration, particularly when dealing with large-scale datasets. Models must efficiently handle data distribution learning while maintaining reasonable computational requirements  [277038852 | Zhang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. This becomes especially challenging when attempting to synthesize relational datasets, which adds another layer of complexity beyond simple tabular data generation  [253510877 | Gueye et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6].

Feature heterogeneity poses a particular challenge, as models must simultaneously manage continuous and categorical variables while accounting for their distinct statistical properties and distributions  [273653942 | Shi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]. This challenge is compounded by the typically smaller size of tabular datasets available for training, which can limit the model's ability to learn complex patterns  [273653942 | Shi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4].

citations.title: [253510877 | Gueye et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]
snippets: Synthetic data generation is an active research topic in machine learning and aims to address data sparsity in development environments and in building data-driven models, especially when the data conveys private and sensitive information about individuals. In recent years, significant progress has been made in synthetic data generation models, particularly with the introduction of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) (Treat et al., 2018)...Promising results are obtained with Tabular GANs (TGANs) (Park et al., 2018)(Chen et al., 2019)[9][10][11](Li, 2020), which are new versions of generative models designed to model and synthesize tabular data. Because of the complexity of tabular data, the scope of previous work was limited to tabular data in a single table with independent rows. Building a generative model to synthesize relational datasets is not a simple task. In addition to the challenges inherent to tabular data, such as modeling the distribution of each column and the relationships between the columns within the table, synthesizing relational databases requires modeling the relationships between tables in the same database, i.e., the relationship between parent and child tables.

citations.title: [272910781 | Umesh et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: In recent years, there has been a significant increase in research efforts focused on generating synthetic tabular data [10,(Xu et al., 2019)12,(Kotelnikov et al., 2022). Along with these models, various performance measures are aimed at evaluating synthetic data's utility, fidelity, and privacy compared to real data [10]. Despite the challenges in creating synthetic tabular data, many models have demonstrated their ability to generate data that maintains privacy while preserving its utility (Wang et al., 2021)(Shi et al., 2022). However, it is worth noting that preserving dependencies among attributes in synthetic data compared to real data can enhance the semantic correctness of the synthetic data.

citations.title: [273653942 | Shi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]
snippets:
Synthesizing high-quality tabular data is an important topic in many data science tasks, ranging from dataset augmentation to privacy protection. However, developing expressive generative models for tabular data is challenging due to its inherent heterogeneous data types, complex inter-correlations, and intricate column-wise distributions.

Unlike image data, which comprises pure continuous pixel values with local spatial correlations, or text data, which comprises tokens that share the same dictionary space, tabular data features have much more complex and varied distributions (Xu et al., 2019;Borisov et al., 2023), making it challenging to learn joint probabilities across multiple columns. More specifically, such inherent heterogeneity leads to obstacles from two aspects: 1) typical tabular data often contains multi-modal data types, i.e., continuous (e.g., numerical features) and discrete (e.g., categorical features) variables; 2) within the same feature type, features do not share the exact same data property because of the different meaning they represent, resulting in different column-wise marginal distributions (even after normalizing them into same value ranges).

In recent years, numerous deep generative models have been proposed for tabular data generation with autoregressive models (Borisov et al., 2023), VAEs (Liu et al., 2023), and GANs (Xu et al., 2019) in the past few years. Though they have notably improved the generation quality compared to traditional machine learning generation techniques such as resampling (Chawla et al., 2002), the generated data quality is still far from satisfactory due to limited model capacity.

citations.title: [277038852 | Zhang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets: The generation of synthetic tabular data plays a critical role in applications such as data enhancement, privacy preservation, and model validation. However, the heterogeneity of tabular data—comprising both continuous and categorical features with intricate interdependencies—presents significant challenges in generating high-quality data.

sections.title: Applications and Use Cases
sections.text:
TLDR; Synthetic tabular data generation finds broad application across multiple domains, from healthcare and finance to privacy-preserving data sharing. The key use cases center around data augmentation, privacy protection, and improving machine learning model performance through increased training data diversity. (9 sources)

## Primary Application Areas

* **Healthcare and Medical Records**

- Generation of synthetic patient records for research while protecting sensitive medical information  [269282531 | Kim et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]

- Support for longitudinal health data analysis without compromising patient privacy  [269282531 | Kim et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]

* **Financial Services**

- Creation of synthetic financial datasets for fraud detection and risk assessment  [269282531 | Kim et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]

- Enhancement of trading model training data while maintaining market confidentiality  [276902574 | Li et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]

* **Supply Chain Management**

- Generation of inventory and logistics data for operational planning  [276775588 | Long et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]

- Enhancement of sales forecasting models with synthetic historical data  [276775588 | Long et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]

## Key Implementation Scenarios

* **Data Augmentation**

- Addressing class imbalance in training datasets  [259503802 | Fonseca et al. | 2023 | Citations: 75]

- Enhancing model training with additional synthetic samples  [276902998 | Stoian et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]

* **Privacy-Preserving Data Sharing**

- Protection of sensitive information while maintaining data utility  [276775588 | Long et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]

- Secure sharing of proprietary business data between organizations  [269282531 | Kim et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]

* **Active Learning Systems**

- Improving data selection and classifier training  [259503802 | Fonseca et al. | 2023 | Citations: 75]

- Semi-supervised learning with both labeled and unlabeled data  [259503802 | Fonseca et al. | 2023 | Citations: 75]

## Domain-Specific Benefits

* **Industrial Applications** 

- Enhanced supply chain visibility and management  [276775588 | Long et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]

- Improved operational decision-making without exposure of sensitive data  [269282531 | Kim et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]

* **Domain Expert Knowledge Integration**

- Incorporation of expert-designed data schemas  [276775588 | Long et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]  [231822017 | Vieira et al. | 2020 | Citations: 169]

- Maintenance of domain-specific relationships and constraints in synthetic data  [276775588 | Long et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]

citations.title: [259503802 | Fonseca et al. | 2023 | Citations: 75]
snippets: The generation of synthetic data can be used for anonymization, regularization, oversampling, semi-supervised learning, self-supervised learning, and several other tasks. Such broad potential motivated the development of new algorithms, specialized in data generation for specific data formats and Machine Learning (ML) tasks. However, one of the most common data formats used in industrial applications, tabular data, is generally overlooked; Literature analyses are scarce, state-of-the-art methods are spread across domains or ML tasks and there is little to no distinction among the main types of mechanism underlying synthetic data generation algorithms. In this paper, we analyze tabular and latent space synthetic data generation algorithms. Specifically, we propose a unified taxonomy as an extension and generalization of previous taxonomies, review 70 generation algorithms across six ML problems, distinguish the main generation mechanisms identified into six categories, describe each type of generation mechanism, discuss metrics to evaluate the quality of synthetic data and provide recommendations for future research. We expect this study to assist researchers and practitioners identify relevant gaps in the literature and design better and more informed practices with synthetic data.

citations.title: [269282531 | Kim et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]
snippets:
Tabular data, consisting of mixed variable types such as numerical and categorical variables, represents a widely applicable and essential data format [30]. It plays a crucial role in enhancing decisionmaking and efficiency in various real-world applications, such as finance, healthcare, manufacturing, and natural sciences [1,3,26]. However, challenges such as data scarcity and class imbalance, particularly for rare yet crucial events, often significantly degrade the performance of machine learning (ML) models, often resulting in reduced accuracy for underrepresented classes. To address these challenges, efficient synthetic data generation methods have been developed to augment tabular datasets. Traditional methods, such as synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) and its variants [5,11,21], focus on generating minority class samples to alleviate class imbalance. Recently, advanced generative models, such as TVAE [35], CTAB-GAN [39], and TabDDPM [19], have shown promising results in producing high-quality synthetic tabular data.

Large language models (LLMs) have also demonstrated significant potential for generating realistic tabular data, effectively handling both numerical and categorical variables [4]37]. However, these models often require extensive, data-specific fine-tuning, which can increase the risk of overfitting to majority classes or dominant feature values, especially in small and highly imbalanced tabular datasets.

citations.title: [276775588 | Long et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]
snippets:
Synthetic tabular data have widespread applications in industrial domains such as healthcare, finance, and supply chains, owing to their potential to protect privacy and mitigate data scarcity. However, generating realistic synthetic tabular data while preserving inter-column logical relationships remains a significant challenge for the existing generative models.

Tabular data, often structured in a table with rows and columns and stored in relational databases (Vieira et al., 2020), is ubiquitous (van Breugel and van der Schaar, 2024) across various industries-ranging from medical records in healthcare and transaction data in finance to sales data in retail to inventory data in warehousing. Such data is often carefully designed and maintained by domain experts, with data schemes or structures that are domain-specific and where columns are interdependent. Compared to unstructured data modalities such as image, video, and text, tabular data is structurally simpler yet semantically more complex, featuring well-defined columns, rich inter-column interactions, high dimensionality and heterogeneity, as well as domain-specific context and complexity. Thus, synthetic tabular data generation is challenging and remains underexplored, with its development significantly lags behind these unstructured data modalities (van Breugel and van der Schaar, 2024).

Nevertheless, many methods (Chawla et al., 2002;Xu et al., 2019;Kotelnikov et al., 2023;Borisov et al., 2022)-mainly adapted from models designed for generating other data modalities-have been proposed in literature to generate tabular data. One of earliest such approaches is the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling TEchnique (SMOTE), originally proposed by Chawla et al. (2002) to address dataset imbalance problem. As a data augmentation method, this interpolation-based method has recently been found effective in generating tabular data (Wang et al., 2024a). However, despite its promising performance on several benchmark datasets, as reported in Long et al. (2025b), SMOTE inherently struggles to preserve data privacy effectively and capture complex column dependencies. To overcome these limitations, deep generative models-leveraging their success in image, text, and audio synthesis-have been increasingly explored for tabular data generation. For instance, Xu et al. (2019) proposed CTGAN, a generative adversarial network (GAN)-based method specifically designed for tabular data. CTGAN learns the distribution of tabular data and generates synthetic rows from the learned representation. Although CTGAN improves privacy preservation (Zhao et al., 2024), it struggles to capture the interdependencies between categorical and continuous columns (Zhang et al., 2023). More recently, diffusion model-based methods such as TabDDPM (Kotelnikov et al., 2023) and TabSyn (Zhang et al., 2023) have been introduced to synthesize tabular data by learning the denoising process in latent space. These approaches demonstrate superior performance compared to CTGAN, particularly in preserving intricate tabular structures. Furthermore, Borisov et al. (2022) proposed GReaT, a large language model (LLM)-based approach for tabular data generation. GReaT transforms tabular data into textual representations and fine-tunes generative models to produce synthetic data, enabling the learning of underlying distributions without requiring complex encoding and decoding processes.

citations.title: [276902574 | Li et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets:
Tabular data synthesis is an important problem with wide range of applications. For example, in fields such as healthcare and finance, real-world data often contain sensitive information that cannot be directly shared for privacy considerations. It is crucial to generate synthetic data which not only closely resembles real data, but also avoids exposing sensitive information [Kotelnikov et al., 2023]. In machine learning applications, data augmentation is done to enrich the data (which often takes a tabular form) for model training, especially for class imbalanced datasets. Model training with both real and synthetic data often improves machine learning performance compared to training with real data alone. 

Early studies on tabular data synthesis are primarily based on statistical models [Aggarwal and Yu, 2004;Barak et al., 2007;Park et al., 2013;Li et al., 2014;Zhang et al., 2014]. With the rise of deep learning, models based on GANs and diffusion [Chen et al., 2019;Xu et al., 2019;Kim et al., 2021;Kotelnikov et al., 2023;Liu et al., 2024] have been widely applied to the task. At the same time, in order to ensure the quality of generated data, some studies have introduced conditional generation models [Xu et al., 2019;Zhao et al., 2023;Liu et al., 2024], aiming to incorporate additional information to guide the table synthesis process.

citations.title: [276902998 | Stoian et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Generative modelling has become the standard approach for synthesising tabular data. However, different use cases demand synthetic data to comply with different requirements to be useful in practice. In this survey, we review deep generative modelling approaches for tabular data from the perspective of four types of requirements: utility of the synthetic data, alignment of the synthetic data with domain-specific knowledge, statistical fidelity of the synthetic data distribution compared to the real data distribution, and privacy-preserving capabilities. We group the approaches along two levels of granularity: (i) based on the primary type of requirements they address and (ii) according to the underlying model they utilise. Additionally, we summarise the appropriate evaluation methods for each requirement and the specific characteristics of each model type.

sections.title: Background & Introduction
sections.text:
TLDR; Recent years have seen growing interest in combining Hebbian learning with deep neural networks for image recognition tasks. This hybrid approach aims to leverage biological plausibility while maintaining practical utility in computer vision applications. (2 sources)

The intersection of Hebbian learning principles and deep neural networks represents an exciting frontier in image recognition research. Hebbian learning, fundamentally rooted in the neuroscience concept that "neurons that fire together wire together," has emerged as a valuable approach for enhancing feature discrimination in image classification tasks  [225392580 | Magotra et al. | 2020 | Citations: 19]. 

This biological perspective finds particular relevance in modern computer vision systems, especially when working with convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which dominate current image recognition implementations. The application of Hebbian learning principles offers a pathway to improve transfer learning efficiency, particularly when working with heterogeneous datasets where traditional uniform training approaches might struggle  [225392580 | Magotra et al. | 2020 | Citations: 19].

One notable advancement in this field has been the development of specialized variants like Adaptive Homogeneous Learning (AHL), which demonstrates strong convergence properties and superior classification results compared to conventional autoencoder-based approaches  [16083305 | Wadhwa et al. | 2016 | Citations: 9]. This has opened new possibilities for unsupervised, bottom-up layer-wise learning in deep convolutional networks, showing promise across various benchmark datasets including MNIST, NORB, and CIFAR  [16083305 | Wadhwa et al. | 2016 | Citations: 9].

citations.title: [16083305 | Wadhwa et al. | 2016 | Citations: 9]
snippets: We demonstrate superior performance, compared to standard alternatives such as autoencoders, in training a deep convolutional net on standard image datasets...We then use AHL as a basis for unsupervised, bottom-up layer-wise learning in a standard deep convolutional net and demonstrate (Section 5) excellent classification results for standard image datasets (MNIST, NORB, CIFAR), using supervised training of a linear SVM as the final layer. Comparing with layered autoencoders, we find that AHL converges faster, and that the features it provides yield better classification performance for CIFAR, and comparable performance for MNIST and NORB.

citations.title: [225392580 | Magotra et al. | 2020 | Citations: 19]
snippets: Transfer learning algorithms have been widely studied for machine learning in recent times. In particular, in image recognition and classification tasks, transfer learning has shown significant benefits, and is getting plenty of attention in the research community. While performing a transfer of knowledge among source and target tasks, homogeneous dataset is not always available, and heterogeneous dataset can be chosen in certain circumstances. In this article, we propose a way of improving transfer learning efficiency, in case of a heterogeneous source and target, by using the Hebbian learning principle, called Hebbian transfer learning (HTL). In computer vision, biologically motivated approaches such as Hebbian learning represent associative learning, where simultaneous activation of brain cells positively affect the increase in synaptic connection strength between the individual cells. The discriminative nature of learning for the search of features in the task of image classification fits well to the techniques, such as the Hebbian learning rule—neurons that fire together wire together. The deep learning models, such as convolutional neural networks (CNN), are widely used for image classification. In transfer learning, for such models, the connection weights of the learned model should adapt to new target dataset with minimum effort. The discriminative learning rule, such as Hebbian learning, can improve performance of learning by quickly adapting to discriminate between different classes defined by target task.

sections.title: Historical Context
sections.text:
TLDR; The journey of Hebbian learning in deep neural networks spans decades, beginning with pioneering models like the Neocognitron in the 1980s. While early theoretical frameworks laid the groundwork, performance gaps compared to contemporary deep learning methods led to renewed research interest in bridging biological plausibility with practical effectiveness. (4 sources)

The historical trajectory of Hebbian learning in deep neural networks reflects a fascinating evolution from early theoretical models to modern implementations. The foundation was established in the 1980s with the Neocognitron, an innovative hierarchical model designed for translation-and-scaling-tolerant object recognition that incorporated essentially Hebbian learning mechanisms  [240354820 | Miconi | 2021 | Citations: 15]. This was followed by developments like the HMAX model, which introduced "imprinting" learning to approximate Hebbian processes in larger networks, and the VISNet model, which explored Hebbian learning with temporal dynamics  [240354820 | Miconi | 2021 | Citations: 15].

A significant shift occurred around 2018, when researchers began systematically exploring ways to implement true Hebbian learning in deep neural networks. A breakthrough came with the introduction of a learning algorithm that could operate without requiring massive amounts of labeled data, moving beyond the traditional backpropagation paradigm  [49479422 | Krotov et al. | 2018 | Citations: 165]. This period saw rapid progression from shallow network architectures (typically 2-3 layers) to deeper structures, culminating in the successful implementation of Hebbian learning in six-layer Convolutional Neural Networks  [231740474 | Talloen et al. | 2021 | Citations: 4].

However, despite these advances, early Hebbian networks consistently underperformed compared to contemporary deep learning techniques  [240354820 | Miconi | 2021 | Citations: 15]. This performance gap became a driving force behind ongoing research efforts to reconcile biological plausibility with practical effectiveness in deep learning systems  [7064552 | Pehlevan et al. | 2015 | Citations: 107].

citations.title: [231740474 | Talloen et al. | 2021 | Citations: 4]
snippets: Recently, unsupervised local learning, based on Hebb's idea that change in synaptic efficacy depends on the activity of the pre- and postsynaptic neuron only, has shown potential as an alternative training mechanism to backpropagation...In particular, the framework is used to expand the Krotov-Hopfield learning rule to standard convolutional neural networks without sacrificing accuracy compared to end-to-end backpropagation.

citations.title: [49479422 | Krotov et al. | 2018 | Citations: 165]
snippets: Significance Despite great success of deep learning a question remains to what extent the computational properties of deep neural networks are similar to those of the human brain. The particularly nonbiological aspect of deep learning is the supervised training process with the backpropagation algorithm, which requires massive amounts of labeled data, and a nonlocal learning rule for changing the synapse strengths. This paper describes a learning algorithm that does not suffer from these two problems. It learns the weights of the lower layer of neural networks in a completely unsupervised fashion. The entire algorithm utilizes local learning rules which have conceptual biological plausibility. It is widely believed that end-to-end training with the backpropagation algorithm is essential for learning good feature detectors in early layers of artificial neural networks, so that these detectors are useful for the task performed by the higher layers of that neural network. At the same time, the traditional form of backpropagation is biologically implausible. In the present paper we propose an unusual learning rule, which has a degree of biological plausibility and which is motivated by Hebb’s idea that change of the synapse strength should be local—i.e., should depend only on the activities of the pre- and postsynaptic neurons. We design a learning algorithm that utilizes global inhibition in the hidden layer and is capable of learning early feature detectors in a completely unsupervised way. These learned lower-layer feature detectors can be used to train higher-layer weights in a usual supervised way so that the performance of the full network is comparable to the performance of standard feedforward networks trained end-to-end with a backpropagation algorithm on simple tasks.

citations.title: [7064552 | Pehlevan et al. | 2015 | Citations: 107]
snippets: Neural network models of early sensory processing typically reduce the dimensionality of streaming input data. Such networks learn the principal subspace, in the sense of principal component analysis, by adjusting synaptic weights according to activity-dependent learning rules. When derived from a principled cost function, these rules are nonlocal and hence biologically implausible. At the same time, biologically plausible local rules have been postulated rather than derived from a principled cost function. Here, to bridge this gap, we derive a biologically plausible network for subspace learning on streaming data by minimizing a principled cost function. In a departure from previous work, where cost was quantified by the representation, or reconstruction, error, we adopt a multidimensional scaling cost function for streaming data. The resulting algorithm relies only on biologically plausible Hebbian and anti-Hebbian local learning rules. In a stochastic setting, synaptic weights converge to a stationary state, which projects the input data onto the principal subspace. If the data are generated by a nonstationary distribution, the network can track the principal subspace. Thus, our result makes a step toward an algorithmic theory of neural computation.

citations.title: [240354820 | Miconi | 2021 | Citations: 15]
snippets: Recent advances in deep learning have greatly improved the state of the art in visual object recognition. Deep learning networks take inspiration from features of the ventral visual cortex (including a hierarchical organization in successive layers and a topological organization of connections). Their internal activity shows similarities, as well as differences, with neural responses to natural images (Yamins et al., 2016)...There is a long history of research in hierarchical Hebbian networks. The Neocognitron (an early hierarchical model for translation-and scaling-tolerant object recognition) used an effectively Hebbian learning rule (Fukushima et al., 1982). The HMAX model used an "imprinting" learning method to approximate Hebbian learning in a large network in a computationally tractable manner (Serre et al., 2007). The VISNet model also studied various forms of Hebbian learning with temporal dynamics to learn invariant representations (Wallis et al., 1997)(Wallis et al., 1997)(Rolls et al., 2000). While these models and others provided rich insight, their performance remained far from current deep learning techniques.

sections.title: Key Architectures & Approaches
sections.text:
TLDR; Several key architectural innovations have emerged to combine Hebbian learning with deep neural networks. These include multilayered networks with structured connectivity, hybrid approaches combining unsupervised pre-training with supervised fine-tuning, and specialized modifications of traditional layers like the Hebbian Softmax layer. (6 sources)

* **Structured Multilayer Networks**: Advanced designs featuring both feedforward and feedback connections utilize Hebbian learning between different layers, while employing anti-Hebbian learning in lateral connections within the same layer. This extends Földiák's original single-layered concept to create more sophisticated architectures  [204401675 | Obeid et al. | 2019 | Citations: 20].

* **Feature Extractor Networks**: Specialized networks have been developed specifically for Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) tasks, using a two-step approach: first unsupervised Hebbian pre-training followed by supervised fine-tuning with Stochastic Gradient Descent. Notably, the Nonlinear Hebbian Principal Component Analysis (HPCA) learning rule has shown promising results on datasets like CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, particularly when limited labeled data is available  [248863047 | Lagani et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6].

* **Online Learning Systems**: Architectures designed for continuous data streams employ Hebbian/anti-Hebbian networks that can process one image at a time with memory requirements independent of the total dataset size. Single-layer implementations have demonstrated superior performance to more complex models like Sparse Autoencoders and Restricted Boltzmann Machines  [5477730 | Bahroun et al. | 2017 | Citations: 3]  [9719611 | Pehlevan et al. | 2014 | Citations: 44].

* **Modified Output Layers**: Innovations like Hebbian Softmax modify traditional output layers by incorporating both smoothed hidden activations and gradient descent learning. This hybrid approach facilitates faster learning of novel classes and improves performance for infrequent classes  [4347492 | Rae et al. | 2018 | Citations: 46].

* **Competitive Learning Networks**: Modern architectures incorporate neural competition mechanisms to prevent redundant feature learning and promote diverse hierarchical representations. Examples include Soft-Winner-Takes-All (WTA) approaches achieving nearly 80% accuracy on CIFAR-10, though harder WTA implementations still face challenges reaching backpropagation-level performance  [275954038 | Nimmo et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

citations.title: [204401675 | Obeid et al. | 2019 | Citations: 20]
snippets: We show that structured and deep similarity matching can be implemented by a new class of multilayered neural networks with structured connectivity and biologically-plausible local learning rules. These networks have Hebbian learning in feedforward and feedback connections between different layers, and anti-Hebbian learning in lateral connections within a layer. They generalize Földiak's single-layered, all-to-all connected Hebbian/anti-Hebbian network (Földiák, 1990).

citations.title: [248863047 | Lagani et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]
snippets: Features extracted from Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have proven to be very effective in the context of Content Based Image Retrieval (CBIR). Recently, biologically inspired Hebbian learning algorithms have shown promises for DNN training. In this contribution, we study the performance of such algorithms in the development of feature extractors for CBIR tasks. Specifically, we consider a semi-supervised learning strategy in two steps: first, an unsupervised pre-training stage is performed using Hebbian learning on the image dataset; second, the network is fine-tuned using supervised Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) training. For the unsupervised pre-training stage, we explore the nonlinear Hebbian Principal Component Analysis (HPCA) learning rule. For the supervised fine-tuning stage, we assume sample efficiency scenarios, in which the amount of labeled samples is just a small fraction of the whole dataset. Our experimental analysis, conducted on the CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 datasets, shows that, when few labeled samples are available, our Hebbian approach provides relevant improvements compared to various alternative methods.

citations.title: [275954038 | Nimmo et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Recent research in Hebbian learning has focused on combining purely Hebbian learning for unsupervised feature extraction in convolutional layers, with supervised classification training on these frozen features. Successful Hebbian integration into DNNs (Amato et al., 2019)(Krotov et al., 2018)Miconi, 2021;(Journ'e et al., 2022) is primarily achieved through neural competition, which allows distinct neurons to respond to input patterns, preventing redundant feature learning and promoting the development of diverse hierarchical representations...Whereas soft-Winner-Takes-All (WTA) competition through (Journ'e et al., 2022)'s SoftHebb model achieves an accuracy on CIFAR-10 of nearly 80%, current hard-WTA Hebbian approaches face challenges to match backpropagation SOTA performance while maintaining biological plausibility and efficiency. citations.title: [4347492 | Rae et al. | 2018 | Citations: 46]
snippets: We propose Hebbian Softmax, a modification of the traditional softmax layer with an updated learning rule. Hebbian Softmax contains the same linear map from the hidden state to the output vocabulary, but learns by smoothing hidden activations into the weight parameters for novel classes whilst concurrently applying gradient descent. This is to facilitate faster binding of novel classes, and improve learning of infrequent classes. We note this corresponds to a learning rule that transitions from Hebbian learning to gradient descent, and we will show that the combination of the two learning rules works better than either one in isolation.

citations.title: [5477730 | Bahroun et al. | 2017 | Citations: 3]
snippets: This study employs a Hebbian learning rule derived from a cost-function and applies it to perform online unsupervised learning of features from multiple image datasets. One of the main focus of this work is to find an online learning principle that is suitable for dealing with a continuous stream of data. Such an architecture can take one image at a time with memory requirements that are independent of the number of samples. A recent model of Hebbian/anti-Hebbian neural network (Pehlevan et al., 2014) was reproduced here and applied for the first time to online feature learning for image classification. The quality of the features is assessed visually and by performing classification with a linear classifier working on the learned features. The simulations show that a simple single-layer Hebbian network can outperform more complex models such as Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) and Restricted Boltzmann machines (RBM) for image classifications tasks. When tested with with the novel multi-layer architecture, the features learned in the different layers improve the classification accuracy, indicating that further layers help to learn additional relevant features.

citations.title: [9719611 | Pehlevan et al. | 2014 | Citations: 44]
snippets: Despite our extensive knowledge of biophysical properties of neurons, there is no commonly accepted algorithmic theory of neuronal function. Here we explore the hypothesis that single-layer neuronal networks perform online symmetric nonnegative matrix factorization (SNMF) of the similarity matrix of the streamed data. By starting with the SNMF cost function we derive an online algorithm, which can be implemented by a biologically plausible network with local learning rules. We demonstrate that such network performs soft clustering of the data as well as sparse feature discovery. The derived algorithm replicates many known aspects of sensory anatomy and biophysical properties of neurons including unipolar nature of neuronal activity and synaptic weights, local synaptic plasticity rules and the dependence of learning rate on cumulative neuronal activity. Thus, we make a step towards an algorithmic theory of neuronal function, which should facilitate large-scale neural circuit simulations and biologically inspired artificial intelligence.

sections.title: Performance Metrics & Results
sections.text:
TLDR; Recent implementations of Hebbian learning in deep neural networks have achieved comparable performance to traditional approaches across multiple benchmark datasets. However, while soft-Winner-Takes-All approaches have reached nearly 80% accuracy on CIFAR-10, hard-WTA implementations and simpler architectures still lag behind backpropagation's current state-of-the-art performance. (5 sources)

Performance evaluations of Hebbian learning in deep neural networks reveal mixed but promising results across different architectures and implementations. On standard benchmark datasets, Hebbian Softmax architectures have demonstrated notable capabilities, achieving approximately 95.5% accuracy on MNIST, 75.2% on CIFAR-10, and 76.2% on STL-10  [252531820 | Journ'e et al. | 2022 | Citations: 48].

When comparing against traditional approaches, Feature Extractor Networks (FENet) incorporating Hebbian learning have shown superior feature extraction capabilities for downstream tasks. Particularly noteworthy is their ability to achieve competitive Top-1 accuracy of 62.0% on CIFAR-10, surpassing conventional ResNet-18 performance (59.5%) and approaching Faster R-CNN results (63.5%)  [247158343 | Cekic et al. | 2022 | Citations: 7].

However, current limitations become apparent when examining specific architectures. Traditional hard-Winner-Takes-All (hard-WTA) implementations face significant performance hurdles, achieving only 72.2% accuracy on CIFAR-10, while simpler architectures with just three CNN layers manage only 64.6% accuracy  [275954038 | Nimmo et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [201666136 | Grinberg et al. | 2019 | Citations: 18]. These results suggest that while Hebbian learning can achieve competitive performance, there remains a substantial gap between current implementations and the performance levels achieved by standard backpropagation approaches <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

An interesting finding emerges regarding network depth and initialization: even when weights are initialized differently and allowed to evolve independently during training, performance can remain comparable to traditional backpropagation approaches  [76667846 | Amit | 2018 | Citations: 43]. This suggests that the relationship between Hebbian learning and network architecture is more nuanced than initially theorized, potentially opening new avenues for architectural innovation <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [247158343 | Cekic et al. | 2022 | Citations: 7]
snippets: While end-to-end training of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) yields state of the art performance in an increasing array of applications, it does not provide insight into, or control over, the features being extracted. We report here on a promising neuro-inspired approach to DNNs with sparser and stronger activations. We use standard stochastic gradient training, supplementing the end-to-end discriminative cost function with layer-wise costs promoting Hebbian ("fire together," "wire together") updates for highly active neurons, and anti-Hebbian updates for the remaining neurons.

Successful Hebbian integration into DNNs (Amato et al., 2019)(Krotov et al., 2018)Miconi, 2021;(Journ'e et al., 2022) is primarily achieved through neural competition, which allows distinct neurons to respond to input patterns, preventing redundant feature learning and promoting the development of diverse hierarchical representations...Whereas soft-Winner-Takes-All (WTA) competition through (Journ'e et al., 2022)'s SoftHebb model achieves an accuracy on CIFAR-10 of nearly 80%, current hard-WTA Hebbian approaches face challenges to match backpropagation SOTA performance while maintaining biological plausibility and efficiency. The SOTA accuracy with a Hard competition WTA model (Hard-WTA) on CIFAR-10 is 72.2% (Grinberg et al., 2019)...A sparse 3-CNN layer Hebbian architecture led to only 64.6% accuracy (Miconi, 2021), and struggled to form meaningful hierarchical representations...By integrating our best-performing learning mechanism (lateral inhibition and BCM Hebbian learning) with Hard-WTA, we achieved 75.2% CIFAR-10 test mean accuracy on the final 50% epochs in Journé et al. (2022)'s 3-CNN layer architecture, setting a new SOTA Hard-WTA performance.

citations.title: [201666136 | Grinberg et al. | 2019 | Citations: 18]
snippets: Local Hebbian learning is believed to be inferior in performance to end-to-end training using a backpropagation algorithm. We question this popular belief by designing a local algorithm that can learn convolutional filters at scale on large image datasets. These filters combined with patch normalization and very steep non-linearities result in a good classification accuracy for shallow networks trained locally, as opposed to end-to-end. The filters learned by our algorithm contain both orientation selective units and unoriented color units, resembling the responses of pyramidal neurons located in the cytochrome oxidase 'interblob' and 'blob' regions in the primary visual cortex of primates. It is shown that convolutional networks with patch normalization significantly outperform standard convolutional networks on the task of recovering the original classes when shadows are superimposed on top of standard CIFAR-10 images. Patch normalization approximates the retinal adaptation to the mean light intensity, important for human vision. We also demonstrate a successful transfer of learned representations between CIFAR-10 and ImageNet 32x32 datasets. All these results taken together hint at the possibility that local unsupervised training might be a powerful tool for learning general representations (without specifying the task) directly from unlabeled data.

citations.title: [252531820 | Journ'e et al. | 2022 | Citations: 48]
snippets: Recent approximations to backpropagation (BP) have mitigated many of BP's computational inefficiencies and incompatibilities with biology, but important limitations still remain. Moreover, the approximations significantly decrease accuracy in benchmarks, suggesting that an entirely different approach may be more fruitful. Here, grounded on recent theory for Hebbian learning in soft winner-take-all networks, we present multilayer SoftHebb, i.e. an algorithm that trains deep neural networks, without any feedback, target, or error signals. As a result, it achieves efficiency by avoiding weight transport, non-local plasticity, time-locking of layer updates, iterative equilibria, and (self-) supervisory or other feedback signals -- which were necessary in other approaches. Its increased efficiency and biological compatibility do not trade off accuracy compared to state-of-the-art bio-plausible learning, but rather improve it. With up to five hidden layers and an added linear classifier, accuracies on MNIST, CIFAR-10, STL-10, and ImageNet, respectively reach 99.4%, 80.3%, 76.2%, and 27.3%. In conclusion, SoftHebb shows with a radically different approach from BP that Deep Learning over few layers may be plausible in the brain and increases the accuracy of bio-plausible machine learning. Code is available at https://github.com/NeuromorphicComputing/SoftHebb.

citations.title: [76667846 | Amit | 2018 | Citations: 43]
snippets: We show that deep networks can be trained using Hebbian updates yielding similar performance to ordinary back-propagation on challenging image datasets. To overcome the unrealistic symmetry in connections between layers, implicit in back-propagation, the feedback weights are separate from the feedforward weights. The feedback weights are also updated with a local rule, the same as the feedforward weights—a weight is updated solely based on the product of activity of the units it connects. With fixed feedback weights as proposed in Lillicrap et al. (2016) performance degrades quickly as the depth of the network increases. If the feedforward and feedback weights are initialized with the same values, as proposed in Zipser and Rumelhart (1990), they remain the same throughout training thus precisely implementing back-propagation. We show that even when the weights are initialized differently and at random, and the algorithm is no longer performing back-propagation, performance is comparable on challenging datasets.

sections.title: Technical Advancements
sections.text:
TLDR; Recent technical innovations in Hebbian learning for deep neural networks focus on scalability, efficiency, and novel learning rules that address biological plausibility. Key advances include fast matrix multiplication optimizations enabling ImageNet-level training, and new 3-factor Hebbian rules that eliminate the need for precise supervision. (7 sources)

Several groundbreaking technical advances have pushed the boundaries of Hebbian learning in deep neural networks. A major breakthrough has been the development of FastHebb, which leverages matrix multiplication optimizations to achieve up to 50x speedup in training, making Hebbian learning feasible at ImageNet scale for the first time  [248863047 | Lagani et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6].

New learning rule families have emerged that address fundamental biological plausibility constraints. Notable among these is a 3-factor Hebbian approach that incorporates pre- and post-synaptic firing rates along with a global error signal (potentially from neuromodulators). This architecture eliminates the need for precise labels while maintaining performance close to backpropagation on image classification tasks  [219636144 | Pogodin et al. | 2020 | Citations: 34].

Innovative adaptations of existing architectures continue to enhance performance. The Hebbian Principal Component Analysis (HPCA) learning rule has shown advantages over traditional Winner Takes All (HWTA) strategies, particularly in transfer learning scenarios  [229349160 | Lagani et al. | 2020 | Citations: 4]. Extensions to the Krotov-Hopfield learning rule have enabled accurate training of standard convolutional neural networks without compromising performance compared to end-to-end backpropagation  [231740474 | Talloen et al. | 2021 | Citations: 4].

A particularly elegant solution involves combining fixed and plastic components in synaptic connections, where the fixed component serves as the connection weight and the plastic component acts as the Hebbian trace  [245876879 | Priyanka et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]  [4714955 | Miconi et al. | 2018 | Citations: 153]. This approach has proven especially valuable in recurrent networks, enabling effective lifelong learning and demonstrating superior performance in both memorization tasks and reinforcement learning scenarios.

citations.title: [219636144 | Pogodin et al. | 2020 | Citations: 34]
snippets: Here we present a family of learning rules that does not suffer from any of these problems. It is motivated by the information bottleneck principle (extended with kernel methods), in which networks learn to squeeze as much information as possible out of the input without sacrificing prediction of the output. The resulting rules have a 3-factor Hebbian structure: they require pre- and post-synaptic firing rates and a global error signal - the third factor - that can be supplied by a neuromodulator. Moreover, they do not require precise labels; instead, they rely on the similarity between the desired outputs. They thus solve all three implausibility issues of backpropagation. Moreover, to obtain good performance on hard problems and retain biologically plausible learning rules, our rules need divisive normalization - a known feature of biological networks. Finally, simulations show that our rule performs nearly as well as backpropagation on image classification tasks.

citations.title: [229349160 | Lagani et al. | 2020 | Citations: 4]
snippets: Recent work has shown that biologically plausible Hebbian learning can be integrated with backpropagation learning (backprop), when training deep convolutional neural networks. In particular, it has been shown that Hebbian learning can be used for training the lower or the higher layers of a neural network. For instance, Hebbian learning is effective for re-training the higher layers of a pre-trained deep neural network, achieving comparable accuracy w.r.t. SGD, while requiring fewer training epochs, suggesting potential applications for transfer learning. In this paper we build on these results and we further improve Hebbian learning in these settings, by using a nonlinear Hebbian Principal Component Analysis (HPCA) learning rule, in place of the Hebbian Winner Takes All (HWTA) strategy used in previous work.

citations.title: [231740474 | Talloen et al. | 2021 | Citations: 4]
snippets: Recently, unsupervised local learning, based on Hebb's idea that change in synaptic efficacy depends on the activity of the pre- and postsynaptic neuron only, has shown potential as an alternative training mechanism to backpropagation...In particular, the framework is used to expand the Krotov-Hopfield learning rule to standard convolutional neural networks without sacrificing accuracy compared to end-to-end backpropagation.

citations.title: [245876879 | Priyanka et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Thomas Miconi et al. (Miconi et al., 2018) in their work, they trained a neural network with backpropagation and explained Hebb's rule. The rule is used to specify a plasticity rule that aids if a neuron participates in making another neuron fire multiple times, the link between them is reinforced. (also known as neurons that fire together then wire together). Thus, a connection between any two neurons contains a fixed and a plastic component, with the fixed component being the connection weight and the plastic component being the Hebbian trace.

citations.title: [4714955 | Miconi et al. | 2018 | Citations: 153]
snippets: How can we build agents that keep learning from experience, quickly and efficiently, after their initial training? Here we take inspiration from the main mechanism of learning in biological brains: synaptic plasticity, carefully tuned by evolution to produce efficient lifelong learning. We show that plasticity, just like connection weights, can be optimized by gradient descent in large (millions of parameters) recurrent networks with Hebbian plastic connections. First, recurrent plastic networks with more than two million parameters can be trained to memorize and reconstruct sets of novel, high-dimensional 1000+ pixels natural images not seen during training. Crucially, traditional non-plastic recurrent networks fail to solve this task. Furthermore, trained plastic networks can also solve generic meta-learning tasks such as the Omniglot task, with competitive results and little parameter overhead. Finally, in reinforcement learning settings, plastic networks outperform a non-plastic equivalent in a maze exploration task. We conclude that differentiable plasticity may provide a powerful novel approach to the learning-to-learn problem.

citations.title: [248863047 | Lagani et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]
snippets: Features extracted from Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have proven to be very effective in the context of Content Based Image Retrieval (CBIR). Recently, biologically inspired Hebbian learning algorithms have shown promises for DNN training. In this contribution, we study the performance of such algorithms in the development of feature extractors for CBIR tasks. Specifically, we consider a semi-supervised learning strategy in two steps: first, an unsupervised pre-training stage is performed using Hebbian learning on the image dataset; second, the network is fine-tuned using supervised Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) training. For the unsupervised pre-training stage, we explore the nonlinear Hebbian Principal Component Analysis (HPCA) learning rule. For the supervised fine-tuning stage, we assume sample efficiency scenarios, in which the amount of labeled samples is just a small fraction of the whole dataset. Our experimental analysis, conducted on the CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 datasets, shows that, when few labeled samples are available, our Hebbian approach provides relevant improvements compared to various alternative methods.

sections.title: Challenges & Limitations
sections.text:
TLDR; Despite progress in combining Hebbian learning with deep neural networks, significant challenges persist around training efficiency, scalability, and performance parity with backpropagation. Key limitations include computational demands at larger scales and difficulties in achieving consistent performance improvements across different architectures and datasets. (4 sources)

While Hebbian learning approaches have shown promise in image recognition tasks, several fundamental challenges limit their widespread adoption and effectiveness. A primary concern is the computational overhead associated with implementing Hebbian learning at scale. Although FastHebb has achieved impressive 50x speedups through matrix multiplication optimizations, the resources required for processing large-scale datasets like ImageNet still pose significant challenges for real-world deployment  [248863047 | Lagani et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6].

The quest for biological plausibility introduces its own set of constraints. While newer architectures like SoftHebb have achieved reasonable accuracy levels (around 80% on CIFAR-10), they still fall short of matching backpropagation's current performance standards  [252531820 | Journ'e et al. | 2022 | Citations: 48]. This gap becomes particularly evident in harder WTA implementations, which struggle to maintain efficiency while preserving biological plausibility  [275954038 | Nimmo et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

Another significant challenge lies in the complexity of maintaining stable feature hierarchies. Simple architectures with limited layers have shown considerable difficulty in forming meaningful hierarchical representations, particularly when scaled beyond three convolutional layers  [275954038 | Nimmo et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. This limitation affects the network's ability to progressively build increasingly abstract representations of visual features.

Data heterogeneity presents yet another hurdle, particularly in transfer learning scenarios. While Hebbian approaches offer potential benefits for handling heterogeneous datasets, ensuring consistent performance across varying data distributions remains a persistent challenge  [225392580 | Magotra et al. | 2020 | Citations: 19]. The discriminative nature of Hebbian learning, while advantageous for feature discrimination, can sometimes lead to instability when adapting to new target datasets <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [225392580 | Magotra et al. | 2020 | Citations: 19]
snippets: Transfer learning algorithms have been widely studied for machine learning in recent times. In particular, in image recognition and classification tasks, transfer learning has shown significant benefits, and is getting plenty of attention in the research community. While performing a transfer of knowledge among source and target tasks, homogeneous dataset is not always available, and heterogeneous dataset can be chosen in certain circumstances. In this article, we propose a way of improving transfer learning efficiency, in case of a heterogeneous source and target, by using the Hebbian learning principle, called Hebbian transfer learning (HTL). In computer vision, biologically motivated approaches such as Hebbian learning represent associative learning, where simultaneous activation of brain cells positively affect the increase in synaptic connection strength between the individual cells. The discriminative nature of learning for the search of features in the task of image classification fits well to the techniques, such as the Hebbian learning rule—neurons that fire together wire together. The deep learning models, such as convolutional neural networks (CNN), are widely used for image classification. In transfer learning, for such models, the connection weights of the learned model should adapt to new target dataset with minimum effort. The discriminative learning rule, such as Hebbian learning, can improve performance of learning by quickly adapting to discriminate between different classes defined by target task.

question: Are there articles on the fusion of coarse and fine granularity related hierarchical ranking?

sections.title: Background/Introduction
sections.text:
TLDR; Multi-granularity information processing combines broad, quick assessments with detailed analysis for better decision-making. The fusion of coarse and fine-grained information helps balance speed and precision in various applications. (3 sources)

Multi-granularity approaches offer a powerful framework for handling information at different levels of detail. Starting with coarse-grained information provides an efficient way to quickly assess large sets of options, making it particularly useful for initial screening processes - whether evaluating candidates, reviewing resumes, or filtering emails  [270765016 | Luo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. This broad initial assessment serves as a foundation that can later be refined through more detailed, fine-grained analysis.

The importance of multi-granularity has been demonstrated across several domains, notably in computer vision tasks. Research has shown impressive results in applications ranging from object recognition to visual classification and text-based question answering  [254823263 | Guo et al. | 2022 | Citations: 15]  [116141508 | Wang et al. | 2018 | Citations: 46]. These approaches are particularly effective because they can handle both coarse-grained and fine-grained features, though implementing them comes with certain challenges. One notable consideration is that while hybrid multi-granularity features offer a straightforward implementation path, they require careful design of the fusion process  [254823263 | Guo et al. | 2022 | Citations: 15].

The integration of different granularity levels creates opportunities for more nuanced information retrieval systems. For example, search engines can now consider both the general topic ("business") and specific aspects ("stock market analysis") of documents to better match user queries  [4959890 | Lau et al. | 2011 | Citations: 8]. This capability highlights how multi-granularity approaches can adapt to users' specific needs while maintaining efficiency in information processing <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [254823263 | Guo et al. | 2022 | Citations: 15]
snippets: This strategy of focusing on multi-granularity characteristics has yielded excellent results in applications such as object recognition (Olszewska, 2022), visual classification (Du et al., 2020), and text-based question answering (Wang et al., 2018). In the task of image-text matching, this method fully considers object elements and non-object elements, which encourages more accurate matching of images and texts, and reduces the impact of the tremendous useless information existing in semantic alignment. Regarding the intermediate granularity, one way is to fuse coarse-grained and fine-grained features as hybrid multi-granularity features (Olszewska et al., 2008), and another way is to obtain features of different granularity by setting different sizes of the visual field to the feature extraction network (Wang et al., 2021). The first method is straightforward and direct, but it necessitates the design of a suitable fusion process, whereas the second one is affected by the choice of the size of each visual field and demanding that the feature extraction module is not a black box.

citations.title: [270765016 | Luo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
snippets: Many decision-making scenarios benefit from starting with coarse-grained information.This approach proves valuable in initial evaluations, as seen in tasks like selecting contestants, screening resumes, or filtering emails.Coarse-grained information allows for a quick and efficient assessment of a large number of alternatives.However, after the initial selection, further refinement of the evaluation process is often required.This is where fine-grained information becomes critical.By continuously refining the decision attributes through successive levels of analysis, decision-makers can make more detailed and precise judgments.This iterative process ultimately improves the overall effectiveness of the decision-making process.While more detailed information is essential for final decisions, coarse-grained information plays a vital role in enhancing decision-making efficiency.After all, decision-making incurs costs related to information collection and the actual situation.Therefore, a multilevel S3WD process offers a compelling approach by progressively analyzing decision-making information, starting from coarse-grained to fine-grained levels.This iterative strategy enables a balance between efficiency and accuracy, leading to better decision results.

citations.title: [4959890 | Lau et al. | 2011 | Citations: 8]
snippets: In the context of IR, we try to apply the concept of information granulation to design a granular IR system which can estimate the "semantic granularity" of documents (e.g., general vs. specific documents) and rank these documents with respect to information seekers' specific granularity requirements.

sections.title: Core Challenges
sections.text:
TLDR; Integrating coarse and fine-grained information faces key obstacles in managing label relationships and computational complexity. The main challenges stem from balancing different granularity levels during training and efficiently scaling hierarchical architectures. (3 sources)

The fusion of coarse and fine-granularity information presents several fundamental challenges that researchers must address. A primary difficulty lies in managing the complex relationships between labels at different granularity levels. While coarse-level classifications tend to suppress fine-grained feature learning, fine-grained features actually prove more beneficial for developing robust coarse-level classifiers. This creates a tension in the learning process due to the loss of relationships between hierarchical multi-granularity labels  [265154530 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

Another significant technical hurdle involves the scalability and computational efficiency of hierarchical systems. When dealing with longer temporal sequences or extended time periods, hierarchical architectures face increased parameter overhead and poor scaling behavior. This limitation becomes particularly apparent when attempting to maintain predictive accuracy while managing larger duration intervals  [276618365 | Lillelund et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

Current approaches primarily focus on discriminative loss functions for ranking purposes, which may not optimally capture the full spectrum of hierarchical relationships. Most methods implement either a rigid nested architecture with fixed feature sharing patterns or restrict themselves to just two levels of granularity, limiting their applicability to more complex, multi-level hierarchies  [214092996 | Achddou et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1].

These challenges underscore why developing effective solutions for multi-granularity fusion remains an active area of research, requiring careful consideration of both architectural design and training strategies <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [214092996 | Achddou et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1]
snippets: For example, while (Kim et al., 2017) propose a nested architecture providing different (potentially nested) outputs, they do not study how to combine these outputs into a refined single prediction, nor provide a reliable confidence measure associated to them. Furthermore, the architecture they propose has key differences with ours, while they propose a nested hierarchy in an end-to-end fashion (i.e., features associated to the coarse and fine levels are shared from the top to the bottom of the network), we enforce sequential information bottlenecks...(Yan et al., 2014) study the problem of nested learning for two nested levels of granularity, and optimize for a final fine prediction. Their design is specific for a two-level category hierarchy while our work generalizes to any number of nested levels, and we can simultaneously train and test up to an arbitrary level of granularity.

sections.title: Fusion Strategies and Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; Various approaches exist for combining coarse and fine-grained information, from neural networks to mathematical frameworks. Key methods include adaptive transformations, bidirectional architectures, and specialized fusion modules that can operate at different levels of the processing pipeline. (9 sources)

Several distinct methodologies have emerged for fusing coarse and fine-grained information:

* **Adaptive Cross-Scale Fusion**: Uses normalized Gaussian functions to compute dynamic mappings between different granularity levels. This approach generates adaptive transformation matrices that can adjust relationships between features at different scales  [268032752 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 9].

* **Bidirectional Architecture**: Implements sequential processing from finest to coarsest granularities, allowing finer-grained classifiers to inform coarser ones. This contrasts with traditional parallel approaches, enabling better flow of hierarchical semantic information  [274789063 | Lu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

* **Dynamic Hierarchical Fusion**: Combines multi-view gated fusion with hierarchical feature fusion to process information across different granularity levels. This approach emphasizes features spanning from coarse to fine granularities while maintaining view consistency  [277005056 | Chen et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

* **Probability-Based Integration**: Constructs probability distributions that link predictions across granularity levels, with finer scale predictions being guided by coarser ones  [276618365 | Lillelund et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

* **Cross-Entropy Combination**: Employs convex combinations of cross-entropy losses at different granularity levels, along with techniques involving soft labels and chained conditional probabilities  [272427238 | Urbani et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

* **Evidence Theory Approach**: Utilizes belief functions and Dirichlet hyperprobability distributions to fuse multilayer classification evidence, moving from coarse to fine granularity  [259744038 | Xu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 6].

* **Query-Based Fusion**: Applies dynamic, nonlinear rank fusion methods that leverage query-document correlations on a per-query basis  [251493187 | Valadez et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0].

* **Progressive Multi-Stage Processing**: Implements a three-stage approach combining coarse-grained unit retrieval, pre-ranking, and fine-grained post-ranking to balance effectiveness and efficiency  [273346467 | Zhao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7].

Each of these methods addresses specific aspects of the fusion challenge, offering different trade-offs between flexibility, computational efficiency, and accuracy <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

sections.title: Applications and Implementations
sections.text:
TLDR; Multi-granularity approaches are actively deployed across diverse domains including image classification, document summarization, and question answering systems. Implementation strategies range from hierarchical architectures to progressive processing pipelines, with applications showing particular promise in areas requiring both broad understanding and detailed analysis. (11 sources)

Recent implementations demonstrate successful deployment of multi-granularity approaches across several application domains:

* **Image Classification and Discovery**: Systems have been developed for fine-grained category discovery using only coarse-grained supervision, helping reduce labeling costs while maintaining classification accuracy. These approaches use hierarchical self-contrasting networks to bridge the gap between coarse and fine-grained representations  [252547561 | An et al. | 2022 | Citations: 17].

* **Document Summarization**: Advanced frameworks employ coarse-to-fine ranking strategies for unsupervised summarization. Notable implementations include semantic block-based approaches that first rank document segments before selecting important sentences  [251622441 | Liang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6].

* **Visual Question Answering**: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have been enhanced with retrieval-augmented frameworks that incorporate hierarchical structures. These systems use both probability-level and instance-level fusion strategies to reduce hallucinations and improve accuracy  [271600627 | Qu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 16].

* **Information Retrieval**: Novel ranking methods have been developed that combine Boolean queries with natural language queries. Systems like COMBSUM demonstrate improved retrieval performance through sophisticated fusion techniques  [261682437 | Wang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 10].

* **Remote Sensing**: Specialized fusion networks have been implemented for land cover classification, using dynamic convolutions and transformers to manage hierarchical information. These systems employ coarse-fine mutual learning strategies to optimize feature fusion  [273743530 | Pan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

* **Cross-Modal Search**: Recent implementations focus on achieving fine-grained hierarchical semantic alignment between different modalities. These systems aim to improve cross-modal representation quality through structured feature mining and relationship identification  [272087386 | Han et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

* **Multi-Task Learning**: Architectures have evolved to support simultaneous processing at multiple granularity levels, using shared feature extractors with independent classification heads  [276928545 | Sani et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [658379 | Wu et al. | 2016 | Citations: 492]  [240354347 | Garg et al. | 2021 | Citations: 12].

* **Medical Imaging**: Enhanced frameworks like CLIP have been adapted for medical imaging tasks, demonstrating strong zero-shot capabilities and transfer learning benefits  [271051547 | Cheng et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [245226112 | Lei et al. | 2021 | Citations: 3908].

sections.title: Evaluation and Performance Considerations
sections.text:
TLDR; Evaluating multi-granularity systems requires specialized metrics that account for hierarchical relationships and varying label granularities. Different approaches to performance measurement reflect the complex nature of assessing both coarse and fine-grained predictions. (6 sources)

Evaluating systems that process information at multiple granularities demands careful consideration of how to measure success across different levels of detail. Traditional evaluation metrics have been modified to accommodate hierarchical structures, with approaches like Hierarchical Average Precision (H-AP) introducing specialized measures that account for partial matches in the hierarchy. This metric is particularly useful as it provides smoother penalties for instances that share coarser semantics even when fine-grained labels differ  [262013617 | Ramzi et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4].

Performance assessment must also consider the inherent subjectivity of label assignments across different expertise levels. Research has shown that domain experts and novices often interpret the same information at different granularity levels, highlighting the need for evaluation frameworks that can account for varying levels of detail  [240354347 | Garg et al. | 2021 | Citations: 12]  [231689408 | Chang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 69].

The construction of hierarchical structures significantly impacts evaluation outcomes. When working with existing datasets, performance can vary based on whether the hierarchy is derived from ontological structures, semantic clustering, or visual clustering methods. This variation affects how closely related concepts are grouped at different granularity levels  [250144476 | Chen et al. | 2022 | Citations: 16].

Modern evaluation approaches have moved toward bi-granularity assessment frameworks that consider both coarse and fine-grained aspects. These frameworks recognize that precise relevance assessment requires more than simple binary discrimination, suggesting that higher-performing systems should incorporate objectives that span multiple levels of granularity  [268032752 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 9]. To ensure consistency across different granularity levels, some approaches now explicitly map between coarse and fine-grained types, incorporating mechanisms to filter out inconsistent classifications  [264288775 | Lee et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3].
