sections.title: Best Practices and Recommendations
sections.text:
TLDR; Effective SFT requires careful consideration of data quality, model selection, and training methodology. Key recommendations include starting with smaller, high-quality datasets and using advanced techniques like knowledge distillation for optimal results. (5 sources)

Based on current research and practical implementations, several best practices emerge for maximizing the effectiveness of supervised fine-tuning:

**Data Generation and Quality**

When working with limited data resources, consider generating synthetic training data through advanced techniques. Research has shown that even training a large model on as few as 125 examples can improve downstream model performance  [263605624 | Kaddour et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]. Alternatively, you can leverage larger language models to annotate or generate new training examples, similar to knowledge distillation approaches but focused purely on data exchange  [263605624 | Kaddour et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]  [246680398 | Meng et al. | 2022 | Citations: 229].

**Parameter Efficiency**

Consider employing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques alongside traditional SFT. Modern approaches like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) offer significant benefits for adapting base models to specific response styles while maintaining computational efficiency  [276724734 | Ross et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]  [271744895 | Zhu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

**Multiple Round Training**

If you're working with newer or less familiar model architectures, implement multiple rounds of training. Breaking down the training process into smaller segments can help prevent confusion and optimize results  [274822521 | Mao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

**Iterative Refinement**

Follow a structured approach combining multiple stages of training: start with basic supervised fine-tuning, progress to reward model training, and finally move to reinforcement learning components if needed  [260334562 | Lai et al. | 2023 | Citations: 130]. This staged approach helps ensure stable and effective model adaptation.

Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT): Starting with a multilingual LLM as the base, e.g., BLOOM (Scao et al., 2022), we fine-tune the model with our instruction dataset for the target language using supervised learning with the autoregressive objective. snippets:
In this work, we attempt to yield the best of both worlds by fine-tuning smaller models with training data generated by an LLM. Following recent work on training data generation [32,27,21], we show that by (i) annotating unlabeled examples or (ii) generating entirely new ones, we can effectively transfer knowledge from the LLM (teacher) to the specialized model (student), which can be several magnitudes of orders smaller, akin to knowledge distillation [18] but only via the exchange of data.

We find that synthetic data generation after fine-tuning the teacher LLM, even on only extremely limited data, improves the synthetic data quality as measured by the downstream model generalization performance. For example, fine-tuning a 20B LLM on as few as 125 examples (5% of the RTE dataset [34]) increases the augmented-data-fine-tuned downstream model's performance by multiple percentage points.

citations.title: [246680398 | Meng et al. | 2022 | Citations: 229]
snippets: Pretrained language models (PLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in various natural language processing tasks: Unidirectional PLMs (e.g., GPT) are well known for their superior text generation capabilities; bidirectional PLMs (e.g., BERT) have been the prominent choice for natural language understanding (NLU) tasks. While both types of models have achieved promising few-shot learning performance, their potential for zero-shot learning has been underexplored. In this paper, we present a simple approach that uses both types of PLMs for fully zero-shot learning of NLU tasks without requiring any task-specific data: A unidirectional PLM generates class-conditioned texts guided by prompts, which are used as the training data for fine-tuning a bidirectional PLM. With quality training data selected based on the generation probability and regularization techniques (label smoothing and temporal ensembling) applied to the fine-tuning stage for better generalization and stability, our approach demonstrates strong performance across seven classification tasks of the GLUE benchmark (e.g., 72.3/73.8 on MNLI-m/mm and 92.8 on SST-2), significantly outperforming zero-shot prompting methods and achieving even comparable results to strong few-shot approaches using 32 training samples per class.

citations.title: [271744895 | Zhu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]
snippets: We primarily focus on the field of large language models (LLMs) for recommendation, which has been actively explored recently and poses a significant challenge in effectively enhancing recommender systems with logical reasoning abilities and open-world knowledge. Current mainstream efforts mainly center around injecting personalized information from recommendation models into LLMs by customizing input templates or aligning representations between semantic and recommendation spaces at the prediction layer. However, they face three significant limitations: (1) LoRA is mostly used as a core component in existing works, but personalization is not well established in LoRA parameters as the LoRA matrix shared by every user may not cater to different users' characteristics, leading to suboptimal performance. (2) Although lifelong personalized behavior sequences are ideal for personalization, their use raises effectiveness and efficiency issues since LLMs require escalating training and inference time to extend text lengths. (3) Existing approaches aren't scalable for large datasets due to training efficiency constraints. Thus, LLMs only see a small fraction of the datasets (e.g., less than 10%) instead of the whole datasets, limiting their exposure to the full training space. To address these problems, we propose RecLoRA. This model incorporates a Personalized LoRA module that maintains independent LoRAs for different users and a Long-Short Modality Retriever that retrieves different history lengths for different modalities, significantly improving performance while adding minimal time cost. Furthermore, we design a Few2Many Learning Strategy, using a conventional recommendation model as a lens to magnify small training spaces to full spaces. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our RecLoRA compared to existing baseline models.

question: how do GNNs perform on graphs with billions of nodes?

sections.title: Background & Scale
sections.text:
TLDR; Modern real-world graphs range from social networks to financial transaction records, with sizes reaching billions of nodes and trillions of edges. These massive graphs pose fundamental challenges for traditional machine learning approaches, leading to the emergence of specialized distributed computing solutions. (6 sources)

The scale of real-world graphs continues to grow dramatically, driven by the increasing digitization of human interactions, business operations, and technological infrastructure. These massive graphs span multiple domains, from social networks to financial systems, with sizes that fundamentally challenge conventional machine learning approaches  [235421912 | Li et al. | 2021 | Citations: 235].

Major platforms exemplify this unprecedented scale. Facebook maintains a social network encompassing over 2.9 billion users connected by more than 400 billion friendship relations  [252684019 | Chai et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3]. Similarly, Alibaba operates a commerce graph connecting more than a billion users with two billion items  [271329060 | Gupta et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [10086579 | Wang et al. | 2018 | Citations: 3621]. Financial institutions face similar challenges - for instance, Alipay processes billions of daily transactions, including cases of embezzlement, fraud, and money laundering  [258762326 | Li et al. | 2023 | Citations: 10].

The scope of these massive graphs extends beyond just social connections. Messaging applications like WeChat maintain graphs containing billions of nodes and ten billion edges representing user relationships  [249538743 | Zhang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 3]. Knowledge bases like Freebase contain over 1.9 billion triples  [252684019 | Chai et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3]. What makes these graphs particularly challenging is that their sheer size exceeds the memory capabilities of single machines, necessitating distributed computing approaches  [265498409 | Mostafa et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1].

sections.title: Major Challenges
sections.text:
TLDR; Processing GNNs on billion-scale graphs faces three main technical barriers: explosive memory requirements for node embeddings, inherent dependencies between training samples, and complexities of distributed computing. These challenges are amplified by the exponential growth in computation needs as graph size increases. (8 sources)

Operating GNNs on large-scale graphs presents distinct challenges that differ significantly from traditional machine learning approaches. One fundamental obstacle is the memory-intensive nature of storing node embeddings, where memory costs increase linearly with the number of nodes  [251492946 | Yeh et al. | 2022 | Citations: 17]. Even modest embedding dimensions of 64 bits per node can quickly escalate to hundreds of gigabytes for billion-scale graphs, far exceeding the capacity of standard GPU memory  [251492946 | Yeh et al. | 2022 | Citations: 17].

Unlike other ML domains where training samples are independent, graphs inherently encode dependencies between nodes through their structure  [222291574 | Zheng et al. | 2020 | Citations: 243]. This characteristic makes traditional mini-batch approaches inadequate, as each batch must account for neighboring dependencies that expand exponentially with depth  [222291574 | Zheng et al. | 2020 | Citations: 243]  [3707621 | Hamilton et al. | 2017 | Citations: 12005].

The distributed computing aspect adds another layer of complexity. When scaling beyond single-machine capabilities, each node representation computation requires reading extensive neighbor data across machines, creating substantial network traffic bottlenecks  [222291574 | Zheng et al. | 2020 | Citations: 243]  [220347100 | Bojchevski et al. | 2020 | Citations: 367]. Current parallelization methods struggle to effectively manage these large and interconnected computation dependencies  [259213239 | Wan et al. | 2023 | Citations: 36].

These challenges become particularly acute in industrial contexts, where graphs can reach sizes requiring hundreds of terabytes of storage simply for IDs and structure, without considering additional features  [276558347 | Zhao et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. The combination of high communication overhead and irregular graph structures makes distributed training particularly demanding, even limiting practical applications to moderate-sized graphs  [278367881 | Ranjan et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. Recent attempts to address these limitations through transfer learning show promise, suggesting that training on manageable subsets while maintaining effectiveness might be a viable path forward  [273507638 | Li et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [220011540 | Ruiz et al. | 2020 | Citations: 335].

citations.title: [220347100 | Bojchevski et al. | 2020 | Citations: 367]
snippets: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful approach for solving many network mining tasks. However, learning on large graphs remains a challenge -- many recently proposed scalable GNN approaches rely on an expensive message-passing procedure to propagate information through the graph. We present the PPRGo model which utilizes an efficient approximation of information diffusion in GNNs resulting in significant speed gains while maintaining state-of-the-art prediction performance. In addition to being faster, PPRGo is inherently scalable, and can be trivially parallelized for large datasets like those found in industry settings. We demonstrate that PPRGo outperforms baselines in both distributed and single-machine training environments on a number of commonly used academic graphs. To better analyze the scalability of large-scale graph learning methods, we introduce a novel benchmark graph with 12.4 million nodes, 173 million edges, and 2.8 million node features. We show that training PPRGo from scratch and predicting labels for all nodes in this graph takes under 2 minutes on a single machine, far outpacing other baselines on the same graph. We discuss the practical application of PPRGo to solve large-scale node classification problems at Google.

citations.title: [222291574 | Zheng et al. | 2020 | Citations: 243]
snippets: Graph neural networks (GNN) have shown great success in learning from graph-structured data. They are widely used in various applications, such as recommendation, fraud detection, and search. In these domains, the graphs are typically large, containing hundreds of millions of nodes and several billions of edges. To tackle this challenge, we develop DistDGL, a system for training GNNs in a mini-batch fashion on a cluster of machines. DistDGL is based on the Deep Graph Library (DGL), a popular GNN development framework. DistDGL distributes the graph and its associated data (initial features and embeddings) across the machines and uses this distribution to derive a computational decomposition by following an owner-compute rule. DistDGL follows a synchronous training approach and allows ego-networks forming the mini-batches to include non-local nodes. To minimize the overheads associated with distributed computations, DistDGL uses a high-quality and light-weight min-cut graph partitioning algorithm along with multiple balancing constraints. This allows it to reduce communication overheads and statically balance the computations. It further reduces the communication by replicating halo nodes and by using sparse embedding updates. The combination of these design choices allows DistDGL to train high-quality models while achieving high parallel efficiency and memory scalability. We demonstrate our optimizations on both inductive and transductive GNN models. Our results show that DistDGL achieves linear speedup without compromising model accuracy and requires only 13 seconds to complete a training epoch for a graph with 100 million nodes and 3 billion edges on a cluster with 16 machines.

sections.title: Scaling Solutions & Techniques
sections.text:
TLDR; Several complementary approaches have emerged to handle billion-scale graphs, including sampling-based methods, parameter sharing, and compression techniques. These solutions aim to balance computational efficiency with model performance while managing memory constraints in distributed settings. (12 sources)

Here are the key approaches for scaling GNNs to large-scale graphs:

1. **Sampling-Based Methods**: These techniques selectively process subsets of nodes and their neighborhoods to reduce computational load. Notable approaches include:

   - Node-centric sampling that uses layered caching and gradient accumulation to minimize disk I/O  [274131701 | Lopushanskyy et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]

   - Neighbor-aware sampling strategies that adapt to varying neighborhood sizes  [3707621 | Hamilton et al. | 2017 | Citations: 12005]

   - Adaptive neighbor sampling that controls computation per sample rather than fixing the number of steps  [4627825 | Zou et al. | 2019 | Citations: 131]

2. **Parameter Sharing and Local Parametrization**: Instead of learning global embedding vectors, these methods learn local mappings that remain consistent regardless of graph size. This approach enables deployment on larger graphs after training on smaller ones  [253157419 | Cervino et al. | 2022 | Citations: 8]  [12742943 | Gilmer et al. | 2017 | Citations: 6907].

3. **Distributed Computing Frameworks**: Specialized frameworks break down the computational workload across multiple machines:

   - Systems that implement distributed sampling for multi-machine training  [246634241 | Liu et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3]  [46949657 | Ying et al. | 2018 | Citations: 3481]

   - Approaches optimized for heterogeneous clusters with varying hardware configurations  [269457375 | Sato | 2024 | Citations: 4]

4. **Memory Optimization Techniques**:

   - Compressed sparse row (CSR) storage formats to reduce memory footprint  [274131701 | Lopushanskyy et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]

   - Edge pruning and filtering to reduce input size while preserving essential patterns  [274860528 | Xia et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]

5. **Precomputed Representations**: Some approaches leverage precomputation of certain components to speed up training, though this comes with tradeoffs in flexibility  [246634241 | Liu et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3]  [220347100 | Bojchevski et al. | 2020 | Citations: 367].

While these solutions have made scaling feasible, they often involve compromises. Sampling methods can introduce redundancy and potential performance losses  [246634241 | Liu et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3], and even with advanced frameworks, processing billion-scale graphs demands substantial computational resources  [59158761 | Sato et al. | 2019 | Citations: 10]  [278367881 | Ranjan et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

However, learning on large graphs remains a challenge -- many recently proposed scalable GNN approaches rely on an expensive message-passing procedure to propagate information through the graph. We present the PPRGo model which utilizes an efficient approximation of information diffusion in GNNs resulting in significant speed gains while maintaining state-of-the-art prediction performance. In addition to being faster, PPRGo is inherently scalable, and can be trivially parallelized for large datasets like those found in industry settings. We demonstrate that PPRGo outperforms baselines in both distributed and single-machine training environments on a number of commonly used academic graphs. To better analyze the scalability of large-scale graph learning methods, we introduce a novel benchmark graph with 12.4 million nodes, 173 million edges, and 2.8 million node features. citations.title: [46949657 | Ying et al. | 2018 | Citations: 3481]
snippets: Recent advancements in deep neural networks for graph-structured data have led to state-of-the-art performance on recommender system benchmarks. However, making these methods practical and scalable to web-scale recommendation tasks with billions of items and hundreds of millions of users remains an unsolved challenge. Here we describe a large-scale deep recommendation engine that we developed and deployed at Pinterest. We develop a data-efficient Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) algorithm, which combines efficient random walks and graph convolutions to generate embeddings of nodes (i.e., items) that incorporate both graph structure as well as node feature information. Compared to prior GCN approaches, we develop a novel method based on highly efficient random walks to structure the convolutions and design a novel training strategy that relies on harder-and-harder training examples to improve robustness and convergence of the model. We also develop an efficient MapReduce model inference algorithm to generate embeddings using a trained model. Overall, we can train on and embed graphs that are four orders of magnitude larger than typical GCN implementations. We show how GCN embeddings can be used to make high-quality recommendations in various settings at Pinterest, which has a massive underlying graph with 3 billion nodes representing pins and boards, and 17 billion edges. According to offline metrics, user studies, as well as A/B tests, our approach generates higher-quality recommendations than comparable deep learning based systems. To our knowledge, this is by far the largest application of deep graph embeddings to date and paves the way for a new generation of web-scale recommender systems based on graph convolutional architectures.

sections.title: Performance Benchmarks
sections.text:
TLDR; Recent benchmarks demonstrate that carefully designed architectures can achieve meaningful results on graphs with hundreds of millions to billions of nodes. Time measurements indicate that modern systems can process billion-scale graphs within hours, though deeper models face diminishing returns. (5 sources)

Recent benchmark results showcase significant progress in processing large-scale graphs, though clear performance boundaries have begun to emerge. On the Papers100M dataset (111M nodes, 1.6B edges), systems can complete preprocessing in under two minutes  [250644137 | Liao et al. | 2022 | Citations: 21]. More ambitious tests have demonstrated success with graphs containing over 60 million nodes and 1.8 billion edges, completing training in less than 30 minutes on standard hardware  [225102916 | Chen et al. | 2020 | Citations: 142].

Temporal graph processing has also shown promising results, with systems able to train on billion-edge temporal graphs within 1-10 hours on standard GPU clusters  [247779292 | Zhou et al. | 2022 | Citations: 86]. The latest developments in architecture design have pushed these boundaries further, with optimizations showing up to 10-20x reduction in matrix operations and 100x acceleration in graph propagation times for billion-edge scale graphs  [268537401 | Liao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

However, important limitations have emerged regarding model scale. Despite ongoing efforts to push boundaries, GNNs with millions of parameters show minimal improvement when scaled beyond this point  [261244034 | Zhang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 20]. This suggests that architectural innovations may be more impactful than brute-force scaling <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

sections.title: Limitations & Future Directions
sections.text:
TLDR; Despite advances in scaling GNNs to large graphs, fundamental limitations persist around computational costs, data transfer bottlenecks, and diminishing returns on model scale. Future directions point toward improved distributed computing frameworks, novel architectures, and hybrid approaches combining multiple scaling techniques. (5 sources)

Current implementations of GNNs face several persistent challenges that suggest room for future innovation. A fundamental limitation is the positive correlation between graph scale and parameter count, which constrains the applicability of these models to truly massive graphs  [226237636 | Weng et al. | 2020 | Citations: 10].

The challenge of training on billion-node graphs remains particularly daunting, even with substantial computational resources  [251403200 | Rahman et al. | 2022 | Citations: 7]. This difficulty stems from the exponential growth in dependencies when expanding neighborhood exploration, coupled with the memory-intensive nature of storing node features and embeddings  [258832806 | Cao et al. | 2023 | Citations: 8].

Looking ahead, several promising directions emerge:

1. Improved Distributed Computing: Development of more efficient distributed training frameworks that can better manage the inherent irregularity of graph structures while minimizing communication overhead <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

2. Novel Architectural Designs: Research into architectures that can maintain performance while reducing parameter counts, possibly through innovative ways to share parameters across large portions of the graph <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

3. Hybrid Approaches: Combining multiple scaling techniques (sampling, compression, and distributed computing) to find optimal trade-offs between computational efficiency and model performance <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

The field appears to be moving toward more pragmatic approaches, recognizing that for some applications, smaller, more efficient models might be preferable to larger ones that show diminishing returns in performance  [261244034 | Zhang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 20].

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are specialized neural networks that compress data into lower dimensional latent spaces while preserving important features. They work by learning the underlying probability distributions of data points and can generate new samples from these learned distributions. (2 sources)

Variational Autoencoders extend traditional autoencoder architectures by focusing on understanding and modeling the probability distributions of the data in the latent space, rather than just finding point estimates of representations  [266374930 | Vora et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]. At their core, VAEs operate through an encoding-decoding process where the encoder maps input data to a lower-dimensional latent space, while the decoder learns to reconstruct the original data from these compressed representations  [271963173 | Cheng et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [187262224 | Baldi | 2011 | Citations: 442].

The fundamental mechanism of VAEs involves two main components: First, they map input data to a lower-dimensional latent space, simultaneously generating parameters for a variational distribution. Second, they use these latent parameters to guide the reconstruction process through a decoder network  [269502481 | Yu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 11]. This approach enables VAEs to serve dual purposes - they can act as powerful compression tools while maintaining the ability to generate meaningful outputs <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [266374930 | Vora et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]
snippets: VAEs are a special case of AEs where the network tries to uncover the underlying distribution associated with these latent variables instead of only finding the latent representation of individual data points. Once the latent distributions are learned, latent representations can be simply sampled from each distribution. In fact, VAE is a type of generative model that can effectively compress signals by mapping them to a lower-dimensional latent space while preserving their essential characteristics. Our VAE encoder maps multi-channel physiological signals into compact latent representations. The decoder reconstructs the original signals from these compressed latent vectors. By training the encoder and decoder together, the VAE learns to compress the signals substantially while retaining critical information. This allows efficient analysis of physiological data even after high compression.

citations.title: [269502481 | Yu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 11]
snippets: The VAE maps the input to a lower-dimensional latent space, generating parameters for a variational distribution.The decoder reconstructs data from this latent space.The loss function combines a reconstruction loss ("distortion") with a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence term ("rate"), acting as a limit on mutual information and serving as a compression regularizer (Bozkurt et al., 2021).

citations.title: [271963173 | Cheng et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: In this paper, we propose VAE (Lopez et al., 2020) as a model compression method. As a variant of Autoencoder (Baldi, 2011), it also consists encoder and decoder, the encoder can downscale the model parameters into latent space, which can be used as a representation of compressed model, and the decoder can be responsible for reconstructing to generate a complete model for use. Through a complete encoding-decoding process, the intermediate latent space as a compressed representation is expected to achieve higher compression rates than previous methods.

sections.title: Staged VAE Architectures
sections.text:
TLDR; Staged VAE architectures involve cascading multiple VAE networks sequentially, where each stage compresses and processes the output of the previous one. This approach improves compression rates and quality by breaking down the compression task into manageable stages. (5 sources)

Staged VAE architectures represent a significant advancement in deep probabilistic modeling by combining the power of sequential VAE applications. Early implementations showed that staged approaches could overcome traditional VAE limitations like blurry reconstructions by introducing intermediate compression steps  [211069015 | Byun et al. | 2020 | Citations: 29].

The basic principle involves training VAEs sequentially, where the first VAE handles initial compression and feature extraction, while subsequent VAEs refine and compress the intermediate representations. This creates a hierarchical manifold learning process, where each stage learns increasingly abstract representations  [211069015 | Byun et al. | 2020 | Citations: 29]. The staged approach has proven particularly useful in scenarios requiring multiple levels of processing, such as handling different types of data transformations or working with multiple domain-specific requirements  [215827763 | Wan et al. | 2020 | Citations: 205].

More sophisticated implementations have emerged that build upon this foundation. For instance, researchers have developed frameworks that stack multiple VAEs hierarchically to enhance model expressiveness and compression efficiency  [236087235 | Ho et al. | 2021 | Citations: 46]. sections.title: Discrete and Hierarchical Compression Techniques
sections.text:
TLDR; Discrete VAEs (DVQ-VAEs) replace continuous latent spaces with discrete codebooks, offering better stability and interpretability. Hierarchical extensions organize multiple VQ-VAE stages to create progressively compressed representations, achieving higher compression rates while maintaining quality. (10 sources)

Discrete VAEs marked a significant advancement by introducing vector quantization to overcome limitations of continuous latent spaces. Instead of using continuous distributions, DVQ-VAEs employ a codebook of discrete embeddings, where the encoder finds the nearest neighbor in this codebook to represent the input  [261529987 | Anisetty et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]. This approach leads to more structured and interpretable representations while avoiding common VAE problems like posterior collapse  [259501111 | Le et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]  [170433891 | Razavi et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1768].

The basic architecture implements a two-stage compression process: first, an encoder compresses input data into continuous representations, then these are quantized to the nearest discrete codebook vectors [261243016 | Corona-Figueroa et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4]. This method has proven particularly effective for various media types, from images to audio, where it reduces the computational burden of generation tasks while maintaining perceptual quality  [268230589 | Xie et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]  [253176366 | Kumar et al. | 2021 | Citations: 0].

Recent innovations have focused on hierarchical approaches to achieve even higher compression rates. Modern systems implement multiple VQ-VAE stages in cascade, where each successive layer compresses the output of the previous one  [268248172 | Rodriguez et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. Some advanced implementations have achieved compression ratios of up to 32× through careful architectural choices and optimization strategies  [277741303 | Yu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. While scaling to high-resolution content remains a challenge, ongoing research continues to push boundaries in both compression efficiency and reconstruction quality  [251903189 | Duan et al. | 2022 | Citations: 43].

These discrete and hierarchical approaches have found successful applications beyond traditional compression tasks, including style transfer, anomaly detection, and super-resolution  [269982228 | Feng et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]  [214749183 | Esser et al. | 2020 | Citations: 1734]. The combination of discrete representations and progressive compression provides a robust framework for achieving state-of-the-art compression performance while maintaining practical utility for real-world applications.

Along with improved neural network blocks, we present a powerful and efficient class of lossy image coders, outperforming previous methods on natural image (lossy) compression. Our model compresses images in a coarse-to-fine fashion and supports parallel encoding and decoding, leading to fast execution on GPUs. Code is made available online.

VAE encoder compresses the spectrogram A ∈ R M ×T into a latent representation P ∈ R M/2 c ×T /2 c ×D , where M, T, D, c denotes the number of mel bands, the sequence length, the codebook dimension, and the compression ratio, respectively. The latent representation P is partitioned into P µ and P σ ∈ R M/2 c ×T /2 c ×D/2 , representing the mean and variance of the VAE latent space. The decoder reconstructs the spectrogram Â based on samples drawn from the distribution P = P µ + P σ  N (0, 1). 

Compared with VAE, VQ-VAE uses a codebook to quantize P m,t into codebook entries, which is utilized to reconstruct the spectrogram by the decoder.

sections.title: Loss Functions and Rate-Distortion Optimization
sections.text:
TLDR; The β-VAE formulation introduced a crucial tradeoff between reconstruction quality and compression through adjustable hyperparameters. Modern approaches optimize compression efficiency using advanced techniques like autoregressive priors and learned discretization, pushing compression rates while maintaining quality. (7 sources)

The fundamental framework for VAE-based compression relies on optimizing a combined loss function that balances reconstruction quality ("distortion") against compression efficiency ("rate"). This balance is primarily controlled through the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence term, which acts as a compression regularizer  [269502481 | Yu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 11]. A notable advancement came with the β-VAE formulation, which introduced a hyperparameter β to explicitly control this tradeoff between reconstruction error and KL divergence  [272689810 | Kim et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

Modern approaches have expanded beyond simple scalar balancing factors to achieve more sophisticated compression control. For instance, learned discretization schemes enable exact bitrate control by learning to map continuous latent variables to exactly discrete values, providing precise control over compression rates  [235358241 | Whang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 20]  [170433891 | Razavi et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1768]. This development represents a significant advance over traditional binning approaches  [46634966 | Oord et al. | 2017 | Citations: 4593].

Hypernetwork-based approaches have demonstrated impressive improvements in compression efficiency by learning optimal parameterizations for distributions over latent codes  [236323264 | Nguyen et al. | 2020 | Citations: 2]. Additionally, conditional VAEs have enhanced controllability in compression by incorporating auxiliary information, allowing for targeted compression of specific attributes while preserving others  [257854759 | Wei et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7].

From an information theory perspective, this optimization framework aligns with rate-distortion theory principles, treating VAE compression as a lossy compression problem where reconstruction error corresponds to distortion and KL divergence serves as the rate measure  [272689810 | Kim et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. This theoretical grounding has guided the development of more efficient and practical implementations that achieve competitive compression rates while maintaining acceptable reconstruction quality  [258999319 | Johnson et al. | 2023 | Citations: 12].

It introduces hyperparameter β into the ELBO that balances the reconstruction error and KL divergence as shown in Equation (3). β influences the regularization by the KL divergence and latent disentanglement [14,5,6,11], which results in the efforts of fine-tuning β in practice [19,28]. Rate-distortion theory on β. The balance of β is explained by ratedistortion theory [16] in which VAE is analogous to lossy compression [1,4]2]. The function of VAE is viewed as compressing a given x into a usually lowerdimensional z and restoring it, resembling a lossy compression system. In this context, reconstruction error corresponds to distortion and KL divergence term corresponds to rate in information theory.

sections.title: Applications and Performance Improvements
sections.text:
TLDR; Advanced VAE architectures have enabled breakthrough compression ratios across multiple domains while maintaining high reconstruction quality. Key innovations include adaptive frame rate handling for video compression, efficient architectures optimized for mobile devices, and refined VAE designs that preserve fine-grained details. (7 sources)

Recent advances in VAE-based compression have led to several practical applications with significant performance gains. In medical imaging and microscopy, improved VAE architectures now achieve near-diffusion model quality while dramatically reducing memory consumption - compressing 1024 × 1024 images to just 16 pixels while maintaining diagnostic usefulness  [258039837 | Keighley et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2].

Video compression has seen particularly innovative developments. Researchers have created flexible frameworks that can adapt to varying frame rates by converting pretrained static-frame VAEs into dynamic versions through strategic modifications to encoder and decoder architectures  [276408758 | Yuan et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]. For mobile deployment, ultra-efficient Video VAE frameworks like LeanVAE have been developed, combining lightweight architectures with wavelet transforms to achieve superior reconstruction quality while reducing computational overhead  [276107045 | Cheng et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

When dealing with compressed representations, refinements to VAE architectures have addressed critical challenges in maintaining image fidelity. Notable improvements include redesigned encoders and decoders that incorporate feature constraints and alignment mechanisms to prevent detail distortion  (Cheng et al._1,  2025). These advances have been particularly valuable in areas like computer vision and image restoration, where preserving fine-grained visual details is crucial  [258039837 | Keighley et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2].

The application scope extends to specialized domains requiring multiple compression targets. For instance, systems have been developed that can simultaneously handle different lighting conditions in image processing by learning distinct latent spaces for various image categories  [268363515 | Zeng et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. Multi-level VAE architectures have also proven effective in handling complex data types, demonstrating versatility across different application contexts  [260900295 | Lv et al. | 2023 | Citations: 13].

citations.title: [258039837 | Keighley et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]
snippets: AEs have some weaknesses, including the inability to deal with previously unseen data. This means that outside the training datasets, the features identified by the encoder are not stable, and may not represent the actual input data. VAE latent space represents a distribution instead of representing the input space. Each distribution represents an approximate learned latent feature; therefore, each latent vector component can use probability distributions to approximate the latent features of unseen data. This architecture may be able to improve on the shortcomings of AEs, while not increasing complexity by an incomprehensible amount. VAE networks can suffer from issues like posterior collapse. VAE variants like the Vector Quantised Variational Autoencoder (VQVAE) and VQVAE2 aim to combat these issues. If the compression of VAEs could compete with existing methods, the compression would allow for the compressed representation to contain meaning within the latent features, possibly allowing for abstraction of clinically relevant features for faster analysis of the biopsy tissue contained on the slide.

snippets: The pre-trained SD model utilizes a VAE to compress images into latent codes, reducing computational costs during diffusion. However, due to the compression inherent in the VAE and the randomness of the diffusion process, using the original SD VAE in deblurring tasks can lead to issues such as detail distortion and loss, resulting in discrepancies between the restored images and the input ones (Zhu et al., 2023). To mitigate this issue, we replace the VAE of SD with a refined-VAE, consistent with previous generativediffusion-based methods (Zhang et al., 2024;Chen et al., 2025). As illustrated in Figure 9, the refined-VAE V ′ introduces feature constraints by adding a refiner to both the encoder and decoder of the original VAE V to align the compressed latent codes and the input images. The encoder refiner performs pre-filtering operations on the degraded features after each layer of the original VAE encoder, thereby reducing content loss during compression. These refined features are then combined with the decoder-refiner via skip connections. The decoder refiner operates after each decoder layer of the original VAE, aiming to combine the features of the original image when decoding the latent codes refined by the diffusion process. This approach helps to minimize the discrepancies between the decoded image and the original one.

snippets: To convert a pretrained static-frame VAE into a dynamicframe version, we exploit the existing capacity of modern video VAEs, which have learned to compress videos into fixed-frame latent spaces [Chen et al., 2024;Xing et al., 2024;Zhu et al., 2023]. question: what are the latest methods to deal with temporal reasoning in llms?

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Temporal reasoning in LLMs is a critical yet challenging aspect of AI that deals with understanding and processing time-related information. Recent developments have led to specialized frameworks and approaches to improve temporal knowledge and reasoning capabilities. (2 sources)

Temporal reasoning represents a fundamental component of natural language understanding that has historically faced significant challenges in artificial intelligence systems. The complexity of temporal reasoning stems from its multifaceted nature, encompassing various aspects such as ordering events, performing temporal arithmetic, analyzing frequencies, and calculating durations  [263605698 | Wang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 10].

A major breakthrough came with the recognition that Large Language Models (LLMs) possess intrinsic temporal knowledge, though this knowledge is not explicitly structured or easily accessible. Research has shown that LLMs contain vast amounts of temporal information accumulated from their training corpus, estimated to be around 80% of temporal triples  [265212665 | Chen et al. | 2023 | Citations: 15]. However, this raw temporal knowledge comes with significant noise and redundancy issues, necessitating sophisticated methods for effective utilization <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

The field has evolved to recognize that traditional approaches to addressing temporal reasoning limitations in LLMs have proven insufficient. Current challenges include managing evolving factual knowledge and handling complex temporal logic, which often result in inaccurate or misleading responses  [265212665 | Chen et al. | 2023 | Citations: 15]. These limitations highlight the need for more structured and systematic approaches to enhance temporal reasoning capabilities in LLMs, setting the stage for innovative solutions that combine knowledge management with advanced reasoning mechanisms <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [263605698 | Wang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 10]
snippets: Reasoning about time is essential for understanding the nuances of events described in natural language. Previous research on this topic has been limited in scope, characterized by a lack of standardized benchmarks that would allow for consistent evaluations across different studies. In this paper, we introduce TRAM, a temporal reasoning benchmark composed of ten datasets, encompassing various temporal aspects of events such as order, arithmetic, frequency, and duration, designed to facilitate a comprehensive evaluation of the TeR capabilities of large language models (LLMs). We evaluate popular LLMs like GPT-4 and Llama2 in zero-shot and few-shot scenarios, and establish baselines with BERT-based and domain-specific models.

citations.title: [265212665 | Chen et al. | 2023 | Citations: 15]
snippets: In this study, we address the challenge of enhancing temporal knowledge reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs). LLMs often struggle with this task, leading to the generation of inaccurate or misleading responses. This issue mainly arises from their limited ability to handle evolving factual knowledge and complex temporal logic. To overcome these limitations, we propose Abstract Reasoning Induction (ARI) framework, which divides temporal reasoning into two distinct phases: Knowledge-agnostic and Knowledge-based. This framework offers factual knowledge support to LLMs while minimizing the incorporation of extraneous noisy data. Concurrently, informed by the principles of constructivism, ARI provides LLMs the capability to engage in proactive, self-directed learning from both correct and incorrect historical reasoning samples. By teaching LLMs to actively construct knowledge and methods, it can significantly boosting their temporal reasoning abilities.

sections.title: Core Frameworks and Architectures
sections.text:
TLDR; Recent frameworks for temporal reasoning in LLMs leverage graph structures, reinforcement learning, and hybrid approaches combining symbolic computation with neural methods. Key architectures include temporal graphs, graph convolutional networks, and neuro-symbolic systems that enable more precise temporal analysis and reasoning. (8 sources)

Recent advances in temporal reasoning architectures for LLMs have taken multiple complementary directions. One prominent approach involves the use of multi-relational graph convolutional networks, which have demonstrated success in capturing complex temporal relationships  [266933295 | Luo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7]. Notable implementations include TANGO, which uses neural ODEs for temporal entity representation, and TITer, which pioneered temporal-path-based reinforcement learning for temporal knowledge graphs  [266933295 | Luo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7]  [233128287 | Han et al. | 2021 | Citations: 24]  [235405508 | Sun et al. | 2021 | Citations: 58].

A significant innovation in architecture design is the introduction of latent temporal representations. The TG-LLM framework demonstrates how transforming input contexts into temporal graphs enhances learning capabilities, supported by Chain-of-Thought bootstrapping and graph data augmentation  [266998999 | Xiong et al. | 2024 | Citations: 74]. Similarly, TLogic has enhanced interpretability through the extraction of temporal logic rules via random exploration  [266933295 | Luo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7]  [245090715 | Liu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 15].

More recent developments have focused on hybrid approaches that combine symbolic computation with neural methods. The TReMu framework exemplifies this trend, implementing a neuro-symbolic approach where temporal questions are translated into executable Python code, leveraging existing libraries for precise temporal calculations  [276107259 | Ge et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]. This approach builds upon notable advances in neuro-symbolic execution, which has shown promise in bridging the gap between declarative specifications and imperative implementation  [259031500 | Pan et al. | 2023 | Citations: 285].

These architectural innovations collectively demonstrate a shift toward more structured and precise temporal reasoning, moving beyond traditional pure-neural approaches to incorporate elements of formal logic and symbolic computation <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [266933295 | Luo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7]
snippets: Recent works have concentrated on leveraging multi-relational graph convolutional networks (Li et al., 2021)(Jin et al., 2019). xERTE (Han et al., 2021) captures query-related subgraph information through dynamic pruning operations. TANGO (Han et al., 2021) adopts neural ordinary differential equations to model the temporal representation of entities. TITer (Sun et al., 2021) stands out as the first model to utilize temporal-path-based reinforcement learning for TKG reasoning. TLogic (Liu et al., 2021) enhances interpretability by extracting temporal logic rules through random exploration of time. TiRGN (Li et al., 2022) and HGLS (Zhang et al., 2023) utilize graph learning methods for comprehensive structural information capture during temporal wandering. (Lee et al., 2023) first explores the potential of ICL in TKGC. Gen-TKG (Liao et al., 2023) provides the most relevant interactions in temporal logic for LLMs to learn and infer.

citations.title: [266998999 | Xiong et al. | 2024 | Citations: 74]
snippets: In this paper, we propose TG-LLM, a novel framework towards language-based TR. Instead of reasoning over the original context, we adopt a latent representation, temporal graph (TG) that enhances the learning of TR. A synthetic dataset (TGQA), which is fully controllable and requires minimal supervision, is constructed for fine-tuning LLMs on this text-to-TG translation task. We confirmed in experiments that the capability of TG translation learned on our dataset can be transferred to other TR tasks and benchmarks. On top of that, we teach LLM to perform deliberate reasoning over the TGs via Chain-of-Thought (CoT) bootstrapping and graph data augmentation. We observed that those strategies, which maintain a balance between usefulness and diversity, bring more reliable CoTs and final results than the vanilla CoT distillation.

citations.title: [276107259 | Ge et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]
snippets:
In this work, we present TReMu (Temporal Reasoning for LLM-Agents in Multi-Session Dialogues), a novel framework designed to enhance temporal reasoning in multi-session dialogues. Our framework introduces time-aware memorization, which uses timeline summarization to generate summaries for each dialogue session, identifying events and associating them with their inferred dates. These summaries, linked to specific times (either session times or inferred event dates), serve as retrievable memory.

During reasoning, we propose a neuro-symbolic temporal reasoning approach inspired by recent work that integrates LLMs with symbolic reasoning, translating questions into symbolic language before using a solver to find answers (Pan et al., 2023;Olausson et al., 2023). Specifically, given a temporal question, we retrieve relevant memory and instruct the LLMs to generate Python code. This approach leverages the LLMs' strong Python coding capabilities and existing Python libraries for temporal calculations. The generated code serves as an intermediate rationale. By executing the code line-by-line, the model follows step-by-step reasoning similar to CoT (Wei et al., 2022), leading the model to select the correct answer.

sections.title: Enhancement Strategies and Techniques
sections.text:
TLDR; Various enhancement techniques have emerged to improve temporal reasoning in LLMs, ranging from structured prompting approaches to sophisticated self-correction mechanisms. These strategies combine multiple techniques like dynamic reflection, temporal graphs, and consistency checking to create more robust temporal reasoning capabilities. (8 sources)

Several key strategies have been developed to enhance temporal reasoning in LLMs:

1. **Structured Prompting and Narrative Approaches**

- Narrative-of-Thought (NOT) methodology breaks down temporal reasoning into structured components, using Python-class based event representation and guided narrative construction  [267636769 | Sahoo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 276]

- Visual-Language assisted Time series reasoning (VL-Time) helps decompress temporal sequences into digestible segments while preserving chronological relationships  [273963297 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7]

2. **Self-Correction Mechanisms**

- Dynamic Reflection schemes implement iterative cycles of probing, critiquing, and reflecting on temporal sequences, helping prevent error accumulation  [263605698 | Wang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 10]

- Temporal Consistency approaches employ multiple-round verification behaviors to improve judgment accuracy  [277103755 | Guo et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]

3. **Knowledge Management Systems**

- Counterfactual prompting techniques generate alternative scenarios to enforce temporal consistency constraints  [276409318 | Kim et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]

- Time-aware retrieval frameworks incorporate temporal constraints and relevance filtering through dedicated modules  [273901401 | Qian et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]

4. **Specialized Training Approaches**

- Pseudo-Instruction Tuning addresses data scarcity issues in temporal QA tasks  [265221318 | Tan et al. | 2023 | Citations: 6]

- Temporal Information-Aware Embeddings enhance model sensitivity to temporal information through matrix augmentation and contrastive reinforcement learning  [272880878 | Yang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]

5. **Multi-Stage Processing**

- TISER framework implements timeline construction combined with iterative self-reflection, leveraging test-time scaling for extended reasoning traces  [277627905 | Bazaga et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]

citations.title: [263605698 | Wang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 10]
snippets: Reasoning about time is essential for understanding the nuances of events described in natural language. Previous research on this topic has been limited in scope, characterized by a lack of standardized benchmarks that would allow for consistent evaluations across different studies. In this paper, we introduce TRAM, a temporal reasoning benchmark composed of ten datasets, encompassing various temporal aspects of events such as order, arithmetic, frequency, and duration, designed to facilitate a comprehensive evaluation of the TeR capabilities of large language models (LLMs). We evaluate popular LLMs like GPT-4 and Llama2 in zero-shot and few-shot scenarios, and establish baselines with BERT-based and domain-specific models.

citations.title: [265221318 | Tan et al. | 2023 | Citations: 6]
snippets: In this paper, we also propose two strategies to improve the robustness and the capabilities of LLMs for temporal reasoning, which are Pseudo-Instruction Tuning and Context Refinement. Pseudo-Instruction Tuning uses pseudo data to alleviate the data scarcity and data imbalance problems of temporal QA, which can improve LLMs' temporal reasoning capability and robustness. The improved reasoning capability also has a positive impact in the ODQA setting. On the other hand, Context Refinement is used to address the long context problem in the ODQA setting.

citations.title: [267636769 | Sahoo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 276]
snippets: Temporal reasoning remains a significant challenge for LLMs, particularly in inferring global temporal relationships from unordered events. To evaluate this capability, Zhang et al. [2024] introduced Temporal Graph Generation (TGG), a benchmark designed to assess LLMs' proficiency in constructing directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) representing event timelines. Experimental results revealed that smaller LLMs (<10B) lagged behind GPT-3.5/4 by approximately 50%, with even GPT-4 facing difficulties due to alignment constraints. To overcome these limitations, the authors proposed Narrative-of-Thought (NOT), a prompting strategy that enhances temporal reasoning without requiring additional model training. NOT comprises three core components: (1) Structural Representation, where events are encapsulated in a Python class and processed through code completion; (2) NOT Prompting template, which generates temporally grounded narratives to guide the construction of temporal graphs; and (3) Narrative-Aware Demonstrations, utilizing GPT-4-generated few-shot examples optimized for both conciseness and accuracy.

citations.title: [272880878 | Yang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]
snippets: In this paper, we introduce a framework to address these challenges. Initially, we implement Temporal Information-Aware Embedding to enhance the model's sensitivity towards temporal information by augmenting its focus on temporal data and adjacent specifics. In our time-aware module, we use SpaCy and identify temporal information within questions and contexts, establishing a question temporal matrix and a context temporal matrix. Furthermore, we advance the model's temporal reasoning capabilities through the Granular Contrastive Reinforcement Learning. We introduce remote negative answers -answers within contexts corresponding to different time periods for the same entities and relationships, and proximal negative answers -answers related to other events within the same time period. Additionally, we propose a more rational reward function to aid the model in reinforcement learning.

citations.title: [273901401 | Qian et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]
snippets: To further enhance LLMs' temporal reasoning ability, this paper aims to integrate relevant temporal knowledge from TKGs into LLMs through a Time-aware Retrieve-Rewrite-Retrieve-Rerank framework, which we named TimeR^4.Specifically, to reduce temporal hallucination in LLMs, we propose a retrieve-rewrite module to rewrite questions using background knowledge stored in the TKGs, thereby acquiring explicit time constraints. Then, we implement a retrieve-rerank module aimed at retrieving semantically and temporally relevant facts from the TKGs and reranking them according to the temporal constraints.To achieve this, we fine-tune a retriever using the contrastive time-aware learning framework.

citations.title: [273963297 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7]
snippets: VL-Time employs two steps using LLMs: (1) acts as a domain expert to plan visualization methods and reasoning guidance. (2) performs TsR using visualization-modeled data and language-guided reasoning. VL-Time effectively compresses time-series data, to empower feature extraction and ICL; mimics the human multi-step decision-making process to unlock LLMs' reasoning capabilities.

citations.title: [276409318 | Kim et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Despite the advanced capabilities of large language models (LLMs), their temporal reasoning ability remains underdeveloped. Prior works have highlighted this limitation, particularly in maintaining temporal consistency when understanding events. For example, models often confuse mutually exclusive temporal relations like ``before'' and ``after'' between events and make inconsistent predictions. In this work, we tackle the issue of temporal inconsistency in LLMs by proposing a novel counterfactual prompting approach. Our method generates counterfactual questions and enforces collective constraints, enhancing the model's consistency.

citations.title: [277103755 | Guo et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]
snippets:
We presented an Temporal Consistency approach for improving mathematical process error identification in language models. Our method leverages temporal consistency patterns in verification behavior, allowing LLMs to recheck their judgments through multiple rounds. We demonstrated how this approach effectively improves verification accuracy across different models and problem types through empirical evaluation. 

Our key insight is that the temporal stability of verifications can serve as a reliable indicator of correctness. This finding opens new directions for developing methods focusing on consistency over time rather than agreement across agents. Our results suggest that incorporating temporal dynamics can enhance the reliability of mathematical reasoning methods.

citations.title: [277627905 | Bazaga et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets: In this paper, we introduce TISER, a novel framework that enhances the temporal reasoning abilities of LLMs through a multi-stage process that combines timeline construction with iterative self-reflection. Our approach leverages test-time scaling to extend the length of reasoning traces, enabling models to capture complex temporal dependencies more effectively.

sections.title: Specialized Applications and Tasks
sections.text:
TLDR; Temporal reasoning in LLMs has expanded beyond basic time understanding to cover specialized applications like temporal graph generation, question-answering, and table data interpretation. These applications require targeted approaches and tools adapted to specific temporal reasoning challenges. (6 sources)

The application landscape for temporal reasoning in LLMs encompasses several specialized domains, each presenting unique challenges and requirements. Temporal Graph Generation (TGG) has emerged as a crucial benchmark for evaluating LLMs' global reasoning capabilities, revealing significant performance gaps between larger and smaller models despite being solvable by advanced models like GPT-4  [273228175 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

Question-answering applications have evolved to encompass more nuanced temporal tasks, including duration calculations, relationship interpretation, and temporal arithmetic operations  [270619481 | Su et al. | 2024 | Citations: 17]. Traditional approaches relying on intermediate reasoning steps like chain-of-thought have shown mixed results in complex temporal QA scenarios, leading to the development of specialized frameworks like TempLogic that incorporate retrieval-guided context distillation and tailored logic reasoning  [273820969 | Li et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0].

For temporal reasoning with tabular data, innovative approaches like the C.L.E.A.R framework have been developed to ground models in evidence and reduce reliance on memorization. This framework emphasizes the importance of auxiliary task training and demonstrates the potential for improvement through synthetic data generation  [271334075 | Deng et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

Current research suggests that temporal reasoning applications can be broadly categorized into three main areas: temporal expression processing, temporal relation extraction, and event forecasting  [277103707 | Yang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. While GraphRAG methods have made progress in these areas, there remains room for improvement, particularly in handling queries that heavily depend on temporal reasoning and requiring sequential retrieval from temporal knowledge bases  [277103707 | Yang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [266998999 | Xiong et al. | 2024 | Citations: 74].

On top of that, we teach LLM to perform deliberate reasoning over the TGs via Chain-of-Thought (CoT) bootstrapping and graph data augmentation. We observed that those strategies, which maintain a balance between usefulness and diversity, bring more reliable CoTs and final results than the vanilla CoT distillation.

citations.title: [270619481 | Su et al. | 2024 | Citations: 17]
snippets: Prior efforts to improve the temporal reasoning capacity of LLMs focus mainly on time-sensitive question-answering (Chen et al., 2021), and utilize methods such as step-by-step reasoning (Zhu et al., 2023b;(Zheng et al., 2023) and ruled-based supervised fine-tuning (SFT) (Tan et al., 2023)Yuan et al., 2023b). More recent studies expand the scope of temporal tasks to include basic temporal concepts understanding (e.g., duration), intricate temporal interpretations (e.g., relation) and computations (e.g., arithmetic) (Wang & Zhao, 2023).

citations.title: [273228175 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]
snippets: In this work, we first study an essential task of temporal reasoning -- temporal graph generation, to unveil LLMs' inherent, global reasoning capabilities. We show that this task presents great challenges even for the most powerful LLMs, such as GPT-3.5/4. We also notice a significant performance gap by small models (<10B) that lag behind LLMs by 50%. Next, we study how to close this gap with a budget constraint, e.g., not using model finetuning. We propose a new prompting technique tailored for temporal reasoning, Narrative-of-Thought (NoT), that first converts the events set to a Python class, then prompts a small model to generate a temporally grounded narrative, guiding the final generation of a temporal graph.

citations.title: [273820969 | Li et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]
snippets: We notice the challenge that large language models (LLMs) face when engaging in temporal reasoning. Our preliminary experiments show that methods involving the generation of intermediate reasoning steps, such as chain-of-thought and program-aided language models, do not consistently boost the performance of complex temporal question-answering tasks. This limitation can be attributed to the LLMs' inadequate understanding of temporal information. To address this problem, we propose TempLogic, a novel framework designed specifically for temporal question-answering tasks across three levels of reasoning. TempLogic incorporates retrieval-guided context distillation, temporal data extraction, and tailor-made logic reasoning.

citations.title: [277103707 | Yang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Recent advancements have increasingly focused on improving the temporal reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Temporal reasoning in natural language processing (NLP) typically falls into three categories: temporal expression detection and normalization, temporal relation extraction, and event forecasting Yuan et al. (2024). The integration of temporal graphs has enabled LLMs to perform more effectively in tasks such as time comparison Xiong et al. (2024) While these methodologies have shown promising results, certain limitations remain: (1) few GraphRAG methods address queries highly dependent on temporal reasoning, and (2) no existing temporal QA dataset requires consecutive retrieval of uncertain amounts of data from a temporal knowledge base.

sections.title: Future Directions and Emerging Trends
sections.text:
TLDR; The evolution of temporal reasoning in LLMs is moving towards more dynamic and adaptive approaches, with emphasis on continuous learning and real-time updates. Key trends include the integration of retrieval-augmented generation systems, time-aware search mechanisms, and automated knowledge updating frameworks. (7 sources)

The future of temporal reasoning in LLMs is being shaped by several emerging trends and technological shifts. A primary direction is the move towards dynamic knowledge management systems that can automatically update and refine temporal information without requiring complete model retraining  [269983033 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]. This includes the development of LLM-guided Dynamic Adaptation methods that can evolve alongside temporal knowledge graphs, ensuring models stay current with the latest temporal patterns and relationships.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are becoming central to advancing temporal reasoning capabilities. These systems are particularly promising as they enable LLMs to access and utilize external information during runtime, eliminating the need for constant full-model retraining  [275906690 | Some et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [276095283 | Khodja et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. The integration of temporal metadata into RAG systems is expected to enhance their ability to retrieve and process time-relevant information more effectively.

Research is also focusing on developing more sophisticated knowledge management techniques, including advanced editing capabilities and automated validation systems  [276095283 | Khodja et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [257919891 | Hartvigsen et al. | 2022 | Citations: 61]  [262253943 | Yu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 41]. These developments aim to create more reliable and maintainable temporal knowledge bases that can be efficiently accessed and updated by LLMs.

The field is witnessing a growing interest in time-aware search technologies, with particular attention to real-time querying and immediate knowledge access  [275906690 | Some et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. This includes the development of predictive systems that can anticipate information needs and automate the updating of knowledge repositories to ensure temporal accuracy and relevance.

Looking ahead, several key areas are expected to see significant advancement <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">:

- Development of more efficient time-aware embedding techniques

- Creation of standardized benchmarks for temporal reasoning assessment

- Implementation of automated temporal knowledge verification systems

- Integration of temporal reasoning with multimodal understanding

citations.title: [269983033 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]
snippets: To address these challenges, in this paper, we propose a Large Language Models-guided Dynamic Adaptation (LLM-DA) method for reasoning on TKGs. Specifically, LLM-DA harnesses the capabilities of LLMs to analyze historical data and extract temporal logical rules. These rules unveil temporal patterns and facilitate interpretable reasoning. To account for the evolving nature of TKGs, a dynamic adaptation strategy is proposed to update the LLM-generated rules with the latest events. This ensures that the extracted rules always incorporate the most recent knowledge and better generalize to the predictions on future events.

snippets:
To address this, research explored methods like continuous learning and dynamic training. Continuous learning enables LLMs to incrementally adapt to new information, allowing them to incorporate evolving language and updated knowledge without needing to retrain from scratch (Karabacak et al., 2023). This is particularly valuable in fields where timely and accurate information is crucial. Dynamic training similarly focuses on updating models continuously, ensuring that LLMs remain relevant over time as new research and discoveries emerge [147]...This has spurred the development of techniques like Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), fine-tuning, and incremental learning. RAG systems are particularly effective because they allow LLMs to retrieve external information during inference, circumventing the need for constant retraining [95,109,127]...Sources advocate future research on several areas time-aware retrieval, forward-looking active retrieval augmented generation, realtime QA, and timeliness in Gen IR [36,99,147].

FLARE anticipates future queries during text generation enabling more timely and relevant access [99].
