sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; RAG systems combine retrieval mechanisms with generative models to leverage external knowledge. Traditional evaluation approaches have focused primarily on end-to-end assessment, but this comes with several important limitations that researchers are actively working to address. (3 sources)

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) represents a hybrid architectural approach that integrates retrieval capabilities with generative models to access and utilize external knowledge sources  [275993400 | Petroni et al. | 2020 | Citations: 1740]. The fundamental premise behind RAG is that by incorporating external information retrieval capabilities alongside generative models, systems can produce more grounded and knowledgeable outputs.

However, evaluating RAG systems presents unique challenges. Traditional evaluation methods have predominantly relied on end-to-end assessment, where generated outputs are compared against ground truth references  [269293655 | Salemi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 62]  [275993400 | Petroni et al. | 2020 | Citations: 1740]. While this approach provides some insights, it faces several significant limitations:

1. Lack of transparency in tracking which specific retrieved documents contribute to the final output

2. High computational requirements, particularly when processing lengthy retrieved documents

3. Resource intensiveness that increases with larger retrieval sets

4. Complex evaluation scenarios due to retrieval result variations

5. Limited ability to provide granular document-level feedback for optimization purposes

These limitations highlight the need for more sophisticated and targeted evaluation approaches that can better assess the individual components of RAG systems <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [269293655 | Salemi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 62]
snippets: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) presents challenges, particularly for retrieval models within these systems. Traditional end-to-end evaluation methods are computationally expensive. Furthermore, evaluation of the retrieval model's performance based on query-document relevance labels shows a small correlation with the RAG system's downstream performance. We propose a novel evaluation approach, eRAG, where each document in the retrieval list is individually utilized by the large language model within the RAG system. The output generated for each document is then evaluated based on the downstream task ground truth labels. In this manner, the downstream performance for each document serves as its relevance label. We employ various downstream task metrics to obtain document-level annotations and aggregate them using set-based or ranking metrics. Extensive experiments on a wide range of datasets demonstrate that eRAG achieves a higher correlation with downstream RAG performance compared to baseline methods, with improvements in Kendall's tau correlation ranging from 0.168 to 0.494. Additionally, eRAG offers significant computational advantages, improving runtime and consuming up to 50 times less GPU memory than end-to-end evaluation.

sections.title: Types of Evaluation Approaches
sections.text:
TLDR; RAG evaluation approaches fall into three main categories: reference-based metrics, LLM-based evaluation, and nugget-based evaluation. Each approach offers distinct advantages and trade-offs, with recent trends moving toward hybrid frameworks that combine multiple evaluation methods. (9 sources)

Current evaluation approaches for RAG systems can be categorized into several key methodologies:

**Traditional Text Quality Metrics**

Reference-based metrics form the foundation of RAG evaluation, using established metrics like BLEU and ROUGE to compare generated responses against reference texts  [276961575 | Abbasiantaeb et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]  [11080756 | Papineni et al. | 2002 | Citations: 26219]  [746379 | Lin | 2004 | Citations: 14246]. These metrics focus primarily on measuring lexical similarity and n-gram overlaps between generated and reference responses.

**LLM-Based Evaluation Frameworks**

A growing trend involves using Large Language Models (LLMs) themselves for evaluation, leading to specialized frameworks like RAGAS and ARES that assess contextual relevance, faithfulness, and informativeness without requiring ground truth references  [267320876 | Lyu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 32]  [257080071 | Es et al. | 2023 | Citations: 367]. However, these reference-free approaches may face reliability challenges when evaluating low-quality retrieved information  [267320876 | Lyu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 32].

**Domain-Specific Evaluation Tools**

Various domains have developed specialized evaluation tools. For instance, in legal applications, tools like FILCO employ lexical and information-theoretic approaches to filter and refine retrieved contexts  [273403982 | Gupta et al. | 2024 | Citations: 19]. Additionally, frameworks like BERGEN now offer combined evaluation approaches that incorporate both reference-based and LLM-based metrics  [276961575 | Abbasiantaeb et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]  [269540052 | Rau et al. | 2024 | Citations: 114].

**Emerging Nugget-Based Assessment**

Building on traditions from early question answering research, newer evaluation approaches focus on breaking down generated content into discrete facts ("nuggets") for more granular assessment  [276961575 | Abbasiantaeb et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]  [7260519 | Voorhees | 2004 | Citations: 237]. This approach allows for more detailed verification of factual accuracy and completeness.

The field continues to evolve rapidly, with researchers increasingly recognizing the importance of developing comprehensive evaluation methodologies that can effectively assess both retrieval and generation components  [269430756 | Fadnis et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

citations.title: [267320876 | Lyu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 32]
snippets: Currently, there are only a few existing benchmarks for evaluating RAG performance, as creating high-quality datasets and experimenting with them entail significant costs. These benchmarks can be classified into two types: reference-required and reference-free evaluation. Reference-free evaluation frameworks, such as RAGAS [13] and ARES [44], use LLM-generated data to evaluate RAG systems on contextual relevance, faithfulness, and informativeness. These frameworks do not depend on ground truth references, but only assess the coherence of the generated text with the retrieved context. This approach may be unreliable if the retrieved external information is low-quality.

citations.title: [269430756 | Fadnis et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]
snippets: There has been increased recognition of the importance of RAG evaluation (Longpre et al., 2024). This consists of 1) designing, 2) running, and 3) analyzing experiments (see Section 2). The research community has mainly limited analyzing to aggregate metrics via benchmark datasets (Liu et al., 2023;Chen et al., 2023), evaluation metrics (Es et al., 2023) as well as evaluation frameworks (such as RAGAs (Es et al., 2023) and ARES (Saad-Falcon et al., 2023)).

citations.title: [273403982 | Gupta et al. | 2024 | Citations: 19]
snippets: FILCO (Wang et. al. 2023) , a method designed to enhance the quality of context provided to generative models in tasks like open-domain question answering and fact verification, addresses issues of over-or under-reliance on retrieved passages, which can lead to problems such as hallucinations in the generated outputs. The method improves context quality by identifying useful context through lexical and information-theoretic approaches and training context filtering models to refine retrieved contexts during test time.

citations.title: [276961575 | Abbasiantaeb et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]
snippets: Despite the advancements in RAG systems and response generation task by the appearance of LLMs, the evaluation of the RAG systems still remains a challenge. The reference-based metrics such as Rouge (Lin, 2004) and BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) are commonly used to evaluate RAG systems by measuring the overlap between generated responses and reference texts, assessing lexical similarity and relevance in terms of precision, recall, and n-gram matching. One line of research focus on using LLMs for evaluation of RAG systems (Shahul et al., 2023)(Kamalloo et al., 2023)(Saad-Falcon et al., 2023)(Zhang et al., 2024)(Zheng et al., 2023). The BERGEN (Rau et al., 2024) tool evaluates the RAG systems by measuring the reference-based and LLM-based metrics. Another line of research [31,37] is attracted to the nugget-based evaluation of the RAG systems. ICAT is an evaluation framework designed to assess the coverage of diverse factual information in long-form text generation. It decomposes the generated text into atomic claims, verifies each claim by retrieving information from a reliable knowledge source, and evaluates the alignment between these claims and the key aspects expected in the output. Nugget-based evaluation has been first proposed in TREC Question Answering Track in 2003 (Voorhees, 2004). The TREC 2024 Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) Track [31] tries to automate nugget-based evaluation with the aid of LLMs to automatically extract and assign the nuggets.

sections.title: Specific Evaluation Methods & Metrics
sections.text:
TLDR; Current evaluation methods encompass both traditional NLP metrics and novel specialized metrics designed specifically for RAG systems. These range from basic text overlap measurements to sophisticated approaches that consider context relevancy, semantic understanding, and information gain. (10 sources)

Here are the key evaluation methods and metrics being used for RAG systems:

1. **Contextual Relevance Metrics**

   - Contextual Precision: Measures the proportion of retrieved documents containing relevant information for the generated response  [270560505 | Balakrishnan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 11]

   - Contextual Recall: Evaluates how much of the relevant information in retrieved documents is actually used in the response  [270560505 | Balakrishnan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 11]

   - Contextual Relevancy: Assesses the alignment between queries, retrieved context, and generated responses  [270560505 | Balakrishnan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 11]

2. **Traditional Text Quality Metrics**

   - BLEU: Focuses on n-gram precision overlap between generated and reference responses  [276939617 | Hindi et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]  [11080756 | Papineni et al. | 2002 | Citations: 26219]

   - ROUGE: Measures overlap through n-grams, word sequences, and word pairs  [276939617 | Hindi et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]  [746379 | Lin | 2004 | Citations: 14246]

   - METEOR: Combines precision, recall, and sentence fluency for more comprehensive evaluation  [276939617 | Hindi et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]

3. **Task-Specific Evaluation Frameworks**

   - Semantic Perplexity (SePer): Quantifies retrieval utility by measuring how much LLM uncertainty decreases after retrieval  [276775668 | Dai et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2]

   - LightEvaluator: Uses dual checkpoints (retrieval and generation) with contrastive pseudo-labeling to assess retrieved document quality  [267312595 | Yan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 72]

   - Retrieval Precision and Answer Similarity: Directly measures the relevance of retrieved context to questions and compares system answers to references  [268819923 | Eibich et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]

4. **Comprehensive Evaluation Systems**

   - Model-based evaluation frameworks like RAGAS use LLMs to assess relevance, faithfulness, and accuracy of both retrieved information and generated responses [265221210 | Saad-Falcon et al. | 2023 | Citations: 105]

   - Multi-metric approaches that combine both retrieval accuracy (precision, recall, F1-score) and generation quality assessments (coherence, fluency, factual accuracy)  [277043297 | Cheng et al. | 2025 | Citations: 3]  [222162263 | Yacouby et al. | 2020 | Citations: 67]

citations.title: [265221210 | Saad-Falcon et al. | 2023 | Citations: 105]
snippets: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems traditionally relies on hand annotations for input queries, passages to retrieve, and responses to generate. We introduce ARES, an Automated RAG Evaluation System, for evaluating RAG systems along the dimensions of context relevance, answer faithfulness, and answer relevance. By creating its own synthetic training data, ARES finetunes lightweight LM judges to assess the quality of individual RAG components. To mitigate potential prediction errors, ARES utilizes a small set of human-annotated datapoints for prediction-powered inference (PPI). Across eight different knowledge-intensive tasks in KILT, SuperGLUE, and AIS, ARES accurately evaluates RAG systems while using only a few hundred human annotations during evaluation. Furthermore, ARES judges remain effective across domain shifts, proving accurate even after changing the type of queries and/or documents used in the evaluated RAG systems. We make our code and datasets publicly available on Github.

sections.title: Challenges in RAG Evaluation
sections.text:
TLDR; RAG evaluation faces significant technical and practical hurdles, including computational demands, scalability issues, and the complexities of handling large knowledge bases. The presence of noisy information in retrieved documents poses particular challenges for maintaining system performance and accuracy. (8 sources)

Evaluating RAG systems presents several interconnected challenges that span both technical implementation and theoretical understanding. At the core of these challenges lies the sheer scale and dynamic nature of potential knowledge bases, which require sophisticated evaluation metrics capable of measuring precision, recall, and relevance across vast amounts of information  [269758033 | Yu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 82].

Computational efficiency emerges as a major concern, particularly as knowledge bases grow larger. Studies have shown that traditional retrieval methods like BM25 struggle with efficiency beyond certain size thresholds, while alternative approaches like approximate dense retrievers (e.g., HNSW) offer significant speed improvements despite minor accuracy compromises  [273345235 | He et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

The management of noise in retrieved documents presents a paradoxical situation: while some irrelevant documents might surprisingly improve accuracy by up to 35%, incorrectly identified relevant documents can severely degrade system performance  [271571143 | Long et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]. This challenge becomes particularly acute as retrieved documents frequently contain noisy or misleading information that can mislead LLMs and potentially reduce overall system effectiveness  [273403480 | Li et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7]  [270210369 | Xu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

Implementation challenges extend to the evaluation methodology itself. Traditional evaluation approaches often rely on fixed chunk sizes and rigid chunking strategies, which fail to capture the full semantic scope of available knowledge  [271874517 | Ru et al. | 2024 | Citations: 13]. Furthermore, the annotation of golden chunks for evaluation is a labor-intensive process that requires constant updates when chunking strategies change  [273375021 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

The integration of multiple retrieval strategies and scaling these solutions in real-world applications remains problematic, particularly for blended approaches that attempt to combine different retrieval methods  [273345967 | Sanniboina et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. These challenges underscore the need for more efficient, scalable, and theoretically sound evaluation approaches that can handle both the practical constraints of deployment and the inherent complexities of information retrieval in RAG systems.

snippets: One primary challenge is the dynamic and vast nature of potential knowledge bases, ranging from structured databases to the entire web.This vastness requires evaluation metrics that can effectively measure the precision, recall, and relevance of retrieved documents in the context of a given query [52,32].Moreover, the temporal aspect of information, where the relevance and accuracy of data can change over time, adds another layer of complexity to the evaluation process [6].Additionally, the diversity of information sources and the possibility of retrieving misleading or low-quality information pose significant challenges in assessing the effectiveness of filtering and selecting the most pertinent information [39].The traditional evaluation indicators for retrieval, such as Recall and Precision, cannot fully capture the nuances of RAG retrieval systems, necessitating the development of more nuanced and taskspecific evaluation metrics [49].

The benefit and detriment in the next token prediction of RAG remain a black box that cannot be quantified or compared in an explainable manner, so existing methods are data-driven, need additional utility evaluators or post-hoc.

sections.title: Latest Trends & Developments
sections.text:
TLDR; Recent developments in RAG evaluation focus on adaptive and self-improving systems that can dynamically adjust their retrieval strategies. There is also a strong emphasis on combining retrieval with robust re-ranking techniques and developing more comprehensive evaluation frameworks that account for incomplete and noisy information. (8 sources)

The landscape of RAG evaluation is evolving rapidly, with several emerging trends addressing previous limitations. Early static retrieval approaches are giving way to more dynamic systems like Adaptive RAG (ARAG), which can adjust its retrieval strategies based on real-time feedback and confidence levels  [277626616 | Qin et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [258863271 | Jiang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 309]. Notable implementations include systems that trigger additional retrievals for uncertain predictions and those that employ self-reflective markers to assess content quality.

Significant progress has been made in corrective approaches, exemplified by Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation (CRAG), which uses dedicated retrieval evaluators to ensure only optimized documents are processed before answer generation  [270688403 | Rackauckas et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8]. Similarly, innovative linking mechanisms between generators and retrievers have demonstrated improved performance across multiple datasets  [277787580 | Lu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

A key area of advancement focuses on context selection and quality enhancement. Researchers are exploring diverse selection methodologies beyond traditional lexical or semantic similarity approaches  [276557931 | Tian et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]. The combination of retrieval with robust re-ranking techniques has emerged as a critical development for ensuring both relevance and precision in retrieved content  [276107364 | Abdallah et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

New evaluation frameworks are increasingly adopting a holistic view of RAG systems, explicitly accounting for scenarios involving incomplete and noisy information  [271693372 | Zhu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 17]. These frameworks are being tested across various specialized applications, including multi-hop question answering, biomedical QA, and text generation  [276408622 | Han et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2].

An interesting parallel development has occurred in utility judgment approaches, where LLMs are being utilized to identify useful retrieved information based on its downstream task applicability  [277622120 | Zhang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. This represents a shift towards more task-aware evaluation methodologies that can better predict the practical usefulness of retrieved information.

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Voice Activity Detection (VAD) has evolved from traditional statistical methods to modern deep learning approaches. The field saw significant advancement when deep neural networks demonstrated superior performance compared to previous approaches like Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM). (3 sources)

Voice Activity Detection systems have undergone substantial evolution in their underlying technologies. Traditional approaches relied on statistical methods, but the introduction of neural networks marked a significant shift in how VAD systems detect speech presence  [46968870 | Saz-Torralba et al. | 2018 | Citations: 5]. This transition accelerated over the past decade, with deep neural networks proving particularly effective at handling frame-level speech/noise classification tasks  [245005974 | Ogura et al. | 2021 | Citations: 0]. Notably, DNN-based VAD systems have demonstrated significantly better performance compared to earlier GMM-based approaches, primarily due to DNNs' enhanced modeling capabilities combined with their ability to process extended context features  [270063503 | Jia et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. Modern implementations often employ a hybrid approach, where neural networks first estimate posterior probabilities for individual frames, and then these estimates are refined using Hidden Markov Models to determine optimal sequences of speech and non-speech segments  [46968870 | Saz-Torralba et al. | 2018 | Citations: 5].

citations.title: [245005974 | Ogura et al. | 2021 | Citations: 0]
snippets: More recently, machine learning-based systems have achieved state-of-theart performance by considering VAD as a frame-level speech/noise classification problem. Methods utilising support vector machines (SVM) [14][15] (Shin et al., 2010) and deep neural networks (DNN) [17][18][19] (Wilkinson et al., 2021) are amongst the most actively studied. X-vectors [21] are 512-dimensional audio embeddings extracted from a DNN [22] trained to classify speakers in the training data.

citations.title: [270063503 | Jia et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
snippets: During the last decade, a kind of more powerful classifier based on artificial neural network has been researched widely (Tong et al., 2016).An impressive improvement in performance of VAD based on deep neural networks (DNN) has been made than one based on GMM due to the super modeling ability of DNN and extended context features (Ryant et al., 2013).

citations.title: [46968870 | Saz-Torralba et al. | 2018 | Citations: 5]
snippets:
Statistical approaches to VAD have produced improved performance, including the use of Neural Networks (NNs) to learn the classification of speech and non-speech [10,14]. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have provided further improvements in this task [37] and are the basis of the VAD proposed in this system. In this setup, the neural networks are trained to classify each frame in one of two classes, one corresponding to speech being present and the other one representing speech not being present.

During VAD implementation, a DNN provides an estimation of the posterior probability for each audio frame, on whether or not it contains speech. Subsequently, a Hidden Markov Model (HMM), that takes as input the posteriors from DNN, determines the optimal sequence of speech and non-speech chunks by considering the speech/non-speech likelihood in a smoothed version over multiple frames.

sections.title: WFST-DNN Hybrid Architecture
sections.text:
TLDR; Weighted Finite State Transducers (WFSTs) are integrated with deep neural networks in VAD systems to handle frame alignments and feature transformations efficiently. This hybrid approach combines the structured alignment capabilities of WFSTs with the power of deep learning for acoustic modeling. (2 sources)

Modern VAD systems implement a sophisticated hybrid architecture that combines weighted finite state transducers (WFSTs) with deep neural networks. At the core of this architecture, WFSTs generate frame alignments and transform features that feed into temporal convolutional neural networks (TCN). This integration allows for precise control over feature extraction and alignment while leveraging the representational power of deep learning  [231749872 | Horiguchi et al. | 2021 | Citations: 36]. The typical workflow involves transforming raw audio inputs through a series of specialized modules - usually five TCN blocks - each consisting of a temporal convolutional layer, ReLU activation function, and batch normalization components  [231749872 | Horiguchi et al. | 2021 | Citations: 36]. While WFSTs alone have historically been used for speech recognition tasks, recent approaches show that neural solutions incorporating contextual information tend to outperform traditional WFST-based methods, especially when dealing with complex scenarios involving rare words or challenging acoustic environments  [257900914 | Chang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4]. Despite these advantages, the combination of WFSTs and DNNs remains valuable for managing feature transformations and maintaining computational efficiency <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [231749872 | Horiguchi et al. | 2021 | Citations: 36]
snippets: TDNN-based VAD: Our...TDNN-based VAD is implemented using a weighted finite state transducer (WFST) and a deep neural network (DNN). The WFST produces frame alignments, which are estimated with the VAD labels. Then the transformed features pass through five TDNN blocks. Each TDNN block consists of a TDNN layer, a Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU), and a batch normalization layer. In the last two TDNN blocks, to capture long temporal contexts, the mean vector for neighboring frames is computed as an additional input. Finally, a linear layer is used to predict the probability for each frame.

snippets: The weighted finite state transducers (WFSTs) (Mohri et al., 2002) on the rare words [12]...The contexts are incorporated to the model either with the shallow fusion (Gourav et al., 2021)(Zhao et al., 2019) or the neural biasing approaches (Pundak et al., 2018)(Bruguier et al., 2019)16,(Sathyendra et al., 2022)(Abro et al., 2019). The neural solutions have been shown outperforming the use of grammars or dynamic WFSTs in the shallow fusion.

sections.title: Working Mechanism
sections.text:
TLDR; WFST-DNN VAD systems operate through a pipeline where WFSTs handle initial feature transformation and frame alignment, while deep neural networks process the temporal aspects of speech detection. The system typically employs multiple processing stages with careful consideration of temporal context and feature dependencies. (4 sources)

The working mechanism of a WFST-DNN VAD system involves several coordinated steps that leverage the strengths of both technologies. The process begins with the WFST producing frame alignments based on the input audio, creating a structured representation of the temporal relationships in the signal  [231749872 | Horiguchi et al. | 2021 | Citations: 36]. These aligned features then undergo transformation through a series of Temporal Deep Neural Network (TDNN) blocks, each combining temporal convolution, rectification, and normalization to progressively extract higher-level representations of the speech signal  [231749872 | Horiguchi et al. | 2021 | Citations: 36]. Notably, the final stages of the neural processing incorporate contextual information by computing mean vectors across neighboring frames to capture longer temporal patterns  [231749872 | Horiguchi et al. | 2021 | Citations: 36].

In some implementations, the system integrates additional signal processing components before reaching the neural network stage. For instance, some architectures incorporate subband Order Statistic Filters (OSFs) to enhance the diversity of the feature space early in the processing chain  [250113874 | Zhao et al. | 2022 | Citations: 1]. The system can be configured with different attention strategies to adaptively handle varying noise conditions and types during runtime  [253826805 | Wang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]  [67926137 | Kim et al. | 2018 | Citations: 13]. Throughout the processing pipeline, the system maintains awareness of ongoing speech activities, allowing it to continuously update its decision-making based on the evolving audio stream  [216142922 | Motlicek et al. | 2013 | Citations: 7].

citations.title: [216142922 | Motlicek et al. | 2013 | Citations: 7]
snippets: More specifically, the core of the TA2 ASR system is represented by the weighted finite state transducer-(WFST) based token passing decoder known as Juicer (Garner et al., 2009). Whilst the decoder is based on a request-driven architecture, the analogues to digital converters (ADCs) are generally interrupt driven. Analysis data flow framework is, in its simplest form, an interface between the decoder's pull architecture and the ADC's push architecture. This framework allows for any directed graph for feature acquisition and is also capable of continuous decoding. Due to the real-time constraints required by the TA2 system, the spotting of keywords is currently performed on 1-best output obtained from the ASR decoder.

sections.title: Implementation Examples
sections.text:
TLDR; Several notable VAD implementations showcase diverse architectural approaches, ranging from energy-based systems to advanced neural networks. These examples demonstrate practical applications across different domains, including robotics, communication platforms, and conversational AI systems. (6 sources)

Here are prominent examples of WFST-DNN based VAD implementations:

* **WebRTC's Production System**: Google implements a frequency-band based VAD system using Gaussian mixture model classifiers within their WebRTC project. This system serves as a standard solution for real-time communications supporting video, voice, and generic data transmission  [246318849 | Strazdas et al. | 2022 | Citations: 31].

* **DE-ENIGMA Robot Interaction System**: A specialized VAD system was developed for human-robot interaction with children on the autism spectrum. Using a BiLSTM-RNN architecture with dense layers, the system analyzes low-level descriptors like fundamental frequency and volume variations to detect child vocalizations in clinical settings  [247216502 | Milling et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0].

* **VoxConverse Multi-Modal System**: This comprehensive approach combines three distinct VAD methods:

  - Energy threshold-based detection

  - Bidirectional LSTM networks pretrained on DIHARD data

  - Wav2vec 2.0 ASR-based detection using phoneme classifications

   [237420981 | Wang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 1]

* **FunASR Enhanced VAD**: Built on Factorized Semi-Markov Models (FSMN), this implementation improves model discrimination by using monophone modeling units and incorporates post-processing techniques like threshold settings and sliding windows for robust performance  [258762651 | Gao et al. | 2023 | Citations: 54]  [52942664 | Zhang et al. | 2018 | Citations: 211].

* **DIHARD Challenge Systems**: Advanced production systems competing in the DIHARD challenge have pushed the boundaries of VAD performance, though specific implementations remain proprietary <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [237420981 | Wang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 1]
snippets:
We design three kinds of voice activity detection, which play a key role in the whole system. We evaluated the following voice activity detection schemes: 

1. An energy-based system. We tune energy threshold of frames on VoxConverse development set. 

2. A bidirectional long short-term memory network (Bi-LSTM) (Bredin et al., 2019) based system with two layers which is trained to output frames decisions. The module was pre-trained on the labeled DIHARD III development set and tuned on VoxConverse development set with 10 epochs. 

3. A wav2vec2.0 [8] based automatic speech recognition (ASR) system. The system was pre-trained on 53k hours unlabeled data. Phoneme classes corresponding to silence and garbage were considered silence for the purpose of VAD and the rest of the classes were considered speech.

citations.title: [246318849 | Strazdas et al. | 2022 | Citations: 31]
snippets: We utilize a VAD developed by Google as part of the WebRTC project [28], which was intended to provide new standards for real-time communications with video, voice, and generic data support. It uses multiple frequency band features with a pre-trained Gaussian mixture model classifier.

citations.title: [247216502 | Milling et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]
snippets: The used VAD system has been trained and evaluated on data recorded under similar conditions as the EMBOA data, namely in the framework of the European Commission's DE-ENIGMA project (Shen et al., 2018; https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/688835; https://deenigma.eu). For the intervention sessions in DE-ENIGMA, the robot Zeno was used. The model was trained on audio data from the British study arm of the project containing audio data from 84 robot-supported intervention sessions of 25 English-speaking children with ASD from the United Kingdom, having a total duration of more than 17 hours. For the experiments reported by Milling et al. (2022), the data was partitioned into train, development, and test partitions in a speakerindependent way. In total, this data contains more than 2 hours of annotated child vocalisations (partially overlapping with other vocalisations). The system was trained to predict the probability of a child vocalisation being present in a given 10-millisecond-long audio frame based on so-called low-level descriptors (LLDs) of the said audio frame. LLDs are a common set of characteristics, which can be extracted from an audio signal, including features such as fundamental frequency (F0), variations in the volume (shimmer), and variations in the fundamental frequency (jitter). The deep learning approach consists of a two-layer bi-directional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) recurrent neural network (RNN), followed by a dense layer, which is designed to allow information flow for several consecutive audio frames. Different thresholds for the predicted probability of the system allow for the adjustment of trade-off between sensitivity and specificity.

citations.title: [258762651 | Gao et al. | 2023 | Citations: 54]

To improve model discrimination, we use monophones as modeling units, given the relatively rich speech information. sections.title: Performance and Applications
sections.text:
TLDR; WFST-DNN VAD systems have found successful deployment across diverse applications, from robotic interactions to personalization-aware speech processing. Recent advances enable targeted speaker focusing and multimodal integration, opening new possibilities in assistive technologies and smart devices. (7 sources)

The performance of WFST-DNN based VAD systems has enabled their adoption across numerous practical applications, demonstrating versatility in handling complex real-world scenarios. In healthcare applications, these systems have proven particularly effective in clinical settings, enabling natural human-robot interaction for children with autism spectrum disorders through robust vocalization detection  [247216502 | Milling et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]. The technology has also evolved to support more sophisticated applications, integrating with various forms of prior information about target speakers, including visual cues and brain signals  [275337196 | Bovbjerg et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [237317465 | Ceolini et al. | 2020 | Citations: 39]  [262897464 | Pan et al. | 2021 | Citations: 4].

A significant advancement has been the incorporation of speaker-specific information to personalize VAD functionality. Modern systems can now utilize speaker characteristics, visual data, and even brain-computer interfaces to deliver customized speech processing  [275337196 | Bovbjerg et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0] [53131436 | Žmolíková et al. | 2019 | Citations: 83]. This capability extends to mobile and wearable devices, where fusing smartphone sensors with microphone arrays creates more robust and accurate speaker diarization systems  [258552270 | Wang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2].

The latest developments in speaker-aware systems have enabled remarkable improvements in word error rates, achieving reductions of up to 41% absolute in certain scenarios  [262897464 | Pan et al. | 2021 | Citations: 4]. These advancements suggest promising future applications in hearing aids, meeting assistants, and driver assistance systems, where accurate speaker identification and voice activity detection are crucial  [258552270 | Wang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]. While current applications continue to evolve, many details of proprietary implementations, particularly in commercial products, remain confidential <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [247216502 | Milling et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]
snippets: The used VAD system has been trained and evaluated on data recorded under similar conditions as the EMBOA data, namely in the framework of the European Commission's DE-ENIGMA project (Shen et al., 2018; https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/688835; https://deenigma.eu). For the intervention sessions in DE-ENIGMA, the robot Zeno was used. The model was trained on audio data from the British study arm of the project containing audio data from 84 robot-supported intervention sessions of 25 English-speaking children with ASD from the United Kingdom, having a total duration of more than 17 hours. For the experiments reported by Milling et al. (2022), the data was partitioned into train, development, and test partitions in a speakerindependent way. In total, this data contains more than 2 hours of annotated child vocalisations (partially overlapping with other vocalisations). The system was trained to predict the probability of a child vocalisation being present in a given 10-millisecond-long audio frame based on so-called low-level descriptors (LLDs) of the said audio frame. LLDs are a common set of characteristics, which can be extracted from an audio signal, including features such as fundamental frequency (F0), variations in the volume (shimmer), and variations in the fundamental frequency (jitter). The deep learning approach consists of a two-layer bi-directional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) recurrent neural network (RNN), followed by a dense layer, which is designed to allow information flow for several consecutive audio frames. Different thresholds for the predicted probability of the system allow for the adjustment of trade-off between sensitivity and specificity.
