citations.title: [211297692 | Li et al. | 2020 | Citations: 5]
snippets: In this paper, two reversible data hiding (RDH) methods for vector quantization (VQ)-compressed images are presented. In the first method, the difference-index table instead of the standard-index table is designed, and all difference indices are then classified into two groups, i.e., the to-be-mapped group and the candidate group, according to the occurrence frequencies of them. Afterwards, the mapping table between those two groups is adaptively constructed and used to serve for data embedding. Furthermore, another joint method is conducted by combining the standard-index based method and the difference-index based method, resulting in a better embedding performance.

citations.title: [233247053 | Hsiao et al. | 2021 | Citations: 4]
snippets: Some researchers have proposed the data hiding scheme based on vector quantization (VQ) compression (Chang et al., 2006)(Hu, 2006)(Chang et al., 2009)(Pizzolante et al., 2011). The data hiding scheme based on side match vector quantization (SMVQ) and search-order code (SOC) is proposed. In this scheme, the VQ image is compressed by SMVQ technology to reduce redundancy, and then the image is recompressed by SOC. In the embedding process, the embedding capacity of image is changed dynamically by threshold to meet different embedding capacity requirements. The experimental results show that the proposed scheme can improve the embedding capacity and reduce the image distortion.

citations.title: [121296137 | Chang et al. | 2006 | Citations: 51]
snippets: Digital data hiding applications have been developed mainly with a view for sending secret information safely through the Internet or other computer networks. Most of the existing vector quantisation (VQ)-based data hiding methods, however, are capable of embedding only a limited quantity of secret data into the medium, usually a secret bit in every block at most. To improve the embedding capacity without seriously sacrificing qualities of carrier media, an adaptive VQ-based data hiding scheme based on a codeword clustering technique is presented. After the adaptive clustering process, the proposed scheme embeds secret data into the VQ-index table by performing codeword-order-cycle permutation. With the help of the cycle technique, more options can be offered for proper codeword substitution, which adds more flexibility to the whole data hiding scheme and therefore improves the quality of the embedded image. As the experimental results demonstrate, the proposed scheme is capable of providing better image quality and embedding capacity than the currently existing VQ-based hiding schemes. In fact, the stego-image quality is so good that it is visually indistinguishable from the VQ-compressed image.

snippets: In this paper, we apply the de-clustering concept and the indicator-free search-order coding (IFSOC) technique to hide information into vector quantization (VQ) compressed images. Experimental results show that the proposed two-layer reversible data hiding scheme for IFSOC-encoded VQ index table can hide a large amount of secret data among state-of-the-art methods with a relatively lower bit rate and high security.

citations.title: [52226768 | Hong et al. | 2018 | Citations: 18]
snippets: Reversible data hiding method can be applied to images in spatial or compressed domains. The spatial domain methods embed data into a cover image by altering its pixel values. The difference expansion scheme proposed by Tian (Tian, 2003) and the histogram shifting scheme proposed by Ni et al. (Celik et al., 2002) are two well-known methods of this type. Many recent works [4][5](Chen et al., 2017)(Lee et al., 2017) have exploited the merits of (Tian, 2003)(Celik et al., 2002) to propose improved methods with better embedding efficiency. In contrast, compressed domain methods modify the coefficients of compressed codes (Chen et al., 2010), or use the joint neighborhood coding (JNC) (Chang et al., 2009) scheme to embed data bits into the compressed code stream. Up to now, RDH methods have been applied to vector quantization (VQ) (Kieu et al., 2016)[13], joint photographic experts group (JPEG) (Liu et al., 2016), and absolute moment block truncation coding (AMBTC) [15](Zhang et al., 2013)[17](Hong et al., 2017)(Chang et al., 2018) compressed images.

sections.title: Advantages & Applications
sections.text:
TLDR; Reversible data hiding in VQ compression offers unique benefits in bandwidth-limited environments and supports reliable data transmission. Its primary applications center around secure communication and authentication, particularly beneficial for scenarios requiring guaranteed image reconstruction. (2 sources)

Key advantages and applications of reversible data hiding in VQ compression include:

* **Bandwidth Efficiency**: Enables efficient transmission of both confidential information and the original image data, making it particularly valuable in bandwidth-constrained scenarios  [203176101 | Basha | 2019 | Citations: 0]

* **Dual-Purpose Communication**: Supports simultaneous transmission of secret messages and authentication information, enhancing data security while maintaining functionality  [12352520 | Wedaj et al. | 2017 | Citations: 55]

* **High Quality Reconstruction**: Guarantees perfect recovery of the original cover image after secret data extraction, ensuring reliability in critical applications  [203176101 | Basha | 2019 | Citations: 0]

* **Superior Image Quality**: Provides better reconstructed image quality compared to traditional VQ compression alone, making it suitable for applications where visual fidelity is important  [203176101 | Basha | 2019 | Citations: 0]

* **Flexible Compression Options**: Works effectively with both Vector Quantization (VQ) and Side Match Vector Quantization (SMVQ), offering versatility in implementation approaches  [203176101 | Basha | 2019 | Citations: 0]

* **Authentication Support**: Particularly valuable for applications requiring image authentication, as the original image can be fully verified after data extraction  [12352520 | Wedaj et al. | 2017 | Citations: 55]

* **Cost-Effective Storage**: Reduces overall storage requirements by combining data compression and hiding functionalities <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

These characteristics make reversible data hiding in VQ compression particularly suitable for healthcare imaging, document authentication, and military communications where both security and accurate reconstruction are essential <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [12352520 | Wedaj et al. | 2017 | Citations: 55]
snippets: Recently, reversible data hiding (RDH) techniques for JPEG images have become more extensively used to combine image and authentication information conveniently into one file. Although embedding data in JPEG image degrades visual quality and increases file size, it is proven to be useful for data communication and image authentication.

citations.title: [203176101 | Basha | 2019 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Since side match vector quantization (SMVQ) provides better image quality of reconstructed image and compression bit rate than vector quantization (VQ) does, it becomes another choice to compress the transmitting images when the bandwidth is limited. To expand the cover media for transmitting confidential information, we propose a novel data hiding scheme which embeds secret data into the SMVQ-compressed image. In terms of the payload capacity, the visual quality, and the compression rate, experimental results confirm that the performances of our scheme are better than that of other information hiding schemes for VQ-based and SMVQ-based compressed images. In addition, the embedded secret data can be extracted from the stego-image without referencing the original cover image.

sections.title: Implementation Challenges & Solutions
sections.text:
TLDR; Implementing reversible data hiding in VQ compression faces challenges including computational complexity and potential image distortion. Key solutions involve optimization techniques like prediction schemes, adaptive clustering, and hybrid approaches combining multiple methods. (7 sources)

While reversible data hiding in VQ compression offers significant benefits, practitioners face several implementation challenges that require careful consideration and innovative solutions. One primary challenge is the computational cost associated with traditional approaches, which can limit their suitability for real-time applications  [14682611 | Fallahpour et al. | 2011 | Citations: 3].

To address these limitations, researchers have developed several effective strategies. Prediction-based schemes have emerged as a promising solution, particularly for handling quantized DC coefficients. These approaches improve accuracy and reduce distortion while maintaining high embedding capacity  [202130927 | Kim et al. | 2019 | Citations: 10]. Similarly, adaptive quantization level difference (QLD) techniques have been successful in achieving better performance in complex image areas while maintaining image quality  [234267428 | Chen et al. | 2021 | Citations: 7].

A significant innovation in addressing reversibility challenges came through the development of Side Match Vector Quantization (SMVQ). This approach helps prevent permanent distortion during the data hiding process by transmitting pixel values directly rather than relying solely on index values  [225611398 | Kashyap et al. | 2020 | Citations: 1]. The SMVQ technique has proven particularly effective as it allows for lossless reconstruction of the original VQ-compressed image while maximizing available embedding space  [31634726 | Lee et al. | 2013 | Citations: 0].

Recent advances have focused on optimizing embedding capacity through intelligent codebook management. Modern approaches allow secret data to be embedded without requiring access to the original cover image, expanding the practical applications of these systems  [203176101 | Basha | 2019 | Citations: 0]. Additionally, researchers have successfully addressed computational efficiency concerns by developing hybrid approaches that combine multiple techniques, resulting in balanced improvements across both payload capacity and visual quality metrics  [211297692 | Li et al. | 2020 | Citations: 5].

snippets:
In [4], to recover the original image from the stego image a novel that cannot be able without any distortion even after the message is extracted from the image reversible data hiding [8] algorithm is proposed.

In [5], The Side Match Vector Quantization (SMVQ) technique was explained in this paper which discusses the scheme that is to be modified and used as a data hiding technique for which is low bit-rate compression. Generally, the images are compressed in SMVQ and the receivers are transmitted with indices values. The indices value will be changed when we try to hide data in it and results in the permanent distortion of the image which cannot be retrieved again. To avoid that problem, the modification of SMVQ technique is in such a way that directly the pixels values are transmitted which leaves the indices values same rather than transmitting the indices values to the receiver, it becomes easy to retrieve the image after the extraction of the data in it as before the data hiding takes place.

citations.title: [234267428 | Chen et al. | 2021 | Citations: 7]
snippets: Hiding a message in compression codes can reduce transmission costs and simultaneously make the transmission more secure. This paper presents an adaptive reversible data hiding scheme that is able to provide large embedding capacity while improving the quantity of modified images. The proposed scheme employs the quantization level difference (QLD) and interpolation technique to adaptively embed the secret information into pixels of each absolute moment block truncation coding (AMBTC)-compressed block, except for the positions of two replaced quantization levels. The values of QLD tend to be much larger in complex areas than in smooth areas. In other words, our proposed method can obtain good performance for embedding capacity and still meets the requirement for better modified image quality when the image is complex.

citations.title: [31634726 | Lee et al. | 2013 | Citations: 0]
snippets: This work presents a novel reversible data-hiding scheme which embeds secret data into a side matched Vector Quantization (SMVQ)-compressed image, and achieves lossless reconstruction of a Vector Quantization (VQ)-compressed image. The rather random distributed histogram of a VQ-compressed image can be re-located to locations close to zero by SMVQ prediction. Thus, fewer bits can be used to encode SMVQ indices with very small values, and no indicator is required to encode these indices, which yields extra hiding space to hide secret data. Consequently, high embedding capacity and low bit rate scenarios can be deposited.

sections.title: Comparison with Other Compression-Based RH Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; Different compression-based reversible data hiding methods offer distinct trade-offs between capacity, quality, and implementation complexity. While JPEG-based methods dominate the field, newer approaches leveraging various compression standards provide alternative solutions tailored to specific use cases. (4 sources)

Compression-based reversible data hiding methods differ significantly in their underlying architectures and capabilities. JPEG-based approaches can be broadly categorized into two main streams: those that modify Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) coefficients and those that work with Huffman table modifications. DCT-based methods, while capable of high embedding capacity, often result in increased file sizes and visible quality degradation. In contrast, entropy coding domain modifications tend to offer lower capacity but maintain better visual quality  [226289970 | Yin et al. | 2020 | Citations: 1].

General compression techniques encompass both lossless methods (like PCX, GIF, TIFF) and lossy approaches (such as JPEG, Vector Quantization, and SMVQ)  [8709651 | Kuo et al. | 2015 | Citations: 13]. Among these, Vector Quantization stands out for its widespread adoption in image compression and data hiding applications  [59288781 | Ali et al. | 2016 | Citations: 15].

Modern implementations have evolved to incorporate multiple compression standards, expanding the range of possible solutions. Notable approaches include methods compatible with Joint Photographic Experts Group (JPEG), Absolute Moment Block Truncation Coding (AMBTC), and other compression formats  [52226768 | Hong et al. | 2018 | Citations: 18]. Each of these formats brings its own strengths - for instance, AMBTC has demonstrated impressive capacity-to-distortion ratios despite being a lossy compression technique  [52226768 | Hong et al. | 2018 | Citations: 18].

The choice of compression method ultimately depends on specific application requirements, including factors such as required embedding capacity, acceptable distortion levels, and computational resources available <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">. When comparing different approaches, it's essential to consider not just theoretical performance metrics but also practical aspects like implementation complexity and real-world deployment considerations.

The existing JEPG reversible data methods can be divided into two categories, one is based on Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) coefficients modification, the other is based on Huffman table modification, the methods based on DCT coefficient modification result in large file expansion and visual quality distortion, while the methods based on entropy coding domain modification have low capacity and they may lead to large file expansion.

In the above two domains, embedding secret data requires large size cover file relatively to the size of secret data and high bandwidth to transmit the cover file,therefore many compression techniques for data hiding have been proposed. sections.title: Introduction/Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Facility layout optimization involves determining the best placement of services and spaces within a building to minimize movement costs and maximize efficiency. Various optimization algorithms have emerged to tackle this complex problem, which is classified as NP-hard. (7 sources)

The facility layout problem (FLP) is a fundamental challenge in operations research that focuses on arranging facilities in a way that minimizes transportation costs and maximizes operational efficiency  [233645248 | Hameed et al. | 2021 | Citations: 9]. At its core, this problem can be formally expressed as finding optimal locations for facilities to minimize total travel cost, which has been established as an NP-hard problem in network theory  [220633135 | Xu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 63].

Mathematically, the problem can be framed as a Quadratic Assignment Problem (QAP), which considers both the flow of activity between departments and the distances between possible locations  [272903605 | Sari et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [120744555 | Koopmans et al. | 1957 | Citations: 2649]. When dealing with locating specific services within a facility, the problem becomes a variation known as the K-median problem, where the goal is to strategically position facilities to minimize the aggregate distance between clients and their assigned facilities [118700862 | Cohen-Addad et al. | 2014 | Citations: 5].

While exact methods exist for solving these problems, they are typically limited to smaller-scale implementations due to computational constraints. This has led to the development of various practical approaches, including heuristic and metaheuristic algorithms, with notable success demonstrated by methods such as Simulated Annealing, Genetic Algorithms, Tabu Search, Particle Swarm Optimization, and Ant Colony Optimization  [272903605 | Sari et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. These algorithms have proven particularly valuable in real-world applications, such as optimizing hospital layouts and fitness center equipment arrangements  [233879126 | Eliguzel et al. | 2021 | Citations: 0].

The evolution of these optimization approaches reflects a broader trend in operations research toward developing practical solutions that can handle increasing problem sizes while maintaining acceptable levels of optimality  [155083909 | Cubukcuoglu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 68]. Recent developments have focused on creating hybrid methods that combine multiple optimization techniques to leverage their respective strengths  [233645248 | Hameed et al. | 2021 | Citations: 9].

citations.title: [118700862 | Cohen-Addad et al. | 2014 | Citations: 5]
snippets: In the facility location problem, given n client points and a facility opening cost f, must choose how many facilities to open and where to open them to minimize the combination of cost of opening facilities and total distance from each client to the nearest open facility. The K-median problem, given n points and an integer k, must choose where to open k facilities so as to minimize the total distance from each client to the nearest open facility.

The goal is to open N facilities in N max so as to minimize the sum of population-weighted travel distances from each residential block to its nearest open facility." We are going to develop a hybrid method based on discrete differential evolution (DDE) algorithm for solving the QAP...we propose to develop a hybrid algorithm (HDDETS) by combining the DDE and tabu search (TS) algorithms to enhance the exploitation mechanism in the DDE algorithm...we propose to apply the proposed algorithm to find the optimal distributions of the advisory clinics inside the Azadi Hospital in Iraq that minimizes the total travel distance for patients when they move among these clinics. Our application shows that the proposed algorithm could find the best distribution of the hospital's rooms, which are modeled as a QAP, with reduced total distance traveled by the patients.

citations.title: [233879126 | Eliguzel et al. | 2021 | Citations: 0]
snippets: In this study, the allocation of sports equipment to the locations in a fitness center is studied. The considered problem contains 19 sport stations (equipment) for 19 alternative locations. Two required information namely the distance matrix between locations and the flow matrix (the number of members who visit the equipment in order) between sports equipment are obtained. The problem is modeled as a QAP and an integer programming formulation is applied. Although the optimal solution of the problem is obtained by the integer programming model using GUROBI package, two heuristic approaches namely 2opt and tabu search algorithms are also applied to find the feasible/optimal solutions in a reasonable time. Optimal solution is also achieved using 2-opt and tabu search algorithms in very short computational times (less than 10 seconds) compared to the integer programming model (4.400 sec). The optimal solution shows that the new layout is 55.47% better than the current layout in terms of the total traveled distance  flow.

snippets: These methods aim to optimize layouts for operational efficiency and effectiveness. The QAP, introduced by Koopmans and Beckmann (Koopmans et al., 1957), provides a mathematical framework for optimizing department placement to minimize factors such as time, cost, and flow between departments. It has applications in various settings, including hospital layout planning (Elshafei, 1977)(Cubukcuoglu et al., 2021)...This model overcomes QAP limitations and utilizes a range of optimization strategies, including exact, heuristic, and metaheuristic algorithms, genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, tabu search, particle swarm optimization, ant colony optimization, and integer linear programming. Exact methods find optimal solutions but are suitable for smaller problems due to scalability issues [58]. Heuristic methods offer quicker, near-optimal solutions without guaranteeing the best solution, while metaheuristic methods enhance heuristic strategies by integrating insights from AI and other fields [59]. sections.title: Core Search & Navigation Algorithms
sections.text:
TLDR; Several fundamental algorithms form the backbone of navigation systems in facility environments. A* and Dijkstra's algorithm are particularly prominent for finding optimal paths, while specialized variations account for crowd dynamics and collision avoidance. (7 sources)

The primary navigation algorithms used in facility environments include:

1. **A* Algorithm**

   - Balances actual movement costs from the start with estimated costs to the target  [272193464 | Zhang | 2024 | Citations: 0]

   - Combines benefits of both Dijkstra's algorithm and greedy search approaches  [272193464 | Zhang | 2024 | Citations: 0]

   - Successfully implemented for optimizing customer movement patterns and autonomous robot navigation  [235376134 | Lacson et al. | 2021 | Citations: 0]  [260482174 | Gui | 2023 | Citations: 1]

2. **Modified Dijkstra's Algorithm**

   - Optimized for calculating realistic trajectories in 2D environments

   - Uses weighted edge capacities to prioritize paths

   - Focuses primarily on distance metrics without additional complexity  [230433910 | Zhan et al. | 2021 | Citations: 4]  [11267487 | Dijkstra | 1959 | Citations: 10966]

3. **Depth First Search (DFS)**

   - Provides systematic path exploration capabilities

sections.title: Advanced Optimization Techniques
sections.text:
TLDR; Modern optimization approaches combine multiple algorithms and introduce novel features like predictive modeling and evolutionary computation to handle complex facility navigation scenarios. These advanced techniques excel at large-scale problems and incorporate real-world considerations like crowd behavior and uncertainty. (8 sources)

Recent advances in facility optimization have introduced sophisticated hybrid approaches that combine multiple algorithmic strategies. Notable among these are combinations of Discrete Differential Evolution (DDE) with Tabu Search (HDDETS), which have shown significant success in solving complex facility layout problems  [233645248 | Hameed et al. | 2021 | Citations: 9]. Similarly, integrated approaches that combine multiple methodologies, such as Ant Colony Optimization with Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedures (ACOR-GRASP), demonstrate enhanced efficiency in finding optimal solutions  [272582175 | Gamot et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [110244750 | Hasle | 2009 | Citations: 23].

Predictive capabilities have become increasingly important in modern optimization systems. These systems now incorporate trajectory prediction models that estimate future pedestrian positions to improve navigation efficiency  [115900278 | Chen et al. | 2018 | Citations: 18]. Some advanced implementations use normal distribution modeling for indoor space partitions and employ learning-based estimators for real-time population distribution predictions  [273654088 | Li et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

Evolutionary optimization approaches have made significant strides by incorporating Boolean grids and implementing two-stage algorithms. These systems utilize randomization stages for generating new topologies and agglomeration stages for forming coherent shapes, proving particularly effective for designing emergency evacuation routes  [37374072 | Helbing et al. | 2013 | Citations: 458]. Additionally, researchers have developed improved variants of existing algorithms, such as the Binary Emphasis Matrix Enhancement (BEME), which show superior performance when dealing with thousands of pedestrians  [237550651 | Wang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 7].

Multi-objective optimization techniques have also gained prominence, exemplified by the use of Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) with adaptive local search operators. These approaches can simultaneously optimize multiple parameters, such as minimizing patient movement distance while maximizing closeness ratings in hospital layouts  [233966780 | Huo et al. | 2021 | Citations: 30]. Specialized algorithms have been developed for specific scenarios, such as the Search and Rescue Optimization Algorithm (SAR), which draws inspiration from human search and rescue operations  [209936129 | Shabani et al. | 2019 | Citations: 102].

sections.title: Dynamic Movement Modeling
sections.text:
TLDR; Dynamic movement modeling captures how groups of people navigate spaces while accounting for interactions, uncertainties, and environmental factors. These models combine velocity calculations, crowd density effects, and real-time adjustments to create realistic simulations of human movement patterns. (6 sources)

Modern dynamic movement modeling approaches integrate multiple layers of complexity to accurately represent how people navigate shared spaces. At the foundation lies the concept of spontaneous velocity, which represents an individual's desired movement speed in the absence of others, with actual velocity being adjusted to account for physical constraints like non-overlapping bodies  [4504136 | Maury et al. | 2009 | Citations: 102].

Advanced tracking systems can predict and estimate multiple human movement paths without requiring prior knowledge of occupancy numbers. These systems build upon historical position data to iteratively refine path estimates, enabling real-time tracking of group movements  [13443259 | Miyazaki et al. | 2015 | Citations: 23]. The accuracy of these predictions depends significantly on managing location uncertainty, with models implementing dynamic speed adjustments based on crowd density. For instance, speeds can automatically adjust between full pace (1.2 m/s), slow walk (0.4 m/s), or stopping entirely based on predefined density thresholds  [273538212 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

Event-driven behavioral models have emerged as an effective approach for understanding how pedestrians navigate facility networks. These models recognize that people actively seek to exit facilities and respond dynamically to changing conditions, such as identifying traffic jams or discovering shorter routes  [13509132 | Wagoum et al. | 2011 | Citations: 112]. The implementation often includes careful attention to specific navigation requirements, such as avoiding obstacles and maintaining clear pathways  [235376134 | Lacson et al. | 2021 | Citations: 0].

Realistic pedestrian movement simulation requires sophisticated optimization techniques to minimize unwanted behaviors like excessive wall crossing. These approaches typically employ multiple correction operators that adjust both speed and turning angles, with searches conducted within error margins to ensure natural-looking movement patterns [3370999 | Torres-Sospedra et al. | 2017 | Citations: 66].

sections.title: Real-world Applications & Performance
sections.text:
TLDR; Optimization algorithms have been successfully deployed in various facility contexts, from search and rescue operations to retail store management. Performance evaluations demonstrate significant improvements in operational efficiency compared to traditional layouts. (7 sources)

The practical implementation of optimization algorithms spans diverse facility types and operational needs. In search and rescue scenarios, novel algorithms have been developed that combine multiple analytical approaches, including hazard assessment and route complexity evaluation, to guide teams through dangerous multi-story buildings during emergencies  [22226642 | Zverovich et al. | 2017 | Citations: 15]. These systems have proven particularly valuable in high-stress situations where quick, accurate routing decisions are crucial.

In educational facilities, backtracking search algorithms have been successfully applied to optimize library layouts, demonstrating measurable improvements in workflow efficiency. Studies comparing these optimized solutions against traditional layouts showed significant reductions in travel distances  [210955755 | Fengtao et al. | 2019 | Citations: 0]. Similar success has been reported in retail environments, where improved pathfinding algorithms help manage pedestrian flows and optimize shopping experiences  [119659389 | Sivers et al. | 2014 | Citations: 91].

Hospital facilities have benefited from local search procedures that systematically evaluate potential facility placements. These algorithms operate by examining possible moves for each site while maintaining computational efficiency through strategic updates of upper bound solutions  [14054783 | Tang et al. | 2016 | Citations: 12]. More recently, mobile facility location algorithms have been developed that can dynamically adjust facility positions to better serve client needs while minimizing movement costs  [6236310 | Ahmadian et al. | 2013 | Citations: 32].

Performance evaluations of optimization systems reveal interesting trade-offs between immediate versus long-term effectiveness. While simpler "go-to-target" strategies may appear intuitive, studies have shown that more sophisticated long-term optimization approaches can actually produce better outcomes, sometimes employing counter-intuitive tactics like temporarily misdirecting occupants to achieve faster overall evacuation  [719490 | Albi et al. | 2015 | Citations: 111]. This highlights the importance of considering system-wide impacts rather than just individual agent performance <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

Human factors play a crucial role in real-world performance, with successful implementations recognizing that optimization algorithms should mirror human cognitive processes. This includes incorporating hesitation steps in path selection and adapting to uncertain environments, which helps create more natural and sustainable solutions  [119659389 | Sivers et al. | 2014 | Citations: 91].

snippets: The pseudocode for the local search procedure is presented as "Algorithm 1": Algorithm 1 The local search procedure upperBound objective value of the upper bound solution while true do for all j 2 J do if j is the only site with a reliable facility opened then continue; else compute the objective value corresponding to move1 and move2 for j, denoted as costMove1J and costMove2J, respectively; upperBound min(upperBound, costMove1J, costMove2J); end if end for if upperBound is updated then select the move that leads to upperBound, i.e., update the location decisions and assignment decisions according to that move; else break; end if end while...Because each site has at most two possible moves and computing the objective value for each move requires O(|I||J|) effort, the time complexity of the internal loop of "Algorithm 1" is O(|I||J| 2 ). sections.title: Introduction to QD-LED Technology
sections.text:
TLDR; Quantum dot light-emitting diodes (QD-LEDs) represent a promising technology for next-generation displays and lighting due to their color tunability and solution-processability. They consist of semiconductor nanocrystals with cores, shells, and organic coatings that can emit light across a wide spectrum when properly excited. (4 sources)

Colloidal quantum dot light-emitting devices have emerged as a compelling candidate for revolutionizing display and solid-state lighting technologies  [104657362 | Kathirgamanathan et al. | 2018 | Citations: 4]. What makes QD-LEDs particularly attractive is their inherent color tunability - simply by adjusting the size of the semiconductor nanocrystals, manufacturers can control the emitted light color  [104657362 | Kathirgamanathan et al. | 2018 | Citations: 4]. 

The basic structure of a quantum dot consists of three main components: an inorganic core made of hundreds to thousands of atoms, an inorganic shell surrounding the core, and organic surfactant molecules called ligands that coat the entire structure  [104657362 | Kathirgamanathan et al. | 2018 | Citations: 4]. Common types include CdSe/ZnS, InP/ZnS, perovskites, and CuInS₂ structures  [104657362 | Kathirgamanathan et al. | 2018 | Citations: 4].

A major breakthrough in QD-LED technology came with the demonstration of nearly 100% quantum yield and precise control over emission color in high-quality QDs  [104657362 | Kathirgamanathan et al. | 2018 | Citations: 4]  [6675749 | Coe et al. | 2002 | Citations: 2105]. This advancement was crucial because traditional organic LEDs struggled to achieve the wide color gamut requirements specified by standards like Rec 2020  [104657362 | Kathirgamanathan et al. | 2018 | Citations: 4].

These versatile QDs find applications beyond just displays and lighting - they have proven valuable in biomedical imaging, solar cells, and various sensor applications  [13108814 | Mordvinova et al. | 2015 | Citations: 15]. Their ability to be processed through various methods including spin coating, inkjet printing, slot coating, or spray coating adds to their manufacturing versatility  [104657362 | Kathirgamanathan et al. | 2018 | Citations: 4].

(Dabbousi et al., 1995)(Coe et al., 2002)(Mashford et al., 2013)(Kim et al., 2013)[16][17][18][19][20][21]26 Colloidal semiconductor nanocrystals (quantum dots, QDs) are composed of an inorganic core (made up of a few hundred to a few thousand atoms) surrounded by an inorganic shell, which in turn is surrounded by an organic surfactant molecules (ligands). Typical quantum dots 20 include CdSe/ZnS, InP/ZnS, perovskites and CuInS 2 . Research on electroluminescence of colloidal quantum dots is gathering momentum as the colour requirement for Rec 2020 (ITU-R-BT2020) cannot be achieved by means of state of art OLED materials 19 with simple device architectures.

sections.title: Types of Quantum Dots Used
sections.text:
TLDR; Various types of quantum dots are used in QD-LEDs, ranging from traditional cadmium-based structures to newer environmentally friendly alternatives. The choice of QD type affects performance metrics like brightness, efficiency, and stability. (7 sources)

Several categories of quantum dots are currently employed in QD-LED applications:

* **Traditional Cd-Based Structures**

   * CdSe/ZnS core-shell QDs - Demonstrated strong emission around 610nm and good stability  [136510536 | Shen et al. | 2011 | Citations: 2]

   * CdS/ZnS QDs - Used effectively in LED applications with emission peaks around 610nm  [16607266 | Kang et al. | 2016 | Citations: 53]

* **Environmentally-Friendly Alternatives**

   * Copper Indium Disulfide (CIS) QDs - Offer viable replacement for cadmium-based QDs with good luminescence properties  [155644920 | Barba | 2019 | Citations: 0]

   * Cu-In-Zn-S (CIZS) QDs - Provide advantages including low toxicity, wide emission range, and large Stokes shifts. Achieve color rendering index of 85.6 and luminous efficiency of 34.8 lm/W  [199651705 | Ting et al. | 2019 | Citations: 5]

   * Na-doped Ag–In–Ga–S (AIGS) QDs in Ga2O3 matrix - Show high photoluminescence quantum yield (58%) with sharp emission peaks  [265227275 | Tozawa et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]

* **Emerging Toxicity-Focused Materials**

   * Cu-Ga-Zn-S (CGZS) QDs - Demonstrate impressive performance with photoluminescence quantum yield exceeding 90% and external quantum efficiency reaching 1.00%  [271268538 | Hou et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]

   * Ternary Quantum Dots (TQDs) - Made with Group I and III elements, offering lower toxicity compared to Cd and Pb-based QDs. Performance can be enhanced through size control and ZnS shell coating [257724205 | Islas-Rodriguez et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4]

snippets: While significant advances in the development of quantum dot light emitting diodes (QLEDs) have been reported, these devices are primarily based on cadmium chalcogenide quantum dot (QD) materials. Both environmental and health concerns arise due to the toxicity of cadmium and consequently, alternative less toxic QDs must be developed for large scale QLED applications such as display and solid state lighting technologies.  In this work, copper indium disulfide (CIS) was investigated as an alternative QD material for QLED applications. Through experimentation with material synthesis and device fabrication, this project aimed to develop high performing CIS QLEDs. Several synthetic approaches were experimented with and it was determined that the injection of shorter chain 1-octanethoil as sulfur precursor with extensive shell reaction time resulted in highly luminescent QDs.  Single color QLEDs were fabricated based on typical device structure, using highly luminescent synthesized CIS QDs as the emissive layer in multilayer devices.

citations.title: [16607266 | Kang et al. | 2016 | Citations: 53]
snippets: For a typical synthesis, 0.1 mmol of cadmium oxide (CdO), 4 mmol of zinc acetate (Zn(CH 3 CO 2 ) 2 ) and 5 ml of oleic acid (OA) were placed in a 50 ml flask and heated to 150 °C in flowing high-purity Ar gas for 30 min. Then 15 ml of 1-octadecene (ODE) was added  to the 3-neck flask and the temperature increased to 300 °C. A stock solution containing 0.2 mmol of selenium (Se) and 3 mmol of sulfur (S) in 2 ml of trioctylphosphine (TOP) was quickly injected into the 3-neck flask. The reaction temperature was maintained for 10 min and then cooled to room temperature. Then, the synthesized QDs were purified by adding toluene, ethanol solution. The mixed solution was centrifuged at 3,000 rpm for 10 min to separate the QDs via precipitation. The supernatant liquid phase was decanted to remove the excess reagent. Subsequently, the QDs were re-dispersed in a non-polar toluene solution (10 mg/ml).

snippets: Cu-In-Zn-S (CIZS) quantum dots (QDs) are considered as promising fluorescent materials owing to their low toxicity, wide emission range and large Stokes shifts, which have a wide prospect in lighting field. CIZS QDs were prepared via ionic liquid assisted microwave method in aqueous solution. The effects of reaction time, addition amount of ligand and pH of precursor solution on phase composition, microscopic morphology and photoluminescence (PL) prop-440 erty were investigated. The size of QDs gradually increased with the increase of reaction time, resulting in red shift of emission peak from 609.2 to 634.6 nm...White LED device was fabricated by combin-ing CIZS QDs and a blue chip, the color rendering index and luminous efficiency of device were 85.6 and 34.8 lm/W, re-spectively, which provided a reference for the application of water soluble multiple QDs in white LEDs.

citations.title: [257724205 | Islas-Rodriguez et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4]
snippets: Different strategies have been developed for TQDs synthesis in organic and aqueous media, allowing to obtain nanoparticles with promising physicochemical properties. So far, the spectroscopic parameters of TQDs (such as QY and FWHM) have not reached the binary QDs values; therefore, further research is needed to improve them. Non-etheless, these nanomaterials have the advantage of using precursors with less toxicity compared to Cdand Pb-based QDs. Optical properties and LEDs parameters are influenced by the size, composition, and solvent used in TQDs synthesis; thus, the critical point to be evaluated is the synthesis strategy and conditions. For instance, some parameters such as the QY (and therefore EQE) can be improved by changing the ratio of the group I and group III concentrations or by coating the core with a ZnS shell.

snippets: I–III–VI-based semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) have been intensively explored because of their unique controllable optoelectronic properties. The obtained QDs showed a sharp band-edge photoluminescence peak at 557 nm without a broad-defect site emission. sections.title: Material Synthesis Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; Quantum dot synthesis typically follows hot-injection methods under inert atmospheres using specific combinations of precursors and solvents. The process involves careful temperature control, ligand exchange steps, and purification phases to achieve desired properties and sizes. (8 sources)

The synthesis of quantum dots for LED applications generally employs hot-injection techniques conducted under inert atmospheres like nitrogen or argon. The base process begins with dissolving metal precursors in organic solvents, typically using combinations of octadecene (ODE) and oleic acid (OA) as primary components  [261372776 | Ribeiro et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]  [240555563 | Kundu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 26].

Temperature control is critical throughout the synthesis process. Initial stages often involve degassing and heating at moderate temperatures (around 100-120°C) to form metal oleate complexes. The core formation typically occurs at elevated temperatures (usually 180-300°C) when chalcogen precursors are rapidly injected into the reaction mixture  [225307153 | Bang et al. | 2020 | Citations: 5]  [240555563 | Kundu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 26].

Shell growth can be performed either in a single step or multiple stages depending on the desired properties. For example, in CdZnS/ZnS QD synthesis, a two-stage shell growth process can be implemented where different ratios of zinc and cadmium precursors are carefully controlled to optimize photoluminescence quantum yield  [225307153 | Bang et al. | 2020 | Citations: 5]. Similarly, CdSe/Zn₁₋ₓCdₓS QDs require precise control over injection rates and temperature profiles to achieve the desired compositional gradient  [240493286 | Baronnier et al. | 2021 | Citations: 5].

Post-synthesis purification is essential for obtaining high-quality QDs. This typically involves multiple washing steps using solvents like acetone, ethanol, and hexane, followed by redispersion in appropriate solvents  [108428151 | Amini et al. | 2015 | Citations: 6]  [225626463 | Pradhan et al. | 2020 | Citations: 26]. For some compositions, such as InP QDs, innovative approaches like using in-situ generated PH₃ instead of expensive elemental phosphorus sources have been developed  [236568155 | Lian et al. | 2021 | Citations: 4].

Recent developments have focused on simplifying synthesis protocols while maintaining quality. One-pot methods have been successful in producing high-performance QDs by eliminating unnecessary steps, though this requires careful optimization of precursor ratios and reaction conditions  [225307153 | Bang et al. | 2020 | Citations: 5]. Additionally, modifications to conventional procedures, such as using thioglycolic acid treatment for PbS QDs, have shown promise in improving crystallinity and reducing defects  [225626463 | Pradhan et al. | 2020 | Citations: 26].

citations.title: [108428151 | Amini et al. | 2015 | Citations: 6]
snippets:
This section provides materials synthesis and fabrication methods of QD-LED devices that are realized by our research group. All of the fabricated devices consist of p-type and n-type materials as HTL and ETL, respectively. Synthesis of these materials will be explained in this section.

CdS is another quantum dot, which has been used in the fabrication of QD-LED. For synthesis of CdS QDs, CdO (1mmol) and TOPO (0.3g) and chloroform (30ml) were mixed together under vacuum conditions at 100°C. Then S (2mmol) dispersed in 2ml of Tri-tertbutylphosphine and this solution was injected to the mixture of CdO (1mmol) and TOPO (0.3g) and chloroform (30ml) at 100°C for 30min. The obtained material was centrifuged with n-hexane, ethanol and acetone for several times.

Surface of the synthesized CdS QDs for applying in QD-LEDs should be improved. For this purpose we got help from FRET mechanism and capping molecules for using as surface modification, selected based on enhancement of illumination of CdS using FRET mechanism. So we carried out surface modification of QDs by organic molecules, which listed as follow:

One of the materials for modification of QD surface is Thioacetamide (TAA). For preparing of CdS with TAA ligands, CdS (0.01g) capped with TOPO (synthesized QD) and TAA (0.01) and 2-propanol (5ml) were mixed together under stirring for 24 hours, after that the obtained material was centrifuged with 2-propanol, n-hexane, ethanol and distilled water for several times.

citations.title: [225307153 | Bang et al. | 2020 | Citations: 5]
snippets: A synthesis procedure of CdZnS/ZnS QDs was adopted with a similar modification as the method described in the literature [8] to enhance their fabrication stability for expanding applications of the most sensitive blue QDs because of their intrinsically small particle size. The structure of CdZnS/ZnS core shell is well-known to provide high photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) and stability by preventing mismatching of unsaturated bonds and dangling bonds on the QD surface. [9] By adopting their properties, the one-pot synthesis method was optimized and simplified by eliminating redundant steps; hence, multiple and complex shell growth processes are not necessary, which enables the improvement in reproducibility and scalability...The synthesis starts with mixing and heating to form Cd-oleate and Zn-oleate by preparing mixed solvents of oleic acid (OA) in 1-octadecene (ODE) with CdO and Zn acetate (Zn(Ac) 2 ) at 140 °C. After increasing the temperature to 300 °C under N 2 flow, S precursor in ODE was quickly injected for the core formation. Because the reactivity of Cd to S is much faster than that to Zn, the amount of Zn precursor was larger than that of Cd to achieve a reaction balance and form the CdZnS alloyed core. Next, the second part of another S precursor in OA was injected at a slow rate of 1 mL min −1 for the thick-ZnS shell growth onto the CdZnS core. Different conditions of shell growth were applied to obtain the PLQY as a function of the amount and concentration of S in OA and the volume of the injection rate. Experimental results show that a large amount of S and a slow injection rate promote the thick-shell growth. 8b] The consequential QDs were annealed for an hour at 310 °C and cooled down to room temperature under ambient conditions. Next, in the purification step, QDs were separated from the precursor, and isolated QDs were dissolved in hexane for further device fabrication.

citations.title: [225626463 | Pradhan et al. | 2020 | Citations: 26]
snippets: Synthesis of PbS QDs: 1.75, 1.5, and 1.32 eV excitonic peak based PbS QDs, used as the matrix materials for the devices, were synthesized using Schlenk technique following the standard recipe. Briefly, 0.446 g (2 mmol) lead oxide (PbO), 1.6 mL (4.7 mmol) oleic acid, and 18 mL 1-octadecene (ODE) were pumped overnight at 90 °C. For 1.75 and 1.5 eV PbS QDs, the temperature was set to 80 °C and 1 mmol hexamethyldisilane (HMS) mixed with 5 mL ODE was immediately injected. The reaction was quenched with cold acetone after a few seconds (20 s for 1.75 eV PbS QDs and 50 s for 1.5 eV QDs) and the QDs were isolated by precipitation. The QDs were further purified by dispersion/precipitation with toluene/acetone three times. For 1.32 eV QDs, the temperature was set at 95 °C and right after the injection, the heating was stopped (without removing the heating mantle) and the solution was allowed to cool down gradually (≈1 h). 0.95 eV excitonic peak based PbS QDs were synthesized by a previously reported multi-injection method with slight modification. [22] Typically, 0.446 g (2 mmol) PbO, 3.8 mL oleic acid, and 50 mL ODE were mixed together at 90 °C under vacuum overnight. Once under Ar, the temperature of the reaction was raised to 100 °C and a solution of 90 μL HMS in 3 mL ODE was quickly injected. After 6 min, a second injection of 65 μL of HMS in 9 mL of ODE was dropwise injected and then the heating was stopped immediately and the solution was cooled down gradually to room temperature. The QDs were purified three times with a mixture of acetone/ethanol, redispering with toluene.

citations.title: [236568155 | Lian et al. | 2021 | Citations: 4]
snippets: InP quantum dots (QDs) are promising down-conversion phosphors for white light LEDs. However, the mainstream InP QDs synthesis uses expensive phosphorus source. Here, economic, in situ-generated PH3 is used to synthesize InP QDs and a two-step coating of ZnS shells is developed to prepare highly luminescent InP/ZnS/ZnS QDs. The QDs show a photoluminescence quantum yield as high as 78.5%. The emission can be tuned by adjusting the halide precursor and yellow emissive InP/ZnS/ZnS QDs are prepared by judiciously controlling the synthetic conditions. The yellow QDs show suppressed thermal quenching and retain >90% room temperature PL intensity at 150 °C for the growth solution. Additionally, the PL spectrum matches with the eye sensitivity function, resulting in efficient InP QD white light LEDs.

citations.title: [240493286 | Baronnier et al. | 2021 | Citations: 5]
snippets: CdSe/Zn 1−x Cd x S Colloidal quantum dots (CQDs) were synthesized following Refs. 31 and 32. To create the CdSe core, 15 mL of octadecene, 1 mmol of cadmium oxide and 3 mmol of myristic acid were introduced in a three-neck flask. The mixture was degassed at 60  C under vacuum for ten minutes before being heated to 300  C under argon. When the mixture became transparent, 0.25 mL of TOPSe at 2 M was introduced to react at 300  C for three minutes. The Zn x−1 Cd x S shell was then created: 3 mL of zinc oleate (Zn(OA) 2 ) at 0.5M and 1 mmol of dodecanthiol (DDT) were injected during one minute. The solution was then left to react 300  C for 30 minutes. The shell created in this first growth step was composed theoretically of 60 % of Cadmium and 20 % of Zinc. Then, 2 mL of cadmium oleate (Cd(OA) 2 ) at 0.5 M, 4 mL of Zn(OA) 2 at 0.5 M and 1.5 mL of TOPS at 2 M were injected in one minute, resulting in a final shell that was equal parts cadmium and zinc. This mixture was heated during 10 minutes to 300  C. This step was repeated 4 times and for each injection, a few nanometers of shell were created. The synthesized QDs were eventually dispersed in hexane.

citations.title: [240555563 | Kundu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 26]
snippets: Synthesis of the PbSe Colloidal Quantum Dots: 2.5 µm excitonic-peakbased PbSe QDs were synthesized under inert atmosphere by the hot injection method. About 2 mmol PbO, 15 mmol OA, and 10 mL ODE were mixed in a three-neck flask and heated at 100 °C, under vacuum, for 1 h to form lead oleate, stirring at 650 rpm. Thereafter, the solution was placed under Ar; the temperature was raised to 180 °C; and a solution of TOP-Se was quickly injected (2 mmol Se, 200 µL DPP, and 1 mL TOP). After 3 min of reaction under these conditions, a second solution of TOP-Se (2 mmol Se in 2 mL TOP) was injected dropwise. Immediately after this second injection, the reaction was quenched with a water bath. Once at room temperature, QDs were separated by centrifugation and redispersed in anhydrous toluene. The addition of 10 µL butylamine was necessary to redisperse the precipitate. Subsequently, the product was washed for three times with a mixture of acetone/ethanol and finally redispersed in anhydrous toluene, adjusting the concentration to 30 mg mL −1 . The final solution was bubbled with N 2 to avoid the oxidation of the material.

citations.title: [261372776 | Ribeiro et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]
snippets:
The chemicals used in the quantum dot synthesis were lead oxide (PbO), oleic acid (OA), octadecene (ODE), hexamethyldisilathiane (TMS), octane, and acetone. These were all purchased from Sigma Aldrich and used with no further processing or purification. 

PbS-OA-capped colloidal QDs were synthesized by the hot injection method. The lead precursor solution was prepared by adding 223 mg of PbO, 1.260 mL of OA, and 9 mL of ODE to a 25 mL three-necked round-bottom flask. The mixture was kept constantly stirring under a vacuum in a Schlenk line at 120 °C for about 1 h until the PbO was completely dissolved. Before the injection of the sulfur precursor solution, a reaction temperature of 70 to 120 °C was set and stabilized under N2 flow. 

The sulfur precursor solution was prepared in a glovebox just before injection by mixing 2.5 mL of pre-degassed octadecene (1 h under constant stirring and vacuum at 120 °C) and 105 µL of TMS. The mixture was transferred to a syringe to inject into the lead precursor solution. Afterward, the sulfur precursor solution was swiftly injected into the lead precursor solution, and a sequence of color transitions from clear to yellow and from yellow to brown was noticed, indicating the formation of QDs in the mixture. 

After injection, the heat source was immediately turned off, leaving the mixture to cool down slowly until a low temperature was reached (~50 °C). The mixture was further transferred to a 45 mL centrifuge tube, and 32.5 mL of acetone was added to precipitate the OA-capped dots. These QDs were centrifuged at 6000 rpm for 5 min. Afterward, the supernatant was discarded, and the precipitate was redissolved in 10 mL acetone, followed by 35 mL of acetone and further centrifugation at 6000 rpm for 5 min. The previous re-dissolution and precipitation step was repeated once more, but now the precipitate was dissolved into 2 to 3 mL of dry octane, filtered through a 220 nm PTFE filter, transferred to a glass flask, and stored in a freezer until used.

sections.title: Processing Techniques
sections.text:
TLDR; QD-LEDs can be manufactured using various solution-based processing methods including spin coating, inkjet printing, and electrodeposition. While spin coating remains common due to its simplicity, newer techniques focus on reducing material waste and enabling better control over film formation. (6 sources)

* **Spin Coating**

   * Traditional method for depositing QD layers, particularly effective for creating uniform thin films  [205623441 | Park et al. | 2017 | Citations: 14]

   * Standard parameters: 2000 rpm speed produces 40 nm thick films for efficient carrier transport  [205623441 | Park et al. | 2017 | Citations: 14]

   * Drawback: High cost of QDs and waste (>96% loss during processing)  [202749584 | Nguyen et al. | 2019 | Citations: 17]

* **Solution-Based Deposition**

   * Low-energy solution processing enables scalable manufacturing  [116875409 | Antolini et al. | 2019 | Citations: 26]

   * Can be combined with various techniques including:

     - Micro-contact printing

     - Inkjet printing

     - Spray coating  [116875409 | Antolini et al. | 2019 | Citations: 26]

* **Electrodeposition**

   * Particularly useful for metal contacts in QD-LEDs

   * Enables sequential deposition of multiple layers including:

     - Hole Transport Layer (HTL)

     - Electron Transport Layer (ETL)

     - Metal contacts (typically Al, Ag, and Au)  [205623441 | Park et al. | 2017 | Citations: 14]

* **Advanced Hybrid Techniques**

   * Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) integration for precise control

   * Multi-step processes combining different deposition methods:

     - Initial QD coating

     - Ligand exchange treatments

     - Surface cleaning steps

     - Final ALD encapsulation  [238423319 | Whitworth et al. | 2021 | Citations: 88]

* **Alternative Material Integration**

   * UV-curable resin systems for patterning applications

   * Requires careful consideration of QD-resin interactions

   * Success depends on proper ligand exchange treatments to prevent QD aggregation  [252155158 | Shiraishi et al. | 2022 | Citations: 4]

* **Emerging Solutions**

   * Electrohydrodynamic (EHD) jet printing shows promise as:

     - Cost-effective

     - Environmentally friendly

     - Suitable for minimal material consumption

     - Capable of precise patterning  [202749584 | Nguyen et al. | 2019 | Citations: 17]

citations.title: [116875409 | Antolini et al. | 2019 | Citations: 26]
snippets: The low-energy solution-based synthesis of QDs enables their scalability and incorporation into devices (processability) (Kathirgamanathan et al., 2015). Owing to colloidal stability and the ability to make films without disrupting the physical integrity of the crystals, the use of QDs in electroluminescent devices has become possible. Deposition techniques such as spin-coating, micro-contact printing, ink-jet printing, can be exploited to manufacture optoelectronic devices such as light emitting diodes (LEDs) and displays onto rigid or flexible substrates.

citations.title: [202749584 | Nguyen et al. | 2019 | Citations: 17]
snippets: Conventional vacuum deposition is used to fabricate OLEDs but is not suitable for heavy metal materials like CdSe/ZnS core/shell QDs. Spin coating has been the most popular approach to fabricate QD-LED devices, mainly due to the simplicity of the method for achieving a near-monolayer of nanoparticles. However, the method results in a relatively high cost of QDs and the loss of more than 96% of the solution during spin coating. Therefore, an alternative deposition route that is capable of patterning and consuming a minimum amount of QD materials is needed...EHD jet printing is a robust, simple, flexible, inexpensive, and powerful technique for a wide range of micro-and nano-particulate patterning and thin-film deposition processes 7,8.

citations.title: [205623441 | Park et al. | 2017 | Citations: 14]
snippets: The colloidal quantum dots (CQDs) of CdSe/CdS/ZnS core-shell-shell were synthesized by the process reported in previous publications 21,22. The CQDs dispersed in cyclohexane were characterized by a UV-vis spectrometer (Varian Cary 5000) and a fluorometer (Fluorolog JOBIN YVON Horiba). The wavelengths of the first excitation absorption and maximum photoluminescence (PL) were measured to be 584 nm and 604 nm, respectively. The FWHM of the CQD emission was ~ 33 nm. ITO-deposited glass was used as a substrate for the CQD LED fabrication. This ITO layer was patterned by chemical wet etching. Poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene)-poly(stryenesulfonate) (PEDOT-PSS) and poly(9,9-dioctyl-fluorene-co-N-(4-butylphenyl)diphenylamine) (TFB) were spin-coated as the HTL for hole injection. The synthesized CQDs were spin-coated at 2000 rpm to match the thickness of 40 nm for efficient carrier transport. After that, gel-type TiO2 was spin-coated as the ETL for electron injection. As the final process, Al, Ag, and Au metals with 50 nm, 240 nm, and 10 nm thicknesses, respectively, were sequentially deposited by electron beam evaporation.

citations.title: [238423319 | Whitworth et al. | 2021 | Citations: 88]
snippets: Quantum dots were deposited on alumina gratings using the following steps; (i) A 30mg/ml solution of CQDs was spun at 2500 rpm on gratings for 30 seconds; (ii) A ligand exchange solution of 7mg/ml EMII in methanol + 0.01 % MPA was applied to the surface for 30 s; (iii) Samples were spun at 2500 rpm for 60 s while methanol was drop cast onto the surface in order to clean the substrate of unwanted ligands; (iv) steps (i)-(iii) were then repeated until the desired thickness of CQDs was reached. For doping the samples were subsequently transferred to an ALD machine for 30 cycles of alumina deposition.

citations.title: [252155158 | Shiraishi et al. | 2022 | Citations: 4]
snippets: Quantum dots (QDs) dispersed in UV-curable resin are used for patterning in photolithography and inkjet printing. However, low affinity between the main component of UV-curable resins known as celloxide, an alicyclic diepoxy compound, and QD surface ligands with alkyl chains causes significant aggregation of QDs. In this study, the dispersibility of core/shell CuInS2/ZnS QDs with adsorbed 1-dodecanethiol and oleic acid in celloxide was improved using the ligand exchange method to prepare transparent fluorescent nanocomposites. Cyclohexyl 3-mercaptopropionate (MPACH) and 3-mercaptopropionic acid (MPA) were successfully adsorbed onto the QDs. MPACH-modified QDs (QD-MPACH) were well dispersed in the UV-curable resin, whereas MPA-modified QDs (QD-MPA) exhibited significant aggregation.

sections.title: Device Fabrication Process
sections.text:
TLDR; QD-LED fabrication involves assembling multiple layered components including hole and electron transport layers, followed by precise metal contact deposition. The process typically combines spin coating for active layers with vapor deposition techniques for electrodes, requiring careful control of layer thicknesses and interfaces. (4 sources)

The fabrication of QD-LED devices follows a systematic multi-layer approach starting with substrate preparation. The process typically begins with indium tin oxide (ITO)-coated glass substrates, which undergo chemical wet etching to create patterned areas for device fabrication  [205623441 | Park et al. | 2017 | Citations: 14].

The construction of QD-LEDs relies heavily on the implementation of both hole transport (HTL) and electron transport (ETL) layers to ensure efficient charge carrier movement. Common materials for these layers include PEDOT:PSS for the hole transport layer and TiO₂ in gel form for the electron transport layer  [205623441 | Park et al. | 2017 | Citations: 14]. The QD emissive layer is typically deposited alongside the transport layers using spin coating techniques, with careful attention paid to achieving optimal thicknesses for efficient carrier transport  [205623441 | Park et al. | 2017 | Citations: 14].

A critical aspect of device fabrication is managing the interface between different layers to prevent QD aggregation while ensuring good electrical contact. This challenge has been addressed through innovative approaches such as directly linking conjugated organic polymers to QD surfaces, which helps eliminate aggregation effects  [46360549 | McDowell et al. | 2010 | Citations: 24]  [1635586 | Skaff et al. | 2004 | Citations: 38].

The final stage involves the deposition of metal contacts through vacuum evaporation techniques. Multiple metal layers are commonly deposited sequentially, with typical configurations including combinations of aluminum (50 nm), silver (240 nm), and gold (10 nm) layers to achieve optimal current spreading and voltage characteristics  [205623441 | Park et al. | 2017 | Citations: 14]. Alternatively, simpler metal-only configurations can also be effective, as demonstrated by devices using solely Al/Ti/Au contacts that still achieved reasonable operational voltages around 10 V  [248979083 | Kelley et al. | 2016 | Citations: 0].

The CQDs dispersed in cyclohexane were characterized by a UV-vis spectrometer (Varian Cary 5000) and a fluorometer (Fluorolog JOBIN YVON Horiba). The wavelengths of the first excitation absorption and maximum photoluminescence (PL) were measured to be 584 nm and 604 nm, respectively. The FWHM of the CQD emission was ~ 33 nm. ITO-deposited glass was used as a substrate for the CQD LED fabrication. This ITO layer was patterned by chemical wet etching. Poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene)-poly(stryenesulfonate) (PEDOT-PSS) and poly(9,9-dioctyl-fluorene-co-N-(4-butylphenyl)diphenylamine) (TFB) were spin-coated as the HTL for hole injection. The synthesized CQDs were spin-coated at 2000 rpm to match the thickness of 40 nm for efficient carrier transport. After that, gel-type TiO2 was spin-coated as the ETL for electron injection. As the final process, Al, Ag, and Au metals with 50 nm, 240 nm, and 10 nm thicknesses, respectively, were sequentially deposited by electron beam evaporation.

citations.title: [248979083 | Kelley et al. | 2016 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Progress in the synthesis of CdSe-ZnS quantum dots and characterization using UV-Vis and fluorescence spectroscopy will be presented. Details of a LED device fabricated from CdSe ZnS quantum dots, 4,4,4-tris-(carbazol-9-yl)-triphenylamine (TCTA) as the hole transport layer, and titatinium (IV) butoxide as the electron transport layer will be reported.

citations.title: [46360549 | McDowell et al. | 2010 | Citations: 24]
snippets: One of the difficulties involved in constructing devices from quantum dots is creating electrical contacts to electrodes that allow charge transport while at the same time preventing quantum dot aggregation. The early photovoltaic devices suffered from aggregation of the particles, which is far from optimal for facilitating charge separation and transport to the respective electrodes. More recent efforts have been directed at directly linking conjugated organic polymers to the surface of the quantum dots such as in composite CdSe-OPV nanostructures described above. A cartoon schematic of a device incorporating such functionalized quantum dots is shown in Figure 7. This direct connection has been shown to eliminate aggregation effects (Skaff et al., 2004) and is expected to lead to much higher device efficiencies. An excellent example of such a device was recently introduced by Zorn et al. (Zorn et al., 2009). In that case, the authors attached block copolymer ligands to CdSe/ZnS quantum dots. The copolymers consisted of both semiconducting blocks and reactive functional blocks that contain multidentate thiol-based anchor groups.

sections.title: Key Components and Materials
sections.text:
TLDR; QD-LEDs rely on several critical components working together, including specialized transport layers, binding agents, and protective coatings. The selection and combination of these materials significantly impacts device performance, stability, and manufacturability. (6 sources)

* **Transport Layers**

   * Hole Transport Layers (HTL):

      - PEDOT:PSS is widely used for efficient hole injection

      - Works well with various QD materials including CdSe/ZnO hybrids  [250064820 | Kim et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3]

   

   * Electron Transport Layers (ETL):

      - Titanium dioxide (TiO₂) in gel form serves as an effective electron transporter

      - Often paired with polymer-based hole transports for balanced carrier mobility  [205623441 | Park et al. | 2017 | Citations: 14]

* **Binding Agents and Resins**

   * Thermally curable epoxy resins (like YD-128) serve as binders for QD mounting

   * Hardeners (such as KFH-271) are essential for curing processes

   * These materials enable secure attachment of QDs to LED chips  [103384131 | Jang et al. | 2018 | Citations: 15]

* **Protective Coatings**

   * Silica coatings protect QDs and improve device stability

   * Shell materials like ZnS can be used to prevent thermal quenching  [21440220 | Xie et al. | 2017 | Citations: 5]

   * Surface modification silanes:

      - APTES (3-Aminopropyltrimethoxysilane)

sections.title:
Introduction to 3D Gaussians
---
sections.text:
TLDR; 3D Gaussians are mathematical constructs that represent 3D spaces using collections of Gaussian distributions characterized by position, scale, and opacity. They've become popular for creating compact, efficient representations of 3D scenes that balance quality and performance. (5 sources)

Recent advances in computer graphics and vision have led to increased interest in using 3D Gaussian distributions as a powerful tool for representing and rendering 3D scenes  [268554137 | Xu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 149]. At their core, 3D Gaussians are mathematical functions that describe points in three-dimensional space, characterized by several key parameters including their mean position, covariance matrix defining spatial extent, opacity, and color information  [277502201 | Li et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

One significant advantage of using 3D Gaussials over traditional volumetric approaches is their efficiency - instead of representing entire volumes densely, they use a sparse set of Gaussian primitives to capture the essential features of a scene  [277502201 | Li et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. This makes them particularly effective for tasks ranging from static scene reconstruction to more complex applications like character animation and dynamic scene capture  [265456237 | Lei et al. | 2023 | Citations: 73].

Their versatility has led to widespread adoption across numerous domains. From basic avatar reconstruction to sophisticated applications involving text-conditioned 3D generation and dynamic scene reconstruction  [268554137 | Xu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 149], 3D Gaussians have proven themselves as a robust representation framework. Notably, they excel at handling both rigid structures like bones and flexible elements in the same representation <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

The success of 3D Gaussians stems from their ability to balance accuracy with computational efficiency, allowing for high-quality reconstructions while maintaining manageable memory requirements and processing speeds  [265456237 | Lei et al. | 2023 | Citations: 73]  [262369712 | Kerbl et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1598]. This has made them increasingly valuable tools in modern computer vision and graphics applications  [257266151 | Keselman et al. | 2022 | Citations: 813].

citations.title: [265456237 | Lei et al. | 2023 | Citations: 73]
snippets: We introduce Gaussian Articulated Template Model (GART), an explicit, efficient, and expressive representation for non-rigid articulated subject capturing and rendering from monocular videos. GART utilizes a mixture of moving 3D Gaussians to explicitly approximate a deformable subject's geometry and appearance. It takes advantage of a categorical template model prior (SMPL, SMAL, etc.) with learnable forward skinning while further generalizing to more complex non-rigid deformations with novel latent bones. GART can be reconstructed via differentiable rendering from monocular videos in seconds or minutes and rendered in novel poses faster than 150fps.

Unlike volumetric methods, which represent a scene as a dense field requiring costly volumetric sampling, 3DGS models a scene as a collection of discrete 3D Gaussian primitives. Each 3D Gaussian is parameterized by its mean position x, covariance matrix Σ, opacity α and view-dependent color represented by spherical harmonics coefficients.

sections.title: Applications in Bone Structure Analysis
sections.text:
TLDR; 3D Gaussian filtering and modeling techniques are widely used in medical imaging to analyze bone microstructure and architecture. These methods help researchers and clinicians visualize, measure, and understand bone properties at microscopic levels, supporting both diagnostic and research purposes. (9 sources)

Microcomputed tomography (microCT) scanning combined with 3D Gaussian processing has become a crucial tool for analyzing bone structure at microscopic levels. Researchers commonly use high-resolution microCT scanners operating at kilovoltage settings (typically 18-55 kVp) to capture detailed internal bone architectures [14584923 | Graham et al. | 2013 | Citations: 68] [220381225 | Wang et al. | 2020 | Citations: 4].

A critical aspect of bone structure analysis involves studying trabecular bone microarchitecture, which forms a complex network governing bone strength and health. Recent studies emphasize that bone morphology doesn't simply follow minimal surface principles but rather presents an intricate pattern of curvatures that can be precisely analyzed using advanced imaging techniques  [235451193 | Callens et al. | 2020 | Citations: 34].

The preprocessing of bone imaging data almost universally incorporates 3D Gaussian filtering to reduce noise while preserving important structural details. Typical implementations use constrained 3D Gaussian filters with sigma values between 0.8-1.2 and specific support parameters  [14584923 | Graham et al. | 2013 | Citations: 68]  [247304764 | Sinzinger et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3]  [235686721 | Goff et al. | 2021 | Citations: 21].

Advanced analytical methods have evolved beyond simple structural measurements. Modern approaches include specialized filters based on the eigenvalues of local Hessian matrices computed using Gaussian derivatives, enabling enhancement of cortical structures while suppressing surrounding tissues  [268741213 | Aldieri et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]. Additionally, innovative techniques now incorporate topology-based analysis through persistent homology integrated with Gaussian mixture models, offering new ways to track morphological changes during disease progression  [271957534 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

Clinical applications have benefited from these technical advances. For instance, in spine interventions, enhanced 3D visualization systems combining ultrasound with Gaussian-filtered CT data have improved the precision of procedures by better revealing anatomical features  [253498957 | Jiang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 1]. Automated segmentation methods have also been developed, employing stepwise approaches from initial thresholding to refined surface reconstruction  [27666641 | Wang et al. | 2012 | Citations: 2].

sections.title: 3D Gaussian-Based Skeletal Modeling
sections.text:
TLDR; 3D Gaussian modeling of skeletons combines anatomically meaningful bone attachments with efficient mathematical representations. This approach uses sets of Gaussians, typically anchored to skeleton joints and bones, to create compact yet detailed representations of human bodies and other articulated structures. (9 sources)

Modern skeletal modeling using 3D Gaussians builds upon foundational work that showed how to attach Gaussian primitives to bone structures to create efficient representations of human anatomy  [1833515 | Sridhar et al. | 2015 | Citations: 249]  [220381225 | Wang et al. | 2020 | Citations: 4]  [663099 | Rhodin et al. | 2016 | Citations: 101]  (Rhodin et al._1,  2016).

These Gaussian-based skeletal models typically consist of two main components: a collection of 3D Gaussian points that capture shape and appearance characteristics, and a comprehensive skeleton model that enables manipulation  [268032552 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 15]. The skeleton structure can vary in complexity, with notable implementations using anywhere from 16 to 55 joints to control different body parts and extremities  [268032552 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 15]  [271089073 | Chatziagapi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

The implementation typically employs a small to moderate number of Gaussians (around 25-91) to represent entire subjects, with each Gaussian maintaining its own position, orientation, and scaling parameters  [272988131 | Tan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]. These Gaussian primitives can be manipulated through established techniques like Linear Blend Skinning (LBS), which allows for natural deformation of the attached Gaussians based on underlying bone movements  [268513551 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 10]  [271903119 | Zhao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

The power of this approach lies in its efficiency and flexibility - it can represent complex shapes with relatively few parameters while maintaining the ability to undergo natural skeletal deformations  [274117016 | Chen | 2024 | Citations: 1]. This makes it particularly suitable for applications ranging from human body modeling to robotic system representation  [276885447 | Hu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

citations.title: [1833515 | Sridhar et al. | 2015 | Citations: 249]
snippets: Markerless tracking of hands and fingers is a promising enabler for human-computer interaction. However, adoption has been limited because of tracking inaccuracies, incomplete coverage of motions, low framerate, complex camera setups, and high computational requirements. In this paper, we present a fast method for accurately tracking rapid and complex articulations of the hand using a single depth camera. Our algorithm uses a novel detectionguided optimization strategy that increases the robustness and speed of pose estimation. In the detection step, a randomized decision forest classifies pixels into parts of the hand. In the optimization step, a novel objective function combines the detected part labels and a Gaussian mixture representation of the depth to estimate a pose that best fits the depth. Our approach needs comparably less computational resources which makes it extremely fast (50 fps without GPU support). The approach also supports varying static, or moving, camera-to-scene arrangements. We show the benefits of our method by evaluating on public datasets and comparing against previous work.
