citations.title: [273098661 | Jeevan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]
snippets: Normalizing flows are generative models built on invertible transformations. Among all the generative models that are widely used, such as, GANs, VAEs, and diffusion, normalizing flows are the only type of model for which the likelihood of data can be computed exactly and efficiently [12](Kobyzev et al., 2020). None of the other models explicitly learn the likelihood of the real data. While VAEs model a lower bound of the likelihood, GANs only provide a sampling mechanism for generating new data, without offering a likelihood estimate (Kobyzev et al., 2020).

sections.title: Advantages and Limitations
sections.text:
TLDR; VAEs excel at handling high-dimensional data and capturing global semantic features but suffer from blurry outputs and distribution assumption constraints. Normalizing flows offer precise density estimation and exact inference but face computational intensity and dimensionality preservation challenges. (6 sources)

**Advantages of VAEs:**

- Effectively captures long-range semantic features and prosodic elements, even with smaller model sizes  [238227056 | Ren et al. | 2021 | Citations: 78]

- Works best with approximately Gaussian distributed variables <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

- Provides compact latent representations and faster training compared to some alternatives  [213340748 | Morrow et al. | 2020 | Citations: 19]

**Limitations of VAEs:**

- Produces lossy recognition and generation processes, potentially losing important details  [214814066 | Nugraha et al. | 2020 | Citations: 29]

- Struggles with strongly skewed or multimodal distributions, requiring larger decoders which can render latent space ineffective  [226282453 | Park et al. | 2020 | Citations: 40]

- Limited flexibility in modeling complex posterior distributions due to assumed factorial structure  [211532721 | Giaquinto et al. | 2020 | Citations: 1]

**Advantages of Normalizing Flows:**

- Enables precise (lossless) recognition and generation processes  [214814066 | Nugraha et al. | 2020 | Citations: 29]

- Offers exact density evaluation without requiring explicit distribution definitions  [214814066 | Nugraha et al. | 2020 | Citations: 29]

- More resistant to common training issues like mode and posterior collapse  [249282520 | Kousha et al. | 2022 | Citations: 27]

**Limitations of Normalizing Flows:**

- Must maintain equal dimensionality between latent and input spaces, potentially being computationally expensive  [214814066 | Nugraha et al. | 2020 | Citations: 29]

- Lack flexibility in modeling varying dimensional features due to bijective nature  [248512570 | Verheyen | 2022 | Citations: 27]

- Cannot perform update operations using recognition models due to bijective property constraints  [214814066 | Nugraha et al. | 2020 | Citations: 29]

citations.title: [211532721 | Giaquinto et al. | 2020 | Citations: 1]
snippets:
A popular approach to generative modeling is with variational autoencoders (VAE, (Lopez et al., 2020)). A major challenge in VAEs, however, is that they assume a factorial posterior, which is widely known to limit their flexibility (Rezende et al., 2015)(Kingma et al., 2016)(Miller et al., 2016)4,(Huang et al., 2018)(Tomczak et al., 2017)(Casale et al., 2018)(Berg et al., 2018). Further, VAEs do not offer exact density estimationa requirement in many statistical procedures. 

Normalizing flows (NF) play an important role in the recent developments of both density estimation and variational inference (Rezende et al., 2015). Normalizing flows are smooth, invertible transformations with tractable Jacobians, which can map a complex data distribution to simple distribution, such as a standard normal. In the context of variational inference, a normalizing flow transforms a simple, known base distribution into a more faithful representation of the true posterior. Flow-based models are also an attractive approach for density estimation because they provide exact density computation and sampling with only a single neural network pass (in some instances).

citations.title: [213340748 | Morrow et al. | 2020 | Citations: 19]
snippets: At a high level, our idea is to combine a simple VAE model with a normalizing flow model in the pixel space. As such, we hope to obtain the benefits of both: the smaller model size, faster training, and compact latent representation of VAEs, as well as the high quality samples of normalizing flows.

citations.title: [214814066 | Nugraha et al. | 2020 | Citations: 29]
snippets:
A major limitation of the VAE framework lies in imprecise (lossy) recognition and generation processes. Its generation process outputs tend to lose some details [15]- (Dai et al., 2019). This would be problematic for speech spectrograms, in particular, because the harmonic structures should be preserved well. Additionally, the distribution of observations (spectrograms) has to be explicitly defined. It is not always easy to do so because in many real cases, we do not know whether a certain distribution is suitable for some observations and assuming an inappropriate one might result in a detrimental effect. 

By contrast, the normalizing flow (NF) (Rezende et al., 2015), (Dinh et al., 2016) provides precise (lossless) recognition and generation processes due to its sequence of bijective transformations. Additionally, the distribution of the observations does not need to be explicitly defined, so NF could be used to model sophisticated ones. However, the dimensionality of the transformed variables is the same as that of the observations due to the bijective property. Therefore, the transformed variables might be high dimensional and their updates, especially by an MCMC method, would be computationally expensive. Moreover, updating using the recognition model (Pariente et al., 2019) cannot be done because of the bijective property.

citations.title: [226282453 | Park et al. | 2020 | Citations: 40]
snippets:
A variational autoencoder (VAE) is, in essence, an autoencoder that samples from a multidimensional Gaussian distribution in the first layer of the latent space. The loss is computed by constructing the cross-entropy between the input dataset and the output dataset. An additional Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence term is added to the loss to encourage the VAE to approximate the posterior with a multidimensional Gaussian distribution [46].

VAEs have several limitations. With a VAE, we assume that the latent space can be approximated using a series of compounded linear transformations of a multidimensional Gaussian distribution. Consequently, VAEs work best when the input variables are approximately Gaussian. If the input variables adhere to a distribution that is clearly skewed or multimodal, we require a large decoder to transform the Gaussian latent vectors to vectors that can accurately reconstruct the input data. If the decoder is too large, the latent space will be rendered useless. This phenomenon is known as the "posterior collapse" [47].

To avoid the limitations of VAEs, one can use normalizing flows to transform a posterior distribution into a much more flexible distribution that is representative of the corresponding data [48]. We incorporate normalizing flows into our VAEs by using them in our latent space.

citations.title: [238227056 | Ren et al. | 2021 | Citations: 78]
snippets: After analyzing two kinds of generative NAR-TTS models (VAE and normalizing flow), we find that: VAE is good at capturing the long-range semantics features (e.g., prosody) even with small model size but suffers from blurry and unnatural results; and normalizing flow is good at reconstructing the frequency bin-wise details but performs poorly when the number of model parameters is limited.

citations.title: [248512570 | Verheyen | 2022 | Citations: 27]
snippets:
Normalizing flows are a class of generative models that enable exact likelihood evaluation. While these models have already found various applications in particle physics, normalizing flows are not flexible enough to model many of the peripheral features of collision events...flows lack in flexibility due to the bijective nature of the transforms, meaning that they are essentially restricted to modelling a continuous feature space of fixed dimension.

On the other hand, GANs and VAEs do not have these limitations, but they do not offer exact likelihood evaluation. GANs are trained adversarially and thus do not offer access to the likelihood at all, but VAEs are able to provide a lower bound estimate of the likelihood. In [1] a method was outlined that combines the favorable properties of normalizing flows with the flexibility of VAEs.

citations.title: [249282520 | Kousha et al. | 2022 | Citations: 27]
snippets: Normalizing flows are a family of generative models that have gained popularity in recent years. Due to their formulation, they admit both efficient sampling and exact evaluation of probability density in contrast to other generative models, like GANs and VAEs [3](Kobyzev et al., 2020). Additionally, flowbased models do not suffer from issues like mode and posterior collapse that are commonly faced when training GANs and VAEs.

sections.title: Applications and Hybrid Approaches
sections.text:
TLDR; Despite their differences, VAEs and normalizing flows can be effectively combined to leverage their complementary strengths. This hybrid approach addresses VAEs' limitations in posterior modeling while maintaining VAEs' benefits of compact representations and efficient training. (7 sources)

Recent developments have demonstrated successful integration strategies that capitalize on the distinct advantages of both approaches. A particularly effective hybrid approach maintains the compact latent representation and faster training characteristics of VAEs while enhancing their posterior modeling capabilities through normalizing flows  [213340748 | Morrow et al. | 2020 | Citations: 19]. This combination helps overcome VAEs' inherent limitation in recovering true posterior distributions while retaining the computational benefits of the VAE framework  [207880657 | Abhishek et al. | 2019 | Citations: 2].

The implementation of normalizing flows in VAE architectures can be achieved through minimal architectural changes to the encoder and decoder components  [216079008 | Tomczak et al. | 2016 | Citations: 173]. This modification enables VAEs to develop richer, more flexible posterior distributions while maintaining their characteristic variational training procedure  [59413778 | Ziegler et al. | 2019 | Citations: 122]. Experimental results have shown that flow-enhanced VAEs can capture more complex posterior geometries, producing multimodal distributions rather than the typical unimodal Gaussian-like distributions of standard VAEs  [36855408 | Saxena et al. | 2017 | Citations: 2].

These hybrid approaches have demonstrated superior performance compared to traditional VAE implementations. sections.title: Background and Fundamentals
sections.text:
TLDR; Depth prediction is a critical component of computer vision that helps machines understand 3D spatial relationships from 2D images. The field combines classical computer vision techniques with modern deep learning approaches to enable applications ranging from robotics to virtual reality. (6 sources)

Understanding depth from visual data is fundamental to artificial intelligence and computer vision systems, serving as a bridge between 2D observations and 3D spatial comprehension  [264832993 | Shvets et al. | 2023 | Citations: 8]. This capability has emerged as a cornerstone technology for numerous practical applications, spanning robotics, autonomous navigation, virtual/augmented reality, and intelligent monitoring systems  [236279966 | Niu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 0].

From a technical standpoint, depth estimation enables computers to derive crucial scene properties including vanishing points, surface normals, obstacle locations, and free space information  [238416095 | Thompson et al. | 2021 | Citations: 4]. The field encompasses various approaches, from traditional computer vision techniques to modern deep learning methods, with notable implementations emerging from stereo vision, multi-view geometry, and active sensing technologies  [131774103 | Gordon et al. | 2019 | Citations: 363]  [17145870 | Saxena et al. | 2007 | Citations: 3078].

While stereo vision systems have traditionally delivered reliable depth information, they face challenges in computational efficiency and hardware implementation costs. Single-image depth prediction, powered by deep learning approaches, offers a compelling alternative by reducing hardware overhead while maintaining acceptable accuracy levels  [131774103 | Gordon et al. | 2019 | Citations: 363]. This advancement has particular significance for mobile and embedded platforms where resource constraints are paramount <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

In industrial applications, depth perception serves distinct purposes depending on the deployment context. For manufacturing applications, depth maps provide crucial dimensional information needed for quality control processes  [238416095 | Thompson et al. | 2021 | Citations: 4]. In robotics and autonomous systems, depth information enables sophisticated navigation capabilities and safe human-robot collaboration  [231808540 | Hadsell et al. | 2009 | Citations: 94].

citations.title: [131774103 | Gordon et al. | 2019 | Citations: 363]
snippets: Estimating scene depth is an important task for robot navigation and manipulation. Historically much research has been devoted to it, including a large bodies of research on stereo, multi-view geometry, and active sensing (Saxena et al., 2007)(Liu et al., 2014)(Eigen et al., 2014). Recently, learning-based approaches for dense depth prediction have gained attention (Eigen et al., 2014)(Liu et al., 2015)19,45]. In these, scene depth is predicted from input RGB images and the depth estimation function is learned using supervision provided by a sensor, such as a LiDAR. Similar approaches are used for other dense predictions such as surface normals (Eigen et al., 2014)(Wang et al., 2014).

sections.title: Evolution of Approaches
sections.text:
TLDR; The evolution of depth prediction spans from hand-crafted features and probabilistic models to sophisticated deep learning architectures. The field progressed through supervised, unsupervised, and self-supervised approaches, with each era bringing increasingly powerful methods for handling geometric understanding from visual data. (14 sources)

Early approaches to depth prediction relied heavily on hand-crafted features and geometric reasoning. Researchers utilized cues such as texture, shading, and structural information, often complemented by probabilistic models and shape-from-motion techniques  [239616762 | Lai et al. | 2021 | Citations: 3]. Notable early work included methods using vanishing points  [1276079 | Hoiem et al. | 2005 | Citations: 1142] and shape-from-shading techniques  [13878671 | Zhang et al. | 1999 | Citations: 151], demonstrating the potential of combining multiple visual cues for depth estimation.

A pivotal moment came with the introduction of supervised deep learning approaches using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The breakthrough work by Eigen et al. established the foundations for monocular depth prediction using deep learning  [2012437 | Eigen et al. | 2014 | Citations: 5121]. This was followed by rapid developments in encoder-decoder architectures, which became the dominant paradigm for dense prediction tasks  [248951321 | Ibrahem et al. | 2022 | Citations: 15].

The field then diversified into three main training paradigms: supervised, unsupervised, and self-supervised approaches  [239616762 | Lai et al. | 2021 | Citations: 3]. Unsupervised methods notably addressed the challenge of requiring ground truth data by leveraging stereo matching or monocular sequences  [7051798 | Godard et al. | 2016 | Citations: 2717]  [207202368 | Fu et al. | 2018 | Citations: 2620].

More recent innovations have focused on addressing specific challenges in depth estimation. These include the integration of local planar priors  [208558939 | Lee et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1028], the development of attention mechanisms for global context understanding  [3666352 | Bahdanau et al. | 2014 | Citations: 26561], and approaches for handling dynamic scenes  [256134310 | Patil et al. | 2022 | Citations: 14].

Current trends show increasing sophistication in architectural designs, with methods incorporating multi-task learning frameworks  [209131483 | Yin et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1024] and specialized components for handling specific challenges like depth ambiguity  [219984159 | Yue et al. | 2020 | Citations: 44]. These advancements reflect the field's maturation and ongoing efforts to improve accuracy and robustness across diverse scenarios  [216042185 | Li et al. | 2019 | Citations: 7].

citations.title: [216042185 | Li et al. | 2019 | Citations: 7]
snippets: Depth prediction has always been a core task to understand the geometric relations within a 3D scene. It provides rich information about the distance of the objects in the image from the viewpoint of camera. This technique is necessary for many applications in computer vision including smoothing blurred parts of an image (Malhotra, 2016) (Li et al., 2018), rendering of 3D scenes (Saxena et al., 2009), virtual reality, selfdriving cars (Hadsell et al., 2009), grasping in robotics [6] and autopilot (Tateno et al., 2017). However, predicting depth from images is a quite complex and challenging task. In absence of the environmental assumptions, the inherent ambiguity of mapping an intensity or color measurement into a depth value makes depth prediction an ill-posed problem. Many unique techniques have been proposed to tackle this problem, such as superpixels based algorithms (Liu et al., 2014), Structure-from-Motion (SfM) (Szeliski, 2015), data-driven methods (Karsch et al., 2012) and CNN based approaches (Laina et al., 2016).

citations.title: [239616762 | Lai et al. | 2021 | Citations: 3]
snippets: Extracting the priors of an image is a vital issue in monocular depth estimation. Before the booming of deep neural networks (DNNs), the mainstream method to solve the monocular depth estimation task was utilizing hand-crafted priors (Hoiem et al., 2005)(Cavoto et al., 2006)[25] or combining them with probabilistic models [3,(Delage et al., 2006). With the coming of the DNN era, the procedure of extracting useful features has been conducted by DNN-based models automatically. Many DNN models have been applied to monocular depth estimation tasks. For example, Xu et al. (Xu et al., 2017) proposed a DNN model combied with conditional random fields (CRFs) for predicting depth images from a single input. Hao et al. (Hao et al., 2018) proposed an end-to-end DNN model, in which a novel dense feature extractor and a depth map generator were presented. Ye et al. [28] proposed a dual-branch network to preserve the spatial and context information of features for monocular depth estimation task. According to the training manners, DNN models can be sorted into three types: supervised (Laina et al., 2016)7,20,(Liu et al., 2021), unsupervised (Godard et al., 2016)(Godard et al., 2018)(Yang et al., 2020)(Johnston et al., 2020) and semi-supervised (He et al., 2018)(Qi et al., 2018)(Yue et al., 2020). For monocular depth estimation, supervised fashion requires a large amount of ground truth depth maps, but unsupervised fashion overcomes this drawback with stereo matching (Godard et al., 2016)(Chang et al., 2018) or monocular sequences (Yang et al., 2020)(Bian et al., 2021). However, due to the lack of ground truth, the accuracies of the unsupervised methods still have a gap with the supervised ones (Fang et al., 2020). Hence, semi-supervised fashion begins to attract our attention, which is a fashion combining a small amount of labeled ground truth with a large amount of relatively cheap unlabeled data to improve depth map prediction performance. Though semi-supervised fashion is a promising method to resolve monocular depth estimation problems, supervised fashion is still valuable for us to research due to its higher accuracy.

citations.title: [248951321 | Ibrahem et al. | 2022 | Citations: 15]
snippets: Depth estimation is a critical task in a variety of computer vision applications, including 3D scene reconstruction from 2D images, medical 3D imaging, augmented reality, self-driving cars and robots, and 3D computer graphics and animations. The recent advances in depth estimation research have shown the effectiveness of the convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in performing such a task (Eigen et al., 2014)(Li et al., 2016)(Liu et al., 2014)(Gan et al., 2018)(Xu et al., 2017)(Kuznietsov et al., 2017)(Fu et al., 2018)(Cao et al., 2016)(Cao et al., 2018)(Niklaus et al., 2019)(Zuo et al., 2020)(Wu et al., 2019)[13](Ibrahem et al., 2022)(Ibrahem et al., 2022). The encoder-decoder CNN architectures are the most used architectures in the dense prediction tasks (Li et al., 2016)(Liu et al., 2014)(Gan et al., 2018)(Xu et al., 2017)(Kuznietsov et al., 2017)(Fu et al., 2018)(Cao et al., 2016)(Cao et al., 2018)(Niklaus et al., 2019)(Zuo et al., 2020)(Wu et al., 2019) (imagelike predictions such as semantic segmentation and depth estimation). The encoder stage compresses the input image to a latent small representation that consists of rich feature maps and the decoder stage uncompress the feature by a sequence of deconvolutional or up-sampling layers in order to obtain pixel-wise predictions. Although the convolutionalbased architectures could perform the depth estimation task efficiently, the convolution algorithm itself lacks the global awareness of the image content as it depends on a limited window (filter) with a small size (3 × 3 or 5 × 5 are the most common filter sizes). Learning of the global content of an image or a sequence of images is very useful for more accurate predictions in all computer vision tasks, so many attention algorithms such as RNN (Bahdanau et al., 2014) or LSTM (Sak et al., 2014) are employed in order to provide a relationship between the images in a sequence of images but those methods are usually computationally expensive and have a limited attention length. Vaswani et al. [18] proposed a solution for those problems in the natural language processing tasks by composing the multi-head self-attention (MSA) mechanism which aims to get the relation between each word and all of the other words in a word sequence.

sections.title: Types of Depth Prediction
sections.text:
TLDR; Modern depth prediction approaches primarily fall into supervised, unsupervised, and self-supervised categories. Each type has distinct characteristics and trade-offs, with supervised methods offering highest accuracy but requiring extensive labeled data, while unsupervised and self-supervised approaches aim to reduce dependency on manual annotations. (12 sources)

* **Supervised Depth Prediction**: Uses ground truth depth maps for training and generally achieves highest accuracy among current approaches  [249251183 | Welponer et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]. Popular architectures include encoder-decoder structures that convert RGB images to pixel-wise depth maps  [51784968 | Laina et al. | 2016 | Citations: 2415]  [209131483 | Yin et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1024]. Common features include skip connections for preserving fine details  [207202368 | Fu et al. | 2018 | Citations: 2620] and support for both ordinal (relative) and Euclidean (absolute) depth estimation  [249251183 | Welponer et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6].

* **Unsupervised Depth Prediction**: Addresses the need for labeled data by leveraging self-supervision signals. Key approaches include:

  - Photometric consistency loss using stereo inputs  [7051798 | Godard et al. | 2016 | Citations: 2717]

  - Multi-view validation using monocular sequences  [3726920 | Garg et al. | 2016 | Citations: 1142]

  - Geometric constraints derived from optical flow  [214605592 | Xiang et al. | 2020 | Citations: 11]

These methods show promising results but typically lag behind supervised approaches in terms of accuracy  [239616762 | Lai et al. | 2021 | Citations: 3].

* **Self-Supervised Depth Prediction**: Emerged as a promising direction to reduce reliance on expensive sensor data. Recent advances include:

  - Learning from unlabeled videos and mono-stereo pairs  [207761721 | Yang et al. | 2020 | Citations: 132]

  - Integration with pseudo-labeling techniques  [235186925 | Bian et al. | 2021 | Citations: 171]

  - Direct depth estimation from monocular cameras  [268889824 | Ren | 2024 | Citations: 0]

* **Specialized Approaches**:

  - Ordinal Regression Networks: Convert depth estimation into a classification problem using discretized depth intervals  [219981387 | Chen et al. | 2020 | Citations: 134].

  - Multi-Task Learning: Combines depth prediction with other tasks like semantic segmentation or optical flow to improve accuracy  [251040172 | He et al. | 2022 | Citations: 53].

  - Surface Normal Integration: Incorporates normal information alongside depth prediction to enhance geometric understanding  [208558939 | Lee et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1028].

Depth prediction tasks predict depth from a single monocular color image. With the absence of depth measurements, depth prediction is even more challenging than depth completion. Handcrafted features (Karsch et al., 2012)(Karsch et al., 2014)(Saxena et al., 2005) are used in the early study of this problem. Recent learning-based methods also integrated those features into novel loss functions to achieve a better result. For example, Zhou et al. (Qi et al., 2018) combined estimated surface normal and depth prediction into a two pathway neural network. 

Even though most approaches achieve promising results on prediction, the scale ambiguity problem still exists because no accurate depth guidance is provided. When it comes to industrial applications, the performance of depth prediction based on a single monocular camera might not be stable.

snippets:
Learning depth from raw images is a fast evolving area in computer vision community. The earliest work formulates depth estimation as a mapping function of input single images, constructed by a multi-scale deep neural network [78] to output the per-pixel depth maps from single images. More accurate depth prediction is achieved by jointly optimizing the depth and self-motion estimation [79]. These supervised learning methods [78], [79], [92] can predict per-pixel depth by training deep neural networks on large data collections of images with corresponding depth labels. Although they are found outperforming the traditional structure based methods, such as [122], their effectiveness are largely reliant on model training and can be difficult to generalize to new scenarios in absence of labeled data.

On the other side, recent advances in this field focus on unsupervised solutions, by reformulating depth prediction as a novel view synthesis problem. [80], [81] utilized photometric consistency loss as a self-supervision signal for training neural models.

citations.title: [235186925 | Bian et al. | 2021 | Citations: 171]
snippets: We propose a monocular depth estimation method SC-Depth, which requires only unlabelled videos for training and enables the scale-consistent prediction at inference time. Our contributions include: (i) we propose a geometry consistency loss, which penalizes the inconsistency of predicted depths between adjacent views; (ii) we propose a self-discovered mask to automatically localize moving objects that violate the underlying static scene assumption and cause noisy signals during training; (iii) we demonstrate the efficacy of each component with a detailed ablation study and show high-quality depth estimation results in both KITTI and NYUv2 datasets. Moreover, thanks to the capability of scale-consistent prediction, we show that our monocular-trained deep networks are readily integrated into ORB-SLAM2 system for more robust and accurate tracking. The proposed hybrid Pseudo-RGBD SLAM shows compelling results in KITTI, and it generalizes well to the KAIST dataset without additional training. Finally, we provide several demos for qualitative evaluation. The source code is released on GitHub.

citations.title: [249251183 | Welponer et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]
snippets: Monocular Depth Prediction. Early methods for monocular depth estimation relied on handcrafted features and used complementary cues to recover the depth since limited information about the scene geometry can be directly extracted from a single image (Saxena et al., 2008). In the deep learning era, the seminal work of Eigen et al. (2014) proposed a scaleinvariant loss function in a coarse-to-fine context using a VGG network. The approach was further extended by adding more layers while predicting surface normals and semantic maps (Eigen et al., 2014). Since then, the problem has been studied in the literature as a supervised (Laina et al., 2016)Xu et al., 2018;(Fu et al., 2018)(Hu et al., 2018) or unsupervised problem (Garg et al., 2016)(Godard et al., 2016)(Tosi et al., 2019)). An architecture often adopted in such methods is the encoderdecoder (e.g., (Fu et al., 2018) with RGB images as input and direct regression of pixel-wise depth maps as output. Indeed, most methods perform pixel-wise supervision, yet Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) have also been used to exploit neighbor relations and include a more global context (Liu et al., 2015). The loss function can be formed either as a regression or a classification problem. Skip connections in a ResNet fashion are used to preserve the fine-grained features of the first layers (Laina et al., 2016). Cues such as texture, shading, and structural information are used, while high quality and pixel-aligned GT depth maps are needed. Depending on the available training data, the scene depth can be estimated as ordinal, i.e., relative (Fu et al., 2018) or Euclidean (Eigen et al., 2014;(Yin et al., 2019). Local planar priors have also been incorporated as guidance (Lee et al., 2019).

citations.title: [251040172 | He et al. | 2022 | Citations: 53]
snippets: Monocular depth estimation aims to predict the scene depth from single color image. Early works [5,24,21,43,16,22,44] estimated continuous depth maps pixel by pixel using convolutional neural networks by minimizing the error between the prediction and ground-truth depths. Furthermore, the geometry [44,(Patil et al., 2022) or multitask constraints [35,47] are imposed on the depth estimation network to predict more accurate depth maps. However, these continuous regression methods usually suffer from slow convergence and unsatisfactory local solutions. Deep ordinal regression network [6] thus introduced a spacing-increasing discretization strategy to discretize depth, where the depth estimation problem is converted into the ordinal depth regression problem. AdaBins [1] proposed a Transformer based depth estimation scheme by dividing the depth range into different bins. Recently, some works [29]23] employed the multimodel learning for depth estimation and further improved its performance.

sections.title: Technical Challenges and Solutions
sections.text:
TLDR; Depth prediction faces several fundamental challenges including scale ambiguity, ill-posed nature of single-image estimation, and difficulty in handling transparent/ambiguous scenes. Various technical solutions have emerged, from self-supervised learning approaches to advanced architectural innovations using attention mechanisms and multi-task learning. (11 sources)

The primary challenge in depth prediction stems from the inherently ambiguous nature of inferring three-dimensional information from a two-dimensional image  [192499627 | Wang et al. | 2019 | Citations: 0]. This creates particular difficulties in regions where objects meet or boundaries exist between different surfaces  [257901029 | Liu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 15].

Scale ambiguity poses a persistent challenge, especially in single-view scenarios where absolute depth measurements cannot be determined  [214605592 | Xiang et al. | 2020 | Citations: 11]. While recent work has shown that networks with sufficient capacity can predict depth from single images when trained adequately  [229180711 | Azaria et al. | 2020 | Citations: 0], achieving consistent scale across varying scenarios remains problematic.

To address these challenges, researchers have developed several innovative solutions:

1. **View Consistency Approaches**: New frameworks ensure depth maps appear reasonable from multiple viewpoints, moving beyond simple pixel-level regression  [199442636 | Liu et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1].

2. **Self-Supervised Learning**: Methods now leverage geometry as the sole source of supervision, allowing networks to learn relationships between visual appearances and 3D properties  [211532626 | Guizilini et al. | 2020 | Citations: 227].

3. **Advanced Architectures**: Attention mechanisms have proven particularly effective for modeling long-range dependencies, helping capture broader contextual information  [225050120 | Liu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 7]  [202169079 | Jiao et al. | 2018 | Citations: 526].

4. **Multi-Modal Integration**: Recent approaches combine depth prediction with other modalities like semantic segmentation and surface normals, creating stronger correlations across tasks  [263310637 | Fang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1].

However, newer challenges continue to emerge, particularly in handling transparent or ambiguous scenes where traditional single-depth estimates prove insufficient. Real-world scenarios involving transparency create situations where pixels don't correspond to unique depth values, requiring more sophisticated approaches that can account for multiple possible depth interpretations  [276903118 | Xu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

The field continues to evolve rapidly, with ongoing research focusing on developing more robust solutions that can handle these complex scenarios while maintaining computational efficiency  [246350124 | Dao et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]. Current emphasis is placed on developing methods that can maintain accuracy across diverse conditions while addressing previously overlooked aspects of depth perception, such as transparency and multiplicative occlusions.

citations.title: [192499627 | Wang et al. | 2019 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Depth prediction plays an essential role in understanding the 3D geometry of a scene. It has been shown that depth information can largely facilitate other vision tasks such as reconstruction (Silberman et al. 2012), recognition (Ren et al., 2012)) and semantic segmentation (Cheng et al. 2017). Stereo images (Kong and Black 2016) or image sequence (Suwajanakorn et al., 2015) usually suffice for accurate depth prediction. While for single-view depth prediction, it is an ill-posed problem due to the lack of geometric information. Ambiguities or uncertainties often happen at those discontinuous regions between objects.

citations.title: [199442636 | Liu et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1]
snippets: This paper addresses the problem of Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE). Existing approaches on MDE usually model it as a pixel-level regression problem, ignoring the underlying geometry property. We empirically find this may result in sub-optimal solution: while the predicted depth map presents small loss value in one specific view, it may exhibit large loss if viewed in different directions. In this paper, inspired by multi-view stereo (MVS), we propose an Adversarial View-Consistent Learning (AVCL) framework to force the estimated depth map to be all reasonable viewed from multiple views.

Due to perspective, there is indeed an equivariance relationship between the visual appearance of an object in 2D and its depth, when conditioned on the object's category. citations.title: [276903118 | Xu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets:
Depth ambiguity is a fundamental challenge in spatial scene understanding, especially in transparent scenes where single-depth estimates fail to capture full 3D structure. Existing models, limited to deterministic predictions, overlook real-world multi-layer depth.

Despite progress in both physical sensors and monocular depth estimation models [5,6,14,17,18,20,22,27,29,[38][39][40][41] (see Fig. 1a&b), a key challenge persists: biased 3D spatial understanding under depth ambiguity.

In real-world 3D scenes, factors such as transparency (see Fig. 1c) break the assumption that each pixel corresponds to a unique depth value. For example, objects viewed through transparent surfaces like glass exhibit a range of plausible depths rather than a single fixed value. While state-of-the-art depth foundation models [38]39] generalize well in unambiguous scenarios, they typically output only a single depth estimate, thereby ignoring inherent depth ambiguity. This limitation results in biased, incomplete 3D representations that undermine both generalization and reliability, especially in safety-critical applications requiring robust spatial reasoning.

citations.title: [216042185 | Li et al. | 2019 | Citations: 7]
snippets: Depth prediction has always been a core task to understand the geometric relations within a 3D scene. In absence of the environmental assumptions, the inherent ambiguity of mapping an intensity or color measurement into a depth value makes depth prediction an ill-posed problem. Many unique techniques have been proposed to tackle this problem, such as superpixels based algorithms (Liu et al., 2014), Structure-from-Motion (SfM) (Szeliski, 2015), data-driven methods (Karsch et al., 2012) and CNN based approaches (Laina et al., 2016).

citations.title: [264818776 | Ciamarra et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Forecasting motion and spatial positions of objects is of fundamental importance, especially in safety-critical settings such as autonomous driving. In this work, we address the issue by forecasting two different modalities that carry complementary information, namely optical flow and depth...Several works have focused on learning to infer depth from monocular RGB cameras (Mertan et al., 2021)(Eigen et al., 2014)(Xie et al., 2019). Nonetheless, relying on depth estimators on predicted future RGBs is hard, due to high uncertainty in predicting raw pixels [20,21,(Kalchbrenner et al., 2016)23,(Kwon et al., 2019). Therefore, other works propose to deal with depth anticipation for future frames, mostly known in the literature as depth forecasting or video depth forecasting. Qi et. al (Qi et al., 2019) introduce an entire framework for predicting 3D motion (both optical flow and depth map) and synthesizing the RGB with its semantic map for unobserved future frames. To this end, they leverage images, depth maps and semantic segmentations of past frames but they make predictions limited to the subsequent future frame, i.e. at the frame t + 1. Also limited to a single future timestep, Hu et. al (Hu et al., 2020) design a probabilistic model for future video prediction, where scene features are learned from input images and are then used to build spatio-temporal representations, incorporating both local and global contexts. These features are finally fed into a recurrent model with separate decoders, each one forecasting semantic segmentation, depth and dense flow at the next future frame. Nag et. al [16] propose a self-supervised method for depth estimation directly at the k-th frame after the last observed one, i.e. at t + k. By means of a feature forecasting module, they learn to map pyramid features extracted from past sequences of both RGBs and optical flows to future features, exploiting a series of ConvGRUs and ConvLSTMs for spatio-temporal relationships in the past. With the same goal, Boulahbal et. al [25] design an end-to-end self-supervised approach by using a hybrid model based on CNN and Transformer that predicts depth map and ego-motion at t + k by processing an input sequence of past frames.

sections.title: Current State of Fraud Challenges
sections.text:
TLDR; Modern fraud challenges are becoming increasingly sophisticated, with criminals adapting their tactics to exploit digital systems and self-service technologies. Key challenges include the scarcity of fraudulent transaction data, high-dimensional transaction data complexity, and the need to maintain accurate detection without overwhelming legitimate users. (6 sources)

The retail and financial sectors face several pressing challenges in their ongoing battle against fraud. One of the most fundamental difficulties is the severe imbalance in transaction datasets, where fraudulent transactions represent a tiny fraction of legitimate transactions  [268048498 | Albone | 2024 | Citations: 0]. This class imbalance creates significant technical hurdles for machine learning systems trying to learn distinguishing patterns between legitimate and fraudulent activities.

Traditional fraud detection methods, which often rely on manual procedures and physical verification, have struggled to keep pace with the sophistication of modern criminal tactics  [272610880 | Adil et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]. Even seemingly straightforward scenarios like self-checkout systems have become vulnerable targets, requiring new technological solutions that integrate multiple sensors and real-time analysis capabilities to achieve reliable fraud detection rates of 90-95%  [274307264 | Smadi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

Technical complexities pose additional challenges for fraud detection systems. These include the difficulty of processing high-dimensional transaction data, which can trigger the "curse of dimensionality" effect, and the challenge of modeling temporal dependencies in transaction sequences  [274253635 | Ileberi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [231842170 | Gorban et al. | 2020 | Citations: 121]. While traditional machine learning algorithms like Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forests, and Gradient Boosting Machines (GBM) have shown promise, they often struggle with these computational challenges  [274253635 | Ileberi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

A notable development in addressing these challenges comes from organizations working on marketplace platforms, where the problem manifests differently as organized retail crime (ORC). Recent research has shown promising results using machine learning approaches that can achieve high detection rates (recall of 0.97) while maintaining reasonable operational efficiency  [260435004 | Mutemi et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4]. Such successes suggest that while the challenges are significant, targeted machine learning solutions can make meaningful progress in addressing modern fraud concerns.

sections.title: Implementation Challenges and Considerations
sections.text:
TLDR; Implementing machine learning fraud detection systems faces several key technical and operational hurdles. Major challenges include data quality and imbalance issues, real-time processing requirements, and the need for continuous model adaptation to emerging threats. (6 sources)

While machine learning offers powerful tools for fraud detection, successful implementation requires careful consideration of several critical challenges. One of the primary obstacles is poor data quality and distribution, which significantly impacts model performance and reliability  [266304296 | Damayanti et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3].

Real-time processing presents another significant challenge, particularly in high-volume transaction environments. Systems must balance the need for immediate fraud detection decisions with computational constraints and processing delays  [266860923 | Khalid et al. | 2024 | Citations: 70]. This requirement for low-latency processing while maintaining high accuracy levels demands careful system architecture planning <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

Data imbalance remains a persistent concern in fraud detection implementations. Since fraudulent transactions constitute a tiny fraction of all transactions, models must be carefully tuned to prevent bias toward majority classes while still maintaining sufficient detection rates  [266304296 | Damayanti et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3].

Concept drift poses an ongoing challenge as fraud patterns evolve over time. Machine learning models require periodic updates and retraining to maintain their effectiveness against new fraud variants  [266860923 | Khalid et al. | 2024 | Citations: 70]. This continuous adaptation need must be balanced against resource constraints and operational overhead.

False positive management represents another crucial consideration. While high detection rates are desirable, systems must carefully calibrate their thresholds to minimize disruption to legitimate users while still catching suspicious activity  [271640328 | Khatib et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [211047919 | Zhou et al. | 2021 | Citations: 29]. Organizations must implement clear escalation protocols and human oversight mechanisms to verify flagged transactions <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

Scalability considerations are particularly important for growing businesses. As transaction volumes increase, systems must maintain their performance levels while supporting expanding feature sets and adapting to new fraud vectors  [258175765 | Moreira et al. | 2022 | Citations: 18]. Cloud-based solutions and distributed computing architectures have emerged as viable options for managing these scalability demands <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

sections.title: Introduction & Evolution
sections.text:
TLDR; Computer vision approaches to corrosion detection evolved from traditional algorithmic methods to sophisticated deep learning techniques. Modern approaches leverage CNNs and other deep learning architectures to automatically extract features and achieve high accuracy in corrosion detection and classification. (8 sources)

The evolution of corrosion detection and monitoring has seen significant advancement in computer vision approaches over the past decades. Early methodologies relied heavily on traditional image processing algorithms, employing techniques such as statistical analysis of grayscale distributions, color and texture descriptors, and binary methods  [251858850 | Savino et al. | 2022 | Citations: 18]  [29185338 | Hutchinson et al. | 2006 | Citations: 44]. These conventional approaches proved particularly valuable in controlled environments where specific conditions could be maintained  [29185338 | Hutchinson et al. | 2006 | Citations: 44].

A major shift occurred with the emergence of deep learning techniques, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), which marked a transition from knowledge-driven to data-driven approaches  [251858850 | Savino et al. | 2022 | Citations: 18]. This shift has been especially impactful in the manufacturing sector, where CNNs have become fundamental tools for solving complex quality control and inspection challenges  [257007271 | Bouguettaya et al. | 2023 | Citations: 16]. Deep learning approaches have demonstrated notable advantages by automatically extracting hierarchical features from raw data, significantly reducing the need for manual feature engineering  [266459127 | Ameli et al. | 2023 | Citations: 20].

The effectiveness of deep learning methods has been extensively documented across various applications. For instance, researchers have achieved classification accuracies exceeding 90% using advanced CNN architectures  [248693134 | Burton et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]. These achievements have led to practical implementations in diverse settings, from underwater vehicle navigation to aerial surveillance and autonomous driving systems  [102330117 | Cha et al. | 2017 | Citations: 227].

However, it's worth noting that while classification tasks have seen widespread success, segmentation remains more challenging due to the scarcity of pixel-level annotated datasets  [248693134 | Burton et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]. Despite this limitation, innovative solutions continue to emerge, combining deep learning with traditional computer vision techniques to address these challenges <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [248693134 | Burton et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]
snippets:
Recently, deep learning based algorithms have revealed promise and performance in the automatic detection of corrosion...To date, research regarding the segmentation of images for automated corrosion detection has been limited, due to the lack of availability of per-pixel labelled data sets which are required for model training.

Recently, much like with the general field of CV, deep learning researchers have looked to convolutional neural networks (CNNs) as the leading method for imaged based deep learning methods [15,16]. In classification, researchers have been able to achieve +90% accuracy for generic corrosion detection using only deep learning methods [15,17]. However, as noted, the segmentation of corrosion has proven more challenging for deep learning based methods, due to the unavailability of suitable training data [15].

Deep learning has also been applied with different levels of success to non-imaged based corrosion detection methods such as utilising Eddy currents in metal plates [18], thermal responses in aluminium [19], and electrochemical data in steel [20].

Recently, several groups have presented deep-learning models for corrosion segmentation to a range with varying levels of performance [5,13,22]. All these methods used small highly accurate labelled data sets and combine them with transfer learning.

A discriminative localisation approach, known as Class Activation Mapping (CAM) and presented by Zhou and co-workers [28], demonstrated that using the last convolutional layer, the predicted class and hidden layers -it is possible to visualise the pixels that have greatest effect on the prediction in a multi class classifier. An approach termed Gradientweighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) [29] expanded the work of Zhou [28] -to produce highly localised heatmaps of the pixels that have the greatest effect on predicting classes, whilst removing the need for any retraining. Thereafter, Grad-CAM++ [30] was developed to overcome some of the shortfalls from the original methodology when applied to images that contain multiple instances of the target class.

sections.title: Performance Comparisons
sections.text:
TLDR; Different deep learning architectures show varying performance levels for corrosion detection, with newer transformer-based approaches showing promising results beyond traditional CNN limits. Comparative analyses reveal trade-offs between accuracy, computational efficiency, and specific use-case requirements. (5 sources)

Recent benchmark comparisons have highlighted significant variations in performance across different deep learning architectures for corrosion detection. Traditional CNN-based architectures like U-Net and DeepLabV3+ have demonstrated baseline performance metrics, with F1-scores of 61.8% and 60.1% respectively in large-scale corrosion detection tasks  [276709441 | Lu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

When comparing specific architectures, certain models have shown exceptional performance in targeted applications. For instance, the Inception v3 model achieved classification accuracy exceeding 95% for Q235 steel corrosion levels  [276216477 | Huang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]. Similarly, mobile-efficient architectures like MobileNetV2 paired with DeepLabv3+ have demonstrated practical utility, achieving validation accuracy of 90.8% while maintaining computational efficiency  [276166963 | Savino et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

A notable advancement has been the introduction of transformer-based architectures, which have broken through the performance saturation typically observed in traditional CNN models. These newer approaches have achieved superior F1-scores of 68.2% in large-scale corrosion detection tasks, outperforming conventional CNN-based models  [276709441 | Lu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

In terms of pixel-level prediction accuracy, specialized architectures like DeepLabv3 and BiSeNetV2 have demonstrated superior performance compared to traditional models such as U-Net, FCN, and Mask-RCNN, while requiring fewer annotated samples for training  [250609082 | Rusakov et al. | 2022 | Citations: 1]. Furthermore, Bayesian deep learning variants have shown promise in providing reliable confidence estimates for corrosion detection tasks, improving overall reliability of the detection systems  [247797898 | Nash et al. | 2022 | Citations: 63].

snippets: Corrosion is one of the main damage mechanisms in civil engineering structures today. Rapid identification and accurate assessment of corrosion in structures are essential to ensure the efficient allocation of limited funds for the maintenance and renewal of existing structures. Vision-based neural networks have been widely used in corrosion detection, in which convolutional neural network (CNN)-like models remain dominant. However, these conventional network models exhibit a saturating performance. Because of the self-attention mechanism, the transformer is the newest breakthrough in computer vision and is becoming state of the art. As the complexity of structures increases, transformer-based methods have no saturating performance. This study proposes a corrosion localization and evaluation architecture for a larger view based on semantic segmentation and image stitching for automatic localization and diagnosis of corrosion from stitched images. The experimental results showed that the proposed method achieved better corrosion detection performance (F1-score = 68.2%) than that of the mainstream CNN-like models U-Net (F1-score = 61.8%) and DeepLabV3 + (F1-score = 60.1%).

sections.title: Challenges & Solutions
sections.text:
TLDR; Key challenges in deep learning-based corrosion detection include data scarcity, implementation complexity, and computational demands. Solutions involve combining traditional computer vision techniques with deep learning, developing efficient architectures, and implementing hybrid approaches. (8 sources)

The primary challenge facing deep learning-based corrosion detection lies in obtaining sufficient pixel-level labeled datasets for training segmentation models  [248693134 | Burton et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]. To address this limitation, researchers have turned to innovative visualization techniques like Class Activation Mapping (CAM) and its derivatives Grad-CAM and Grad-CAM++, which can generate meaningful activation heatmaps without requiring additional training  [248693134 | Burton et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]  [14947863 | Zhou et al. | 2016 | Citations: 23632].

Implementation complexity presents another significant hurdle, particularly in industrial settings. This has led to the development of simplified yet effective approaches, such as threshold methods, morphological operations, and edge detection techniques  [276891697 | Yan et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [111357458 | Palakal et al. | 2001 | Citations: 524]  [115820879 | Dorafshan et al. | 2018 | Citations: 144]. These traditional methods can serve as complementary tools alongside deep learning approaches, helping to reduce the overall system complexity.

Background interference and environmental factors pose persistent challenges for accurate corrosion detection. Various solutions have emerged to address these issues, including background subtraction techniques and eigenvalue decomposition methods  [276891697 | Yan et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [257665966 | Pedram et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]. The integration of spectral analysis has proven particularly effective, allowing for independent processing of material-specific wavelength ranges and separation of reflected intensities from illuminated backgrounds  [116858624 | Ahuja et al. | 2017 | Citations: 24].

Computational efficiency remains a crucial consideration, especially for real-world applications. This has driven the development of lightweight architectures and hybrid approaches that maintain high accuracy while reducing computational demands. For instance, recent innovations include YOLO-based models optimized for rapid deployment  [276891697 | Yan et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [267237872 | Tan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3], and modified versions of ShuffleNet that achieve significant accuracy improvements while maintaining computational efficiency  [276891697 | Yan et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [254730073 | Huang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 27].

citations.title: [248693134 | Burton et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]
snippets:
Recently, deep learning based algorithms have revealed promise and performance in the automatic detection of corrosion...To date, research regarding the segmentation of images for automated corrosion detection has been limited, due to the lack of availability of per-pixel labelled data sets which are required for model training.

Recently, much like with the general field of CV, deep learning researchers have looked to convolutional neural networks (CNNs) as the leading method for imaged based deep learning methods [15,16]. In classification, researchers have been able to achieve +90% accuracy for generic corrosion detection using only deep learning methods [15,17]. However, as noted, the segmentation of corrosion has proven more challenging for deep learning based methods, due to the unavailability of suitable training data [15].

Deep learning has also been applied with different levels of success to non-imaged based corrosion detection methods such as utilising Eddy currents in metal plates [18], thermal responses in aluminium [19], and electrochemical data in steel [20].

Recently, several groups have presented deep-learning models for corrosion segmentation to a range with varying levels of performance [5,13,22]. All these methods used small highly accurate labelled data sets and combine them with transfer learning.

A discriminative localisation approach, known as Class Activation Mapping (CAM) and presented by Zhou and co-workers [28], demonstrated that using the last convolutional layer, the predicted class and hidden layers -it is possible to visualise the pixels that have greatest effect on the prediction in a multi class classifier. An approach termed Gradientweighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) [29] expanded the work of Zhou [28] -to produce highly localised heatmaps of the pixels that have the greatest effect on predicting classes, whilst removing the need for any retraining. Thereafter, Grad-CAM++ [30] was developed to overcome some of the shortfalls from the original methodology when applied to images that contain multiple instances of the target class.

citations.title: [276891697 | Yan et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets: The detection of corrosion areas mainly includes metal surface corrosion detection based on traditional algorithms and metal surface corrosion detection based on deep learning. Metal surface corrosion detection based on traditional algorithms is mainly divided into threshold methods (Pedram et al., 2023)(Palakal et al., 2001) , morphological methods (Dong et al., 2017)(Perez et al., 2006) , edge detection method (Dorafshan et al., 2018)18 , and texture analysis (Sun et al., 2023)(Ahuja et al., 2017)(O'Byrne et al., 2013) . These traditional methods are simple and easy to implement, but they generally have the disadvantages of low detection accuracy and being susceptible to background noise. In contrast, deep learning methods can automatically extract corrosion features from images, thus ensuring high-precision segmentation of the detected object. Liu et al. 22 used the VGG19 model to extract the damage and corrosion characteristics of steel plate coating, and combined it with the Faster R-CNN algorithm for defect detection. Srivastava et al. 23 used the UNet-8 layer architecture to analyze and classify corroded areas in images. Fondevik et al. 24 used PSPNet and Mask R-CNN for automatic image analysis of the self-built corrosion dataset. Tan et al. (Tan et al., 2024) built the DSNet model based on YOLOx, and demonstrated its accurate detection accuracy and segmentation performance in tunnel bolt detection and corrosion region segmentation tasks. Huang et al. (Huang et al., 2022) used the idea of ShuffleNetv2 to build a lightweight residual deep learning model, which achieved significant accuracy improvement in the metal surface corrosion segmentation task. Yin et al. 27 combined edge information and class balance loss with UNet to build a DeepSC-Edge model, and achieved excellent segmentation accuracy on the self-built corrosion image dataset.

sections.title: Introduction/Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Activation functions are fundamental components in neural networks that enable non-linear learning and pattern recognition. They serve as crucial decision-makers in neural networks by transforming inputs into meaningful outputs while satisfying specific mathematical requirements. (7 sources)

Neural networks rely heavily on activation functions as essential building blocks that enable them to learn and process complex information  [225922639 | Sharma et al. | 2020 | Citations: 940]. These functions operate at the intersection of biology and technology - working similarly to biological neurons by transforming input signals into meaningful outputs  [271218561 | Hammad | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [248756597 | Yamamoto et al. | 2022 | Citations: 2].

At their core, activation functions address a fundamental challenge in neural networks: they prevent values from growing indefinitely while maintaining the network's ability to learn effectively. Specifically, they multiply input values by weights, sum the results, and scale these values within a manageable range before passing them to subsequent layers  [210694524 | You et al. | 2020 | Citations: 25].

Two key requirements must be met by activation functions to be practically useful in neural networks: they must be non-linear and ideally differentiable to enable gradient-based optimization methods  [210694524 | You et al. | 2020 | Citations: 25]. This mathematical foundation is crucial because it allows neural networks to handle complex, real-world problems through non-linear transformations  [259171775 | Qi et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0].

Modern deep learning has particularly benefited from advances in activation function design. Notably, the introduction of non-saturating activation functions has helped solve persistent challenges like gradient explosion and vanishing gradient problems that plagued earlier approaches  [210694524 | You et al. | 2020 | Citations: 25]. These improvements have contributed to breakthrough achievements in various domains, including speech recognition, visual object localization, and face detection  [7102196 | Krizhevsky et al. | 2012 | Citations: 115420].

The widespread adoption of these principles has established deep learning as a transformative tool across industries, from healthcare diagnostics to autonomous vehicles  [7102196 | Krizhevsky et al. | 2012 | Citations: 115420]  [207897253 | Ciresan et al. | 2012 | Citations: 2601]. Their success stems from their ability to create systems that can learn from raw, unstructured data while requiring minimal preprocessing <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [210694524 | You et al. | 2020 | Citations: 25]
snippets:
Activation functions are crucial elements in deep learning neural networks. These functions perform transformations on the input to maintain their values in a manageable range. In a neural network, feedforward propagation is the process of multiplying various input values of a particular neuron by their associated weights, summing the results, and then scaling the values between a given range before forwarding this information to the succeeding layer. Activation functions perform scaling operations.

Only hidden and output layer neurons possess activation functions. In general, values in the input layers are appropriately scaled. Hence, input layers do not require any activation function. However, once these values are multiplied by weights and summed in the first hidden layer, they rapidly become larger than the range of their original scale, where activation functions become necessary. Activation functions can force these large values back within the acceptance range and make them useful. Consequently, this process affects the succeeding layer's input and thus the computation of new weights. Lastly, activation functions affect the distribution of weights, which is back-warded through the entire network. Therefore, the final output values of the CNN are influenced. Accordingly, activation functions determine the output of the neural network from the given input dataset.

To guarantee the usefulness of the processing values, activation functions must be 1) nonlinear and 2) continuously differentiable or at least nearly completely differentiable. Most neural networks are optimized with some form of gradient descent. Therefore, a continuously differentiable function is necessary for gradient-based optimization methods and allows efficient backpropagation of errors throughout the network. Theoretically, any function can be used as an activation function as long as it meets the above requirements. However, only a few such functions are used in practice. In a traditional CNN, activation functions generally use saturated nonlinear functions (saturating nonlinearity), such as sigmoid and tanh functions. Unlike saturated nonlinear functions, unsaturated nonlinear functions (non-saturating nonlinearity) can solve the gradient explosion and disappearance problems of saturated functions. In addition, unsaturated nonlinear functions can enhance the convergence rate and are theoretically suitable for neural networks.

sections.title: Basic Requirements and Properties
sections.text:
TLDR; Effective activation functions must meet several key mathematical and practical requirements to ensure proper network learning and optimization. These requirements balance competing needs like non-linearity, computational efficiency, and stable gradient flow. (5 sources)

Key requirements and properties of activation functions:

1. **Non-linearity**

   - Must introduce non-linear curvature to enable complex pattern learning  [250089226 | Dubey et al. | 2021 | Citations: 641]

   - Essential for networks to learn non-linear relationships between inputs and outputs  [260811291 | Lee | 2023 | Citations: 49]

2. **Differentiability**

   - Should be continuous or nearly continuous to enable gradient-based optimization

   - Necessary for backpropagation through the network  [210694524 | You et al. | 2020 | Citations: 25]

3. **Gradient Behavior**

   - Must avoid vanishing or exploding gradients during training  [250089226 | Dubey et al. | 2021 | Citations: 641]

   - Should allow gradients to propagate effectively when input is positive  [259847235 | Zhang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 17]

4. **Computational Efficiency**

   - Cannot increase model complexity excessively

   - Should maintain reasonable computational costs  [250089226 | Dubey et al. | 2021 | Citations: 641]

5. **Input Range Characteristics**

   - Unboundedness is preferable to avoid saturation

   - Smooth transitions help with optimization and generalization  (2022)

6. **Data Distribution Preservation**

   - Should maintain data distribution for better training

   - Can incorporate regularization through behavior with extreme inputs  (2022)

7. **Optimization-Friendly Features**

   - Should allow for effective learning algorithm convergence

   - Need to balance expressivity with computational efficiency  (2022)  [264145788 | Biswas et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]

These properties collectively determine how well an activation function can enable the network to learn complex patterns while remaining computationally tractable  [264145788 | Biswas et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1].

sections.title: Common Types of Activation Functions
sections.text:
TLDR; Various types of activation functions exist, each with distinct mathematical properties and trade-offs. The most prominent categories include traditional functions like Sigmoid and Tanh, ReLU family members, and newer adaptive functions like Swish. (10 sources)

Common activation functions fall into several main categories:

1. **Traditional Saturating Functions**

   - Sigmoid: Maps outputs to range [0,1], widely used historically but suffers from vanishing gradients  [234785880 | Abirami et al. | 2021 | Citations: 56]

   - Hyperbolic Tangent (Tanh): Produces outputs in range [-1,1], performs slightly better than Sigmoid but shares similar saturation issues  [234785880 | Abirami et al. | 2021 | Citations: 56]  [273998106 | Mulindwa et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]

2. **ReLU Family**

   - Standard ReLU: Simple threshold function that outputs 0 for negative inputs and passes positive values unchanged  [234785880 | Abirami et al. | 2021 | Citations: 56]

   - Leaky ReLU: Addresses ReLU's "dead neuron" problem by allowing small negative slopes  [273691147 | Lu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]

   - Parametric ReLU (PReLU): Learns the optimal negative slope during training  [10520992 | Jin et al. | 2015 | Citations: 216]

3. **Adaptive Functions**

   - Maxout: Computes maximum of multiple linear functions, can approximate any convex function  [10520992 | Jin et al. | 2015 | Citations: 216]  [193707725 | Goodfellow et al. | 2013 | Citations: 6606]

   - Swish: Combines multiplication and squashing of input with sigmoid function  [196831891 | Molina et al. | 2019 | Citations: 77]  [55017405 | Ramachandran et al. | 2018 | Citations: 1819]

   - SiLU (Sigmoid Linear Unit): Combines linear and non-linear properties through element-wise multiplication with sigmoid function  [273691147 | Lu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]

4. **Trainable Functions**

   - Learned Piecewise Linear Activations (LPLA): Allows separate control over negative and positive segments  [231592494 | Liang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 21]

   - Automatically searched activations: Recent research has focused on developing automated approaches to find optimal activation functions  [196831891 | Molina et al. | 2019 | Citations: 77]

Each type offers distinct advantages and faces certain limitations. While ReLU and its variants remain popular due to their simplicity and effectiveness  [246786369 | Wang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 61], newer functions aim to address specific challenges in neural network training and optimization  [247881354 | Sule | 2022 | Citations: 27].

sections.title: Advantages and Challenges
sections.text:
TLDR; Activation functions are crucial for enabling complex pattern learning but face inherent trade-offs between different desirable properties. While various solutions have been proposed, finding the perfect activation function remains an ongoing challenge in deep learning research. (8 sources)

The primary advantage of activation functions lies in their ability to introduce non-linearity, enabling neural networks to learn and capture complex patterns in data  (2022). This non-linearity is essential because it allows networks to fit any complex data distribution and explore richer function spaces during optimization  (2022).

However, selecting the right activation function comes with significant challenges. Key considerations include balancing gradient behavior, computational efficiency, and the need to preserve useful signal characteristics  [235455798 | Alkhouly et al. | 2021 | Citations: 40]. Even though many activation functions are theoretically capable of universal approximation, their practical performance can vary dramatically depending on the specific task and network architecture  [235455798 | Alkhouly et al. | 2021 | Citations: 40].

Despite extensive research, no single activation function has proven universally superior  [49427911 | Sutfeld et al. | 2018 | Citations: 28]. For instance, ReLU, while widely adopted, faces notable challenges including the "zero-mean problem," "negative coordinate misspecification issue," and "unbounded output issue"  [211677960 | Zhou et al. | 2020 | Citations: 25].

Recent innovations have attempted to address these limitations through various approaches. Some researchers focus on developing theoretically-grounded activation functions that satisfy specific optimization criteria  [250560156 | Amrouche et al. | 2022 | Citations: 5]. Others explore adaptive mechanisms, such as dynamic slope adjustment during training, to better handle varying input conditions  [271903877 | Chakraborti et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

The field continues to evolve with new proposals addressing specific challenges, though finding the optimal activation function for a given task remains an open research question  [277781524 | Chidiac et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. This ongoing evolution reflects the fundamental importance of activation functions in enabling effective deep learning while acknowledging the complex trade-offs involved in their selection and design.

sections.title: Selection Criteria and Recommendations
sections.text:
TLDR; Selecting an activation function requires careful consideration of task-specific requirements and model characteristics. While ReLU remains popular due to its simplicity and effectiveness, the optimal choice depends on factors like computational constraints, gradient behavior, and the specific demands of the application. (5 sources)

When selecting an activation function for a deep learning project, several key factors should guide the decision-making process. The choice should align with the specific requirements of the task and the characteristics of the model architecture  [273691147 | Lu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

A critical consideration is the computational efficiency versus performance trade-off. ReLU and its variants remain popular choices due to their lightweight computational requirements and efficiency  [28413187 | Liu et al. | 2017 | Citations: 128]. However, newer functions like SiLU offer interesting compromises by combining linear and non-linear properties to potentially improve training efficiency and performance  [273691147 | Lu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

The dynamic nature of modern deep learning tasks suggests that activation functions should be selected with careful consideration of their impact on both learning capacity and computational efficiency  (Lee_1,  2023). Recent developments indicate that GELU has shown promising results in various applications, demonstrating superior performance across multiple evaluation metrics compared to traditional functions  (Lee_1,  2023).

It's worth noting that traditional activation functions still have valid use cases. Sigmoid and Tanh functions, while having limitations with deep networks, can be effective in shallow networks or specific architectural contexts  [7179166 | Agostinelli et al. | 2014 | Citations: 472]. The trend in activation function selection appears to be moving toward hybrid approaches that combine the benefits of different activation strategies  [7179166 | Agostinelli et al. | 2014 | Citations: 472]  [193707725 | Goodfellow et al. | 2013 | Citations: 6606].

For optimal results, practitioners should consider conducting empirical evaluations of different activation functions on their specific tasks, as theoretical advantages don't always translate to practical benefits <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.
