question: Find some existing work on LLM and inductive qualitative analysis.

sections.title: Background/Introduction
sections.text:
TLDR; There has been limited adoption of machine learning in qualitative analysis primarily due to technical barriers among social scientists. Recent developments have introduced Large Language Models (LLMs) as potential tools for both inductive and deductive qualitative analysis, though this field is still emerging with relatively little scholarly attention. (5 sources)

Qualitative analysis traditionally follows structured approaches like Thematic Analysis (TA) and Grounded Theory (GT), with TA being particularly prominent in empirical legal studies and other social science domains [264590595 | Dr'apal et al. | 2023 | Citations: 23]. While these methods acknowledge that interpretations can vary and be subjective based on analysis goals, they typically require significant manual effort, including line-by-line review, iterative coding, and constant comparison of themes  [269214633 | Lam et al. | 2024 | Citations: 42].

The adoption of machine learning in qualitative analysis has faced notable resistance, primarily due to social scientists lacking necessary computing expertise  [258832411 | Paoli | 2023 | Citations: 26]. This technological barrier has created a gap between the availability of advanced analytical tools and their practical implementation in social science research <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

However, the emergence of LLMs represents a potential paradigm shift in qualitative data analysis. These models align naturally with traditional qualitative approaches since both textual analysis and LLMs share foundational principles in language understanding  [269756830 | Khan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]. Early implementations have shown promise, with frameworks like GATOS demonstrating that LLMs can effectively identify themes and sub-themes in qualitative data, requiring minimal human intervention once implemented [271544514 | Gebreegziabher et al. | 2023 | Citations: 12].

It's important to note that while LLMs show potential for automation, current research emphasizes maintaining balance - suggesting that domain-specific knowledge and human judgment remain crucial components of the analysis process  [269214633 | Lam et al. | 2024 | Citations: 42]. This hybrid approach acknowledges both the capabilities of LLMs and the irreplaceable value of human expertise in qualitative research.

citations.title: [258832411 | Paoli | 2023 | Citations: 26]
snippets:
There has been a limited uptake of machine-learning in qualitative analysis, also because of social scientists' lack of computing skills.

We should consider that using LLMs for qualitative analysis is a subject in its statu nascendi, in the state of being born. Therefore, there is very limited literature available. To the author's knowledge there are only two scientific papers on the use of LLMs for qualitative data analysis (Xiao et al., 2023; Gao et al. 2023). An additional online post is also worth discussing (Schiavone et al., 2023), due to its findings. The first two contributions also place emphasis on the labor-intensive process of qualitative coding of large datasets. Both papers promote the use of LLMs to automate the qualitative coding process. Neither engages substantially with the problem of 'interpretation' which is part of qualitative analysis. Xiao et al. (2023) focus on two aspects: the agreement of LLMs deductive coding with coding done by human analysts, and how the design of the prompt (i.e. what is asked to the LLM) impacts the analysis. They deploy LLMs for deductive coding, which in their paper means assigning predefined labels to text. They found that "it is feasible to use GPT-3 with an expert-developed codebook for deductive coding." (p. 76) and that a "codebook-centered design performs better than the example centered designs" (p. 77), where the prompt is based on the actual codes, rather than on examples of using the codebook. They use Cohen's Kappa to measure the inter-reliability between the analysist and the model, however this measure can only be used when different analysts use the same codes on the same material. Gao et al. (2023) focus on the creation of a support tool for collaborative coding. They connect the use of LLM to social sciences and follow the approach proposed by Richards and Hempill (2018), focusing on "open coding", "iterative discussion", and "codebook development". The research is also supported by user evaluation, which contributes to establishing some agreement across the scientific community.

citations.title: [264590595 | Dr'apal et al. | 2023 | Citations: 23]
snippets: Thematic analysis and other variants of inductive coding are widely used qualitative analytic methods within empirical legal studies (ELS). We propose a novel framework facilitating effective collaboration of a legal expert with a large language model (LLM) for generating initial codes (phase 2 of thematic analysis), searching for themes (phase 3), and classifying the data in terms of the themes (to kick-start phase 4). We employed the framework for an analysis of a dataset (n=785) of facts descriptions from criminal court opinions regarding thefts. The goal of the analysis was to discover classes of typical thefts. Our results show that the LLM, namely OpenAI's GPT-4, generated reasonable initial codes, and it was capable of improving the quality of the codes based on expert feedback. They also suggest that the model performed well in zero-shot classification of facts descriptions in terms of the themes. Finally, the themes autonomously discovered by the LLM appear to map fairly well to the themes arrived at by legal experts.

citations.title: [269214633 | Lam et al. | 2024 | Citations: 42]
snippets: In contrast to common machine learning approaches, qualitative analysis methods have long acknowledged that data interpretations are varied, subjective, and highly dependent on one's analysis goals [2,44]. Qualitative coding processes, such as grounded theory methods, have the researcher engage in manually reviewing and interpreting the data, typically starting from line-by-line, lowerlevel summaries and proceeding to rounds of thematic grouping and synthesis into codes [8,43]. Once codes have been synthesized, they are applied back to the data in a process of "constant comparison," which both elucidates the data and tests the robustness and richness of the current codes. These synthesized codes also serve as the input for each successive round of coding to derive broader, more abstractive insights...Given the substantial labor involved in conducting qualitative analysis, researchers have explored algorithmic systems that use AI to aid qualitative analysts with both inductive coding (generating codes from data) and deductive coding (applying codes back to data) [9,19,52]. Most recently, research at the intersection of LLMs and qualitative analysis has focused on amplifying deductive coding processes and found that LLMs perform fairly well in coding data with existing codebooks, though not enough for full reliance [62,64]. Meanwhile, novel systems designed to aid inductive coding, such as PaTAT [22] and Scholastic [27], have explored opportunities for human-AI collaboration that keep the inductive code generation work in the hands of human analysts and leverage AI to sample and re-organize data or to formalize themes into decision rules.

citations.title: [269756830 | Khan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]
snippets: As flexible instruments of language processing, it is unsurprising that LLMs should offer promise as tools for qualitative data analysis.Textual analysis and LLMs build upon a shared history of language theorisation and practice, and in the case of LLMs, draw upon earlier experiments on text prediction [9], which use related ideas of meaning to estimate the next most likely word or token.This can be thought of as an inductive process: using patterns of phrases to infer the next word that should follow.

sections.title: Types of Qualitative Analysis with LLMs
sections.text:
TLDR; LLMs can support both inductive and deductive approaches in qualitative analysis, with distinct differences in how they process data and generate insights. Inductive analysis uses LLMs to discover themes from raw data, while deductive analysis applies predetermined codes or frameworks to categorize content. (4 sources)

Qualitative analysis with LLMs encompasses two primary methodological approaches: inductive and deductive analysis, each serving different analytical purposes and utilizing distinct processing strategies  [271843504 | Breazu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

Inductive thematic analysis represents a bottom-up, discovery-oriented approach where LLMs identify and develop themes directly from unstructured data without prior theoretical assumptions or constraints  [271843504 | Breazu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. This process mirrors natural language pattern recognition, drawing parallels to early text prediction experiments where models inferred probable subsequent words based on contextual patterns  [269756830 | Khan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6].

Deductive coding, in contrast, operates as a top-down approach where LLMs apply predetermined codebooks or analytical frameworks to organize and classify data according to established categories  (Paoli_1,  2023). This method has shown promising results, with studies indicating that combining LLMs with expert-created codebooks can achieve substantial agreement with human-coded results  [273025601 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

While both approaches demonstrate utility in modern qualitative research, their relative maturity and validation differ significantly. Deductive coding using LLMs has received more rigorous examination and validation in published research, particularly in fields such as psychology, education, and public health  [272683044 | Qiao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]. However, inductive analysis remains an area of active exploration, with ongoing discussions about optimal implementation strategies and validation methods <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [269756830 | Khan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]

sections.title: Applications and Use Cases
sections.text:
TLDR; LLMs have been successfully deployed across diverse research domains, from healthcare customer service analysis to mathematics education and legal studies. These applications demonstrate particular strength in reducing analysis time while maintaining acceptable accuracy levels for large-scale qualitative datasets. (5 sources)

* **Healthcare Customer Service Analysis**: Fine-tuned open-source LLMs have been used to analyze patient feedback, successfully identifying critical issues such as care delivery delays and communication problems in healthcare settings. This approach has proven particularly effective in processing large volumes of patient feedback while significantly reducing analysis time requirements  [274192664 | Barros et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [268109260 | Mathis et al. | 2024 | Citations: 22].

* **Mathematics Education Research**: Studies have shown successful deployment of LLMs for analyzing transcribed math tutoring sessions, comparing their outputs against human expert analysis using standardized metrics like Fleiss' κ coefficients. When properly integrated with human oversight, these systems achieved impressive F-scores of 0.92 for code identification and 0.89 for category creation  [276781981 | Liu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [266091865 | Barany et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8].

* **Legal Empirical Research**: Specialized frameworks have been developed for analyzing court opinions, particularly in criminal law cases. These approaches enable efficient processing of large document collections (e.g., 785+ fact descriptions) for discovering patterns in legal cases, such as classifications of theft types [264590595 | Dr'apal et al. | 2023 | Citations: 23].

* **Educational Assessment**: Automated essay scoring systems powered by LLMs have evolved to incorporate sophisticated linguistic features beyond simple lexical measures, addressing historical criticisms about the technology's capability for deep comprehension <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

* **Social Media Analysis**: LLMs have been adapted for analyzing social media conversations, particularly excelling in tasks such as detecting deception and identifying behavioral markers across thousands of posts  [266091865 | Barany et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8].

snippets: Thematic analysis and other variants of inductive coding are widely used qualitative analytic methods within empirical legal studies (ELS). We propose a novel framework facilitating effective collaboration of a legal expert with a large language model (LLM) for generating initial codes (phase 2 of thematic analysis), searching for themes (phase 3), and classifying the data in terms of the themes (to kick-start phase 4). We employed the framework for an analysis of a dataset (n=785) of facts descriptions from criminal court opinions regarding thefts. The goal of the analysis was to discover classes of typical thefts. Our results show that the LLM, namely OpenAI's GPT-4, generated reasonable initial codes, and it was capable of improving the quality of the codes based on expert feedback. They also suggest that the model performed well in zero-shot classification of facts descriptions in terms of the themes. Finally, the themes autonomously discovered by the LLM appear to map fairly well to the themes arrived at by legal experts.

sections.title: Methodological Considerations
sections.text:
TLDR; Key methodological considerations for LLM-supported qualitative analysis include careful attention to prompt engineering, validation metrics, and iterative refinement processes. Researchers emphasize the importance of developing structured workflows while acknowledging the need for standardization in evaluation approaches. (7 sources)

The successful implementation of LLMs in qualitative analysis requires careful attention to methodological details and systematic approaches. Prompt engineering emerges as a critical factor, with researchers noting that well-designed prompts incorporating clear task backgrounds, specific processing instructions, and explicit output expectations significantly improve analysis quality  [275212618 | Gao et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

Validation and reliability of LLM-generated analyses present unique challenges. While some researchers have attempted to adapt traditional inter-rater reliability measures like Cohen's Kappa for LLM-human comparisons, these adaptations face limitations given the fundamental difference between human and machine interpretation approaches  (Paoli_1,  2023). New metrics are being developed to address this gap, such as Initial Thematic Saturation (ITS), which helps assess the validity of LLM analysis transactions  [266844800 | Paoli et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

Methodological frameworks for LLM-supported analysis typically follow established qualitative traditions while incorporating LLM capabilities. One successful approach adapts Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic analysis framework for LLM implementation, with studies showing encouraging results in matching human analysis outcomes  [278312852 | Wang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. Similar success has been observed when adapting Grounded Theory methodologies for LLM implementation  [269137326 | Paoli | 2024 | Citations: 1].

The evolution of ML approaches in qualitative analysis reveals a progression from traditional supervised learning methods to more sophisticated generative approaches. While earlier efforts focused on deductive coding using classification-based methods  [277596177 | Chen et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [156098872 | Zheng et al. | 2019 | Citations: 21], current research emphasizes the importance of iterative, generation-based approaches that can handle open coding more effectively  [277596177 | Chen et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

An important methodological insight is that the goal isn't necessarily perfect replication of human analysis but rather achieving sufficient capture of key patterns in datasets  [269137326 | Paoli | 2024 | Citations: 1]. This pragmatic approach allows researchers to leverage LLM capabilities while maintaining methodological rigor and realistic expectations about the technology's role in the analysis process.

snippets:
Existing ML/GAI Approaches for Open Coding Qualitative analysis enables in-depth explorations of human experiences by focusing on nuanced interpretations, emotions, and subjective experiences that shape individual and social realities (Rahman, 2016). Thematic Analysis (TA) and Grounded Theory (GT), two widely used qualitative methods, advocate for open coding as an essential first step to uncover the underlying reasons and processes that form and transform meanings (Corbin & Strauss, 2008;Rahman, 2016). 

ML and GAI techniques have been extensively studied by the CSCL community to support qualitative analysis, particularly for large discourse datasets, yet past studies have mostly focused on deductive analysis. In deductive coding, algorithms aim to mimic humans' results, making way for classification-based methods, such as supervised ML (Zheng et al., 2019) or rule-based systems (Erkens et al., 2008). For open coding, however, the number and nature of underlying codes are unknown before the analysis, necessitating the study of generation approaches. To help with qualitative researchers' open coding processes, recent studies focus on: 

1. Topic modeling, an unsupervised ML technique, identifies semantically similar word groups (topics) in text-based datasets and has been used for inductive or open coding (Baumer et al., 2020;Cai et al., 2023). 

The resulting topics help researchers focus on key data patterns. Despite efforts, the difficulty in interpreting and evaluating the results limits its power (Grootendorst, 2022;(Sievert et al., 2014). 2. GAI models have been more recently adopted for open, inductive coding. By iteratively providing data pieces with relevant instructions (e.g., research questions, coding instructions, desired output format), GAI models can produce codes that humans find more interpretable and useful (De Paoli, 2023;Sinha et al., 2024).

sections.title: Challenges and Limitations
sections.text:
TLDR; Major challenges in using LLMs for qualitative analysis include reproducibility concerns due to ad hoc prompt engineering and varying depths of theme extraction. Technical barriers persist around inconsistent performance metrics and the need for extensive validation protocols, particularly affecting adoption in sensitive research areas. (6 sources)

Despite promising developments in LLM-supported qualitative analysis, several significant challenges continue to limit widespread adoption and reliable implementation. One fundamental concern relates to the reproducibility and replicability of LLM-based analyses, with many practitioners taking an opportunistic approach to prompt engineering that undermines methodological rigor  [277451847 | Khalid et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

Performance consistency remains a persistent challenge, with researchers noting that while LLMs can effectively capture certain themes, they often fall short in producing nuanced, multidimensional interpretations. Studies across various disciplines, including medicine and education, consistently report that LLMs tend to miss subtle variations in themes and struggle with complex categorical structures  [276724675 | Schroeder et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]  [268109260 | Mathis et al. | 2024 | Citations: 22].

Technical limitations are particularly evident in scenarios requiring deep contextual understanding. While LLMs show promise in supporting basic coding tasks, their application becomes more challenging when dealing with sensitive personal narratives or situations requiring delicate ethical handling  [276724675 | Schroeder et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]  [268109260 | Mathis et al. | 2024 | Citations: 22]. This limitation is especially pronounced in health-related qualitative research, where nuances in patient narratives require careful consideration of cultural and social factors <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

Another significant barrier is the lack of standardized validation protocols. While some progress has been made in developing metrics for assessing LLM performance in qualitative analysis, the field lacks consensus on unified evaluation criteria  [276724675 | Schroeder et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]. This absence of standardization creates difficulties for researchers attempting to validate or replicate previous work, particularly when different prompt engineering approaches yield varying results  [277501797 | Overton et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

Furthermore, the complexity of integrating LLM outputs into existing qualitative research frameworks poses practical challenges. While LLM-human collaboration shows promise in speeding up analysis processes, ensuring proper integration with established qualitative research methodologies requires additional methodological development and validation  [277501797 | Overton et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [268649903 | Izani et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4].

They have also been used to code interviews successfully (Bano et al., 2024). A key theme in the use of LLMs in qualitative research is that, while they can automate tasks and perform at similar or better levels than human analysts, LLM-human collaboration results in faster, higher quality analysis on both inductive and deductive tasks (Izani & Voyer, 2023).

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Task vectors represent specialized information embedded in neural networks through fine-tuning, typically captured by subtracting pre-trained weights from task-specific fine-tuned weights. Their discovery came independently through different approaches, from analyzing few-shot learning to studying weight interpolation in transformers. (6 sources)

The concept of task vectors emerged through several parallel discoveries in machine learning research. Initially, Achille et al. introduced task embeddings as a meta-learning method for visual classification, utilizing Fisher information matrices derived from model gradients  [207846479 | Achille et al. | 2019 | Citations: 725]. Later, in the domain of Large Language Models (LLMs), researchers found that task-specific information could be encoded through manipulation of model parameters and activations  [267782482 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

A notable breakthrough came with the observation that when fine-tuning models, the learned task information actually exists as sparse vectors in the weight matrix. This finding led to the development of efficient methods to store and transfer task-specific knowledge  [237447914 | Wortsman et al. | 2021 | Citations: 1094]. Building on this understanding, weight interpolation became a powerful tool for exploring model capabilities, showing that GPT-2 could generate coherent outputs even after extreme interpolation steps  [246426451 | Ramesh et al. | 2021 | Citations: 1792].

The fundamental definition of a task vector remains consistent across implementations: it represents the difference between weights of a pre-trained model and those of the same model after being fine-tuned for a specific task  [254408495 | Ilharco et al. | 2022 | Citations: 435]. This approach has proven remarkably versatile, with task vectors exhibiting several useful mathematical properties - notably, they can be added, subtracted, and scaled arbitrarily, making them valuable tools for model manipulation  [254408495 | Ilharco et al. | 2022 | Citations: 435]. While earlier research suggested that task-specific information might be difficult to isolate due to complex pre-training processes  [275570381 | Yang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1], the development of task vectors has provided concrete methods for identifying and leveraging this information <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [254408495 | Ilharco et al. | 2022 | Citations: 435]
snippets: Changing how pre-trained models behave -- e.g., improving their performance on a downstream task or mitigating biases learned during pre-training -- is a common practice when developing machine learning systems. In this work, we propose a new paradigm for steering the behavior of neural networks, centered around \textit{task vectors}. A task vector specifies a direction in the weight space of a pre-trained model, such that movement in that direction improves performance on the task. We build task vectors by subtracting the weights of a pre-trained model from the weights of the same model after fine-tuning on a task. We show that these task vectors can be modified and combined together through arithmetic operations such as negation and addition, and the behavior of the resulting model is steered accordingly. Negating a task vector decreases performance on the target task, with little change in model behavior on control tasks. Moreover, adding task vectors together can improve performance on multiple tasks at once. Finally, when tasks are linked by an analogy relationship of the form ``A is to B as C is to D", combining task vectors from three of the tasks can improve performance on the fourth, even when no data from the fourth task is used for training. Overall, our experiments with several models, modalities and tasks show that task arithmetic is a simple, efficient and effective way of editing models.

snippets: Task embedding, initially introduced as a task vector (Achille et al., 2019), as a meta-learning method for visual classification tasks. This concept utilizes the empirical Fisher information derived from model gradients to encode task-specific information into a vector representation, demonstrating that the model parameter can provide detailed task information. Expanding into NLP, (Vu et al., 2020) applied Fisher information to capture task-specific details in fine-tuned language models, formalizing it as task embedding...(Ilharco et al., 2022) introduced a method with arithmetic operations by subtracting the original parameters from its fine-tuned parameters to extract task vectors...Recent investigations into the task embedding of LLMs by (Hendel et al., 2023) extracted task vectors from parameters and activations of LLMs.

sections.title: Core Concepts & Properties
sections.text:
TLDR; Task vectors represent the difference between pre-trained and task-fine-tuned model weights, acting as carriers of task-specific knowledge. These vectors exhibit mathematical properties like linearity and additivity, enabling sophisticated model manipulation through arithmetic operations. (6 sources)

At its core, a task vector τt is formally defined as the difference between a model's parameters Θ(t) after fine-tuning for task t and its initial pre-trained parameters Θ(0): τt = Θ(t) - Θ(0)  [271865581 | Yang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 68]. This simple mathematical formulation captures the essential modifications made to the base model during the fine-tuning process.

Task vectors possess several remarkable properties that make them powerful tools for model manipulation. Most fundamentally, they behave like regular vectors in the weight space of the model, supporting basic arithmetic operations including addition, subtraction, and scalar multiplication  [271693681 | Belanec et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]. This enables three primary operations:

1. Task Addition: Combining multiple task vectors to create a model that performs all associated tasks simultaneously  [271865581 | Yang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 68]

2. Task Negation: Removing previously learned tasks by subtracting their corresponding task vectors  [271865581 | Yang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 68]

3. Zero-shot Transfer: Using linear combinations of task vectors to enable models to generalize to new tasks without additional training  [277787405 | Li et al. | 2025 | Citations: 4]

Recent theoretical analyses have revealed that these properties emerge from a phenomenon called weight disentanglement, where different directions in the weight space independently control distinct aspects of the model's behavior  [274788575 | Choi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]. This explains why task vectors can be manipulated independently and reliably.

From an implementation perspective, task vectors offer significant advantages over traditional fine-tuning approaches. They require substantially less computation since they can be created using existing pre-trained models without additional training  [273228310 | Kim et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. However, challenges remain in efficiently combining multiple task vectors and managing potential interference between different tasks  [274788575 | Choi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]  [265351803 | Yadav et al. | 2023 | Citations: 13].

citations.title: [265351803 | Yadav et al. | 2023 | Citations: 13]
snippets: Many past works have shown that task vectors can be compressed by adopting various techniques like (1) sparsification (Yadav et al., 2023)(Sattler et al., 2019)Sung et al., 2021) -removing some parameters that are not crucial for the performance; or (2) quantization (Dettmers et al., 2023;(Sattler et al., 2019) -reducing the number of bits that represent each parameter. These are two complementary ways to reduce the amount of information stored, reducing the number of nonzero entries in the task vector, and reducing the amount of information in each of each entry...Past works (Yadav et al., 2023) have shown that for any given task, 70 − 90% of the values in the task vector can be pruned without hurting the performance of the tasks.

citations.title: [271693681 | Belanec et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]
snippets: As a method of adapting model weights without training, task vectors (Ilharco et al., 2022) compute the difference between pre-trained weights and finetuned weights on a specific task. The task vector is simply defined by the element-wise difference between the pre-trained weights of the whole model and the weights after fine-tuning. Task vectors can be then applied to any model weights θ of the same dimensionality (architecture) by element-wise addition. The representation of task vectors in the weight space of the model has the same properties as standard vectors, therefore it is possible to include them in arithmetic expressions like addition, negation, or combinations via the addition of two or more vectors together. We further build on the findings from (Ilharco et al., 2022) and (Lester et al., 2021) in the following parts of this section.

citations.title: [271865581 | Yang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 68]
snippets: Recently, Task Arithmetic [71] introduced the concept of "task vector" (in Figure 4(a)), which represents the model parameter Θ (t) fine-tuned on task t subtract the pre-trained  model parameter Θ (0) , i.e., τ t = Θ (t) − Θ (0) . In other words, task vectors are thought to steer the behavior of a neural network meaningfully. For example, multitask learning (MTL) can be accomplished by adding task vectors, forgetting can be achieved by subtracting task vectors, and task analogies can be performed using analogous task vectors. Specifically, when we want the pretrained model to perform MTL, we can add multiple task vectors {τ 1 , . . . , τ T } to the pretrained model, i.e., Θ (merge) = Θ (0) + λ  T t=1 τ t in Figure 4(b), where λ is a hyperparameter. Conversely, when we want the pretrained model to forget a function t, we can subtract the corresponding task vector from pretrained model as Figure 4(c), i.e., Θ (merge) = Θ (0) − τ t . As shown in Figure 4(d), we can also implement task analogies by task vector analogies, thus enabling zeroshot learning of new tasks. Similarly, PEMs [234] combines Adapters with different capabilities by extending task arithmetic [71] to parameter-efficient fine-tuning settings.

Specifically, the vectors are the result of subtracting (negating) the weights of a pre-trained model θ pre from those of a model θ t f t fine-tuned on a target task t. We can adjust the model in the desired direction by adding or subtracting the sum of these task vectors τ = t τ t from the original model's weights, according to the formula θ new = θ pre + λτ . This approach is more computationally efficient than fine-tuning, as it leverages pre-trained models from public repositories and eliminates the need for additional training.

snippets: Intriguingly, Ilharco et al. [52] introduced a method that employs test-time adaptation [46] to dynamically determine the coefficients for the weighted sum of task vectors based on the input data distribution, thereby reducing task interference.

citations.title: [277787405 | Li et al. | 2025 | Citations: 4]
snippets: The task vector approach first fine-tunes a pre-trained model on several simpler tasks to obtain task vectors, which represent the weight differences between the fine-tuned models and the pre-trained model. To handle more complex tasks, a proper model can be edited by adding a linear combination of these task vectors to the pre-trained model. Since this approach only requires determining the appropriate arithmetic hyperparameters, with no need for further fine-tuning on complicated tasks, the task vector method offers a significant efficiency advantage and is particularly effective when adapting to a wide range of downstream tasks. Empirical evidence shows that adding multiple task vectors can improve the model's performance on corresponding tasks, while subtracting certain task vectors allows the model to forget associated tasks. A proper linear combination of task vectors can even enable the model to generalize on an out-of-domain task that has an analogous relationship with the given task vectors, without needing labeled data.

sections.title: Recent Applications
sections.text:
TLDR; Task vectors have found widespread adoption across domains including speech recognition, language modeling, and image processing. Recent applications showcase their versatility in areas ranging from improving model safety to enabling efficient few-shot learning. (13 sources)

Recent advances in applying task vectors span multiple domains and functionalities:

1. **Language Model Enhancement**: Researchers have developed methods to improve language models' reliability and safety using task vectors. Notable applications include mitigating hallucination through negative task vectors  [259203355 | Daheim et al. | 2023 | Citations: 163] and developing safety-focused alignment techniques through dedicated safety vectors  [267819324 | Bhardwaj et al. | 2024 | Citations: 9]. The concept of "Chat Vectors" has emerged as a specific application for enhancing dialogue capabilities and safety in conversational AI  [268253329 | Huang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 14].

2. **Speech Recognition**: In automatic speech recognition (ASR), task vectors have been successfully applied to Whisper models, enabling efficient downstream task adaptation without requiring extensive computational resources  [272332568 | Kang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

3. **Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Integration**: Task vectors have been combined with efficient adapters and lightweight modules, creating flexible frameworks for model enhancement  [259843861 | Zhang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 168]  [235458009 | Hu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 6608]  [246411503 | Liu et al. | 2022 | Citations: 2756].

4. **Cross-Modal Applications**: Task vectors have expanded beyond single-modal applications to facilitate transfer learning between different modalities, particularly in multimodal scenarios  [276580677 | Lin et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]  [264335880 | Liu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 205].

5. **Few-Shot Learning**: Task vectors have enabled improved few-shot learning capabilities, particularly through the discovery that they can capture task information independent of specific input-output examples  [277940330 | Kharlapenko et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [261051667 | Hendel et al. | 2023 | Citations: 438].

citations.title: [268253329 | Huang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 14]
snippets: Recently, the development of open-source large language models (LLMs) has advanced rapidly. Nevertheless, due to data constraints, the capabilities of most open-source LLMs are primarily focused on English. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of $\textit{chat vector}$ to equip pre-trained language models with instruction following and human value alignment via simple model arithmetic. The chat vector is derived by subtracting the weights of a pre-trained base model (e.g. LLaMA2) from those of its corresponding chat model (e.g. LLaMA2-chat). By simply adding the chat vector to a continual pre-trained model's weights, we can endow the model with chat capabilities in new languages without the need for further training. Our empirical studies demonstrate the superior efficacy of the chat vector from three different aspects: instruction following, toxicity mitigation, and multi-turn dialogue. Moreover, to showcase the adaptability of our approach, we extend our experiments to encompass various languages, base models, and chat vectors. The results underscore the chat vector's simplicity, effectiveness, and wide applicability, making it a compelling solution for efficiently enabling conversational capabilities in pre-trained language models. Our code is available at https://github.com/aqweteddy/ChatVector.

citations.title: [272332568 | Kang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Recently, the size of automatic speech recognition (ASR) models has been increasing, similar to large language models (LLMs), and efficient tuning to enhance the performance of downstream tasks with limited resources remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose a simple and effective downstream task tuning method using task vectors. We utilize task vectors to orient the pre-trained Whisper model in the weight space, moving in that direction to achieve downstream task adaptation. We demonstrate that the model can be adjusted through arithmetic operations of the task vector, and this adjustment is reflected in the Whisper. Furthermore, we can efficiently construct a generalized model by summing vectors.

citations.title: [276580677 | Lin et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]

Following these works, Huang et al. (2024a) characterizes multimodal task vectors as pairs of attention head activations and indices and applies those task vectors to generative VLMs in in-context learning settings to compress long prompts that would otherwise not fit in limited context length. Luo et al. (2024) further analyzes the transferability of task vectors from different modalities, which extends the application of task vectors.

citations.title: [277940330 | Kharlapenko et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets:
Task vectors were independently discovered by Hendel et al. (2023) and (Todd et al., 2023). The key idea behind task vectors is that they capture the essence of a task demonstrated in a few-shot prompt, allowing the model to apply this learned task to new inputs without explicit fine-tuning. Task vectors have several important properties: 

1. They can be extracted from the model's hidden states given ICL prompts as inputs. 2. When added to the model's activations in a zero-shot setting, they can induce task performance without explicit context. 3. They appear to encode abstract task information, independent of specific input-output examples.

sections.title: Technical Developments
sections.text:
TLDR; Recent technical developments in task vectors focus on compression methods and optimization techniques to make them more efficient and practical. Key innovations include sparsification, quantization, and dynamic grouping methods that improve performance while reducing storage requirements. (8 sources)

Several major technical advancements have shaped modern task vector implementations. Early research established foundational compression techniques through sparsification and quantization, showing that 70-90% of task vector values could be removed without affecting performance  [265351803 | Yadav et al. | 2023 | Citations: 13]  [196232309 | Sattler et al. | 2019 | Citations: 280].

Recent optimization approaches have evolved along multiple paths. One stream focuses on advanced compression methods, including singular value decomposition (SVD)-based techniques for exploiting low-rank structures  [277435010 | Lee et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. Parallel developments have explored model sparsification, alternative optimization algorithms, and the assumption that fine-tuned weights lie within thin Gaussian shells  [276094680 | Zeng et al. | 2025 | Citations: 3].

A notable advancement comes from the integration of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with task vectors, leading to more modular and efficient implementations  [276094680 | Zeng et al. | 2025 | Citations: 3]  [255364773 | Hu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 10420]. This approach has been further refined with router-based adapter reuse algorithms, enabling more flexible model architectures  [268970004 | Ostapenko et al. | 2024 | Citations: 11].

Dynamic improvements continue to emerge in how task vectors are managed and optimized. Recent work includes the development of Dynamic Task Vector Grouping (DTVG), which uses sophisticated similarity metrics and knowledge consistency measures to optimize task transfers  [277272320 | Zhang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. Additional enhancements focus on improving fusion performance through removal of insignificant parameters and resolution of symbol conflicts  [274233792 | Tian et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]  [265351803 | Yadav et al. | 2023 | Citations: 13].

citations.title: [265351803 | Yadav et al. | 2023 | Citations: 13]
snippets: Many past works have shown that task vectors can be compressed by adopting various techniques like (1) sparsification (Yadav et al., 2023)(Sattler et al., 2019)Sung et al., 2021) -removing some parameters that are not crucial for the performance; or (2) quantization (Dettmers et al., 2023;(Sattler et al., 2019) -reducing the number of bits that represent each parameter. These are two complementary ways to reduce the amount of information stored, reducing the number of nonzero entries in the task vector, and reducing the amount of information in each of each entry...Past works (Yadav et al., 2023) have shown that for any given task, 70 − 90% of the values in the task vector can be pruned without hurting the performance of the tasks.

snippets: Given shared pretrained weights for different downstream models, the task arithmetic method calculates the task vector for each task by computing the difference between the fine-tuned weights and the pretrained weights. This method multiplies the sum of these task vectors by a coefficient and adds them to the pretrained weights to construct a model capable of performing multiple downstream tasks. Recently, several studies have proposed methods to enhance task arithmetic. For instance, (Yadav et al., 2023) improve fusion performance by removing smaller parameters and symbolic conflict parameters during the fusion of task vectors. (Yu et al., 2023) employ a random mask to ensure parameter sparsity, thereby reducing noise during fusion. [4] optimize the coefficients of task vector fusion using test set data to enhance fusion performance. A recent work, PCB-Merging [5], proposes making trade-offs in task fusion by measuring competition between parameters.

citations.title: [276094680 | Zeng et al. | 2025 | Citations: 3]
snippets:
Task vectors (Ilharco et al., 2022) is a practical model editing and merging technique that navigates the weight space of pretrained models. These vectors provide a direction that enhances task-specific knowledge in parameter space by subtracting the pretrained model weights from the updated parameters after fine-tuning a specific task. Beyond their simplicity, task vectors have an intriguing property: they can be manipulated through arithmetic operations such as addition and negation, allowing for the composition of models with tailored behaviors or hybrid task capabilities.

There were attempts that address this problem either through model sparsification (He et al., 2024;Wang et al., 2024a), alternative optimization algorithms (Li et al., 2024), or assuming all fine-tuned weights lie in a thin Gaussian shell when fine-tuning tasks are the same (Jang et al., 2025) each model.

Another interesting recent work proposed the LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) Adapter library (Ostapenko et al., 2024), which uses a similar clustering approach to enable more modular large language models, along with a router-based adapter reuse algorithm. Such advantage was also proved to be successful for LoRA merging (Zhao et al., 2024), which can be seen as a special case under our bases framework.

citations.title: [277272320 | Zhang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets: We propose a method called Dynamic Task Vector Grouping (DTVG). Specifically, We first introduce a novel task similarity metric, the dot product between task prompt vectors (TPV), which steadily achieves a better transfer performance than the current metric, the cosine similarity between soft prompts. Based on this metric, we introduce a source task grouping method to select the transfer source task group for each target task with two metrics, including target similarity and knowledge consistency. Then, a multi-task merging method is used to weighted sum the task vectors from the target task and the selected source tasks, synthesizing the initialization soft prompt for the target task. During the fine-tuning stage of the target task, we track the task similarity changes and dynamically update the source task group, which will effectively improve transfer performance.

citations.title: [277435010 | Lee et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Model merging has emerged as a promising approach for unifying independently fine-tuned models into an integrated framework, significantly enhancing computational efficiency in multi-task learning. Recently, several SVD-based techniques have been introduced to exploit low-rank structures for enhanced merging, but their reliance on such manually designed rank selection often leads to cross-task interference and suboptimal performance.

sections.title: Challenges & Solutions
sections.text:
TLDR; Major challenges in task vector applications include maintaining model stability during arithmetic operations, managing memory constraints, and ensuring reliable task transfers. Recent solutions leverage insights from continual learning and gradient dynamics to develop more robust manipulation strategies. (7 sources)

Despite their promise, task vectors face several key technical and operational challenges that researchers are actively addressing. A fundamental issue lies in understanding exactly how models acquire and organize new capabilities during fine-tuning, as this affects how task vectors can be effectively manipulated  [276409016 | Jiang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]  [257674697 | Jain et al. | 2023 | Citations: 458].

Early approaches to learning task embeddings faced limitations in accurately predicting transferability between tasks, though newer methods have shown improvement through techniques like pooled BERT representations and layer-wise gradient analysis  [248376935 | Padmakumar et al. | 2022 | Citations: 18]. More recent work has expanded these concepts to include prompt transfer learning, where task-specific prompts can mutually benefit each other  [248376935 | Padmakumar et al. | 2022 | Citations: 18].

A significant breakthrough in addressing these challenges came from analyzing the relationship between task vectors and gradient dynamics. Research has shown that the evolution of Fisher Information Matrices (FIM) follows deterministic dynamics that resemble classical gradient descent, providing a theoretical foundation for better understanding and controlling task vector manipulations  [257674697 | Jain et al. | 2023 | Citations: 458].

Practical challenges in deploying task vectors have spurred innovation in visualization and debugging techniques. New approaches allow researchers to understand how models adapt to task transformations and visualize the geometric relationships between different tasks  [269005382 | Hojel et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7]. These tools have proven particularly valuable in computer vision applications, where task vectors can now be identified and guided without requiring input-output examples  [269005382 | Hojel et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7].

Recent solutions have also addressed the challenge of combining multiple task vectors effectively. Linearization techniques have enhanced the compositional nature of task vectors  [270924160 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8], while new frameworks for mixing different types of adaptations (including weight, activation, and input adaptations) have emerged to overcome previous limitations in capturing complex model behaviors  [268253329 | Huang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 14]  [259203355 | Daheim et al. | 2023 | Citations: 163].

citations.title: [248376935 | Padmakumar et al. | 2022 | Citations: 18]

(2020) proposed two methods to learn task embeddings capable of predicting transferability between source and target tasks-one by pooling the representations of the textual task data from BERT and the other by using the layer-wise gradients of a BERT model. Vu et al. (2021) learned task specific prompts that can benefit each other via prompt transfer.

snippets:
In this work, we analyze the activations of MAE-VQGAN, a recent Visual Prompting model, and find task vectors, activations that encode task-specific information. Equipped with this insight, we demonstrate that it is possible to identify the task vectors and use them to guide the network towards performing different tasks without providing any input-output examples.

In [11,17,38], Task Vectors or Function Vectors are sets of latent activations derived from particular positions inside a transformer [40] model which serve as internal representations of a task implicitly described by an ICL prompt with input-output demonstrations. These latent activations at particular positions can consequently be used in a new forward pass in the absence of the ICL prompt (or with a corrupted prompt) while still managing to guide the model to perform the desired task. The investigation of Task Vectors aligns with broader efforts in the field to make neural networks more adaptable and tailored to specific tasks [23,26] as well as boosting the performance [19,30]47] by gaining a deeper understanding of how different attention heads within a model contribute to its overall function. Our work is the first to explore Task Vectors in computer vision.

sections.title: Background on Reward Model Evaluation
sections.text:
TLDR; Reward models are essential components in machine learning systems that attempt to capture human preferences. Their evaluation traditionally relies on accuracy metrics against manually labeled data, though this approach has significant limitations. (4 sources)

Traditional evaluation of reward models primarily centers around measuring their accuracy in predicting human preferences using manually annotated datasets  [273228350 | Wen et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5]. This straightforward approach, while widely adopted, faces fundamental challenges - even small variations in reward model accuracy can lead to dramatically different outcomes when these models guide policy optimization  [273228350 | Wen et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5].

A critical aspect of reward model evaluation involves assessing their ability to differentiate between outputs, which becomes particularly complex when dealing with multiple responses per prompt. One common approach is to break down partial rankings into pairwise comparisons for evaluation purposes  [276574585 | Wen et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

The field has evolved beyond simple binary classification accuracy metrics. Modern evaluation frameworks now incorporate more sophisticated measures, including correlation analysis between model predictions and human judgments, assessment of multi-dimensional preferences, and specialized metrics for detecting problematic aspects like implausible content or misaligned keywords  [271270563 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7]. Additionally, some researchers employ innovative evaluation methods such as analyzing correlations between model-simulated and human-simulated reward signals to assess the effectiveness of different learning approaches  [271270563 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7]  [266374653 | Zeng et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1].

The complexity of modern reward modeling necessitates comprehensive evaluation strategies that go beyond traditional accuracy metrics <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">. This sets the stage for understanding why simple accuracy measurements alone are insufficient for properly evaluating reward models.

citations.title: [266374653 | Zeng et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]
snippets: There are several ways to collect comparison-based user preference data. For instance, LMs can be prompted to produce multiple versions of outputs y ∼ π(y|x) by conditioning on the prompt x. Also, the answers generated by LMs can be compared with the outputs generated by heuristics, such as using the first sentence of the input context. We use the latter method to create binary preference data. After pairs of answers (y i , y j ) are generated, we then surface them to different treatment groups through live experiments to determine users' implicit preferences via click-through-rates, and create ranked pairs for model training.

snippets: Recent work (Chen et al., 2024) noted a discrepancy between the learned (implicit) reward model and the learned policy model in DPO in terms of their capabilities of correctly ranking candidate outputs according to their quality. Particularly, the ranking accuracy of the learned reward model (Eq. 6) is usually high, indicating that the better output y w is assigned a higher reward. i.e., r θ (x, y w ) > r θ (x, y l ). However, Chen et al. (2024) found that the ranking accuracy of the learned policy p θ remains low even after DPO fine-tuning. They partly attributed this to the generally low ranking accuracy of the reference policy p ref , noting that DPO fine-tuning rarely reverses the preference (i.e., p(y w |x) vs. p(y l |x)) due to the KL-constraint.

Currently, the evaluation of RMs depends on measuring accuracy against a validation set of manually annotated preference data. Although this method is straightforward and widely adopted, the relationship between RM accuracy and downstream policy performance remains under-explored...Our findings reveal that while there is a weak positive correlation between accuracy and downstream performance, policies optimized towards RMs with similar accuracy can exhibit quite different performance. Moreover, we discover that the way of measuring accuracy significantly impacts its ability to predict the final policy performance...This underscores the inadequacy of relying solely on accuracy to reflect their impact on policy optimization.

sections.title: Limitations of Ranking Accuracy
sections.text:
TLDR; Simple ranking accuracy metrics fail to capture important nuances in reward model performance and can be misleading indicators of actual utility. Even high ranking accuracy doesn't guarantee effective downstream performance or alignment with true human preferences. (5 sources)

Research has revealed several critical limitations of relying solely on ranking accuracy metrics for evaluating reward models. A fundamental issue is that ranking accuracy only ensures monotonic relationships between rewards, allowing for non-linear or non-unit slope mappings that don't necessarily reflect true reward structures  [274822838 | Hong et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

The practical implications of these limitations become apparent when examining real-world performance. Recent studies have shown that reward models, even advanced ones, achieve remarkably modest accuracy rates - around 46.6% in comprehensive evaluations - often barely exceeding random chance  (Liu et al._1,  2024).

A notable concern is the disconnect between ranking accuracy and actual downstream performance. Studies have consistently shown that higher alignment scores between estimated and ground truth rewards don't reliably predict better reinforcement learning performance  [271855284 | Mattson et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [257426979 | Tien et al. | 2022 | Citations: 40]. This creates a concerning situation where models with seemingly strong accuracy metrics might actually be poorly suited for guiding policy optimization.

Furthermore, current evaluation methods can be vulnerable to systematic biases. Research has identified that reward models may disproportionately favor responses from certain policy models, creating artificial advantages that distort genuine performance assessments  [277780346 | Zhu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. This bias isn't just theoretically concerning - it can lead to exploitation by policy models that optimize for reward in ways that diverge from authentic human preferences, potentially resulting in deceptive or unintended outcomes  [277780346 | Zhu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

citations.title: [271855284 | Mattson et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Interestingly, we find that higher alignment scores between the cumulative estimated reward and the cumulative ground truth reward does not necessarily lead to better RL performance during policy training, a phenomenon reported in other work on preference learning (Tien et al., 2022). Both Goal Classifier and XIRL trained on MQME data score better on both reward learning metrics when compared with XIRL-Buckets and XTriplets, yet the latter approaches far outperform the former methods during RL training (Figure 1). Furthermore, our results indicate that X-RLHF has the best Kendall correlation and accuracy on the validation set, surpassing even XIRL which was trained on X-Magical (near-optimal demonstrations). These findings suggest that quantifying the alignment between rewards is not necessarily a good indicator of down-stream RL performance.

citations.title: [257426979 | Tien et al. | 2022 | Citations: 40]
snippets: Learning policies via preference-based reward learning is an increasingly popular method for customizing agent behavior, but has been shown anecdotally to be prone to spurious correlations and reward hacking behaviors. While much prior work focuses on causal confusion in reinforcement learning and behavioral cloning, we focus on a systematic study of causal confusion and reward misidentification when learning from preferences. In particular, we perform a series of sensitivity and ablation analyses on several benchmark domains where rewards learned from preferences achieve minimal test error but fail to generalize to out-of-distribution states -- resulting in poor policy performance when optimized. We find that the presence of non-causal distractor features, noise in the stated preferences, and partial state observability can all exacerbate reward misidentification. We also identify a set of methods with which to interpret misidentified learned rewards. In general, we observe that optimizing misidentified rewards drives the policy off the reward's training distribution, resulting in high predicted (learned) rewards but low true rewards. These findings illuminate the susceptibility of preference learning to reward misidentification and causal confusion -- failure to consider even one of many factors can result in unexpected, undesirable behavior.

citations.title: [274822838 | Hong et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]
snippets:
Reward models in the past only need to satisfy ranking consistency with the corresponding true rewards. However, for ideal offline optimization of the RLHF loss, a learned log ratio reward and its corresponding true reward have to satisfy the slope-1 linearity, a much stronger requirement than ranking consistency. The reason is that, to satisfy ranking consistency, the relationship between the two rewards can be any monotonically increasing function, including those that are non-linear or linear with the slope being any positive number. 

Therefore, metrics that are based on ranking consistency to evaluate the log ratio reward (i.e., the learned reward model) is not meaningful when it comes to offline alignment.

citations.title: [277780346 | Zhu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets: In this paper, we identify a model preference bias in RMs, where they systematically assign disproportionately high scores to responses from certain policy models. This bias distorts ranking evaluations and leads to unfair judgments...When biased, RMs can be easily exploited, where policy models optimize for reward in ways that deviate from genuine human preferences (Eisenstein et al., 2023;(Gao et al., 2022)Pang et al., 2022). This phenomenon, referred to as reward hacking (Skalse et al., 2022), allows models to exploit vulnerabilities in the RM rather than achieving genuine behavioral improvements, potentially leading to deceptive or unintended outcomes.

sections.title: Alternative Evaluation Metrics and Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; Beyond simple accuracy metrics, researchers have developed diverse evaluation approaches ranging from detailed preference correlation analyses to specialized benchmarks. These alternatives include measuring multi-dimensional preferences, analyzing global ranking quality, and establishing connections to downstream policy performance. (7 sources)

* **Benchmark-Based Evaluation**: Researchers have created comprehensive evaluation frameworks like RM-Bench that correlate strongly with policy model performance. However, some earlier benchmark approaches showed limited correlation with actual alignment performance  [273346208 | Zhou et al. | 2024 | Citations: 18].

* **Binary Classification Accuracy**: A fundamental baseline measurement involves testing how well reward models assign higher rewards to responses explicitly chosen by human annotators  [273482364 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7].

* **Multi-Dimensional Preference Analysis**: Advanced evaluation frameworks examine complex aspects beyond simple binary choices, including:

  - Correlation between model and human Elo ratings

  - Win ratio correlation with humans

  - Specialized metrics for detecting implausible content and misaligned keywords  [271270563 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7]

* **Global Ranking Quality Assessment**: Traditional metrics like Spearman's correlation have limitations since they only require correct relative rankings within problem contexts, not absolute global ordering  [277502118 | Ficek et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

* **Consistency-Regularized Evaluation**: Some approaches combine ranking accuracy with consistency regularization to improve reliability despite potentially noisy annotations  [273375180 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7].

* **Self-Generated Data Validation**: Novel methods evaluate models' ability to generate high-quality preference data for training, recognizing that ranking accuracy impacts the quality of self-training signals  [273375180 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7].

* **Policy-Invariant Comparison**: More recent approaches emphasize comparing learned reward functions using common evaluation datasets rather than on-policy data, helping isolate issues related to reward specification versus optimization  [258947033 | Bewley et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]  [220041972 | Gleave et al. | 2020 | Citations: 66].

(Gleave et al., 2020) recently highlighted the importance of comparing and evaluating learnt reward functions in a policy-invariant manner, by using a common evaluation dataset rather than on-policy data generated by agents optimising for each reward.

citations.title: [220041972 | Gleave et al. | 2020 | Citations: 66]
snippets: For many tasks, the reward function is too complex to be specified procedurally, and must instead be learned from user data. Prior work has evaluated learned reward functions by examining rollouts from a policy optimized for the learned reward. However, this method cannot distinguish between the learned reward function failing to reflect user preferences, and the reinforcement learning algorithm failing to optimize the learned reward. Moreover, the rollout method is highly sensitive to details of the environment the learned reward is evaluated in, which often differ in the deployment environment. To address these problems, we introduce the Equivalent-Policy Invariant Comparison (EPIC) distance to quantify the difference between two reward functions directly, without training a policy. We prove EPIC is invariant on an equivalence class of reward functions that always induce the same optimal policy. Furthermore, we find EPIC can be precisely approximated and is more robust than baselines to the choice of visitation distribution. Finally, we find that the EPIC distance of learned reward functions to the ground-truth reward is predictive of the success of training a policy, even in different transition dynamics.

They partly attributed this to the generally low ranking accuracy of the reference policy p ref , noting that DPO fine-tuning rarely reverses the preference (i.e., p(y w |x) vs. p(y l |x)) due to the KL-constraint.

sections.title: Challenges and Considerations in Reward Model Evaluation
sections.text:
TLDR; Evaluating reward models presents unique technical and practical challenges due to the interdependence between reward assessment and policy optimization. Additional complications arise from computational costs, potential biases in evaluation methods, and the risk of reward model manipulation. (6 sources)

The evaluation of reward models faces several interconnected challenges that complicate efforts to accurately assess their performance. A fundamental difficulty lies in the inherent circularity of evaluation - reward models must be assessed indirectly through their influence on policy optimization, rather than through direct comparison with ground truth  [260316010 | Casper et al. | 2023 | Citations: 473].

This indirect evaluation approach introduces significant practical constraints. The assessment becomes heavily dependent on various arbitrary choices in the policy optimization process, including the selection of RL algorithms, architectural decisions, computational resources allocated, and numerous hyperparameters  [260316010 | Casper et al. | 2023 | Citations: 473]. This dependence makes it challenging to establish consistent and reliable evaluation protocols.

Another critical consideration emerges in the realm of Large Language Model (LLM) evaluators. These tools, while offering scalability benefits, can themselves harbor biases that affect reward model assessment. Worse still, the policy models being evaluated may learn to exploit these same biases present in the reward models  [267627509 | Chen et al. | 2024 | Citations: 52]  (Zeng et al._1,  2023).

Practical implementation challenges persist in the training phase as well. Current practices often involve spending excessive computational resources searching for "stable" training runs showing increasing reward  [264832734 | Lambert et al. | 2023 | Citations: 32]. This pursuit can inadvertently lead to mismatches between the intended reward objectives and the achieved outcomes. Realistically, even with optimal conditions, achieving perfect accuracy (around 75% being considered successful) remains elusive due to the complexity of the underlying tasks  [264832734 | Lambert et al. | 2023 | Citations: 32].

The field has seen recognition of these challenges leading to innovations in evaluation methodology. Notably, researchers have moved away from purely uncertainty-based reward learning objectives toward regret-based techniques  [268036634 | Ellis et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [218571321 | Wilde et al. | 2020 | Citations: 43], acknowledging that the parameter space representation might not fully capture the true solution space structure.

citations.title: [260316010 | Casper et al. | 2023 | Citations: 473]
snippets: Tractable: Evaluating reward models is difficult and expensive. When the true reward function is known, several methods can be used to judge the quality of the learned reward model (Gleave et al., 2020a;(Wulfe et al., 2022). However, in most cases, reward modeling is used only when the true reward function is not known, making direct evaluation impossible. Hence, the reward model is typically evaluated in an indirect way by optimizing an RL policy using the learned reward model and then evaluating the generations from the RL policy. This makes the reward model evaluation intricately dependent on the policy optimization process which is inherently expensive and noisy. It is also not clear how robust a reward model evaluation is to many ad-hoc choices made in the policy optimization process: e.g., choice of RL algorithm, policy network architecture, compute spent, and other various hyperparameter choices (Gao et al., 2022).

citations.title: [264832734 | Lambert et al. | 2023 | Citations: 32]
snippets:
Common practice in RLHF, especially with larger models where gradients are less stable, is to spend additional compute in search of "stable" training runs with increasing reward, which induces further likelihood of mismatch.

While relatively little work and resources exist for the study of state-ofthe-art reward models, the matching of the reward signal they provide to the intended use-case of the final policy is central to solving the objective mismatch issue, particularly through the methods used to collect preference data. The reward models are trained on aggregated datasets to maximize agreement of the model on a held out set of data, which in practice often yields a maximum accuracy of 60-75% (Bai et al., 2022;Ouyang et al., 2022). Given the complex task encompassed in reward modeling, it is unlikely that the models converge to 100% accuracy, but studying the sources of this performance delta could indicate sources of mismatch.

citations.title: [267627509 | Chen et al. | 2024 | Citations: 52]
snippets: It is challenging to evaluate the policy automatically through LLM evaluators, as these LLM evaluators can often be biased in practice (Zeng et al., 2023), Zheng et al., 2023a, Singhal et al., 2023], and the policy can learn to exploit these biases which also exist in the reward model.

citations.title: [268036634 | Ellis et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
snippets: Recently, Wilde et al. (Wilde et al., 2020) demonstrated existing reward learning objectives that largely depend on parameter-space uncertainty can be suboptimal and proposed a regret-based technique.

citations.title: [218571321 | Wilde et al. | 2020 | Citations: 43]
snippets: We study active preference learning as a frame-work for intuitively specifying the behaviour of autonomous robots. A user chooses the preferred behaviour from a set of alternatives, from which the robot learns the user’s preferences, modeled as a parameterized cost function. Previous approaches present users with alternatives that minimize the uncertainty over the parameters of the cost function. However, different parameters might lead to the same optimal behaviour; as a consequence the solution space is more structured than the parameter space. We exploit this by proposing a query selection that greedily reduces the maximum error ratio over the solution space. In simulations we demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms other state of the art techniques in both learning efficiency and ease of queries for the user. Finally, we show that evaluating the learning based on the similarities of solutions instead of the similarities of weights allows for better predictions for different scenarios.
