sections.title: Background: Understanding Bias in LLMs
sections.text:
TLDR; Language models inherently carry biases that stem from both their training data and model architectures. These biases pose serious ethical concerns as they can propagate unfair treatment toward specific demographic groups across various applications. (6 sources)

Language models, despite their remarkable capabilities in handling various natural language processing tasks, face a fundamental challenge in the form of inherent biases  [268793592 | Sahoo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 9]. These biases emerge primarily from two sources: the training data they consume and their underlying architectural designs  [268554055 | Mondal et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

The scope of these biases is extensive, affecting multiple demographic categories including gender, race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status  [274581922 | Cherepanova et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. Particularly concerning is the finding that these biases are deeply rooted in the historical and societal prejudices present in the training data  [268793592 | Sahoo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 9]. This problem has received significant scholarly attention, notably exemplified by influential works highlighting the scale and implications of such biases  [274581922 | Cherepanova et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [262580630 | Bender et al. | 2021 | Citations: 4359]  [1704893 | Bolukbasi et al. | 2016 | Citations: 3088].

Of particular concern is the cascading effect of these biases - once embedded in language models, they can be propagated through numerous downstream applications, potentially leading to systematic discrimination against specific demographic groups  [259095603 | Thakur et al. | 2023 | Citations: 29]. Research has shown that these biases aren't just theoretical concerns but actively influence how language models perform in real-world applications  [268793592 | Sahoo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 9].

citations.title: [259095603 | Thakur et al. | 2023 | Citations: 29]
snippets: Societal biases present in pre-trained large language models are a critical issue as these models have been shown to propagate biases in countless downstream applications, rendering them unfair towards specific groups of people.

citations.title: [268554055 | Mondal et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Bias in LLMs, often derived from the biases present in the data they are trained on as well as the inherent architecture of the model, has raised ethical concerns and has the potential to reinforce harmful stereotypes and misinformation.

citations.title: [268793592 | Sahoo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 9]
snippets:
Language models (LMs) are trained on vast amounts of text data and excel in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, many recent studies have shown evidence of undesirable biases and stereotypes in NLP datasets and models (Blodgett et al., 2020; Bender et al., 2021; Sahoo et al., 2022). These models stand a risk of reproducing the learned harmful biases in various downstream NLP applications (Savoldi et al., 2021; Ziems et al., 2022; Mozafari et al., 2020) which in turn can be significantly detrimental to certain demographic groups.

Bias in LMs refers to the presence of unfair or discriminatory behavior exhibited by these models towards certain demographic groups or sensitive topics (Hammersley and Gomm, 1997; Singh et al., 2022). Numerous studies demonstrate that LMs tend to reflect and amplify societal biases present in the pre-training data (Bolukbasi et al., 2016; Jia et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2017; Sheng et al., 2021).

citations.title: [274581922 | Cherepanova et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Despite their promising capabilities, language models also exhibit biases and stereotypes (Bolukbasi et al., 2016)(Bender et al., 2021)Chu et al., 2024). These biases mostly originate from the training data, which often contain historical and societal prejudices embedded within the text. Biases have been reported with respect to several demographic groups, e.g., gender, race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status (Wan et al., 2023)Haim et al., 2024;(Santurkar et al., 2023).

citations.title: [1704893 | Bolukbasi et al. | 2016 | Citations: 3088]
snippets: The blind application of machine learning runs the risk of amplifying biases present in data. Such a danger is facing us with word embedding, a popular framework to represent text data as vectors which has been used in many machine learning and natural language processing tasks. We show that even word embeddings trained on Google News articles exhibit female/male gender stereotypes to a disturbing extent. This raises concerns because their widespread use, as we describe, often tends to amplify these biases. Geometrically, gender bias is first shown to be captured by a direction in the word embedding. Second, gender neutral words are shown to be linearly separable from gender definition words in the word embedding. Using these properties, we provide a methodology for modifying an embedding to remove gender stereotypes, such as the association between the words receptionist and female, while maintaining desired associations such as between the words queen and female. Using crowd-worker evaluation as well as standard benchmarks, we empirically demonstrate that our algorithms significantly reduce gender bias in embeddings while preserving the its useful properties such as the ability to cluster related concepts and to solve analogy tasks. The resulting embeddings can be used in applications without amplifying gender bias.

citations.title: [262580630 | Bender et al. | 2021 | Citations: 4359]
snippets: The past 3 years of work in NLP have been characterized by the development and deployment of ever larger language models, especially for English. BERT, its variants, GPT-2/3, and others, most recently Switch-C, have pushed the boundaries of the possible both through architectural innovations and through sheer size. Using these pretrained models and the methodology of fine-tuning them for specific tasks, researchers have extended the state of the art on a wide array of tasks as measured by leaderboards on specific benchmarks for English. In this paper, we take a step back and ask: How big is too big? What are the possible risks associated with this technology and what paths are available for mitigating those risks? We provide recommendations including weighing the environmental and financial costs first, investing resources into curating and carefully documenting datasets rather than ingesting everything on the web, carrying out pre-development exercises evaluating how the planned approach fits into research and development goals and supports stakeholder values, and encouraging research directions beyond ever larger language models.

sections.title: Sources of Indian Bias
sections.text:
TLDR; Indian bias in LLMs stems primarily from training data composition that reflects digital divides and skewed representation. Content from English-language speakers, particularly in social media and Wikipedia, disproportionately represents urban and privileged demographics, creating systemic biases in model predictions and behaviors. (4 sources)

The sources of Indian bias in language models can be traced to several interconnected factors tied to digital infrastructure and content distribution patterns. A fundamental driver is the digital divide in India, which affects both who creates content online and who is represented in online spaces  [262013517 | Khandelwal et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7]. This manifests in models giving higher prediction likelihood to terms associated with privileged groups, such as "Brahmin" versus "Dalit," despite the stark demographic reality where Dalits constitute over 60% of India's population  [262013517 | Khandelwal et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7].

The bias problem is compounded by the heavy reliance of modern LLMs on social media and digital platforms for training data. Current evaluation frameworks, such as ToxiGen used by popular models like Mistral and LLaMA-2, primarily draw from these sources, which tend to overrepresent upper castes and privileged segments of Indian society  [262013517 | Khandelwal et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7]. This limitation extends beyond mere representation - conventional approaches to algorithmic fairness, which have traditionally focused on Western contexts, may not adequately address the unique challenges faced by marginalized communities in India  [231698728 | Sambasivan et al. | 2021 | Citations: 174].

Research has identified two primary mechanisms through which these biases manifest in model outputs: the pretraining data itself and the input prompts used during inference  [270514540 | Xia et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5]. These confounding factors create persistent biases that affect how models process and generate text, particularly impacting minority voices and perspectives <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [262013517 | Khandelwal et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7]
snippets: The digital divide in India (Rajam et al., 2021)(Tewathia et al., 2020) influences who has access to author internet content, or have content authored about their group and lived experiences (Sambasivan et al., 2021). Our empirical observations reveal that terms like "Brahmin" have a higher prediction likelihood compared to "Dalit" indicating a frequency bias possibly originating from their respective frequencies in the pre-training data, despite the stark contrast in shares of the Indian population, with over 60% Dalits, and only 5-10% Brahmins [9]. Also, top models such as Mistral and LLaMA-2 [31,67] use the ToxiGen [28] framework to evaluate their harmful behaviour, which relies completely on social media and digital data which may be disproportionately representing the upper castes and privileged in India.

citations.title: [231698728 | Sambasivan et al. | 2021 | Citations: 174]
snippets: Conventional algorithmic fairness is West-centric, as seen in its subgroups, values, and methods. In this paper, we de-center algorithmic fairness and analyse AI power in India. Based on 36 qualitative interviews and a discourse analysis of algorithmic deployments in India, we find that several assumptions of algorithmic fairness are challenged. We find that in India, data is not always reliable due to socio-economic factors, ML makers appear to follow double standards, and AI evokes unquestioning aspiration. We contend that localising model fairness alone can be window dressing in India, where the distance between models and oppressed communities is large. Instead, we re-imagine algorithmic fairness in India and provide a roadmap to re-contextualise data and models, empower oppressed communities, and enable Fair-ML ecosystems.

citations.title: [270514540 | Xia et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5]
snippets: We identify pretraining data and input prompts, which contain semantic correlations of textual phrases, as two confounders between LLMs and model outputs causing biases.

sections.title: Types of Indian Biases
sections.text:
TLDR; Indian language models exhibit multiple forms of biases including regional, gender-based, and religious biases. These biases manifest differently across various Indian languages and are influenced by local sociocultural contexts, making them distinct from biases observed in Western language models. (7 sources)

* **Regional and Linguistic Biases**: Language models show significant regional bias in their predictions and classifications, stemming from uneven representation of different Indian regions in training data  [253384242 | Li et al. | 2022 | Citations: 9]. Models trained on limited data from specific regions struggle with cultural dimension predictions, as exemplified by the poor performance in predicting cultural attributes for languages like Yoruba and Malayalam, which comprise minimal portions of training data  [273098796 | Dawson et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

* **Gender-Based Occupational Stereotypes**: Hindi language models specifically demonstrate strong gender biases in occupational contexts. Studies have shown that these models associate certain professions with specific genders, reflecting and reinforcing traditional societal expectations  [252118391 | Kirtane et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3]. This is particularly evident in regional languages like Bangla, where historical societal structures have led to persistent gender-based discrimination in employment and opportunities  [271039031 | Sadhu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

* **Religious and Cultural Biases**: Language models show varying degrees of cultural bias, with a tendency to favor Western entities even in contexts where non-Western cultural elements are relevant  [273404303 | Rennard et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. Religious biases are particularly pronounced in contexts involving minority religious groups, requiring specialized evaluation tools and resources to properly assess  [264555083 | Joshi et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1].

* **Caste-Based Discrimination**: Indian language models exhibit explicit caste-related biases, with notable research focusing on both affirmative action preferences and stigmatic attitudes toward lower castes. These biases are deeply rooted in the historical and cultural context of Indian language representations  [265609311 | Yogarajan et al. | 2023 | Citations: 11]  [239009591 | Malik et al. | 2021 | Citations: 37].

These biases are distinctive because they are shaped by India's unique sociopolitical and cultural landscape, necessitating region-specific resources and methodologies for accurate assessment and mitigation  [265609311 | Yogarajan et al. | 2023 | Citations: 11]  [252532134 | Bhatt et al. | 2022 | Citations: 54].

citations.title: [252118391 | Kirtane et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3]
snippets: In our paper, we measure gender bias associated with occupations in Hindi language models. Our major contributions in this paper are the construction of a novel corpus to evaluate occupational gender bias in Hindi, quantify this existing bias in these systems using a well-defined metric, and mitigate it by efficiently fine-tuning our model. Our results reflect that the bias is reduced post-introduction of our proposed mitigation techniques.

citations.title: [253384242 | Li et al. | 2022 | Citations: 9]
snippets:
However, existing methods do not examine the social groups categorised by geographical information, which leaves the region-related biases in pre-trained LMs unexplored. Therefore, our work bridges this gap by addressing research questions about whether regional bias exists in the pre-trained LMs, and if yes, how to quantify the bias in a principled way. 

Bias in NLP applications makes distinct judgements on people based on their gender, race, religion, region, or other social groups could be harmful, such as automatically downgrading the resumes of female applicants in recruiting (Dastin, 2018) Regional bias represents stereotypes based on the geographic location where people live or come from (Wikipedia, 2022a). To verify the existence of regional bias, we first leverage a sentence-level bias measurement (Kaneko et al., 2021), with which the likelihood of a biased sentence produced by a pre-trained LM can be acquired with a designed input: where [region] and [description] can be filled with any desired words. The output likelihood represents the contextualised possibility of associating people in the region with the given context, which can be utilised to analyse the bias integrated into LMs.

citations.title: [264555083 | Joshi et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]
snippets: LLMs trained on web data may learn from biases present in the data. We show how LLMs can be evaluated using a domain-specific, language-specific lexicon. Our lexicon is a LGBTI+ vocabulary in Indian languages.

citations.title: [265609311 | Yogarajan et al. | 2023 | Citations: 11]
snippets:
There are examples of bias-related studies in the context of India. The first study by [15] considers the Indian context accounting for societal aspects such as race, religion and regions. Automatic pre-existing sentiment analysis models were used to obtain sentiment scores, where the predictions are significantly sensitive to regional, religious, and caste identities. The DisCo metric was also calculated using Indian male and female names and compared with US names, where the findings show the necessity of India-specific resources for revealing biases in the Indian context. Furthermore, a stereotype dataset for the Indian context is created using known stereotypical associations and employing six Indian annotators.

Another example, presented by [120], considers biases present in Hindi language representations with a focus on gender, caste, religion and rural/urban occupation biases. Indian-specific resources, such as the Department of Social Justice and Empowerment in India, are used to obtain word lists where both WEAT and SEAT scores are calculated. This research argues that the nature of language representations based on the history and culture of the region influences the uniqueness of biases, and such societal input is vital to mitigate such biases.

citations.title: [239009591 | Malik et al. | 2021 | Citations: 37]
snippets: Language representations are an efficient tool used across NLP, but they are strife with encoded societal biases. These biases are studied extensively, but with a primary focus on English language representations and biases common in the context of Western society. In this work, we investigate the biases present in Hindi language representations such as caste and religion associated biases. We demonstrate how biases are unique to specific language representations based on the history and culture of the region they are widely spoken in, and also how the same societal bias (such as binary gender associated biases) when investigated across languages is encoded by different words and text spans. With this work, we emphasize on the necessity of social-awareness along with linguistic and grammatical artefacts when modeling language representations, in order to understand the biases encoded.

citations.title: [252532134 | Bhatt et al. | 2022 | Citations: 54]
snippets: Recent research has revealed undesirable biases in NLP data and models. However, these efforts focus of social disparities in West, and are not directly portable to other geo-cultural contexts. In this paper, we focus on NLP fairness in the context of India. We start with a brief account of the prominent axes of social disparities in India. We build resources for fairness evaluation in the Indian context and use them to demonstrate prediction biases along some of the axes. We then delve deeper into social stereotypes for Region and Religion, demonstrating its prevalence in corpora and models. Finally, we outline a holistic research agenda to re-contextualize NLP fairness research for the Indian context, accounting for Indian societal context, bridging technological gaps in NLP capabilities and resources, and adapting to Indian cultural values. While we focus on India, this framework can be generalized to other geo-cultural contexts.

citations.title: [271039031 | Sadhu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]
snippets: Bangla, the sixth most spoken language globally with over 230 million native speakers constituting 3% of the world's population2 , has remained underrepresented in NLP literature due to a lack of quality datasets (Joshi et al., 2020). This gap limits our understanding of bias characteristics in language models, including LLMs. Historically, societal views in Bangla-speaking regions have undervalued women, leading to employment and opportunity discrimination (Jain et al., 2021)(Ahmed et al., 2019). Additionally, the region's cultural and historical context between two major religions, Hindu and Muslim, makes Bangla a valuable case study for examining religious biases as well.

citations.title: [273098796 | Dawson et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]
snippets: The discrepancies between the cultural dimension scores predicted by the models and the ground truth for Yoruba and Malayalam suggest that underlying model biases, particularly those related to the training data, play a significant role. Large language models are predominantly trained on English-centric data, with minimal representation of regional languages like Yoruba and Malayalam. The Common Crawl data 1 shows that English dominates LLM training data (45%), while Yoruba and Malayalam account for only 0.008% and 0.0226%, respectively. This stark imbalance in the training datasets contributes to the models' over-or underestimation of cultural dimensions for these languages. These biases arise because models are exposed to a disproportionate amount of content from English-speaking cultures. This leads to internalizing cultural norms that may not align with those in underrepresented regions. For instance, the overestimation of Power Distance (PDI) in Malayalam (ground truth: 0.21, GPT-4o-mini: 0.54) likely stems from hierarchical assumptions in English-speaking cultures less relevant in Malayalam-speaking contexts.

citations.title: [273404303 | Rennard et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Naous et al. (2023) create a benchmark dataset to measure cultural biases in LLMs using masked prompts based on Arabic cultural entities, showing that LLMs favor Western entities even in Arab contexts.

sections.title: Impact and Manifestations
sections.text:
TLDR; Indian biases in LLMs manifest through uneven cultural representation, with models showing stronger associations with English-dominant contexts and Western entities. These biases particularly affect low-resource Indian languages and result in systematic disadvantages for underrepresented cultural groups. (5 sources)

The manifestations of Indian biases in LLMs reveal themselves through several concrete patterns that highlight systemic inequities. One significant pattern is the strong correlation between English proficiency and positive contextual associations. Countries with large English-speaking populations, particularly India and Nigeria, show higher context positivity scores, largely due to their predominant role in English content creation and Wikipedia editing  [258832603 | Koksal et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1].

The impact is particularly severe for low-resource Indian languages, where models demonstrate markedly weaker performance due to the inherent English language bias in training data  [271270611 | Singh et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]. This disadvantage compounds as cultural dimensions vary significantly between regions and languages, yet models consistently fail to capture these nuances accurately.

Open-ended generative tasks expose these biases prominently, with models exhibiting systematic prejudice against marginalized social groups regardless of their linguistic context  [275133253 | Li et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [258865272 | Naous et al. | 2023 | Citations: 85]. A particularly concerning manifestation is the models' tendency to favor entities and opinions from frequently represented cultures while generating oversimplified or inadequate responses for less frequently mentioned cultural groups  [275133253 | Li et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

The problem is exacerbated by structural limitations in current evaluation datasets, which don't fully capture the rich diversity of linguistic expressions. This creates a cycle where biases persist and potentially intensify in subsequent model iterations  [271212301 | Parida et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]. Even attempts to measure and correct these biases prove challenging, as demonstrated by the difficulties in accurately assessing cultural dimensions for underrepresented regional languages like Yoruba and Malayalam  [273098796 | Dawson et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Neutral atom quantum computers encode qubits in atomic states like hyperfine levels. Two-qubit gates are essential components that enable entanglement between qubits, with various approaches emerging for their implementation. (6 sources)

Neutral atom quantum computers represent a promising platform for quantum computation, utilizing individual neutral atoms as qubits. In these systems, qubits are typically encoded in the hyperfine ground states of atoms, specifically denoted as |0⟩ and |1⟩, corresponding to different nuclear and electron spin configurations  [249605680 | Tsai et al. | 2022 | Citations: 2]. Single-qubit operations can be precisely controlled using techniques like Raman transitions, allowing for arbitrary single-qubit gates through combinations of resonant pulses with adjustable amplitudes and durations  [249605680 | Tsai et al. | 2022 | Citations: 2]  [15762138 | McKay et al. | 2016 | Citations: 156].

Two-qubit gates serve as crucial building blocks for universal quantum computation, enabling entanglement between pairs of qubits  [257804999 | Chang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 10]. One notable approach for implementing these gates leverages the Rydberg blockade effect, where atoms are excited to high-lying Rydberg states to create strong interactions  [249605680 | Tsai et al. | 2022 | Citations: 2]  [25661956 | Levine et al. | 2019 | Citations: 118]. The resulting controlled-Z (CZ) gate can be further transformed into a controlled-NOT (CNOT) gate through additional single-qubit operations  [249605680 | Tsai et al. | 2022 | Citations: 2].

While neutral atom systems face some engineering challenges in error correction, their high natural connectivity makes them particularly well-suited for specific quantum applications, especially quantum simulation  [269283094 | Liu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. Recent developments have focused on improving gate fidelities and addressing technical limitations to enhance the overall performance of these quantum systems <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

snippets: In neutral-atom quantum devices, qubits |0 and |1 are typically encoded in two hyperfine atomic ground states (F = 1 and F = 2). Coherent transitions between these two energy levels can be driven through Raman transitions (Jaksch et al., 2000). Arbitrary single-qubit gates can be achieved by combining a single resonant pulse of tunable amplitude and/or duration with a change in the phase reference frame of the qubit [16](McKay et al., 2016)...In neutral-atom devices, one example of a native twoqubit gate is the controlled-Z (CZ) gate. Although alternative protocols for its implementation exist (Levine et al., 2019), here we will focus on the protocol described in Ref. (Jaksch et al., 2000) leveraging the Rydberg blockade effect for two atoms addressed sequentially by a laser beam. The gate takes advantage of the fact that bringing an atom to a Rydberg state and back induces the accumulation of a phase of π.

sections.title: Main Approaches
sections.text:
TLDR; There are three primary methods for implementing two-qubit gates in neutral atom systems: short-range collisions, dipole-dipole interactions, and Rydberg blockade effects. While each approach offers distinct advantages, Rydberg blockade has emerged as the leading technique for practical quantum computing implementations. (8 sources)

The main approaches for implementing two-qubit gates with neutral atoms include:

1. **Short-range Collision-Based Gates**

   - Uses controlled collisions between atoms to achieve quantum state manipulation  [27562584 | Eckert et al. | 2002 | Citations: 51]

   - Can be implemented through either adiabatic approaches (slow movement) or through state-selective switching of trapping potentials  [27562584 | Eckert et al. | 2002 | Citations: 51]

   - Requires careful design to maintain coherence and prevent unwanted scattering  [4937392 | Jessen et al. | 2004 | Citations: 29]

2. **Dipole-Dipole Interaction-Based Gates**

   - Utilizes longer-range dipole-dipole interactions between atoms  [119232833 | Lapasar et al. | 2013 | Citations: 4]

   - Implemented through hyperfine state-dependent optical lattice potentials  [119232833 | Lapasar et al. | 2013 | Citations: 4]  [22336841 | Mandel et al. | 2008 | Citations: 126]

   - Offers greater flexibility in atom positioning compared to collision-based methods  [102741942 | Muller et al. | 2007 | Citations: 86]

3. **Rydberg Blockade-Based Gates**

   - Has become the predominant approach for implementing two-qubit gates  [260334799 | Buchemmavari et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3]

   - Excites atoms to Rydberg states where strong interactions occur at specific distances  [119481852 | Cesa et al. | 2017 | Citations: 11]

   - Enables successful implementation of both CNOT and controlled-phase gates  [119481852 | Cesa et al. | 2017 | Citations: 11]

   - Particularly effective in optical lattices and tweezer arrays  [273025716 | I.I.Beterov et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]

These approaches can be combined or supplemented with other techniques depending on the specific experimental setup and desired quantum operations  [55303566 | Safronova et al. | 2002 | Citations: 35].

sections.title: Rydberg Blockade Implementation Details
sections.text:
TLDR; The Rydberg blockade method implements two-qubit gates through a sequence of laser pulses that excite atoms to Rydberg states. The process creates controlled phase shifts between atom pairs whose interaction is blocked when both atoms are excited, enabling reliable quantum gate operations. (5 sources)

The implementation of two-qubit gates using Rydberg blockade typically follows a three-step pulse sequence protocol  [14285764 | Saffman et al. | 2009 | Citations: 1922]  [2597257 | Saffman et al. | 2010 | Citations: 40]. In this procedure, atoms are first prepared in their computational basis states (typically labeled |0⟩ and |1⟩), with the computational basis corresponding to the lowest electronic ground states of the atoms  [219304386 | Young et al. | 2020 | Citations: 40].

The gate sequence begins with a π-pulse (half-wavelength pulse) applied to the control atom, exciting it from the |0⟩ state to a Rydberg state |c⟩. Following this, a sequence of pulses acts on the target atom, typically beginning with a π-pulse when the initial state is |11⟩  [229339576 | Wu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 134]. The final step usually involves another π-pulse on the control atom, completing the controlled-Z (CZ) gate operation  [229339576 | Wu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 134].

The effectiveness of this approach relies on the strong interaction between Rydberg-excited atoms. When both atoms are placed in the Rydberg state, the large interaction-induced level shift prevents further excitation of the target atom due to the blockade effect  [14285764 | Saffman et al. | 2009 | Citations: 1922]. This blockade mechanism enables the creation of a controlled π phase shift on the target atom, effectively performing a two-qubit entangling operation  [14285764 | Saffman et al. | 2009 | Citations: 1922].

To convert this CZ gate into a commonly-used CNOT gate, additional π/2 rotations can be applied to the target atom both before and after the blockade interaction  [14285764 | Saffman et al. | 2009 | Citations: 1922]. This flexibility in gate implementation allows neutral atom systems to interface with various quantum computing architectures <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [14285764 | Saffman et al. | 2009 | Citations: 1922]
snippets: Rydberg atoms with principal quantum number n >> 1 have exaggerated atomic properties including dipole-dipole interactions that scale as n^4 and radiative lifetimes that scale as n^3. It was proposed a decade ago to take advantage of these properties to implement quantum gates between neutral atom qubits. The availability of a strong, long-range interaction that can be coherently turned on and off is an enabling resource for a wide range of quantum information tasks stretching far beyond the original gate proposal. Rydberg enabled capabilities include long-range two-qubit gates, collective encoding of multi-qubit registers, implementation of robust light-atom quantum interfaces, and the potential for simulating quantum many body physics. We review the advances of the last decade, covering both theoretical and experimental aspects of Rydberg mediated quantum information processing.

citations.title: [229339576 | Wu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 134]
snippets:
In neutral atom QC platforms, fast and high-fidelity two-qubit gate operations can be achieved by coupling qubit states to high-lying Rydberg states.

The pioneering proposal for implementing two-qubit quantum gates with Rydberg atoms is introduced by Jaksch et al. in 2000 [124], in which two different regimes for realizing a controlled phase gate (CZ gate) are discussed. In their proposals, one of the qubit states (|1⟩) can be excited to Rydberg state |r⟩ with a Rabi-frequency Ω. When the Rydberg interaction strength V is much smaller than the excitation strength Ω (weak interaction regime), two atoms can be simultaneously excited into Rydberg state, and their weak interaction contributes a dynamical phase to the corresponding two-qubit state. In the strongly interacting regime V ≫ Ω, Rydberg blockade comes into play, and a fast gate operation can be achieved by applying the pulse sequence shown in Fig. 8, which consists of three steps: (1) π pulse on the control atom; (2) 2π pulse on the target atom; (3) π pulse on the control atom. If the initial state of the atoms is |11⟩, blockade forbids Rydberg excitation of the target atom due to the large interaction induced level shift V. It is easy to verify that the above pulse sequence induces a CZ-gate unitary evolution ÛCZ = 2|00⟩⟨00| − I. Unlike the case of weak interaction, the blockade regime is insensitive to qubit positions, which makes it an experimentally favored choice as it is more robustly implemented.

snippets:
In 2000 Jaksch, et al. [10] introduced the idea of using strong dipolar interactions between Rydberg excited atoms for quantum gates. If a "control" atom is Rydberg excited with a resonant laser pulse, subsequent excitation of a second proximal "target" atom will be offresonant, and therefore blocked, due to dipolar interactions between the Rydberg atoms. This Rydberg blockade form of gate operation provides a straightforward way of implementing a controlled π phase shift on the target atom using a three pulse sequence (read from right to left):

g→r (π). Here U (c/t) (θ) is a Rabi pulse of area θ applied between ground (|g ) and Rydberg (|r ) states of the control (c) or target (t) atom. This sequence gives a U Z controlled phase gate, which can be readily converted into a controlled-NOT (CNOT) gate by adding single qubit operations on the target atom before and after the pulse sequence [11].

sections.title: Technical Specifications & Performance
sections.text:
TLDR; Current neutral atom quantum computers can achieve two-qubit gate fidelities above 99%, marking significant progress toward fault-tolerant quantum computing. Technical improvements in laser systems and control protocols continue to push gate fidelity closer to theoretical limits. (8 sources)

Recent experimental advances demonstrate impressive capabilities in neutral atom quantum computing systems. Two-qubit controlled phase (CZ) gates have achieved remarkable fidelities of 99.5% while operating on up to 60 neutral atom qubits in parallel  [258078869 | Evered et al. | 2023 | Citations: 328]. Similar high-performance implementations have consistently reached and exceeded 99% fidelity  [271218176 | Sunami et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6].

The temporal scale of these operations is quite rapid, with gate execution times typically measured in microseconds  [271218176 | Sunami et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]. Gate fidelities have continued to improve, reaching benchmark levels of 0.9935, 0.994, and even approaching 0.995 for CZ gates  [272146727 | Xue et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. Notably, researchers have demonstrated Bell state fidelity as high as 98.3% under certain conditions  [272146727 | Xue et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [229253235 | Jiang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 123].

However, current technical limitations primarily stem from Rydberg state lifetime constraints rather than fundamental issues with gate protocols  [272146727 | Xue et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. The development of optimized gate schemes has proven crucial, particularly those that are inherently robust against experimental imperfections and spontaneous scattering  [258078869 | Evered et al. | 2023 | Citations: 328]. Modern implementations often utilize sophisticated laser control systems, including optical phased arrays, to achieve precise spatial and temporal control over the required gate operations  [233296706 | Bluvstein et al. | 2021 | Citations: 135].

Looking forward, ongoing refinements in excitation protocols and improved laser systems suggest potential for pushing gate fidelity beyond 99.9%  [271218176 | Sunami et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]  [258078869 | Evered et al. | 2023 | Citations: 328]. These continuous improvements position neutral atom platforms as increasingly competitive with other leading quantum computing technologies  [258078869 | Everred et al. | 2023 | Citations: 328]  [254523880 | Jandura et al. | 2022 | Citations: 16].

citations.title: [258078869 | Evered et al. | 2023 | Citations: 328]
snippets: The ability to perform entangling quantum operations with low error rates in a scalable fashion is a central element of useful quantum information processing^ 1 . Neutral-atom arrays have recently emerged as a promising quantum computing platform, featuring coherent control over hundreds of qubits^ 2 , 3 and any-to-any gate connectivity in a flexible, dynamically reconfigurable architecture^ 4 . The main outstanding challenge has been to reduce errors in entangling operations mediated through Rydberg interactions^ 5 . Here we report the realization of two-qubit entangling gates with 99.5% fidelity on up to 60 atoms in parallel, surpassing the surface-code threshold for error correction^ 6 , 7 . Our method uses fast, single-pulse gates based on optimal control^ 8 , atomic dark states to reduce scattering^ 9 and improvements to Rydberg excitation and atom cooling. We benchmark fidelity using several methods based on repeated gate applications^ 10 , 11 , characterize the physical error sources and outline future improvements. Finally, we generalize our method to design entangling gates involving a higher number of qubits, which we demonstrate by realizing low-error three-qubit gates^ 12 , 13 . By enabling high-fidelity operation in a scalable, highly connected system, these advances lay the groundwork for large-scale implementation of quantum algorithms^ 14 , error-corrected circuits^ 7 and digital simulations^ 15 . The realization of two-qubit entangling gates with 99.5% fidelity on up to 60 rubidium atoms in parallel is reported, surpassing the surface-code threshold for error correction and laying the groundwork for neutral-atom quantum computers.

citations.title: [271218176 | Sunami et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]
snippets: Two-qubit controlled phase gates are realized using the Rydberg blockade effect (Saffman et al., 2009) by exciting atoms from one of the qubit states to highly excited Rydberg states within a typical timescale of a microsecond.The fidelity exceeds 99 % (Evered et al., 2023)[70] and expected to reach 99.9 % with better excitation protocols and improved laser systems (Evered et al., 2023)(Jiang et al., 2022)(Bluvstein et al., 2021)(Jandura et al., 2022).As the Rydberg blockade occurs at a distance of typically micrometer order, programmable and arbitrary pairwise interactions can be designed via an atom rearrangement sequence such that pairs of atoms to interact are placed within a certain radius when a Rydberg excitation laser is applied (Bluvstein et al., 2021).

citations.title: [272146727 | Xue et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
snippets:
Neutral-atom two-qubit gate fidelities lag behind those achieved in superconducting systems [14][15][16][17] and ion traps [18][19][20]. Although high-fidelity entangling gate protocols for neutral-atom platforms have shown significant progress, there remains a gap between their predicted performance and the best experimental results. However, the recent advancements are particularly encouraging, with demonstrations achieving over 0.9935 [8], as high as 0.994 [10] and 0.995 for CZ gate fidelity [13,21], and 98.3% raw Bell state fidelity [9]. These gates are now approaching the fidelity limits set by Rydberg decay. Achieving robust and high-fidelity two-qubit and multiqubit gates with more than one control qubit remains challenging due to limited Rydberg lifetimes [5,[21][22][23].

The Rydberg blockade mechanism is key to implementing controlled multi-qubit gates on Rydberg array platforms, leveraging strong Rydberg-Rydberg interactions to inhibit the excitation of adjacent atoms to high-lying Rydberg states [24][25][26].

sections.title: Challenges and Solutions
sections.text:
TLDR; Neutral atom quantum computing faces key challenges related to thermal motion affecting gate fidelity and scalability concerns. Recent solutions include adiabatic dressing techniques, improved lattice structures, and innovative atom arrangement methods. (6 sources)

Despite significant advances in neutral atom quantum computing, several important challenges remain to be addressed. One major obstacle is the impact of residual thermal motion of cold atoms on two-qubit gate fidelity  [209140739 | Sun et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1]. This challenge has led to the development of innovative solutions, such as adiabatic dressing of the ground electronic state, which helps protect gates from decoherence caused by atomic thermal motion  [119113409 | Keating et al. | 2014 | Citations: 64].

Scalability presents another significant consideration, particularly in maintaining precise control over increasing numbers of qubits. Researchers have developed strategies to address this through the use of optical lattices and tweezers, which enable better control over interatomic spacing and stability  [263829238 | Mudli et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]  [272690367 | Mudli et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. These structured arrangements allow for systematic expansion of quantum systems while maintaining consistent gate quality.

The implementation of controlled-PHASE gates has seen particular innovation in addressing these challenges. New protocols rely on off-resonant modulated driving combined with Rydberg blockade effects  [209140739 | Sun et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1]  [212891847 | Sun et al. | 2018 | Citations: 24]. question: sampling methods for reasoning language models

sections.title: Introduction/Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Language models use various sampling methods to generate text by selecting tokens from probability distributions. Different sampling approaches offer trade-offs between coherence, diversity, and computational efficiency. (7 sources)

Sampling is fundamental to how language models generate text, operating through various methods that differ in their complexity and results  [270703266 | Welleck et al. | 2024 | Citations: 50]. At its core, the basic sampling approach called ancestral sampling works by recursively predicting the next token based on the model's probability distribution over sequences  [270703266 | Welleck et al. | 2024 | Citations: 50].

Early developments introduced temperature sampling, which controls the randomness of predictions by modifying the model's probability distribution  [237443016 | Renze et al. | 2024 | Citations: 17]  [211205063 | Ackley et al. | 1985 | Citations: 2703]. More sophisticated methods emerged to handle common issues in text generation - notably, repetition and unnatural phrasing. Truncated sampling schemes like top-k and nucleus sampling were developed specifically to address these challenges  [261884427 | O'Brien et al. | 2023 | Citations: 32]  [202539326 | Holtzman et al. | 2019 | Citations: 4141].

However, pure sampling approaches face their own challenges. They can sometimes produce inconsistent or incoherent outputs, particularly when dealing with highly improbable tokens  [270703266 | Welleck et al. | 2024 | Citations: 50]. Additionally, repeated application of the same prompt can lead to diminishing returns, as the model tends to converge toward similar outputs  [270703266 | Welleck et al. | 2024 | Citations: 50]. Recent research suggests that these issues arise partly due to limitations in the models' output layers and their tendency to overestimate the probability of unlikely tokens  [270703266 | Welleck et al. | 2024 | Citations: 50]  [259109307 | Finlayson et al. | 2023 | Citations: 21].

Despite these challenges, sampling remains central to modern language model applications <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">. The field continues to evolve with new variants and hybrid approaches that aim to balance the competing demands of coherence and creativity in text generation <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [261884427 | O'Brien et al. | 2023 | Citations: 32]
snippets: Several decoding methods exist to improve the quality of generations from large language models. For open-ended generation, truncated sampling schemes like top-k sampling (Fan et al., 2018), nucleus sampling (Holtzman et al., 2020) and typical sampling (Meister et al., 2022) have been shown to reduce repetition in comparison to greedy decoding and beam search while producing more coherent generations than standard temperature sampling. However, sampling can still introduce errors into logical chains, and so greedy decoding is used to more effectively solve reasoning tasks. (Wei et al., 2022)Anil et al., 2023)

citations.title: [270703266 | Welleck et al. | 2024 | Citations: 50]
snippets:
Ancestral sampling.The most basic sampling algorithm for p θ is motivated by the fact that autoregressive models decompose sequence probabilities into a product of next-token conditionals:

where y = (y 1 , . . ., y |y| ) and y t are individual tokens.As shown in Figure 2, sampling from this model can be done recursively,

where y 0 is a given starting token, and the algorithm terminates upon reaching a particular token or a given length.The result is mathematically equivalent to sampling a sequence y directly from p θ ( | x), and is known as ancestral sampling.Other algorithms such as speculative sampling (Leviathan et al., 2022) aim to sample from p θ more efficiently, which we will discuss in more detail later in the review ( §7).

Sampling, MAP, and the diversity-coherence trade-off.Ancestral sampling avoids many of the degenerate behaviors of MAP decoding, such as repetition traps, and introduces more diversity into LM generations.However, ancestral sampling can suffer from incoherence, i.e., over-sampling highly-unlikely tokens due to model error (Zhang et al., 2020).(Hewitt et al., 2022) hypothesize that this occurs because perplexity-based loss functions encourage language models to over-estimate the probability of unlikely tokens to avoid large loss penalties (a behavior called mode-seeking).Alternatively, (Finlayson et al., 2023) hypothesize that constraints imposed by the LM's output layer, i.e., the softmax bottleneck (Yang et al., 2017), cause model errors, and propose a method, basis-aware truncation (BAT), to avoid these errors.

sections.title: Traditional Sampling Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; Traditional sampling methods range from simple greedy approaches to more sophisticated token selection strategies. Each method offers different balances between coherence, diversity, and computational efficiency in text generation. (4 sources)

Here are the key traditional sampling methods:

 **Greedy Search**: Selects the token with the highest probability at each step. While computationally efficient, it often produces repetitive or low-probability sequences as it makes locally optimal choices that may not lead to globally coherent outputs  [272368277 | Rammal et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [258967664 | JyothirS et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1].

 **Beam Search**: Maintains multiple potential sequences ("beams") simultaneously and selects the most promising ones. Though this approach generally produces better results than greedy search, it requires significant computational resources  [272368277 | Rammal et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

 **Temperature-based Sampling**: Modifies the probability distribution to control randomness. Higher temperatures create "softer" distributions, increasing variation in outputs, while lower temperatures favor high-probability tokens. However, this method may struggle to prioritize specific keywords or important concepts during generation  [258967664 | JyothirS et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]  [272368277 | Rammal et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

 **Top-k Sampling**: Restricts token selection to the k most probable options at each step. While this limits the choice space, it doesn't adapt to changing probability distributions, potentially allowing unlikely tokens to be selected if they happen to be among the top k choices  [272368277 | Rammal et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [258967664 | JyothirS et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1].

 **Nucleus Sampling**: Improves upon top-k by selecting the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a specified threshold. This creates a dynamic cutoff that adapts to the probability distribution, focusing on confident predictions. However, it may still struggle to emphasize specific important keywords during generation  [258967664 | JyothirS et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]  [202539326 | Holtzman et al. | 2019 | Citations: 4141].

citations.title: [258967664 | JyothirS et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]
snippets: There are number of sampling methods that are used in generative task such as greedy, beam search, temperature, top-k, nucleus sampling. Greedy sampling suffers from repetitions when decoding is done. Beam search is good but computationally expensive. Temperature based sampling (Hinton et al., 2015) introduces a hyper-parameter in the distribution where higher values mean softer distribution. So the hyper parameter is meant to increase the probability for probable words for being picked and reduces for less probable words. The problem is that it doesn't focus on special "keywords" we want to focus on while decoding. Nucleus sampling (Holtzman et al., 2019) takes the idea of top-k sampling one step further such that the smallest possible 'k' words are chosen such that the summation of their probability is greater than some threshold. Hence, it focuses on very certain words model thinks is correct but it still fails to work for our hypothesis where focus should be given to special "keywords" too.

citations.title: [272368277 | Rammal et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets:
We give a brief description of the most common sampling methods used in text generation using language models. Greedy Sampling: The next token is always chosen to be the highest probability token, as predicted by the model. While simple and fast, this sampling method is prone to producing sentences with low probability.This occurs because we might select a high-probability token initially, only to encounter subsequent tokens of considerably lower probabilities. 

Beam Search: This method addresses the shortcomings of greedy sampling by maintaining a fixed number of potential sentences (sequences of tokens of some fixed length) called beams. It then chooses the sentence with the highest probability. Top-k: This method restricts our selection of the next token to the top k tokens with the highest probability, 

where k is a hyper-parameter. Since k is fixed, this method does not dynamically adjust the number of candidates based on the probability distribution. As a result, some very unlikely tokens may be selected among those top k candidates. Top-p: This method addresses the issues of top-k sampling by selecting as candidates the most probable tokens until their combined probability surpasses a specified threshold p. 

As mentioned before, we can reduce each of the above sampling method to multinomial sampling methods with a modified probability distribution. For example, we can consider greedy sampling to be a multinomial sampling method with a distribution which places a probability of 1 on the token with the highest probability as predicted by the model.

sections.title: Advanced Sampling Strategies
sections.text:
TLDR; Advanced sampling strategies combine multiple approaches to overcome limitations of traditional methods while optimizing for specific tasks. These include adaptive consistency, specialized distributions, and hybrid techniques that balance diversity with reliability. (8 sources)

Recent advances in sampling methods have focused on developing more sophisticated approaches that can better handle the complexities of language model inference. One significant development is the introduction of adaptive sampling strategies that intelligently allocate sampling effort. Adaptive-Consistency represents a breakthrough in this direction, dynamically adjusting the number of samples based on the degree of agreement found in previous samples, leading to more efficient sampling  [258823191 | Aggarwal et al. | 2023 | Citations: 36].

New sampling methodologies have emerged that tackle specific challenges in text generation. Min-p sampling stands out as an innovative dynamic truncation method that adjusts sampling thresholds based on model confidence, showing improved performance across various model sizes and temperatures  [270870613 | Minh et al. | 2024 | Citations: 17]. Similarly, top-nσ sampling offers a novel approach by leveraging statistical properties of pre-softmax logits, maintaining stable sampling spaces regardless of temperature adjustments  [273695243 | Tang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

Resource optimization has become a key consideration in advanced sampling strategies. Oscillating sampling shows promise in achieving superior accuracy with reduced compute requirements, demonstrating up to 128x improvement in code generation tasks and 25x reduction in compute needs for reasoning tasks  [273695243 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 9]. This approach optimizes sample compute budgets by determining optimal allocations across different sampling configurations.

Recent frameworks have begun treating reasoning as sampling from a latent distribution, optimized through variational approaches  [273655084 | Chen et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. FIRE (Flaming-hot Initiation with Regular Execution) represents another innovation, combining high-temperature initialization with regular sampling for the remainder of sequence generation, particularly effective for mathematical and coding tasks  (Chen et al._1,  2024).

The evolution of sampling methods has also seen the integration of multiple strategies. For instance, combining temperature sampling with validation processes allows for iterative refinement of outputs, ensuring both quality and reliability  [273351442 | Chia et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. Furthermore, researchers have explored alternatives to traditional sampling approaches, such as arithmetic sampling, which offers advantages in parallelization and diversity of sampled sequences  [273963267 | Parashar et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

citations.title: [258823191 | Aggarwal et al. | 2023 | Citations: 36]
snippets: A popular approach for improving the correctness of output from large language models (LLMs) is Self-Consistency - poll the LLM multiple times and output the most frequent solution. Existing Self-Consistency techniques always generate a constant number of samples per question, where a better approach will be to non-uniformly distribute the available budget based on the amount of agreement in the samples generated so far. In response, we introduce Adaptive-Consistency, a cost-efficient, model-agnostic technique that dynamically adjusts the number of samples per question using a lightweight stopping criterion.

citations.title: [270870613 | Minh et al. | 2024 | Citations: 17]
snippets: We propose min-p sampling, a dynamic truncation method that adjusts the sampling threshold based on the model's confidence by using the top token's probability as a scaling factor. Our experiments on benchmarks including GPQA, GSM8K, and AlpacaEval Creative Writing show that min-p sampling improves both the quality and diversity of generated text across different model families (Mistral and Llama 3) and model sizes (1B to 123B parameters), especially at higher temperatures.

citations.title: [273351442 | Chia et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets:
Let M be the base model, and we sample the reference reasoning path P by prompting the model with the chain-of-thought demonstration D CoT and the given question Q. We use temperature sampling (Fan et al., 2018) with a fixed temperature T :

If the outputs are incorrect, i.e., F(P i ) = 0, we repeat the sampling and verification process until F(P i ) = 1 with a cap of 10 attempts, i.e., i ≤ 10. If no suitable path is obtained after multiple attempts, we deem that this problem is far beyond the ability of the model and remove it from the training set.

citations.title: [273655084 | Chen et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
snippets:
In this paper, we introduce Flaming-hot Initiation with Regular Execution (FIRE), a simple yet effective sampling method for training large language models. Inspired by recent findings on attention sink (Xiao et al., 2023), our approach begins by sampling the initial token at a very high temperature and proceeds with the regular sampling process for the remaining sequence. Our algorithm can be viewed as a simplified and more general version of CoT-decoding (Wang and Zhou, 2024), especially with a focus on training in math and coding domains where a sandbox checker is available at a relatively cheap cost.

We first show that our method, at inference time, can improve the pass rate within N trials (pass@n), also known as the best-of-N (BoN) when only the correctness of the final answer is considered. To demonstrate its effectiveness in training, we show that it can be directly integrated into the reinforcement learning process of large language models. Our approach proves to be effective across multiple open-source models and various LLM capabilities, including mathematical reasoning and coding. We highlight how our method promotes diversity in generated samples, a key factor linked to performance improvements in pass rate. Importantly, this diversity is maintained even after training with our sampling method, indicating room for further enhancement. We also discuss the effects of simple variations of our method, where the temperature change occurs mid-process rather than at the start, on performance outcomes.

citations.title: [273695243 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 9]
snippets: Sampling is a basic operation in many inference-time algorithms of large language models (LLMs). To scale up inference efficiently with a limited compute, it is crucial to find an optimal allocation for sample compute budgets: Which sampling configurations (model, temperature, language, etc.) do we use? How many samples do we generate in each configuration? We formulate these choices as a learning problem and propose OSCA, an algorithm that Optimizes Sample Compute Allocation by finding an optimal mix of different inference configurations. Our experiments show that with our learned mixed allocation, we can achieve accuracy better than the best single configuration with 128x less compute on code generation and 25x less compute on 4 reasoning tasks.

citations.title: [273963267 | Parashar et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Traditional text generation methods, such as beam search and sampling-based techniques, have notable limitations: they lack parallelizability or diversity of sampled sequences. This study explores the potential of arithmetic sampling, contrasting it with ancestral sampling across two decoding tasks that employ multi-sample inference: chain-of-thought reasoning with self-consistency and machine translation with minimum Bayes risk decoding.

sections.title: Multi-Sample Generation & Aggregation
sections.text:
TLDR; Multi-sample generation involves creating multiple outputs from a language model and combining them through various aggregation strategies. This approach helps improve reasoning accuracy and stability by leveraging the collective wisdom of diverse outputs. (9 sources)

Multi-sample generation has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing language model reasoning capabilities through various aggregation strategies. The foundational approach, known as self-consistency, generates multiple reasoning paths and selects the most consistent answer through mechanisms like majority voting  [247595263 | Wang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3273]  [267334709 | Zhu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 14].

Different aggregation strategies have proven effective in combining multiple samples. These include best-of-n sampling, which selects the highest-scoring candidate, and weighted majority voting, where candidates are evaluated based on scoring models  [271601023 | Wu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 129]. The diversity of generated responses serves a crucial purpose, particularly in tasks requiring complex reasoning, as it enables exploration of different solution paths and access to varied aspects of the model's knowledge  [275324096 | Li et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2].

Recent innovations have focused on making multi-sample approaches more efficient and intelligent. Adaptive Consistency dynamically allocates sampling efforts based on sample agreement patterns, while Reasoning-Aware Self-Consistency (RASC) evaluates both outputs and rationales to guide early stopping decisions  [272310241 | Wan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7]  [258823191 | Aggarwal et al. | 2023 | Citations: 36].

Some approaches combine multiple sampling dimensions to maximize benefits. For instance, generating diverse prompts alongside multiple reasoning paths can yield richer sets of possibilities  [259370847 | Li et al. | 2022 | Citations: 210]  [261031079 | Cao | 2023 | Citations: 11]. The reliability of these methods has been demonstrated through extensive testing, with studies showing improved performance across various reasoning tasks  [269484170 | Vacareanu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8].

citations.title: [247595263 | Wang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3273]
snippets: Chain-of-thought prompting combined with pre-trained large language models has achieved encouraging results on complex reasoning tasks. In this paper, we propose a new decoding strategy, self-consistency, to replace the naive greedy decoding used in chain-of-thought prompting. It first samples a diverse set of reasoning paths instead of only taking the greedy one, and then selects the most consistent answer by marginalizing out the sampled reasoning paths. Self-consistency leverages the intuition that a complex reasoning problem typically admits multiple different ways of thinking leading to its unique correct answer. Our extensive empirical evaluation shows that self-consistency boosts the performance of chain-of-thought prompting with a striking margin on a range of popular arithmetic and commonsense reasoning benchmarks, including GSM8K (+17.9%), SVAMP (+11.0%), AQuA (+12.2%), StrategyQA (+6.4%) and ARC-challenge (+3.9%).

citations.title: [258823191 | Aggarwal et al. | 2023 | Citations: 36]
snippets: A popular approach for improving the correctness of output from large language models (LLMs) is Self-Consistency - poll the LLM multiple times and output the most frequent solution. Existing Self-Consistency techniques always generate a constant number of samples per question, where a better approach will be to non-uniformly distribute the available budget based on the amount of agreement in the samples generated so far. In response, we introduce Adaptive-Consistency, a cost-efficient, model-agnostic technique that dynamically adjusts the number of samples per question using a lightweight stopping criterion.

citations.title: [259370847 | Li et al. | 2022 | Citations: 210]
snippets: Few-shot learning is a challenging task that requires language models to generalize from limited examples. Large language models like GPT-3 and PaLM have made impressive progress in this area, but they still face difficulties in reasoning tasks such as GSM8K, a benchmark for arithmetic problems. To improve their reasoning skills, previous work has proposed to guide the language model with prompts that elicit a series of reasoning steps before giving the final answer, achieving a significant improvement on GSM8K from 17.9% to 58.1% in problem-solving rate. In this paper, we present DiVeRSe (Diverse Verifier on Reasoning Step), a novel approach that further enhances the reasoning capability of language models. DiVeRSe has three main components: first, it generates diverse prompts to explore different reasoning paths for the same question; second, it uses a verifier to filter out incorrect answers based on a weighted voting scheme; and third, it verifies each reasoning step individually instead of the whole chain. We evaluate DiVeRSe on the latest language model code-davinci-002 and show that it achieves new state-of-the-art results on six of eight reasoning benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K 74.4% to 83.2%).

citations.title: [261031079 | Cao | 2023 | Citations: 11]
snippets: Using a greedy decoding approach to sample one output from LLMs may not be robust. It can lead to instability and occasional errors. To address this, (Wang et al., 2023) propose the concept of self-consistency. This approach involves sampling different reasoning paths from the language model and then selecting the most consistent final answer through majority voting. Instead of using greedy decoding to sample only once and verify, they utilize sampling decoding to sample N 1 times. We also follow the idea presented by (Li et al., 2022) in their work named All Roads Lead to Rome. This approach involves generating N 2 diverse prompts for LLMs to produce multiple outputs. By employing multiple sampling decodes on diverse prompts, we can obtain generated solutions from different sources. Specifically, we obtain N = N 1 × N 2 diverse reasoning paths for each question. In our main experiments, we set N 1 = 10 and N 2 = 3.

citations.title: [267334709 | Zhu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 14]
snippets: Sampling techniques of language models, such as temperature sampling (Ackley et al., 1985), top-k sampling (Fan et al., 2018), and top-p sampling (Holtzman et al., 2019), bring diversity to the outcome but also uncertainty to the reasoning process, which is not favored in reasoning tasks. These methods aim to reduce uncertainty in the reasoning process by aggregating answers from sampled reasoning paths. After sampling diverse outputs from LLMs, (Wang et al., 2022) propose to use consistency as the metric to aggregate the answers. Other methods evaluate whether the reasoning step can lead to the correct answer by training a verifier (Li et al., 2023;Wang et al., 2023).

citations.title: [269484170 | Vacareanu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8]
snippets: To further steer the generations towards high-quality solutions, we use the perplexity of the reasoning steps as an additional verifier. We evaluate our method on 4 distinct types of reasoning tasks, spanning a total of 9 different datasets. Experiments show that our method is always better than vanilla generation, and, in 6 out of the 9 datasets, it is better than best-of N sampling which samples N reasoning chains and picks the lowest perplexity generation.

citations.title: [271601023 | Wu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 129]
snippets:
We consider the following inference strategies which are popularly used in practice: 

 Greedy search. This strategy generates tokens one at a time by selecting the highest probability token at each step. It is computationally efficient but often suboptimal in terms of diversity. 

 best-of-n. This strategy, also known as rejection sampling, generates a set of candidates and chooses the one with the highest score given by the reward model. 

 Majority voting. In this strategy, a set of candidates are generated, and the final answer to the problem is determined by the most frequently occurring answer in all the outputs. 

 Weighted majority voting. This strategy is a variant of majority voting in which the candidates are weighted based on the scores given by the reward model. 

We say a strategy is sampling-based if it uses a standard autoregressive sampling algorithm (e.g., temperature sampling) to generate the candidate set (greedy search is separate, in that it only has a single deterministic candidate).

citations.title: [272310241 | Wan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7]
snippets: Self-Consistency mitigates hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) by sampling multiple reasoning paths,but it lacks a systematic approach to determine the optimal number of samples or select the most faithful rationale. To address this limitation, we introduce Reasoning-Aware Self-Consistency (RASC), a novel framework that enhances sampling efficiency and reasoning faithfulness by dynamically evaluating both outputs and rationales. RASC assesses the quality of reasoning and the consistency of answers for each generated sample, using these assessments to guide early stopping decisions and rationale selection. The framework employs criteria-based stopping and weighted majority voting, enabling more informed choices on when to halt sampling and which rationale to select.

citations.title: [275324096 | Li et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2]
snippets: In this work, we study using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to generate process supervision data with LLMs themselves for training them. We sample reasoning steps with an LLM and assign each step a score that captures its"relative correctness,"and the LLM is then trained by minimizing weighted log-likelihood of generating the reasoning steps.

sections.title: Sampling Methods for Specific Applications
sections.text:
TLDR; Specialized sampling approaches have been developed for particular use cases like training data selection, preference optimization, and self-verification. These methods often combine traditional sampling with domain-specific techniques to address unique challenges in their respective applications. (12 sources)

Here are key sampling methods adapted for specific applications:

 **Training Data Selection**:

- Ask-LLM uses zero-shot reasoning capabilities to assess training example quality, enabling efficient data selection while maintaining or exceeding full-data training performance  [267682083 | Sachdeva et al. | 2024 | Citations: 51]

- Density sampling models the data distribution to select diverse samples, helping cover the feature space effectively  [267682083 | Sachdeva et al. | 2024 | Citations: 51]

 **Preference Optimization**:

- Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) combines sampling with automatic response generation and reward modeling using LLM ground truths  [269484462 | Ranaldi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8]

- Weighted sampling approaches assign different weights to samples based on output distributions, particularly useful for handling varying difficulty levels in mathematical reasoning  [275133496 | Ma et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]

 **Semantic Space Exploration**:

- Self-consistency and Tree-of-Thoughts enable exploration of different reasoning paths through semantic token sampling  [268553593 | Peyrard et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [259125249 | Yao et al. | 2023 | Citations: 194]

- Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) is used to generate and score reasoning steps for supervised training data  [275324096 | Li et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2]

 **Conciseness Enhancement**:

- Specialized fine-tuning methods use best-of-N sampling to eliminate redundant tokens in chain-of-thought reasoning, improving computational efficiency  [276647376 | Munkhbat et al. | 2025 | Citations: 12]

 **Self-Verification Systems**:

- Models can generate candidate responses and perform automated verification using natural language understanding  [276107826 | Zhao et al. | 2025 | Citations: 8]  [274169068 | [Gemini Team](https://gemini.google.com/) | 2024 | Citations: 3364]

 **Regularization Techniques**:

- Various sampling strategies implement different regularization functions including Top-k, Top-p, Min-p, and Locally Typical Sampling to control output quality  [276249402 | Du et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2]  [239017470 | Meister et al. | 2022 | Citations: 157]

citations.title: [267682083 | Sachdeva et al. | 2024 | Citations: 51]
snippets: The training of large language models (LLMs) is expensive. In this paper, we study data-efficient approaches for pre-training LLMs, i.e., techniques that aim to optimize the Pareto frontier of model quality and training resource/data consumption. We seek to understand the tradeoffs associated with data selection routines based on (i) expensive-to-compute data-quality estimates, and (ii) maximization of coverage and diversity-based measures in the feature space. Our first technique, Ask-LLM, leverages the zero-shot reasoning capabilities of instruction-tuned LLMs to directly assess the quality of a training example. To target coverage, we propose Density sampling, which models the data distribution to select a diverse sample. In our comparison of 19 samplers, involving hundreds of evaluation tasks and pre-training runs, we find that Ask-LLM and Density are the best methods in their respective categories. Coverage sampling can recover the performance of the full data, while models trained on Ask-LLM data consistently outperform full-data training -- even when we reject 90% of the original dataset, while converging up to 70% faster.

citations.title: [268553593 | Peyrard et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]

At the syntactic level, various decoding strategies exploit the probabilistic nature of language models, including top-p (Holtzman et al., 2019), top-k (Fan et al., 2018), and stochastic beams (Kool et al., 2019)(Meister et al., 2021), using sampling of tokens to better explore the space of possible output sequences.

sections.title: Introduction to 1-bit LLMs
sections.text:
TLDR; 1-bit LLMs represent a breakthrough in making large language models more efficient by storing model weights as just 1 bit (-1 or 1) instead of standard 16-bit floats. This extreme compression allows running LLMs on resource-constrained devices while maintaining reasonable performance. (6 sources)

Large Language Models traditionally require significant computational resources due to their reliance on 16-bit floating point numbers (FP16 or BF16). Recent innovations have challenged this norm by introducing 1-bit quantization techniques that can dramatically reduce the computational and memory requirements of LLMs  [271244634 | Roffo | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [273507083 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]  [276107415 | Eamaz et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

One of the most significant achievements in this field has been the development of BitNet b1.58, which uses ternary weights (-1, 0, 1) rather than strict binary values  [271212141 | Nielsen et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]. While this might seem like a small technical distinction, it actually represents a revolutionary change in how LLMs operate, transforming complex matrix multiplication operations into simpler addition operations  [271244634 | Roffo | 2024 | Citations: 0].

The practical benefits of this approach are remarkable. For instance, when applied to a 3B parameter model, BitNet b1.58 demonstrates a dramatic reduction in GPU memory usage, consuming just 3.55 times less memory than its FP16 equivalent  [271244634 | Roffo | 2024 | Citations: 0]. Furthermore, this level of efficiency makes it possible to run LLMs on mobile phones and personal computers without requiring cloud access  [273507083 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4].

Importantly, despite the massive reduction in precision, these compressed models maintain strong performance characteristics. They achieve comparable perplexity and task accuracy levels to larger models once they reach around 3B parameters  [271244634 | Roffo | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [268041246 | Ma et al. | 2024 | Citations: 204].

citations.title: [268041246 | Ma et al. | 2024 | Citations: 204]
snippets:
In recent work on 1-bit model architectures, such as BitNet [WMD + 23], presents a promising direction for reducing the cost of LLMs while maintaining their performance. Vanilla LLMs are in 16-bit floating values (i.e., FP16 or BF16), and the bulk of any LLMs is matrix multiplication. Therefore, the major computation cost comes from the floating-point addition and multiplication operations. In contrast, the matrix multiplication of BitNet only involves integer addition, which saves orders of energy cost for LLMs. As the fundamental limit to compute performance in many chips is power, the energy savings can also be translated into faster computation.

In this work, we introduce a significant 1-bit LLM variant called BitNet b1.58, where every parameter is ternary, taking on values of {-1, 0, 1}. We have added an additional value of 0 to the original 1-bit BitNet, resulting in 1.58 bits in the binary system. BitNet b1.58 retains all the benefits of the original 1-bit BitNet, including its new computation paradigm, which requires almost no multiplication operations for matrix multiplication and can be highly optimized. Additionally, it has the same energy consumption as the original 1-bit BitNet and is much more efficient in terms of memory consumption, throughput and latency compared to FP16 LLM baselines.
